en: The *Hetubinduṭīkā* composed by the illustrious Arcata.
Homage to the Omniscient One.
[May there be auspiciousness through homage to the Victors:
He who, having generated great compassion to protect all people from calamity,
has accumulated a vast cause consisting of merit and wisdom, and has shaken off all weariness;

I bow my head in homage to that Sun of the Jina, who, having ascended the mountain of the arising of exceedingly pure wisdom that spreads over all objects of knowledge, dispels the darkness within the hearts of the world. // 1 //
[1] Merit: [An introduction to the demonstration of the supreme sweetness of Dharmakīrti’s words:
For indeed, among the words of Dharmakīrti, there is a better chewing even of that which has already been chewed. [1.2]
For does the grape, even when squeezed, ever lose its sweetness? // 2 //
[2] Even regarding what has already been chewed, there is further chewing—[T.
having proclaimed his own lightness, the promise to explain the treatise:
That mind of his which, like a scale placed upon the path of logic, holds the entire world together as one;
Where could his profound words prevail, and where am I, of dull intellect? // 3 //
Nevertheless, there are some of dull intellect even among those [who follow me]; it is for their sake that this *Hetubindu* is being analyzed by me as well. (4)
[The revelation of the purpose of the opening statement:
With the words "In the absence of... and so forth, he states the purpose for commencing the treatise.
Some maintain that this is for the sake of engaging the audience.
As it has been said: "For of any treatise whatsoever, or even of any action, as long as the purpose has not been stated, by whom shall it be grasped? (Ślokavārttika 1.12).
Thus it has been said. That is incorrect, because the purpose of this treatise is as follows:

[In order to demonstrate] that the treatise is a specific means toward a particular purpose, and since it is impossible for discerning persons to engage in what is not a means when they have ascertained its status as such, their engagement in listening to the treatise and so forth—driven by the desire for that purpose—will occur; therefore, the meaningfulness of stating that purpose is described.

And this is not tenable; for the activity of discerning persons who seek a purpose proceeds toward the means to that end only because they have ascertained the existence of that [purpose] therein— just as, for example, farmers and others, having determined the nature of seeds and so forth by distinguishing them from non-seeds, proceed toward the means such as grain.

Otherwise, if those who seek an end were to act without having ascertained the means, their very status as discerning persons (*prekṣāvattā*) would be lost. However, regarding the end (*upeya*), although there can be no operation of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and thus no certainty, those who have distinguished the means proceed by way of a probability (*saṃbhāvanā*), thinking: "This is capable of accomplishing this intended effect," provided that there is no possibility of obstacles or deficiencies in the causal conditions.
For a discerning person, [the treatise] would not fail its purpose;
moreover, certainty arises from valid cognition alone,
and the statement of the purpose possesses no such validity.
Because words lack a necessary connection with external objects,

and because— even if they possess validity regarding the speaker’s intention— they lack a rule for engaging with things as they actually exist, there can be no certainty that they serve as a means toward the specific purpose of a particular treatise.

For those who intend to express a certain object in a particular way do not necessarily act accordingly; since we observe that those with the intention to deceive speak in one way and act in another, there is no confidence whatsoever in the world.

Because a specific purpose is presented, a doubt arises as to whether this treatise is a means to achieve that [purpose]. Therefore, in order to determine its existence—just as a farmer seeks to ascertain the presence of a seed—one proceeds [to state the subject matter].
If it is argued that activity is justified [by this doubt], we say no; for the doubt regarding whether [the scripture] is a means to a specific purpose exists even prior to its being stated,
since such a doubt is established by logic (*nyāya*) in the absence of any valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that either proves or refutes it.

Furthermore, since one observes treatises intended for the purpose of explaining inference and other such topics, by what could the doubt that previously arose— namely, "What is the purpose of this [work], is it the explanation of inference, or something else, or is there no purpose at all?"— be dispelled? Moreover, is this [work] indeed devoid of purpose?

Furthermore, since the engagement of one who desires to know is possible even through a statement possessing a purpose, or through a purpose intended by oneself, or through something similar to that, the presentation of a statement of purpose is indeed superfluous.
Therefore, "that statement which is devoid of a purpose... [S. 3a]
Or, if it lacks that purpose, it is not undertaken to be composed or explained by a discerning person; for example,
the sentence "ten pomegranates" and so forth, or the examination of a crow’s teeth.

In order to point out the lack of proof (*asiddhatā*) for one who objects on the grounds that "this treatise or its subject matter is purposeless" by means of the non-perception of a pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*), the statement of the purpose is presented at the outset.
[This is the consideration of the purpose of the treatise and its subject matter.
Therein, with the phrase "for the sake of explaining that," he states the purpose of this very treatise himself.
For the purpose of a sentence is indeed the comprehension of its respective meaning;
and that exists here, because through the mutual connection of the words and the intermediate sentences, there is the comprehension of the composite meaning.
To explain: in this treatise, inference is being elucidated; thus, that is the subject matter (*abhidheya*).
Because that very [inference] is connected with the word "that" (tat).

Although inference is subordinate when there is the comprehension of an imperceptible object, nevertheless, because the function of a word conforms to the speaker's intention, it is referred to by the word "that";
otherwise, there would be no contact with the primary element.
And how could this be so?
Because words cannot be inherently connected [to their objects],
and because inference alone is being expounded by means of the statement beginning with "the property of the subject" (pakṣadharma).
The purpose of this treatise is the derivation of that [inference], which is the non-erroneous cognition of its true nature, because that is what is to be accomplished.
For this very reason, he indicates the operation of the treatise—whose object is the derivation of inference—by means of the causative suffix (*ṇic*), stating: "for the sake of deriving that."
Consequently, the relationship between the treatise and its purpose, characterized as that of the means and the end to be accomplished (*sādhyasādhanalakṣaṇa*),

is also stated. Although, according to the linguistic usage (*śabdavṛtta*), the primary importance belongs to the function of the treatise— the object of which is the mastery of inference— nevertheless, according to the actual state of things (*vastuvṛtta*), the mastery itself is primary, because it is that which is to be accomplished by the treatise.

Furthermore, because the other [means of knowledge] is subordinate as being merely a means to that [inference], it is understood that the purpose is indeed the mastery of inference (*anumāna-vyutpatti*) itself, and not the operation of the treatise (*prakaraṇa-vyāpāra*). By the statement, "Because the comprehension of objects beyond the senses (*parokṣārtha-pratipatti*) is based upon inference," he states the purpose of the subject matter of the treatise, which is the definition of inference.

For a person of discernment does not engage [with a statement] merely because the sentence possesses a result characterized by the cognition of its own literal meaning; rather, they do so when that expressed meaning is useful for human goals, and such utility exists here. This is because the cognition—meaning the ascertainment—of an imperceptible object has inference—the three-featured logical mark—as its cause, since the term for the effect is used metaphorically for the cause.
This is stated in order to demonstrate that it cannot be established by any other means.
{p. 4.1} For the purpose of refuting the views of others, the "basis" (*āśraya*)—meaning the cause—is analyzed in a general sense as that for which inference (*anumāna*) is the basis.

Subsequently, when there is a requirement for a specific [explanation] regarding what it is that has inference as its basis—it is said that, although in the connection between the word and the cognition of an imperceptible object...

Nevertheless, although femininity is understood, because it is not present to the intellect at the time of the formation of that word-base (*pada*), it is considered "external" (*bahiraṅga*); thus, it does not serve as the cause for the feminine suffixes, as in the examples *iyaṃ brāhmaṇī* ("this Brāhmaṇī woman") and *iyam uṣṭrikā* ("this female camel").
[3] The statement of the purpose; [4] its being for the sake of engaging the audience;
[5] by virtue of the desire for that purpose.
[6] A description of the determinative nature of the initial statement that expresses the purpose; [7] the purpose—
[9] From the doubt regarding the means; [10] because it is the means for a specific purpose.
[12] Of doubt, [13] its analysis,
[14] by means of verbal logic.
[15] The function of the treatise;
[16] the treatise;
[17] the purpose—T.
[18] Womanhood [is established];
by this very fact—that it arises from a mark (*liṅga*)—it is indicated that it is an inference (*anumāna*).
And by this, every cognition of an imperceptible object (*parokṣārtha*) is shown to be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Because it is impossible to realize that [object] through anything else, it is stated that [the realization] is based solely on a logical mark (*liṅga*) possessing the three characteristics; this is because of the restriction [implied by the phrase] "precisely because it is based on inference.
Consequently, if words and so forth possess validity, they are nothing other than inference.

Otherwise, it would follow that those [other means of knowledge] must also be explained, since the reason is the same. For instance: every cognition of an imperceptible object that constitutes a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is not independent.
Because there is an absence of a necessary connection with its own object, it is impossible for that [cognition] to be invariably in conformity with it;
furthermore, since the defining characteristic of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is non-contradiction (*avisamvāda*).

If [cognition] were to arise from something else even when it is unrelated, then the undesirable consequence would follow that everything could be cognized by everyone; for even if there is no connection with the subject (*dharmin*), it would produce a cognition regarding everything.

Because there is no absence of proximity or distance, such an object is indeed a three-featured mark (*trirūpaliṅga*). Thus, every cognition of an imperceptible object (*parokṣārtha*) does not differ from inference, since it arises from a three-featured mark. And what is this object? It is the reason (*hetu*), which is a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) pervaded by a part of that [subject]. Of what [is it the reason]?
It is shown by its connection with the subject at hand— that "the cognition of an imperceptible object" (parokṣārthapratipatti)—

because of the restriction that "only that which is a property of the subject (pakṣadharma) and is pervaded by a part of it (tadaṃśavyāpta) is the reason for the cognition of an imperceptible object. In the absence of such a restriction, [the definition would be too broad].
[20] being the cause for the realization of objects not present to the senses,
[21] independent realization,
[22] for one's own benefit—

[23] [The establishment that the nature of a real entity belongs only to the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) and not to the universal (*sāmānya*), which is connected to and bound by its own side.

However, the inclusion of the term "object" (*artha*) is for the sake of demonstrating that even inference (*anumāna*), as the comprehension of an imperceptible object, has the particular characteristic as its domain of validity (*prāmāṇya*).
For an object is that which is capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), and it is the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) alone that possesses this nature.
For this very reason—since the establishment of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has as its basis a real entity (*vastu*)—he will state [later]: "Because the real entity is the substratum."

Otherwise, one who seeks purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) would not engage with that [object] based on inference. Even though the universal (*sāmānya*) is not a real entity, its purposeful action consists merely in being a cognition; and since that [cognition] is established as being produced by that [universal], the universal is not actually employed for such things as burning or cooking.
Because it is the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) itself that is operative there.

If it is argued that [the word] functions there because of its connection with that [particular], we say no; for since an eternal entity cannot be assisted by anything, it lacks any connection with anything at all.
Even if a relation exists, how could there be activity toward one thing upon the cognition of another?
For that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
If it is argued that activity occurs there due to error (*bhrānti*), because the distinction is not determined owing to the subtlety of inherence (*samavāya*);
If that is the case, then let it be mere illusion;
what is the use of a superfluous universal (*sāmānya*) as an internal tumor?
If you argue that this is because an illusion without a seed (*nirbbījabhrānti*) is impossible;
Those very individuals, when performing that single effect, are the seed of error;
for the cognition of a universal has a form identical to the color and shape [of the individual],
yet the universal does not possess that nature.
How, then, can that [universal] be the seed of error?
For others maintain that error is based on similarity.
However, since individuals themselves are excluded from those of a different class and possess the very nature of cognitions with a universal form, they alone are the seed of error.
Because the exclusion of what is not that nature (atadrūpavyāvṛtti) exists in those [particulars],
and because it is impossible for a real entity (vastubhūta) such as a universal to exist in them due to the impossibility of its connection with them.

However, for those who postulate that the universal (*sāmānya*) is indeed of the nature of the individual (*vyakti*), they have effectively accepted that the validity (*prāmāṇya*) of inference has as its object the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
But how could a universal that is of the nature of a particular characteristic appear in inference?
For that would entail the undesirable consequence of adopting the Vaiśeṣika view.
{p. 6.1} [1. General definition of the reason (*hetu*);
[§ 1. Discussion on how pervasion (*vyāpti*) is established by means of the threefold nature of the reason;
[24] And because of the absence of color and shape.
[25] By the Sāṃkhyas [26] it has been stated that when the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) does not appear... [S. 7a] ...indeed.

In that regard, since the effect (*kārya*) and the essential nature (*svabhāva*) function as means of establishing a positive affirmation (*vidhi*), they have no operation when a negation (*pratiṣedha*) is to be proven.

Furthermore, from non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) alone, there is no certainty regarding the absence of other causes; for it is established in four ways: non-apprehension of the essential nature (*svabhāva*), the cause (*kāraṇa*), and the pervader (*vyāpaka*), as well as the apprehension of the contradictory (*viruddhavidhi*).

Among these, the non-apprehension of the essential nature—which consists in the apprehension of something else and pertains to that which is associated with a single cognition (*ekajñānasaṃsargin*) in a form possessing equal fitness (*tulyayogyatārūpa*)—is accepted as the cause for the conventional usage of non-existence (*abhāvavyavahārahetu*).
Nor is another reason (hetvantara) accepted as being an absolute non-existence (atyantābhāva) for that which has followed the form [of the negation];
for if it were so, there would be merely a negation of its location and so forth, not an absolute non-existence.

However, the non-perception of the cause and the pervader (kāraṇavyāpakānupalabdhi) occurs only when the relationship of effect-to-cause and pervaded-to-pervader (kāryakāraṇavyāpyavyāpakabhāva) is established.
Furthermore, this mode [of negation] is not possible when another cause is admitted to be absolutely non-existent.
Therefore, how could those two lead one to understand its absence?

As for contradiction (*virodha*), it is understood through the non-existence of something that possesses its complete causes when another thing exists; thus, even the perception of the contradictory (*viruddhopalabdhi*) is impossible in this case.
Or, if [the reason] were possible, how could there be an absolute negation through the non-perception of the cause (*kāraṇānupalabdhi*) and so forth?

Anticipating this objection, he says: "The fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) are other than those. Since the fallacious reasons are other than those three kinds of valid reasons, therefore that [negation] is indeed threefold.
He thinks as follows: here, when something is restricted to a certain domain, that restriction is established through the pervasion of its opposite by the reverse of that [domain].

For example, when it is stated that "whatever exists is necessarily momentary," this restriction of existence (*sattva*) to momentary things is established through the pervasion of the non-momentary—the opposite of the momentary—by non-existence (*asattva*), which is the reverse of existence.

Likewise, here too, when the reason is restricted to being threefold, it becomes restricted to the number three itself, through the pervasion of objects outside the number three by the state of being a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsatva*), which is the reverse of being a valid reason.
Thereupon, he demonstrates that objects distinct from the three kinds of valid reasons are merely pseudo-reasons (*hetvābhāsa*).

Consequently, by the perception of what is incompatible with the essential nature (*svabhāvaviruddhopalabdhi*), one ascertains the absence of causal status for those objects other than the non-perception of effect (*kārya*) and essential nature (*svabhāva*).
Furthermore, the contradiction between a valid reason and its pseudo-counterpart consists precisely in their being defined by mutual exclusion (*parasparaparihārasthitalakṣaṇatā*).
At the very moment of cognizing the characteristic of the cause, [the object] is already apprehended;
for, precisely from the cognition whose manifestation is restricted to that nature, there arises the cognition of its appearance as such by virtue of its being other than its opposite,
since there is a mutual determination of the absence of each other's form.

In that regard, the status of being a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsatva*), which is observed in objects excluded from the three types of valid reasons, negates the status of being a valid reason (*hetutva*) which is its own opposite.
Furthermore, those objects external to the three types of reasons are neither characterized by absolute non-existence nor is the status of being a reason actually denied of them;

rather, it is simply that the status of being a reason—well-established elsewhere—is projected upon them due to delusion, or merely suspected, and is thereby removed through the perception of its opposite.

Why, then, is it said: "How can there be contradiction for that which is absolutely non-existent"? Contradiction is not characterized solely by the impossibility of coexistence, such that this principle would have to be applied in all cases. Nor is it to be understood that contradiction exists only between a thing and the very locus where it is negated, such that one might ask how there could be a cognition of contradiction with anything at all regarding a non-existent thing?
Thus it might be objected:

"Is it not the case that there is no cold touch here because of fire"? [The answer is: It is not only in the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*) that the contradiction between cold touch and fire exists, but rather everywhere; for instance, although this [cold touch] is known elsewhere to be contradicted by fire, its negation occurs in the subject of the thesis.

Likewise, because they are perceived as fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*), the status of being a valid reason is excluded for those objects that lie outside the three types of valid reasons. Furthermore, even in the case of that which is absolutely non-existent, a contradiction based on its defining characteristic (*lākṣaṇika-virodha*) is recognized—just as momentariness contradicts non-momentariness because the latter is impossible in any real entity—or as existence contradicts non-existence, which is characterized by the absence of all causal capacity. Enough with these ramblings of the dull-witted!

This has been established with great care: the state of being a reason, when restricted to the triad, becomes necessarily fixed therein provided that there is pervasion even in its contrapositive. With this intention, in order to demonstrate the pervasion of the contrapositive, the following was stated: "pseudo-reasons" (*hetvābhāsa*).
"Another has arisen," and so forth; therein, there is another object associated with the same cognition (*ekajñānasaṃsargi-vastvantara*).
[29] The state of being a cause;
[30] the cause;
[31] characterized by non-existence when that which exists is absent.
[32] Of this very thing as it is perceived— T. [33] of the cold touch [34] in its threefoldness.

[§2. Discussion on the pervasion of the three types of external objects by the nature of fallacious reasons] In this regard, it might be argued: "In that case, the pervasion of the opposite of momentariness by the absence of existence is established by the force of a subverting means of valid cognition (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*);
but here, by which means of valid cognition is the pervasion of objects external to the three numbers established as being fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*)?"
Here [the opponent] says: "Because of the necessity of inseparable connection" (*avinābhāvaniyamāt*).

This means that even when a thing—distinct from the three types of logical reasons—is accepted or suspected as a mark (*liṅga*), there is an absence of inseparable connection despite the presence of the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*).
And so he will state: "It does not exist elsewhere than in the three kinds of reasons; it is said to be restricted to this very [context].

Furthermore, the deficiency of inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) is ascertained in cases such as "knowability" (*prameyatva*) to be pervaded by the general property of being a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*), namely the unestablished (*asiddha*), the contradictory (*viruddha*), and the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). Thus, when "being a fallacious reason" is the probandum (*sādhya*), the deficiency of inseparable connection is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).

Furthermore, the absence of the inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) is established through the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*), precisely because [those other reasons] are distinct from the three types of valid reasons.
For it is thus: the inseparable connection is pervaded by identity (*tādātmya*) and causality (*tadutpatti*), since these two necessarily exist therein.

And because that [effect] exists only when those two [cause and essential nature] exist, and because for that which does not possess their intrinsic nature or arise from them, there is no dependence upon them; consequently, there is no rule of non-deviation from them. As it has been said:

"From the relation of cause and effect, or from an essential nature that acts as a regulator, there is the rule of inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*); it is not established by mere observation or non-observation."
"What is the necessity of an invariable concomitance for another [property] in a different way through other [means],
or when the cause is not a distinct entity, as in the case of dye on a cloth?

For even the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) of taste and so forth with form and so forth is not intrinsic (*svataḥ*), but rather occurs by way of the non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*) from their own causes; thus, the very production from those causes is the basis for invariable concomitance.

Otherwise, if one were to postulate invariable concomitance with something that is not dependent on it, or not dependent on its cause, then everything would be invariably concomitant with all things, as there would be no distinction.
If it is argued that the invariable concomitance of color, taste, and so forth is caused by their inherence in a single substance (*ekārthasamavāya*):
Now, it might be argued that inherence (*samavāya*) is also described as existing between things that stand in the relation of the supported and the support;

yet, since that relation of support and supported cannot be established through a mere contingency when there is no mutual benefit, inherence as a dependence upon a single causal complex (*ekasāmagryadhīnatā*) must be understood as "inherence in a single object" (*ekārthasamavāya*).

Alternatively, any other real entity (*vastubhūta*) as a connection is impossible, as this has already been demonstrated at length by the author of the treatise in the *Examination of Relations* (*Sambandhaparīkṣā*). Therefore, this should be understood from that very source. Asa... [fragmentary]... #
Or rather, [is it not the case that] even when the relationship of producer and produced does not exist?

Or, if [it is argued that] "in the case of identity (*tādātmya*), there is an inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) with that very thing and not with another," then the answer must be given by the very nature of things (*vastusvabhāva*): "Only those things which exist in such a way [are so connected], not those posited by us;
we are merely observers. If this is said:
In that case, the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of things would be accidental; thus, it would not belong to anything at all.
For a restriction of place, time, and substance is not logical for that which is causeless.
Indeed, such a thing might be brought about somewhere or not, depending on whether it is contingent or non-contingent upon something and somewhere.

Otherwise, since there would be no distinction, who could prevent its existence in other places and times, just as it exists in its desired place, time, and substance? For there would be no difference.
Therefore, when one thing is observed to be invariably concomitant with another, the thinkers of reality (*tattvacintaka*) must state the cause for that non-deviation;
they should not resort to a mere "stretching out of the feet" (i.e., a lazy, unreasoned assumption).

And since that non-deviant cause is not logically possible as anything other than what has been described, those lacking it do not possess the characteristics of a valid reason (*hetu*). Thus it has been said:
"Among those such as the conjoined (*saṃyogin*) and so forth, there exists no such necessary connection;
they are not reasons, because deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is possible."
[As stated in] PV 4.203.

Herein is the formal argument (*prayoga*): that which lacks both identity (*tādātmya*) and origination from it (*tadutpatti*) with respect to another thing is not invariably concomitant (*avinābhāvī*) with that other;
for example, "knowability" (*prameyatva*) and so forth are not invariably concomitant with "impermanence" (*anityatva*) and so forth.

Furthermore, for those things that are distinct from essential nature (*svabhāva*) and effect (*kārya*), neither identity (*tādātmya*) nor causality (*tadutpatti*) exists with anything else; this is the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*).

Non-perception of essential nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*), however, is included within the reason of essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*); thus, its logical connection (*pratibandha*) is characterized solely by identity.

As for the non-perceptions of the pervader and the cause, they establish the absence of the pervaded and the effect precisely through the force of the logical connections characterized by identity and causality.
As it has been said: "Therefore, either an essential nature connected with that alone, or a cause, would exclude the entity itself, or the effect, because of the absence of deviation" (PV 3.22).

Thus, in this verse, the definition of the logical reason (hetu-lakṣaṇa) [1], the restriction of its number (saṃkhyā-niyama) [2], and the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) that demonstrates it [3] have been indicated.
[35] Regarding the inseparable connection (avinābhāva), it arises from identity (tādātmya). [36]
[37] Of the probandum; [38] of the probans;
[39] in the dissimilar instance.
[40] In the case of the similar instance (sapakṣa),
[41] when there is an absence of identity (tādātmya) or origination from that (tadutpatti) for the probans (sādhana), [42]...
[43] In the case of the probandum (sādhya), [44] such as a hammer and so forth, [45] or eternality and so forth.
[46] In the absence of a restriction by a single causal complex,
[47] that which is not dependent on the probandum,
[48] and that which is not dependent on the causes of the probandum.
[49] If there is no assistance provided to that which is to be supported, such as color, taste, and so forth, [50] then [the reason] is not connected [to the probandum],
[51] such as impermanence and the like.

[52] The pervaded (*vyāpya*) is such properties as being produced (*kṛtakatva*), etc. [§ 3. An alternative explanation of the phrase "due to the restriction of inseparable connection" (*avinābhāvaniyamāt*):

Alternatively, regarding the statement "it is only threefold," that property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) is indeed of three kinds—namely, called essential nature (*svabhāva*), effect (*kārya*), and non-perception (*anupalambha*)—and it is pervaded by its own part (*tadaṃśena*), but nothing else is.
The connection is that it is indeed pervaded by its own part in those three ways.
What is the reason?
Because of the rule of inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*).
That is, because of the necessity of *avinābhāva*— which is to say, pervasion (*vyāpti*)—
it is restricted solely to the three types of property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*).
And because there is a rule of invariable concomitance for the three kinds of property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*),

and because nothing other than the three kinds of property of the subject— consisting of essential nature (*svabhāva*), effect (*kārya*), and non-perception (*anupalambha*)— is pervaded by that part [of the reason],

it follows that the threefold property of the subject, which takes the form of effect, essential nature, and non-perception, is indeed pervaded by that part; thus, it is stated that such a [property] is not a non-reason (*ahetu*).

Consequently, those Cārvākas who— by asserting that the designation "reason" (hetu) applies only to things external to the three types of reasons because of the absence of inseparable connection (avinābhāva) there,
and by declaring that these are not reasons because inseparable connection necessarily exists within the three types of reasons—
are thereby refuted.
[§ 4. The indication of fallacious reasons even without stating their definitions:

In this regard, one might think: "The definition of fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) should also be stated there, so that students may desist from treating them as valid reasons. To this he says: "Fallacious reasons are other than those" (*tato 'pare*). This means that since fallacious reasons—being other than the definition of a valid reason, namely "that which is a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) and is pervaded by its part" (*tadaṃśena vyāpta*)—are understood as being deficient in that definition, their specific definition is not stated.
For instance: when it is stated that "it is a property of the subject" (*pakṣadharma*), that which lacks the status of being a property of the subject is not a [valid] reason (*hetu*).

When it is stated that "it is pervaded by a portion thereof" (*tadaṃśena vyāptaḥ*), since there is necessarily an absence [of the reason] wherever there is an absence of pervasion by that portion—due to the absence of pervasion by the contrary (*viparyaya-vyāpti*) or of the pervader—it follows that these are understood as fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*), namely the unestablished (*asiddha*), the contradictory (*viruddha*), and the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because they are deficient in the essential form of a reason.

For instance: when an object of a certain characteristic has been explained to a student, he will himself initiate the conventional usage of that term for an object lacking that characteristic, because the apprehension of its own nature occurs precisely through the exclusion of what is not of that nature; thus, effort in that regard would not be fruitful.
As for the exposition of fallacious reasons (hetvābhāsa) found elsewhere, that is intended for those of dull intellect;
however, this present treatise was composed for those of vast intelligence, as it is stated: "It is presented in brief."

For only those who are capable of understanding what has been stated in brief exactly as it is— not those of dull intellect— are able to do so, because for the latter, there is an absence of comprehension of the meaning exactly as it is without an extensive explanation.
For this very reason, the definition of fallacious reasons (hetvābhāsa) was described therein precisely by first introducing them through their implications.
Thus, in this explanation, six topics are indicated in this verse: (1) the definition of the reason (*hetu-lakṣaṇa*);

(2) the restriction regarding the number of reasons (*hetu-saṃkhyā-niyama*); (3) the determination that those three possess the status of being reasons (*tasya ca trividhasya hetutvāvadhāraṇam*); (4–5) the cause for the combined presentation of both [the definition and the number];
and (6) the cause for not stating the definition of pseudo-reasons (*hetvābhāsa-lakṣaṇānabhidhāna-kāraṇam*). These are the six meanings set forth here in the verse.

Something more—this too is well observed: that logical reason (*hetu*) is indeed threefold, being divided by the distinctions of effect (*kārya*), essential nature (*svabhāva*), and non-perception (*anupalabdhi*).

Likewise, it is of exactly three types and possesses exactly three characteristics (*trirūpa*), due to the distinction between the forms of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), positive concomitance (*anvaya*), and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*);
for positive and negative concomitance are expressed by the statement of "pervasion by its part" (*tadaṃśavyāpti*).
That reason is not even capable of possessing other forms such as having a non-contradicted object (*abādhitaviṣayatva*).

Why? Because: (1) the fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) are other than that; (2) they are other than those three types, namely [the three kinds of] essential nature (*svabhāva*) and so forth, or other than the three forms consisting of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) and so on; or (3) they are others, such as the "conjoined" (*saṃyogin*) and so forth, or those possessing forms distinct from having a non-contradicted object and the rest.
Why?

Because the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) is restricted solely to this threefold and three-characterized reason; the meaning is that elsewhere—in cases where other forms exist apart from [the three types such as] essential nature (*svabhāva*) and so forth—there is an absence of invariable concomitance.

For indeed, there is no possibility of an inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*)—which is the basis for a logical bond—existing apart from the essential nature (*svabhāva*) and so forth, nor of another form existing within that which possesses such a nature. And he will state later, beginning with "if the six characteristics are not present," that just as another form is impossible when the inseparable connection does not exist, so too is it here. [54] Whatever form...
[55] The cause of this twofold restriction regarding the number of reasons—that is, the determination of the causal status—is the restriction of inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*). ...
[§ 5. According to Dignāga, the word *pakṣa* refers solely to the locus (*dharmin*]:
Even when the definition of a reason is formulated as "a property of the subject" (*pakṣadharma*), if the term *pakṣa* refers to the whole [subject and predicate],...

If that which is grasped as the object of inference were [already] established, then every reason (*hetu*) would be unestablished (*asiddha*); or, if it were established, inference would be redundant. Thus he says: "The subject (*pakṣa*) is the locus of the property (*dharmin*). But if it is asked: how can the word *pakṣa*, which denotes a composite whole, be used here for the locus alone?
Because of the metaphorical application of the whole to its part:
for the whole known as the "thesis" (*pakṣa*) has two parts, namely the property-bearer (*dharmin*) and the property (*dharma*).
Therefore, in this context, the word "thesis" (*pakṣa*) is applied to the mere property-bearer through the metaphorical application of the whole.

Furthermore, being a "part" (*ekadeśatva*) is the basis for the metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) of the whole; thus, there is no risk of that [designation] applying elsewhere than to the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*). As it has been said:

"Because the whole is what is to be proven (*sādhya*), and because it is a part even when the property alone is the subject (*dharmin*)—though not the primary one—the status of being the 'probandum' (*sādhyatva*) is metaphorically attributed [to the subject]."
Thus:
"For when something is a part of another, there is a metaphorical attribution (*upacāra*) of that [whole's] nature to it;
for when one part of a cloth is burnt, there is no metaphorical attribution that 'the blanket is burnt'. (PS III 9; cf. HBtransl 835) [56]
[§ 6. Īśvarasena’s objection to the explanation of Dignāga and its refutation.

This explanation by the Master (Ācārya) was challenged by Īśvarasena; [the author], wishing to refute that challenge, sets forth the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) and says, beginning with "In the absence of a purpose," etc.: "Without a purpose, it is not desired..."
"Transgressing the primary meaning of a word" (PS III 39cd)—
in the absence of a purpose, figurative usage is not appropriate.
To this, the opponent replies: "Let there simply be the subject (dharmin) and the property (dharma).
It is not that there is a lack of purpose.
Why? Because the purpose of the negation is the object of dispute, which is every other subject (dharmin).

Since that which is the state of a metaphorical designation (upacāra) consists in the negation of all properties of the subject (dharmin), the reason [adduced by the opponent]—namely, "because of the absence of purpose"—is unestablished (*asiddha*).

If it is asked, "What is the merit in this being so?", he replies: "For when such a metaphorical designation exists, [properties such as] visibility (*cākṣuṣatva*) and so forth [are thereby excluded]."

By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), fallacious reasons such as "because of the blackness of a crow" (*kākasya kārṣṇyāt*), which are unestablished due to being in a different locus (*vyadhikaraṇāsiddha*), are excluded and rejected as valid reasons.
However, since the term "property of the subject" (*dharmidharma*) is stated in a general sense, one might think that even those [unestablished reasons] could function as reasons;
therefore, this [fallacy] is established even by the explicit mention of the "subject" (*dharmin*) when no figurative usage (*upacāra*) is intended.

To this, the opponent says that the metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) is indeed useless—meaning not only by the expression of the property (*dharma*), but also by the expression of the substratum (*dharmin*). [The phrase "dharmyāśrayasiddhau" means: when there is the establishment of the dependence upon the substratum; "dependence" (*āśraya*) here refers to the taking up (*parigraha*) of the substratum (*dharmin*), and it is in the presence of that establishment [that the metaphor is used]. If it is asked: "What, then, is the cause for the property to imply its substratum? [59]
Because it is dependent on another— since a property (dharma) is dependent upon a property-bearer (dharmin)— it necessarily implies that property-bearer.
Therefore, the mention of the property-bearer, being redundant [if stated separately], indicates only the specific subject of the thesis (sādhyadharmin),
and not the property-bearer in general.
It might be thought: "From the mention of the *dharmin* (the subject), it is understood that some specific *dharmin* qualified [by the property] is intended here;

but why is it understood that this is the *sādhyadharmin* (the subject possessing the property to be proven)? To this he says: "By the principle of proximity (*pratyāsatti*). And here, proximity is understood to be intended by the force of the word *dharmin*.

In the case of pervasion (*vyāpti*), however, since even the mention of the property (*dharma*) implies the locus (*dharmin*) alone according to the rule of logic, the explicit mention of the locus would be redundant.
Furthermore, proximity belongs to the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*) alone, because it is there that the reason (*hetu*) is first presented.
The selection of the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*) does not arise from proximity.
Why?
Because it applies to the subject of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadharmin*) as well, and not solely to the subject of the thesis.
Sometimes, in an application preceded by the observation of pervasion (*vyāpti*), the existence of the reason (*hetu*) is first demonstrated even in the subject of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadharmī*).
If the establishment of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharmin*) does not occur through proximity, then it will occur through elimination (*pāriśeṣya*);
for, by means of the pervasion with that part (*tadaṃśavyāpti*) which serves as the reason, the existence of the property is established in the subject of the example.
For it is thought that without an example, the pervasion (vyāpti) of the reason by the probandum cannot be demonstrated.

Therefore, since the term "property-possessor" (dharmin) is distinct from what follows, it is understood as referring specifically to the property-possessor that is the subject of the thesis (sādhyadharmin).

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "by its part" (tadaṃśena), the word "that" (tat) will connect with the property-possessor implied by the mention of the "property" (dharma); thus, one should not suspect that the inclusion of the term "property-possessor" is for the sake of establishing that connection.
That for which no other purpose is possible is the domain of *pāriśeṣya* (presumption by elimination); however, another purpose for the mention of the subject (*dharmin*) is indeed conceivable.
Therefore, how can the inclusion of the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*) follow from the mention of the subject by way of *pāriśeṣya*?

Thinking thus, the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādin) says: "If it were already established that the property of existence (sattva) is present in the subject of the example through its pervasion by that [reason], then the further mention of the 'subject' (*dharmī*) might be suspected of having the restrictive purpose of implying that only that which is a property of the very subject of the example is the reason.
Consequently, properties such as visibility (*cākṣuṣatva*) and the like would alone be reasons."

"It would be undesirable [to claim] that 'being produced' (kṛtakatva) and so forth [are not reasons]; therefore, a figurative usage (upacāra) must be employed. To the question, "But what is seen in the treatises on logic (tarkaśāstra) as a statement for the sake of restriction? he says: "It is seen [in the rule] 'only in what is of the same class' (sajātīya eva)," and so forth.

In that regard, concerning the definition of a logical reason (*hetu*) given by the Teacher— namely, "that which exists in the similar class" (*san sajātīye*)— although the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) of the reason is established by the restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) "existence only in the similar class," [one might ask:
where?

Regarding the statement, "That which is non-existent when the probandum is absent is [the reason] when that [probandum] is excluded" (NMu 7), the Teacher explained the mention of "non-existence" for the sake of restriction: so that non-existence may occur only where [the probandum] is absent, and not elsewhere, nor in what is contradictory. Likewise here too, the mention of the locus (*dharmī*) might be suspected to be for the sake of restricting existence to that very [locus].
When? Even when the subject of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadharmin*) has been established. Why?
Because of the statement regarding the pervasion by its part (*tadaṃśavyāpti*).
For what purpose? To ensure the necessity of its existence (*bhāvaniyama*).
In that very same subject of the example,
when a possibility of doubt exists—
why is this so?
By the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), there is the grasping of the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*).

Now, one might object: since that which is not a property of the subject (*apakṣadharma*) cannot be a logical reason (*hetu*), there can be no suspicion regarding the necessity [of the reason being a property of the subject].

For instance, even if a property were pervaded by the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*), if it were perceived in some particular subject, it would produce the cognition of its own pervader only in that very place and not elsewhere, due to proximity (*pratyāsatti*) and remoteness (*viprakarṣa*).
"In successive order:

but how can that which is not perceived in any locus (*dharmī*) be a means of cognition? Or, if it were so [perceived], it would cause its own pervader to be known everywhere, because there is no distinction between proximity and remoteness. To this he says: "Therefore, by implication," and so forth.

This capacity that has just been described brings about, for listeners of keen intellect, the comprehension of the meaning characterized by the inclusion of the subject (*sādhyadharmin*) through this very capacity; however, there would be a burden of cognitive effort for those who themselves pursue the meaning without its verbal expression.

Therefore, by means of a mere metaphorical designation—devoid of the listener's own inference of the non-verbal meaning from the phrase "property of the subject" (*dharmidharma*)—there is the identical reference as "property of the thesis" (*pakṣadharma*).
And "respect for practice" is avoided.

By the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "and respect for practice," this is what is meant: those who require instruction from another must understand this meaning from the statement of the definition (*lakṣaṇa*). [S.15a]
"Since it is understood according to its own definition, how can it be that 'that which is not a property of the subject (apakṣadharma) is not a logical reason'?"—
this is the doubt. Therefore, for those who follow such definitions, the employment of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) is made both to establish the rule and to dispel that doubt.
[57] Because those [reasons] possess the property of being attributes of subjects such as a jar and so forth,
[58] there is the rejection of the fallacy of the unestablished due to a different locus (vyadhikaraṇāsiddha).
[59] If it is argued that— parā— T.

[60] The principle of pervasion (*vyāpti*) is that whatever property (*dharma*) belongs to any given subject (*dharmin*) may serve as the reason (*hetu*). If this were intended, then [61] there would be an implication of the mere subject (*dharmimātra*), because a property is dependent upon its subject.

[62] For there are two kinds of formal argument (*prayoga*): that which possesses the restatement of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) preceded by the statement of pervasion (*vyāpti*), and that which possesses the statement of pervasion preceded by the restatement of the property of the subject.
"Whatever is produced is impermanent."
Just like a jar;
and sound is produced.

That which exists in the similar class (sajātīya) and is present in the homologous set (sapakṣa), and which is absent in its opposite—the absence of the probandum (sādhyābhāva)—in the heterologous set (vipakṣa), being in two ways non-existent, whether as existent or as non-existent, if it does not so occur.
However, the intended meaning is that only when [the reason] is indeed non-existent in the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*) is it a valid logical reason (*samyag-hetu*).
Here, the aphorism of the Master Dignāga—"that which exists in the similar class (*sajātīya*) and is non-existent in its absence"—is explained as follows:
the meaning is that a logical reason is that which possesses non-existence either in the form of a non-entity, in another form, or in a contradictory form.
[66] The expression of the property-bearer and the property— T. [67] Even when [the reason] is unperceived, it possesses the capacity for proof [68] for those who desire instruction from another.
[§ 7. The establishment of the restriction regarding "the property of the subject" (pakṣadharma):
Here, because the employment of words necessarily has the result of exclusion (vyavaccheda), it must certainly be determined.
Furthermore, in the case of the genitive compound *pakṣadharma*, no other type of compound is possible.

And thus, because of the restriction that "it is a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) alone," the pervasion by its own part (*tadaṃśavyāpti*) is contradicted. Pointing out this contradiction in the definition, he says: since the qualification of the subject requires exclusion from others, a property that depends on such a qualification does not follow elsewhere—in other words, it does not occur in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) other than the subject itself. For instance, that which is qualified by the subject belongs to the subject alone, and not to anything else.
For example: he who is Devadatta’s son is his son alone, and not Yajñadatta’s as well.
Because it does not extend to anything other than that, there is uniqueness (*asādhāraṇatā*); it would not be common (*sādhāraṇatā*).
This means, in short, that there is a contradiction with the pervasion of its own part (*tadaṃśavyāpti*).
Because commonality [of the reason] is established through its pervasion by that part [of the subject];
therefore, if the property of the subject is not pervaded by that part, [the reason is inconclusive].
[S. 15b. Now, if it is argued that "pervasion by a portion of that" (*tadaṃśavyāpti*) is not the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), then the definition is contradictory.

But surely, "pervasion by a portion of that" will be explained as having the characteristic of inseparable connection with its own probandum (*svasādhyāvinābhāva*): namely, that when the pervading probandum-property exists in the reason, it necessarily exists in the subject which is its locus; or alternatively, that the pervaded reason exists only when that very pervading probandum-property exists.
Nor does this necessarily imply that the reason must occur elsewhere than in the subject (pakṣa), such that a contradiction with its definition might be suspected.
For indeed, when the reason exists in that very subject which has been made the locus of the thesis, it certainly establishes its pervasion by the property to be proven (sādhyadharma).

And that very fact of its being inseparably connected with its own probandum (sādhya) in the subject of the thesis (sādhyadharmin) is the basis for its capacity to prove; it is not based on [such a connection] in another subject.
Furthermore, that inseparable connection with its own probandum is based on the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) that establishes the necessary relation (pratibandha);
it is not based merely on observing coexistence (sahabhāva) frequently or even once in some similar instance (sapakṣa).

For it is not the case that "diamond is not scratchable by iron because it is earthy, like wood and so forth," since even though there is an invariable concomitance (avinābhāva) between being earthy and being scratchable by iron elsewhere, such a state does not necessarily hold true in all cases.
Furthermore, if there were a rule that pervasion must be demonstrated only in instances other than the subject (*pakṣa*), then how could existence (*sattva*) establish momentariness?
How could one establish [the reason] with respect to entities?
For, against one who maintains that momentariness pervades all things, there is no similar instance (sapakṣa) whatsoever.
Furthermore, even if some accept the momentariness of a flame and the like, that too is not established through direct perception,
because the distinction between moments is so subtle that it is imperceptible.
Moreover, what logic is this— that pervasion (vyāpti) must be demonstrated elsewhere [in an example] and not even in the subject of the thesis (sādhyadharmin)?
For in this way, the definition of a logical reason (*hetu*) would be understood as being merely conceptual,
rather than functioning by the force of real entities (*vastubala*);
therefore, it is established that the reason is pervaded by its own probandum (*sādhya*) due to an essential connection (*pratibandha*).

And since that [logical reason] is established even in the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*) through the operation of a subverting proof (*bādhakapramāṇa*) regarding its opposite, there is no need whatsoever for it to depend on [its presence] elsewhere.

For this very reason, it has been stated elsewhere: "Whatever is observed somewhere, if it possesses a connection of that same kind with something else, that [reason] makes that [other thing] known in that [subject]."
The nature of the thing (*vastugati*) consists in its occurrence (*vṛtti*),
which is characterized by positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).
[71] In the determination;
[72] the characteristic; [73] in the section.
[74] Certain;
[75] of the logical mark (liṅga); [76] in fire and so forth.
[77] The indicator of fire [78] for those who know the connection [79].
Wherever it has been observed, there alone and not elsewhere—

this definition, beginning with "its presence in the object of inference (anumeya) and in what is similar to it," likewise refers to the *sapakṣa* as being precisely that which possesses the property to be proven (*sādhyadharmin*).
Therefore, this [definition] ultimately means simply that [the reason] exists only when the property to be proven is present.
Consequently, even for the subject (*sādhyadharmin*) which possesses that same property, its actual status as a similar instance (*sapakṣatva*) is not excluded;
for it is impossible to negate it by means of its being a "subject" (*pakṣatva*), a status established by the desire to prove it as the probandum (*sādhyatveneṣṭi*).

Therefore, since the statement of "pervasion by a part of that" (*tadaṃśavyāpti*) expresses the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) consisting in the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāvitva*) with its own probandum—because otherwise such [pervasion] would be impossible—it does not necessarily require occurrence elsewhere.
How is this doubt raised?
Truly, this should not be doubted at all,

provided that the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) of every reason with its own probandum could be ascertained through valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) within the very subject (*dharmin*) that has been made the locus of the thesis (*pakṣīkṛta*).

[As in the case of the essential reason (svabhāvahetu) characterized by existence when momentariness is the property to be proven, there is identity (tādātmya) established through the operation of a subverting proof (bādhakapramāṇa) against the contrary; however,
for the effect-reason (kāryahetu),
the necessary connection (pratibandha) is established by means of perception and non-perception with respect to some essential reason whose locus has been made the subject of the thesis.]
How could it be apprehended when the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is imperceptible?

Therefore, since its establishment occurs only elsewhere, and because that [reason] which depends on such a qualification must depend upon that [property], it does not follow there; thus, its "uniqueness" (*asādhāraṇatā*) is suspected by the mere possibility [of its occurrence]. For at that time, not occurring elsewhere, it would lack the exclusion (*vyatireka*) from the opposite of the property to be proven...

Since it is impossible for [the reason] to exist outside of those two [categories], and since all things are subsumed within that locus through either its presence in the probandum or its exclusion from it, it becomes a cause for doubt.

It might be argued: "In some cases, regarding a locus, the occurrence [of the reason] elsewhere must be taken into account for the sake of recollecting the proof of the necessary connection (pratibandha) previously grasped but now forgotten."
He addresses this objection with the words "No," and so forth:
"It is not the case that there is no non-occurrence elsewhere. Why?"
Non-connection (*ayoga*) means lack of relation; it is by the exclusion of that [non-connection] that the subject (*pakṣa*) is qualified.
For qualification does not occur solely through the exclusion of connection with another (*anyayogavyavaccheda*), but also through the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*).
Where the existence of a property in a subject is doubted, there the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*) is logically required;
and here the example is: "Caitra is an archer. For in the case of Caitra, it is doubted whether archery exists or does not exist.

Therefore, the scriptural statement "Caitra is an archer," which establishes his existence as such, excludes the alternative possibility of his being a non-archer that has been brought to mind by the listener's doubt;
thus, the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*) is what is logically established here.
Desiring to refute the exclusion intended by others, he says: "No."
The connection is that because it is qualified by the exclusion of connection with anything else (*anyayogavyavaccheda*), there is "uniqueness" (*asādhāraṇatā*) due to its non-occurrence elsewhere.
Here too, the example is "Arjuna is a bowman.
Although this word "bowman" is a general term, by virtue of [contextual] capacity and so forth, it functions to denote one who possesses preeminent qualities.

In this case, since Pārtha’s status as an archer is already established, there is no suspicion of non-connection (*ayoga*). However, when the statement "Pārtha is an archer" is made to a listener who suspects whether such an excellence exists elsewhere or not— thereby harboring a suspicion of connection with another (*anyayoga*)— then the exclusion of connection with another (*anyayogavyavaccheda*) follows as a logical necessity.

Because the two positions established by the doubt to be resolved are mutually contradictory, the exclusion of connection with another (*anyayogavyavaccheda*) is necessarily entailed by the force of logic through the mention of one [of them].

Thus, when there is a doubt as to whether this property exists or does not exist in the subject (*pakṣa*), the statement "it is a property of the subject" (*pakṣadharma*) means that it is indeed a property of the subject and not a non-property.

Furthermore, because a property is a qualifier due to its being dependent [on a substratum], non-connection (*ayoga*) is excluded; it is not the case that connection with something else (*anyayoga*) is excluded, because its pervasion by a portion of that [subject] has already been established, and thus there is no doubt regarding the example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
"A part of that" means "a property of that.
By the word "that," the subject (*pakṣa*) is referred to, not the property (*dharma*), because it is impossible for a property to possess another property.
And "part" (*aṃśa*) refers to the property (*dharma*), not a single portion [of the subject], because the word "side" (*pakṣa*) denotes the mere locus of the property (*dharmī*);
it is not a part of that [locus], since that [locus] lacks any single portion.

[81] The three types of reasons— known as the essential nature (*svabhāva*), the effect (*kārya*), and the non-perception (*anupalabdhi*)— are those whose presence in the object of inference (*anumeya*) and in what is similar to it (*tattulya*), and their absence in the dissimilar case (*avipakṣa*), are certain.
[82] That is the property to be proven (*sādhya-dharma*) of the subject to be proven (*sādhyadharmin*).

[83] Of that which possesses an inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) with its own property to be proven— namely, [84] the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*) and the essential-nature reason (*svabhāvahetu*)— its...
And that is the compound *sa cāsau dharmī* ("that which is both it and the subject").
There is an alternative reading, *taddharmaṇaḥ*, which should be explained as "of that which has such a property," meaning "of that which possesses that uncommon property."
And that is the subject (dharmin);
[the word] "of that" means "of the subject to be proven" (sādhyadharmin).

The compound is to be analyzed as follows: "that which occurred previously," "that which was grasped," "that which was forgotten," and "the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes the necessary connection (*pratibandha*)," all of which constitute its recollections.

Regarding that which exists as a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), there is pervasion (*vyāpti*)—namely, that which pervades and that which is pervaded—because it is cognized as possessing the nature of both. [§ 8. Pervasion consists in being a property of both the pervaded and the pervader. [87] Because it is perceived as having the nature of both.
When it is intended to be expressed as a pervading property (*vyāpakadharma*), then "therein" (*tatra*) refers to the pervader which is the object of cognition (*gamyasya*).

Here, the locative case (*saptamī*) has the meaning of the object (*artha*) as its primary sense, not the locus (*ādhāra*) as its primary sense, because it is impossible for properties (*dharmas*) to have other properties as their locus.

Therefore, this is the meaning: wherever the pervaded (vyāpya) exists in a subject (dharmin), there the pervader (vyāpaka) necessarily exists; this is pervasion (vyāpti), which is a property inherent to the pervader itself.

Consequently, the cognition of the pervaded as being "pervaded" occurs in relation to the existence of the pervader. However, it is not determined in this way [that the pervaded is the locus of the pervasion].

It is not the case that "only a pervader exists there," because this would entail the consequence of the absence of the logical reason (*hetu*), since even non-pervaders such as corporeality (*mūrtatva*) exist there.
Nor is it the case that "only in that [locus]" [exists], because this would result in the fallacy of non-effort-immediacy (*aprayatnānantarīyakatva*) and other such properties being non-reasons.
And the reason would be inconclusive (*sādhāraṇa*),
because eternality exists only among those things that are objects of cognition (*prameya*).
However, when [it is established] by way of being a pervading property (*vyāpyadharman*)...

When there is an intention to express the pervasion (*vyāpti*), it exists only where the pervader (*vyāpaka*)—the object to be understood (*gamya*)—is present; that is, wherever the pervader exists in a given subject (*dharmin*), the pervaded (*vyāpya*)—the means of understanding (*gamaka*)—exists there as well, and not its presence even when that [pervader] is absent. This is what constitutes pervasion.
In this case as well, the restriction that "the pervaded (vyāpya) exists only there" has not been adopted because it would entail the non-existence of the reason (*hetu*),
since even that which is not pervaded (*avyāpya*) may exist there.

Nor has the restriction "the pervaded exists only there" been adopted, because that would result in something existing in only a portion of the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) being established as a valid reason.
And there would be the status of being a common reason for *prameyatva* (knowability), because it necessarily exists in eternal things; thus,
this is a description of the relationship between the pervaded and the pervader.

However, this is for the purpose of demonstrating that because pervasion (*vyāpti*) possesses the same property in both cases, there should not be a cognition of a single form as if it were a conjunction (*saṃyoga*).

For instance—since in the former case the restriction is by way of excluding non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*), while in the latter it is by way of excluding connection with another (*anyayogavyavaccheda*)—how could there be a single form of pervasion in both? As it has been said: "The probandum (*liṅgin*) exists only where the mark (*liṅga*) is; conversely, the mark exists only where the probandum is."
"In the reversal of the rule, there is no connection between the mark and that which possesses the mark.
By this, the fault stated by the Teacher regarding the capacity to indicate based on the force of conjunction is addressed: "The fire is not non-conjoined with it in any respect."

"Or smoke [is not pervaded] in every way; therefore, illumination is obtained from smoke"—this [argument] does not apply here, as has been explained. For, since conjunction (saṃyoga) is indistinguishable in both cases, this undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) follows from that, but not from pervasion (vyāpti).
For the pervasion in the pervading property (*vyāpakadharma*) is not exactly the same as that in the pervaded property (*vyāpyadharma*). Thus it has been said:
"Although the relation between the mark (*liṅga*) and the bearer of the mark (*liṅgin*) resides in both and exists through coexistence,"
"Its occurrence is like that of the container and the contained, but not like that of things in conjunction.
Therefore, the pervader is not the pervaded, and the pervaded is not the pervader.
Because of the statement, "the reason is pervaded by a portion of that," the fault mentioned regarding the position of things in conjunction does not apply.
Nor does it follow that both [the pervader and the pervaded] would be the object of inference and the means of inference;
for, according to the definition of the reason as stated, it is understood that only the pervader is the object of inference,
while only the pervaded is recognized as the means of inference.
The connection is that it is precisely the relationship of the pervaded and the pervader;
[this refers to] "of the pervader."
[90] In every way, [91] regarding total annihilation, [92] it is determined within the cause.
[93] Because pervasives such as impermanence and so forth exist even in things like lightning that do not follow immediately upon effort;
[94] [the term] "annihilation" [is used];
[95] the meaning is "of a pervasive such as impermanence and so forth."
[96] Because of being immediately subsequent to effort,
[97] even in the case of impermanent things such as lightning and so forth, there is an absence of the pervader— namely, being immediately subsequent to effort—
due to [98] the cause.
[99] In every respect, the relationship between the signifier and the signified would be established.
Just as the general properties (*sāmānyadharma*) of fire are signified, its specific properties (*viśeṣadharma*) such as being produced from grass or leaves would also have to be signified.

Likewise, for smoke, its general properties such as substantiality (*dravyatva*) and earthiness (*pārthivatva*), just like its specific properties such as "smokeness" (*dhūmatva*) and whiteness (*paṇḍutva*), would become signifiers. This is because the relation of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is equal in both cases.
[§ 9. Indication of the nature of pervasion as positive and negative concomitance:

If, then, the definition of a reason is that "the property of the subject (pakṣadharma) is pervaded by its own part," then the reason would have two forms—namely, being a property of the subject and being pervaded by its own part—whereas elsewhere it is stated to have three forms. How, then, is there no contradiction?

The connection is as follows: by this statement regarding the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of that part, it should be understood that either positive concomitance (*anvaya*) or negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) has been stated.
The underlying sense is that pervasion consists in the nature of positive and negative concomitance.

For instance, when one thing is invariably accompanied by another, and when that [second] thing is absent, the [first] thing also ceases to exist, then that very thing is said to be "pervaded" by the other; thus, because pervasion is of the nature of that [concomitance], the expression of pervasion denotes both positive and negative concomitance.
Therefore, because the two aspects [of the reason] are expressed by the statement of pervasion (*vyāpti*), there is no contradiction; [for example:
smoke [is pervaded] by fire.
[102] Fire [103] Smoke [104] By fire
[§ 10 The ascertainment of pervasion is by means of either perception or inference.
And these two are ascertained under the heading of "indicative reasons" (jñāpaka-hetu);
furthermore, their ascertainment is not by means of only one instrument of knowledge (pramāṇa), but rather by each according to its own [appropriate means].
By whatever means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) determines what belongs to someone;
and as for which means of valid cognition determines what for whom, that will be explained later.
The word "or" (*vā*) is used to indicate that positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) are of equal status.

This indicates that because the second [form of the argument] is understood through one alone—whether by way of affirmation or negation—among the two types of formal application (prayoga), namely those characterized by similarity (*sādharmya*) and dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), there is no need to present both; for they are ultimately identical in nature despite the difference in their exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*).

Indeed, the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)—the property of the logical mark (*liṅga*) being absent when the probandum (*sādhya*) is absent—is a property inherent to its very nature; thus, its positive concomitance (*anvaya*) form is not in fact contradictory to it.
And what is the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*)? It is that which is ascertained by its respective means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

The connection is with the word "stated" (*ukta*). That [inference] is also explained here in the context of certainty (*niścaya*), in order to declare that what is certain possesses the capacity to convey meaning (*gamakatva*).
The word "or" (*vā*) is for the purpose of illustration. Furthermore,

even though perception itself has the form of its own unique particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), it is established as such because it generates a subsequent conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of a universal (*sāmānya*).

The term "ascertainment" (*niścaya*) is used figuratively (*upacārataḥ*) in order to demonstrate that the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) which follows upon perception lacks the capacity to apprehend an object not already apprehended.

Therefore, although the logical mark (*liṅga*) is established in the form of a universal (*sāmānya*), the basis for its establishment is nonetheless the very cognition of the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*); thus, it is said that the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) is established in the locus of the probandum (*sādhyadharmin*) by means of perception.

This will be clarified immediately hereafter. Alternatively, "ascertainment through inference" means the establishment or certainty of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) with respect to the unproven locus (*asādhyadharmin*). He says "through inference" (*anumānataḥ*) because of the distinction between the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and its result (*phala*); that is, ascertainment is by means of inference (*anumānena*).
In this example, the ascertainment of smoke—that is, of the universal *dhūmasāmānya*—occurs through direct perception (*pratyakṣataḥ*) according to its sequence and according to its location.
It is not, however, a mere absence (*nivṛttimātra*) consisting of a non-entity (*tuccharūpa*).
[Objection: But how can a universal, which is the nature of the logical mark (*liṅga*), be apprehended by non-conceptual direct perception? To this, he says:
[107] In the Buddhist view, there is no result of valid cognition (*pramāṇaphala*) that is distinct from the nature of the cognition itself (*pramiti*).
However, having provisionally accepted a distinction, it is said that "ascertainment occurs through inference.
For in this regard, there is this delusion... [this is a synonym].
[§ 11. Refuting the view of Uddyotakara and stating that the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*) is a means of cognition when it depends on place and other factors:

But as for the one who thinks: "That portion of space which is connected with fire is imperceptible; whereas that which is perceptible—consisting of the nature of light and so forth, like the sky—is not possessed of fire even though it is seen together with smoke. Therefore, how can there be smoke in a [specific] location..."
[Opponent: "Establishment is through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Therefore, it is logical that smoke alone is the subject (*dharmin*). The relationship between the probandum and the probans is as follows: 'This smoke possesses fire, because it is smoke.'"—[Reply: Even for him, that portion of the smoke which possesses fire is not perceptible.

Furthermore, since that which is being perceived exists in the upper portion and is thus not in contact with the fire, how can the generality of smoke (*dhūmasāmānya*) be established through perception in the subject of the inference (*sādhyadharmin*)?
If it is argued that the composite whole (*avayavin*) of smoke is perceptible, we say no.
Because it does not exist apart from its constituent parts,
or— if its unity were established through worldly convention— the imagined unity of that much space would likewise not be precluded.
Furthermore, people perceive fire only in its specific location, not in the smoke itself;
and it is only by depending on place, time, and other such factors that the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*) is a prover. As it has been said:
"Even in the case of an effect that is contradictory [to the probandum], dependence on place, time, and so forth is required."
In the case of sound, the property of being unproduced is established by inference based on such reasons as its varying according to the variation of its cognition;
[108] and fire is proven at the time of smoke [109], not at the time of ashes.

[110] Not only in the case of the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*), but here, Kumārila—failing to understand the intended meaning regarding the establishment of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) in the locus of the probandum (*sādhyadharmin*) through perception as it has been described—asks: "How [can it be said that] perception... [S. 23a] ...is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*) yet grasps a universal (*sāmānya*)? This is the response to Kumārila’s objection.

"Even the apprehension of the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of a mark (*liṅga*), such as smoke, which is by nature a universal (*sāmānyātman*) through conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), is not possible;
how much less, then, can there be an apprehension of its relation to a subject (*dharmin*)?"—thus he objected.

For by that [objection], the following *bhāṣya*—"Because inference and the other means of knowledge are preceded by perception, they are not causes for [the cognition of] *dharma*" (ŚBh 1.1.4)—is [undermined].
How could inference and the other means of knowledge be preceded by perception,
when sensory cognition is non-conceptual because it lacks the capacity for recollection?
And there can be no apprehension of a mark that is not conceptually constructed, nor likewise of its connection with the subject; having thus raised this objection—
As for the claim that there is no apprehension by perception because the inferential mark (*liṅga*) and so forth lack conceptualization (*vikalpa*),
that is not accepted, since even conceptualization is helpful in the form of the object itself.
For there exists first a non-conceptualizing awareness of mere observation,
which arises from the pure object itself and is similar to the cognition of infants, the mute, and others.
Furthermore, when an object is subsequently determined by the intellect through its properties such as birth and so forth, that too is accepted as being of the nature of direct perception.

By saying this, it is effectively stated: "This defect—characterized by the non-apprehension of the mark (liṅga), the subject (dharmin), and their relationship—belongs only to the Buddhists for whom perception is exclusively non-conceptual (nirvikalpaka); it does not belong to us, who accept that perception is also conceptual (savikalpaka)."
Then, in order to provide a rebuttal to the faults described therein, he says: "For that which is accompanied by smoke," and so forth.

The collective meaning here is as follows: perception indeed apprehends that which stands before one—such as the locus of smoke and so on—in its positive form (*vidhirūpeṇa*) as the unique particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) of smoke and the like, excluded from all similar and dissimilar classes, because it is established in its own intrinsic nature.

Because all capacities (*sāmarthya*) possess mutually non-confounded forms, that which arises through their capacity conforms to its respective place [as described in verse 111] and generates two subsequent conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*), namely affirmation (*vidhi*) and negation (*pratiṣedha*).
