By means of these, one conceptualizes the property-bearer (*dharmin*) and the properties (*dharma*) called "smoke" and "absence," as well as their spatial relationship—
superiority and inferiority— thinking, "It is thus, and not otherwise."
Because conceptual constructions arise through the assistance of other conditions, such as the proficiency gained from repeated practice, in accordance with [prior] experience; therefore,
the determination of the essential natures of the property and the substratum, as well as the determination of their relationship, is accomplished based upon perception.
For instance—the very ascertainment of the relation between smoke and its locus is the determination that "this is here.
And that is indeed accomplished by non-conceptual perception in the manner already described.

Nor is there any relation characterized as a container-and-contained (ādhārādheya) relationship distinct from the two things situated in a vertical arrangement, since such a relation is not experienced by perception.
There would be conceptual construction,
because that which exists as a real entity is negated elsewhere.
Therefore, this [negation] is merely a superimposition of conceptual construction based upon those two objects as they actually exist.

Thus, the linguistic convention in the world regarding property (*dharma*) and substratum (*dharmin*)—based on the relation "this is related" and "this is the relatum"—occurs through the exclusion or non-exclusion of other distinctions; it is not, however, ultimate.
Even the conventional usage of universals is merely projected by conceptual construction and is extended only by relying upon entities that are excluded from those of a different class.

Even though they are distinct, those very things—by way of experience and by virtue of being excluded from what is heterogeneous—are, by their very nature, the causes for a conceptual cognition that has a single form; and thus it has been said:

"Even though there is difference, certain things are restricted by their own nature to the accomplishment of a single purpose, such as a single reflective awareness, an object, or a cognition, just like the sense faculties and so forth. (PV 3.72)
[111] Perception arising from the efficacy of an object situated in front; [112] situated in a superior-inferior relationship;
[113] characterized by smoke and location.

Therefore, by way of generating a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of a universal, the aspect of smoke appearing therein—which has a nature excluded from what is of a different class—is grasped as a universal-form by perception itself.
For the exclusion from what is of a different class is not something other than that which is excluded; there is nothing else whose non-apprehension by perception would need to be accounted for.

Consequently, it is the very particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of smoke and so forth, exactly as it was perceived, that is conceptually constructed as having a nature excluded from others. Thus, by virtue of the determinative judgment (*adhyavasāya*) of the cognizer, this is merely a recollection (*smṛti*).
Conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is of two kinds: that which follows upon perception and that which, in reality, has no object at all.

Therefore, as for what was said—"If one were to say that this cognition, which is a recollection, [perceives] the universal non-differently, since the universal is not experienced [in that way]"—it is as follows:
It is indeed apprehended only by inference;
and in that case, there would be an infinite regress, because the inference that grasps the logical mark (liṅga) arises through the power of another logical mark distinct from it,

and since that [mark], being of a general nature, is itself the object of yet another inference, and so on for each subsequent one, the realization of even a single possessor of the mark (liṅgin) would not occur even in a thousand aeons.
It is not possible;
how much less so within the span of a single human lifetime? And thus it has been said:
"That universal which is not cognized without inference..."
And inference does not proceed without being freed from its logical mark (liṅga).
Furthermore, no one accepts that what is non-common can function as a logical mark (liṅga),
nor does any unperceived mark exist that can serve as an illuminator [of its object].
And fearing that there might again be the apprehension that "the understanding of that [fire] too would occur through another inference," he says: "For where there is smoke...
and so forth. He thinks as follows:
For one for whom the universal (*sāmānya*) is not cognized without inference, this fault may indeed apply;
however, for us, the universal is cognized through a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that arises subsequent to direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), due to a natural delusion.

Furthermore, because the conceptualization of the logical mark (*liṅga*) is based on the perception of the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), it possesses non-contradiction (*avisamvādakatva*) by virtue of its indirect connection with the real entity.

Just as there is the error of perceiving a jewel in the luster of a jewel, so too the status of being an effect-reason (*kāryahetu*) belongs to the universal smoke (*dhūmasāmānya*) which appears in conceptual construction; this is because that universal is established as a logical mark (*liṅga*) by virtue of its being based on the observation of an effect and through the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of it as such.
Indeed, it is not proper to establish the particular characteristic of smoke (*dhūmasvalakṣaṇa*) as a logical mark.
Because that [reason] which is unique lacks presence in the similar class (sapakṣa), because it is impossible for it to be pervaded by a portion of that [class],
and because it is impossible to perceive a real entity when conceptualizing the probandum and the probans.

As for what was stated—that "inference has the universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) as its object"—it is not restricted in such a way that "inference alone has the universal characteristic as its object.
This is because conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) occurring subsequent to perception also have that as their object, as do other conceptual constructions.
Rather, it is restricted so that "inference has only the universal characteristic as its object," for the purpose of negating its having the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object.

In that context, "sadhūma" means that which exists together with smoke; this is stated for the purpose of demonstrating the property of being a characteristic of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*). And this very point is the seed for the conceptualization of affirmation (*vidhi-vikalpa*).

The connection is: "for one who has seen that region with smoke by means of direct perception. Of what nature is it? It is "one whose form is distinguished from other things"; the analysis of the compound is: its form (*rūpa*) is distinguished (*vivikta*), that is, unmixed (*asaṅkīrṇa*), from other things, namely from those of the same class and those of different classes. This is because all entities are established in their own respective natures (*svabhāva*), and thus there is no confusion of natures.
Otherwise, because everything would be applicable to everything, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

By this, the cause for the conceptualization of negation (*pratiṣedha-vikalpa*) has been explained, as well as the seed for the mental construction of a universal (*sāmānya-utprekṣā*). As it has been said:
"The mutual difference [of things] is the seed for the designation of the last [term]," as stated in PV 3.71.

For instance: conceptual construction arises by concealing the distinct form of these [particulars], which are mutually excluded from one another, and by superimposing upon them a non-distinct nature that appears common to them despite their exclusion from other objects.
This occurs "by way of its own uncommon essence," meaning by way of a nature excluded from other objects.

It is not, however, as Kumārila thinks—that "the exclusion from other objects is grasped by the means of cognition known as non-apprehension (*abhāvapramāṇa*) and is not to be determined by perception."
For it is impossible for perception, which arises through the power of real entities (*vastubalabhāvin*), to perceive otherwise, as that would entail the consequence of being erroneous.

The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: for a person who has perceived [an object] in its true nature, immediately thereafter there arises a cognition of the mark (*liṅga*) based on memory (*smārta*).
"Based on memory" (*smārta*) means memory itself.
The cognition in which the logical mark (liṅga) appears is "knowledge of the logical mark" (liṅgajñāna).
By this, he states the formal determination of the logical mark for that universal which appears in the conceptual construction (vikalpa) occurring subsequent to direct perception (pratyakṣa).
What, then, is its object in the ultimate sense?

[§ 14. The establishment of validity and invalidity regarding conceptual constructions of affirmation and negation in perception: [114] Regarding memory and so forth, [the object is the ultimate reality of the distinctions as they have been perceived... *Sphuṭārthā*, 27a and 27b... [The determination of validity and invalidity among the conceptual constructions of the rules and prohibitions of perception. Memory and so forth...
[115] Regarding the universal (*sāmānya*), [116]—when conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arises—[T. S.

28a. he begins an investigation into the validity and invalidity of conceptual constructions concerning the affirmation and negation of perception (*darśana*). In that regard, among those conceptual constructions of the affirmation and negation of perception, that which is the first...

That which has been described at the outset as "there is indeed an initial cognition of mere observation" (ŚV, Pratyakṣapariccheda 112ab)— that is, the vision which arises prior to the operation of conceptual construction, which is called "initial," and which has the unique particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object— has a non-common (*asādhāraṇa*) object.

That alone is valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and not even the conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) of injunctions and prohibitions, because that [alone] possesses the defining characteristic of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-lakṣaṇa*), whereas those two do not. For instance, the definition of valid cognition consists in having as its object that which has not been previously apprehended and having as its object that which accomplishes purposeful action (*arthakriyā*). This...

In this context, "the first" refers to the state of being a cognition of an object not previously known; it is described as having an uncommon object, meaning it has as its object the means for accomplishing a purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), because only the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is the means for accomplishing a purposeful action. [§ 15.
Establishing the Invalidity of Negating Conceptual Cognitions]

[117] Due to the first qualification, even though the conceptual cognition of negation has as its object the accomplishment of a purposeful action (arthakriyā) that is to be determined, it lacks validity.
Due to the second, however, even though the conceptual cognition of an affirmation has as its object a universal not previously apprehended, it lacks validity.
In this regard, demonstrating that the conceptual cognition of negation is essentially a form of memory because its object is an entity already grasped by perception—

He says: when that unique [particular], being of such a nature and having a form unmixed with other objects, has been seen—that is, apprehended—by means of a perception whose capacity arises from its own unmixed form. For instance, even by one who maintains that the non-existent part (*abhāvāṃśa*) is distinct from the existent part (*bhāvāṃśa*), the existent part must be conceived as having a nature that is unmixed in form.

Otherwise, that very portion consisting of non-existence could not be established. Furthermore, if there were no state of having a nature unmixed by way of its own-being (*svabhāva*), then even if a separate portion of non-existence were present, it would not be logical;

for it is impossible to abandon a mixed nature that has come about through the power of its own causes, even if an ineffective portion of non-existence were to occur alongside it. Nor can that [portion of non-existence] itself effect the destruction of that [mixed nature].

Because it will be demonstrated that there is no logical possibility for a cause of destruction, it is better that things arise from their own causes with unmixed forms by their very nature rather than having those mixed forms destroyed.
Therefore, the non-existence of other forms in things is simply their nature;
it is nothing else. And such a state is indeed apprehended by perception. When that state is thus seen—
That object is unique (asādhāraṇa) because it does not possess a common nature with that other entity, since its nature is devoid of the form of the latter;
[the text] clarifies this very point by stating its uniqueness—that is, its lack of a common nature—through each of those non-corresponding forms.
Thus, by expressing and manifesting its distinction from other objects, its dissimilarity, and the fact that "this is not of another form," [it reveals its own specific nature].
Memory arises by the force of a non-perceptual [cognition] because it operates upon what was seen as distinct.
The point is that if it were to arise by the force of a logical mark (*liṅga*), memory—even though its object is exclusion—would not exist.

What is its object? Its object is the exclusion of what is not that (*atad-vyāvṛtti*). By the word "that" (*tat*), there is a reference to the real entity (*vastu*) which was the object of the perception. "Not that" (*atat*) refers to that which is of a different class (*vijātīya*).
Exclusion from what is not that (atasmād vyāvṛttiḥ) is "exclusion from the non-that" (atadvyāvṛttiḥ).
That which has this as its object is "such" (tathā).
The cognizer [thinks]: "Just as it was perceived, even I postulate the distinction [of the object] from other things."
And this was stated from the perspective of conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*);

in ultimate reality (*paramārthatas*), however, because it lacks an object, it is neither a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) nor the result of the means of non-apprehension (*abhāvapramāṇaphala*). This is the meaning.
For it is not logical that validity should consist in being the producer of memory.
Why is it not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)?
Because it apprehends a particularity—the form of what was previously perceived—which depends upon other conditions such as the proficiency of repeated practice.

For it is not the case that whatever is seen is grasped by conceptualization simply because it has been seen; for if there were no distinction in the act of seeing, it would follow that conceptualization would arise regarding all aspects [of an object].
Rather, only a certain [aspect] arises depending on conditions such as repeated practice (*abhyāsa*). Thus, he explains this by means of the term "grasping of the aspect" (*ākāragrahaṇa*).
"Let it be that there is a grasping of the object as it is perceived;

however, why does this [perception] not constitute a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)? One who, out of a lack of confidence that [the source] might ever be deceptive,

For instance, even in common worldly usage, a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is said to be non-discrepant and non-deceptive.
And if one does not apprehend that which accomplishes a purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), one will not engage with it;
how much less could one attain it? How then could a person acting with foresight designate such a thing as a means of valid cognition on the grounds of its non-discrepancy?
[§ 18. Detailed Proof that the Universal is Not a Real Entity:

If it is argued that the universal (*sāmānya*) is likewise capable of accomplishing purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), and therefore the affirmative conceptual cognition (*vidhi-vikalpa*) directed toward it will be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), he replies: "No; indeed, the universal does not provide any purposeful action—whether characterized as a single cognition or a single designation, or otherwise produced by individuals—that is accepted as being accomplished by it."

Of what kind [is it]? It is that which is to be grasped by the conceptual cognition (*vikalpavijñāna*) produced through the power of that [perception], occurring at a subsequent stage after the apprehension of the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), that is, the apprehension of the individual (*vyakti*) known as "indeterminate cognition" (*ālocanājñāna*).
By the word "that" (*tat*), the apprehension of the specific characteristic is connected.

He speaks thus because of the subsequent statement beginning with "furthermore, the object thereafter," in order to refute the status of perception as a valid means of knowledge (*pratyakṣapramāṇatā*) for the conceptualization that arises following a sensory observation.
However, every universal (*sāmānya*) by itself does not accomplish any causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*).

But that universal which is grasped by inferential conceptualization (*anumānavikalpa*)—having arrived through the ascertainment of a logical mark (*liṅga*) connected with causes and pervaders—does, by virtue of a mediated connection (*sambaddhasambandha*), accomplish a causal efficacy whose object is the accomplishment of a purpose not yet attained; therefore, it is the object of that [conceptualization].
Conceptual construction is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);
however, this [subsequent cognition] is not so,
because the capacity for causal efficiency has already been apprehended by the initial sensory perception.
An example here is as follows: the remainder of the sentence is "appearing in the cognition that perceives blue as 'blue'";
it connects with the context that "the universal does not accomplish any purposeful action.
Now, one might object: since the universal appearing in the inferential mark (liṅga) and conceptual construction (vikalpa) is the subject under discussion, why is another example being cited?

This is in order to refute, by means of an identical line of reasoning, the opponent’s assertion that every conceptual cognition (*vikalpa*) arising subsequent to a direct perception (*darśana*) possesses the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pratyakṣapramāṇa*).

Furthermore, what universal (*sāmānya*) appearing in the conceptual cognition "What is blue?"—which arises subsequent to a direct perception—does not provide for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*)? If [it is argued that it does not provide] that which is to be accomplished by the particular (*vyakti*); [then...]

In that case, another entity would likewise not perform the causal efficiency belonging to another; thus, because it too would not accomplish causal efficiency, the consequence would follow that it is a non-entity (*avastu*).
If, on the other hand, it performs its own specific causal efficiency, that is unproven.
Anticipating the objection that this is because it produces its own effect, characterized by non-differentiated cognition and designation, he says:

"For that very thing which was perceived by the sensory awareness (*ālocanājñāna*)—namely, the particular blue (*nīlasvalakṣaṇa*), the individual instance of blue—is what performs such causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) as the object to be accomplished.
By the word 'such' (*tathāvidha*), the universal (*sāmānya*) is intended here."
Because this [subject] possesses such a synonymy,
and because its common form is likewise [of that nature],
it [establishes] a corresponding probandum characterized by non-differentiated cognition and designation, namely the probandum of the universal "blue."
It is so called because it has the nature (*śīla*) of performing a causal function (*arthakriyā*); that is, it is a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).

He thinks as follows: just as individual instances (*vyakti*), though distinct, assist that single, undivided universal (*sāmānya*) characterized by their restriction to a single effect through a certain proximity, even without connection to another universal; [so too does the particular].
Otherwise, there would be the consequence of an infinite regress;
therefore, they will establish even the causal efficiency consisting of non-different cognition and designation.
What is the use of accepting a universal that lacks any means of valid cognition and is contradicted by valid cognition?
For instance—in inferential and other such cognitions, we do not perceive in individual objects that same kind of indistinct form which appears in them;
rather, at the time of perceiving an individual, we discern only a single distinct form, such as blue.
So how can I deceive myself by postulating something that has never been seen?
If it is argued that there is no perception [of the universal] due to its association with the form of the individual, like fire in a mass of iron; we say no,
because this would entail the absence of any established distinction between difference and non-difference in all cases,
since this same answer could be easily applied elsewhere as well.

Furthermore, a universal does not possess two forms— a distinct and an indistinct one— by which it might appear through one form in perception and through the other in inferential and other types of cognition;
for that would entail the undesirable consequence of admitting two separate entities.
Because the distinction between entities everywhere is based solely on the distinction between their appearances,
and because it is accepted that a universal cannot possess another universal and that this [universal] is itself devoid of universals;
this is an adverbial modifier.
[132] Because that which has not been assisted cannot be the locus of such an addition,

By this, the following argument is also refuted, which he stated:

It arises as having a dual nature, and that [dual nature] is not possible without [the existence of both]. Because an indistinct form such as blue is not perceived there within a clear appearance of blue and so forth; and because even a second distinct [form] that persists is not observed.
Furthermore, if that were the case, how could there be a persistence [of a single entity] for one who reaches the interval between two individual instances?

If it is argued that even when [the universal] is seen, the determination of its perception occurs only in that one substratum and not everywhere; we say no.

Even in that [conceptual cognition], since the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) does not appear, how could there be a dual nature?

Furthermore, because it does not appear as such within its own cognition, and because it is impossible for a single thing to possess multiple forms,

this non-differentiated universal cognition— which would otherwise grasp distinct objects— does not appear as something arising from the manifestation of particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*). Furthermore, the firmness of cognition does not consist in its indestructibility, since momentariness is admitted; rather, it consists in its being uncontradicted.
And that is not possible for this [cognition].
A refutation has been stated even in brief;

Therefore, just as individuals assist that single [universal] without another universal, so too will they bring about non-differentiated cognition and designation; thus, it is that very particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of blue—

Because they desire the universal to be distinct from the particular, it is therefore established as permanent.
"For those [particulars] would be false if they were produced without that [universal], even in the absence of an object;

Because it is accepted that the falsity of general cognitions is based on subverting cognition; for instance: why is "cowness" restricted only to those things possessing a dewlap and so forth?
Because it has that as its nature.
If it is asked why this [universal] has identity with that [particular], let it be understood that it is "from its own nature" (*svabhāvāt*),

And it is incorrect to say that "the unique [universal] does not possess arising and passing away when the individual instances arise and perish," because it would entail a difference [between them] due to the superimposition of contradictory properties. And it has been said:

If it is argued that the individual is unproduced at birth because it has come from another substratum, then how could it have existed previously in its own place without being connected to anything else? How could it exist there without being conjoined?

If it is argued that [the cognition] is not destroyed when the individual is destroyed, nor has it reached another individual, then the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) which apprehends it will be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). To this he says: "And that blue particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) has indeed been seen by the perceptual awareness (*ālocanā-pratyaya*) in its very nature—that is, as a self-essence capable of performing the causal function (*arthakriyā*) to be accomplished by the blue."
Then, how could a conceptual cognition that produces no further distinction regarding an action whose purpose has already been accomplished be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)?
Now, if it is thought: "In that case, let the conceptualization of blue be a valid means of knowledge as it apprehends the universal (*sāmānya*) itself;
and that universal is capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyākārin*)."

Since that which is to be accomplished as blue will perform its causal function (arthakriyā) by acting in conjunction with the blue [particular], he says that universals (sāmānya) are indeed of the same nature as particulars: "And it is not the case that..."— meaning that for a universal which is imagined and whose nature is to exist at a time subsequent to the perception of a blue particular, and which exists at a time subsequent to the apprehension of a logical mark (liṅga) in the manner previously described, there is no causal function to be accomplished by a particular.
The meaning is that it can be established as follows:

by means of the blue universal (*nīlasāmānya*), which is the object of the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of blue, the causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) to be accomplished by the blue—such as dyeing and so forth—is performed.

This is because, given the impossibility of that [causal efficiency] belonging to the nature of the individual instance (*vyakti*), it cannot exist in that which has a purely imagined form (*kalpitarūpa*).

Furthermore, no purposeful action—whether the production of blue or any other—is performed by an object that possesses a permanent nature as the referent of the conceptualization of "blue," because such permanence is incompatible with both succession and simultaneity; this is what is intended.
[§ 22. Observation of defects in the definition of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) as accepted by the Mīmāṃsakas.]

Thus, having established that the universal appearing in the cognition "this is blue" upon seeing blue does not accomplish any purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), the Mīmāṃsakas [state] that the definition of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—"the cognition of a previously unknown object"—is overly broad (*ativyāpti*). This is because it would follow that even a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arising after perception—which has as its object something that performs no purposeful action—would be valid. Therefore, they maintain this definition.

Showing that the qualification must be adopted, he says: "Therefore. Since it is thus untenable for a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arising subsequent to perception to possess validity because its object is the accomplishment of a purposeless action, therefore, having set aside our opponent's definition of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—namely, that it is "non-contradictory cognition"—[our own position stands].
Valid cognition has as its object a thing not yet apprehended;

even regarding the claim that "valid cognition is the cognition of a previously unknown object," if one were to formulate another definition of valid cognition out of mere self-aggrandizement, [one would still have to provide] a means to avoid over-extension.

The qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) is to be employed as that which is to be qualified (*viśeṣaṇīya*). How is it to be qualified? [By the phrase] "when the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) has not been apprehended.
For by this qualifier, the validity of inferential conceptualization (*anumāna-vikalpa*) is established, [as well as that of] sensory perception (*ālocanājñāna*).

Furthermore, since the validity of the subsequent conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is excluded, everything is well-established. Thus, having refuted the validity of the affirmative conceptual construction (*vidhi-vikalpa*)— on the grounds that its object is not the accomplishment of a purposeful action even though it apprehends a previously unapprehended universal— it is shown that the status of being a memory (*smṛtitva*), which is common to both the negative conceptual construction (*pratiṣedha-vikalpa*) and the conceptual construction associated with words, is likewise negated.

Showing the cause of its validity, he says: "But when the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) has been apprehended by sensory perception (*ālocanājñāna*), the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)— which arises through the power of that [perception], exists by the force of the apprehension of the particular characteristic, and imitates it— is [the means of knowledge] because it is not produced directly [from the object],
but rather by the impregnation (*āvedha*) deposited by the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) of the perception."

And because it follows the form of the indistinct particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of blue, and because of the unification of the perceived and the conceptualized, it is described in this way;
but in reality, it does not resemble anything at all—
it is simply memory (*smṛti*).
Why? Because it has that as its object only from the perspective of practical efficacy (*kāryataḥ*), not from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*).
Here, "practical efficacy" consists in the person's engagement with the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) and the conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*) thereof.

And because it functions as a result [of a prior cognition] and has that [prior object] as its domain, conceptual construction arising from the force of perception is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), for it is merely recollection (*smṛti*).
To explain: even for recollection, which takes as its object a portion of the perceived particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), there is no objective reality (*paramārtha*) as its domain;
this is because the particular characteristic does not appear in recollection with a clear form, as it does in sensory cognition.

However, it arises precisely from the aforementioned causal efficiency (*kārya*); and since that is the same even in the case of a conceptual construction of affirmation (*vidhivikalpa*), how could this not be a memory?
[§ 23. Establishing the validity of inference by distinguishing it from the conceptual construction of affirmation.]
In this regard, it might be argued: "But surely even a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) based on inference is accepted as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

In the same way, an affirmative conceptual construction (*vidhivikalpa*) will also be a means of valid cognition. To this, he says: "Because the form of an object not yet cognized has not been cognized... [S. 37a]

Thus it is thought: that mere entity which was previously experienced in the kitchen and so forth as being excluded from non-fire is not remembered by the inferential conceptualization solely as being connected to that specific place and so on; rather, it is [remembered] in whatever location...
That [object] was not previously experienced as being related [to fire].

Therefore, because there is the apprehension—by way of excluding non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*)—of a real entity that is excluded from non-fire and which was not apprehended by the two perceptions grasping the property-bearer (*dharmin*) of the probandum and the property-bearer of the example, its status as a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) is justified;
but this is not the case for the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that arises subsequent to perception.
"Because it is the opposite of that," as [the manifestation] is by means of a cause.

[§ 24. The establishment of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is based upon real entities (*vastu*), and only the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is a real entity.]

If it is argued that [this cognition] does not apprehend a previously unapprehended nature of the object, why then is it not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)? To this he replies: "Because it has a real entity as its basis," and so forth.

Furthermore, the fact that the establishment of a valid means of knowledge has a real entity as its basis is stated with reference to the objective domain of the operation of the means of knowledge, and not to the definition of its objective support (*ālambana*).

Otherwise, since inference would have as its object a mentally constructed universal (*parikalpita-sāmānya*), it would lack a real entity (*vastu*) as its basis, and the established system of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) would be non-comprehensive.

If it is asked: "If the system of the means of valid cognition is based on real entities, how can non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*)—which has a remote object as its domain—be a valid means of cognition? [The answer is:

Even in that case, because the conceptualization of *pradhāna* and so forth is itself established by proving that it does not have a real entity as its material cause (*bhāvānupādānatā*), that [non-apprehension] also indeed has a real entity as its basis; thus, there is no fault.
Now, one might ask: "How is it that the establishment of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is based solely on real entities (vastu)?

To this he says: because the activity of those seeking an object—namely, the acquisition or avoidance characterized by the attainment of what is desired—occurs with respect to that which is capable and potent for purposeful action (arthakriyā), defined as pleasure or pain.

Even if the activity of those seeking an object is directed toward what is capable of purposeful action, how does this still establish that the system of the means of valid cognition is based on real entities?

If it is argued that "in that case, there would indeed be a substratum capable of causal efficiency (arthakriyā)," he replies: "For that which is capable of causal efficiency is precisely what defines a real entity (vastu). Therefore, since it has the nature of being a substratum for what is capable of causal efficiency, how could it not be a substratum for a real entity? This is the intended meaning. [T. 229b]

And this demonstration of the establishment of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) based on the object-entity (*vastu*), by stating "when the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) has not been apprehended," might lead someone else to say: "The establishment of the means of valid cognition is indeed dependent upon the mere entity (*vastumātra*), and not solely upon the particular characteristic.
Therefore, even if it does not apprehend an unapprehended particular characteristic, it nonetheless apprehends an unapprehended form of the entity."
In order to point out that this is unestablished—namely, that the validity of a conceptual cognition (*vikalpa*) which apprehends [an object] will come to be—it was stated:
"of one who apprehends the nature of an object not yet apprehended," and so forth.
And when its lack of establishment is pointed out, why [is it said] that validity belongs only to that which apprehends the nature of an object not yet apprehended, and not to any other?

To this objection, it was stated that [validity] consists in being capable of purposeful action (*arthakriyā-yogya*), and so forth. Thus, even for one who asserts that validity has a real entity (*vastu*) as its object, it follows that it has only the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object,
because only that is characterized by the capacity for purposeful action.
And because the universal (*sāmānya*) is the opposite of that [particular], so he thinks.

Furthermore, in order to remove the validity of the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of blue which arises at a time subsequent to the direct experience, he states the supporting reason: "From that aforementioned conceptual construction as well—not only from the experience of the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) of blue—[the cognition] does not [engage] with the real object itself."

The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: because a person's activity is directed toward the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) itself through the determination of that [object], that is, through the determination of the particular characteristic—otherwise, activity toward it would be impossible—the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arising from the capacity of that [perception] once the particular characteristic has been apprehended is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Previously, its lack of validity was stated on the grounds that it does not apprehend a form of an object not already apprehended.

Now, however, because there is the apprehension of that which has already been apprehended, there is a distinction between the two [types of inference] by way of their being positive and negative in form.
Alternatively, what was stated—that [inference] has that as its object by virtue of its effect—has been made clear under the guise of providing a corroborative reason (*upacayahetu*).
[This concerns] the state of being an instigator (*pravartakatva*)—

Even if, by means of that conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*), a person’s activity is directed toward the very object itself, why should this [conceptual construction], which grasps a universal not previously apprehended, lack a separate validity from perception?

If this is argued, he says: because when there is activity directed toward the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) itself, it shares the same acquisition and preservation (*abhinnayogakṣema*) with the perception known as "indeterminate cognition" (*ālocanājñāna*).
Acquisition (*yoga*) is the attainment characterized by the determination of an object not yet reached;
preservation (*kṣema*) is its protection, characterized by the performance of its purposeful action (*arthakriyā*).
It is so called because its acquisition (*yoga*) and preservation (*kṣema*) are non-distinct from that [object].
In this regard, the acquisition of conceptualization is non-distinct from non-conceptual perception by virtue of its determination of the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).

Its preservation is non-distinct [from perception] because, just as in the case of sensory awareness (*ālocanājñāna*), activity proceeds toward the particular characteristic itself even from conceptualization.

This is his intention: if conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) were to have as its object a different cognizable from the non-conceptual consciousness (*nirvikalpacetas*), then it would either cause the person to engage with that very [conceptualized] object in order to attain the purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) to be accomplished by it, or it would not cause engagement at all;

for [the opponent] admits that the only purposeful action belonging to the universal (*sāmānya*)—which is intended to be the object of that [conceptual construction]—is characterized by a single, undifferentiated cognition, and because that [universal] is established precisely through the arising of conceptual construction.

When successive sensory cognitions arise regarding one and the same object, such as blue, then because the subsequent sensory cognitions share the same *yogakṣema* (identical acquisition and preservation) as the preceding one, it would follow that they are invalid;

For those whose minds possess direct perception as they observe all phenomena moment by moment, even a single objective moment of the Blessed Ones may be either beneficial or obstructive to some particular aim of others; this is because those moments, which are the objects of such perception, are employed in diverse causal functions and thus possess distinct modes of acquisition and preservation (*yogakṣema*). Therefore, if this is stated with reference to those who perceive the distinction between moments at every instant, then there is no inconclusiveness (*anekānta*), since each [moment] possesses its own separate validity due to its distinct utility.

Now, if it is said with reference to those persons engaged in worldly transaction (*sāṃvyavahārika*) who determine unity among all objects, then the entire continuum of blue is determined as a single object, stable in nature, and its causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is determined as being of a single essence. Thus, since even the validity (*prāmāṇya*) of subsequent cognitions is undesired [by the opponent], how can there be any inconclusiveness (*anekānta*)?
Demonstrating this, he says: "For [it is] common" (*sādhāraṇe hi*).
For those who engage in worldly transaction (*vyavahartṛ*), all moments (*kṣaṇa*) occurring within that continuum—which are determined as one—are common;
although they are distinct in every moment due to having different causes, they are, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), adhered to as one through error (*viparyāsa*).
Regarding the effects such as dyeing or the perception of blue and so forth, there is no difference in the capacity—namely, the power of attaining the object—of those subsequent moments of cognition.
Since activity proceeds from them toward the very same object as the initial moment of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), validity belongs to that first one alone in that regard.

For instance, for those seeking purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), the conventional usage of "valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*) applies to a cognition capable of bringing about the means to achieve that action.

For those whose intellects are unimpaired, it is logical that the conventional distinction between valid cognitions (*prāmāṇya*) is based solely on the difference in their capacity to accomplish a purposeful action (*arthakriyā*). Otherwise, how could one avoid the consequence that even memory and the like would be considered valid cognitions?
Or else, why would a discerning person care for a useless classification of means of knowledge?

In what case, indeed, would there be no difference in capacity regarding a common task? To this he says: [173] "Those various fires, those which have been cognized by them, and those fires that are proximate—in relation to these, as well as to the inferential cognitions whose objects are those [fires], when a purpose such as kindling is desired, which is to be accomplished by fire in general..."

Since there is no difference in the manifestation of the attainment of the means for achieving that purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), it is not logical for the wise to maintain a distinction in validity (*prāmāṇya*) in those cases; the same applies here as well.

However, when one desires to perform the "five-fire" austerity (*pañcatapa*), then even for those inferences whose objects are proximate fires cognized through various successive instances of smoke, their validity is certainly not precluded, because of the difference in their functional capacity (*sāmarthyabheda*).
Since the cognitions of a yogin characterize the transformation of moments (*kṣaṇavivarta*), they do not share the same status of security or success (*aikyogakṣema*).

Consequently, the moments are distinct and the causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is distinct from the moment of cognition.

It is established by the aforementioned reasoning that the very first perception whose object is the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)— which is designated by others as "subsequent determinative cognition" (*ālocanājñāna*)— is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and not the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arising from its power; for it has been settled that the "ascertainment" (*niścaya*) consists in the establishment of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) in the locus of the probandum (*sādhyadharmin*) through either direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) or inference (*anumāna*).

Thus, by stating that the determination of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharman*) is established through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), and by incidentally refuting the validity of the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that follows upon perception,
it has been demonstrated that "perception is free from conceptual construction" (*pratyakṣaṃ kalpanāpoḍham*).
[§ 28. Demonstrating the Primacy of Inference:
If this is so, why was it stated that "this [treatise] is commenced for the purpose of explaining inference," rather than simply "for the purpose of explaining right cognition" in general?
Furthermore, misconceptions regarding number and other such categories concerning its object have already been refuted herein.
Inference alone is the basis for the comprehension of objects that are beyond the senses.

Why? Because it has been stated that only a reason (hetu) which is a property of the subject (pakṣadharma) and is pervaded by its part (tadaṃśena vyāpta) is the cause of that comprehension, and nothing else; thus, all means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) whose object is an imperceptible thing are included within inference. In brief, this refutes the disagreement regarding the number [of pramāṇas] concerning the domain of correct knowledge.

Likewise, because the pervaded aspect is understood as the object of cognition, it is stated by the expression "pervasion of that aspect" that inference has a universal (sāmānya) as its object and not a particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa); for the latter is unique (asādhāraṇa),
and what is unique cannot be a pervader,
nor can it be an object of conceptual construction (vikalpa).

In this context, by stating that the first [type of cognition] has an uncommon object (*asādhāraṇaviṣaya*), it is declared that perception (*pratyakṣa*) has only the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object.

By the statement that "perception itself is the means of valid cognition" (*darśanam eva pramāṇam*), it is indicated that the means of valid cognition is itself the result (*phala*), because that [perception] consists in the cognition of the object.

Likewise, since it will be stated that its application is twofold, inference for the sake of others (parārthānumāna) will be discussed, because it consists in the communication of a logical mark (liṅga) possessing the three characteristics (trirūpa).
Furthermore, a concise exposition of inference is also intended.
And since that [inference] exists everywhere, why was it said [by the author] that it is for the purpose of explaining inference?
True; however, its mention is due to its predominance.
For instance, its predominance arises because the reality characterized by the four noble truths—which is essential for the primary goal of human beings—is ascertained through inference alone.
Likewise, even when a dispute arises regarding an object of perception, there is no basis for its definitive determination other than inference; for this reason also, it possesses primacy.
Furthermore, its primacy is due to its being the motivator [of action].
For instance— that which has already yielded its fruit, whether as a means to pleasure or pain,
or that whose fruit is currently being experienced and is thus perceived, is not an object of purposeful activity because the result has already been accomplished.
Therefore, even in the case of a perceptible means to pleasure or pain whose fruit is yet to come, it is inference alone that prompts one to act.
For perception does not determine the capacity of that [cause] with respect to future pleasure and pain, because the result is imperceptible.
As it has been said: "For when the effect is imperceptible, there is no cognition of the causal relation."

Therefore, because of the similarity with the means of pleasure and pain previously experienced, the determination of the suitability for future results regarding even an object of direct perception does not arise from perception itself.
As it has been said: "That which is established in such a way through similarity with what has been observed does not transcend the status of being inferable.
How, then, do both [perception and inference] function as motivators?
For it has been stated that one who acts after having determined an object by means of these two is not deceived regarding purposeful action (*arthakriyā*).
Since the nature of water, fire, and so forth— which are the means for achieving pleasure and pain— is established through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*),
and their capacity toward a future result is established through inference (*anumāna*), both serve as motivators for action.

It has been stated that the attainment of the beneficial and the avoidance of the harmful are preceded by correct knowledge (*samyagjñāna*), but not because the capacity regarding future results can be ascertained through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). For those of limited vision (*arvāgdarśin*), there is no ascertainment of the capacity for future results through such means;
therefore, inference (*anumāna*) is mentioned because of its predominance. Enough of this excessive detail.

Thus, first demonstrating the determination of positive concomitance for the reason of essential nature as being based on its own specific means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), he says: "The determination of positive concomitance..."

The implication is that not only is the ascertainment of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) stated, but the ascertainment of positive concomitance (*anvayaniścaya*) is also stated in the case of an essential reason (*svabhāvahetu*).

The mere existence—that is, the mere presence—of the probans (*sādhanadharma*), which does not depend on other causes such as a hammer and so forth, its "concomitance" (*anubandha*) or following along, which is its pervasion (*vyāpti*); the establishment of that is what constitutes the ascertainment of positive concomitance in the case of an essential reason.
Of what is there the establishment of the necessary concomitance with the mere existence of the probans-property (*sādhanadharma*)?

It is of the property to be proven (*sādhya-dharma*). It is called "the property" because it is that which is to be proven—since it is unestablished—and because it is one part of the aggregate consisting of both the property and the locus (*dharmin*). The establishment of this meaning—that wherever the probans-property exists, there the property to be proven also exists without depending on any other cause—is the determination of positive concomitance (*anvaya-niścaya*) in the case of an essential reason (*svabhāva-hetu*).

But how, again, does the property to be proven (sādhyadharma) follow upon the mere existence of the property that proves it (sādhanadharmabhāvamātra)? It is by way of being its very nature (*tadbhāvatayā*). That is, by way of being the nature (*bhāvatayā*) of that which has the proving property as its own-being (*svabhāva*); that is, by way of being its very nature.
For how could a proving property that is the very nature of the property to be proven not follow upon it?
Because it would follow that it lacks form? The property to be proven [is related to] the property that proves it.
[§ 30. The Establishment of the Relationship between Probandum and Probans Even in the Case of Identity in the Reason of Essential Nature.
Now, one might object: "If there is identity because of being that very nature, how can there be a relationship between probandum and probans?
To this he says: "In reality," that is, from the perspective of ultimate truth.

However, at the time of conceptualizing the probandum and the probans, because they appear as distinct within a conceptual cognition— which is based on various entities excluded from others through a causal chain— the relationship of probandum and probans is not undermined.

For this [conceptual cognition] does not rely upon an ultimate distinction between the properties of the probandum and the probans, nor between these and the locus (dharmin), such as in the case of "producedness" and so forth.
Because, in the absence of a relation, the state of being the probandum and the probans is untenable.

If it is argued that the relation between "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) and "impermanence" (*anityatva*), etc., is inherence in a single object (*ekārthasamavāya*); we say no, because if that [inherence] were also a different entity from those two, the absence of a relation—namely, that "this is the inherence of these two in this object"—would remain in the same state.

Furthermore, if one were to postulate another relation, it would lead to the fallacy of infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Moreover, if one were to postulate that [properties] such as being produced (*kṛtakatva*) exist through inherence (*samavāya*), then these properties would also exist in things like the self (*ātman*), which are considered eternal;
for the very same inherence by whose power being produced exists in sound, exists in those things considered eternal as well.
Since that [property] is apprehended as being one and the same, by what could the occurrence of "producedness" (*kṛtakatva*) and so forth in the self (*ātman*) and other such things be prevented?

Now, if it is established that "only in that entity which has the nature of coming into being after not having existed, and which, having come into being, has the nature of ceasing to exist— that is, an unstable form— do properties such as producedness reside," then it is precisely this very nature of coming into being after not having existed, and this nature of instability in what has come into being, that serves as the basis for conceptual cognition whose object is the exclusion of the superimposition of forms contrary to those [two natures].
Why is this not accepted?

Since those two properties—which possess non-difference at the level of ultimate reality—subsist in the subject (*sādhyadharmin*) by that very fact, what is the use of an intermediate obstacle such as "producedness" (*kṛtakatva*) and so forth?
For it is not by their mere existence that properties such as producedness serve as the basis for the cognition of the property to be proven.
Because those [entities] would be constantly present, it would follow that their properties are apprehended incessantly;
however, they appear only within conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

And that conceptual construction, following after an aspect appearing within itself which is determined (*adhyavasita*) as having an external form, apprehends the entity as having such characteristics as being produced and impermanent.
Although from the perspective of ultimate reality there is no contact with that form [of consciousness],
it is so designated because, through a succession of causes, those other phenomena serve as its material cause; whereas other phenomena are merely conceptualized as the conditions for its arising.
Therefore, let that very thing which is the basis for that conceptualization be the cause for the production of such a mental construction;
and since the properties possessing distinctness have fulfilled their purpose upon the acceptance of that [conceptualization], enough with that further conceptualization.
Furthermore, even by way of impermanence as something distinct, one necessarily perceives the non-abiding nature of the entity itself.
