And by that, through the fact that [the probandum] is in reality of the same nature as that [probans], the necessary concomitance of the property to be proven with the mere presence of the proving property is established; thus, the certainty of positive concomitance (*anvayaniścaya*) arises in the form: "Wherever there is the proving property, there is the property to be proven."
An example here is as follows: "Whatever exists is necessarily momentary. By this restriction, he states the pervasion (*vyāpti*).
And this form has been explained as the necessary concomitance (*anubandha*) with the mere presence of the property to be proven (*sādhanadharma*).

Because [the object] is shown to be momentary simply on the basis that it exists, even in the absence of any other sign; and since that [momentariness] is established in reality as being the very nature of that [existence], he demonstrates the means for establishing it—the operation of a subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*)—as follows: "If there were non-momentariness, which is the opposite of momentariness, there would be a contradiction with causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), that is, with the activity of the effect."

Its accomplishment [is established] through its opposition; that is its characteristic. That "characteristic" refers to the nature of reality (*vastutva*), which has causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) as its defining mark—that is, whose essence consists in the capacity for causal efficiency.
This is what was stated.
For causal efficiency (arthakriyā) is what characterizes the reality of a thing as consisting in its capacity for such action;
thus, this kind of reality is lost or withdrawn,
because it entails the induction of non-existence, which is the opposite of that [reality].

And this subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*), which consists in the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*), will be explained by himself later when its occasion arises. Therefore, by means of this operation of the subverting proof, the fact that the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is in reality the very nature of the proving property (*sādhanadharma*) is established.
And by virtue of that being its nature in reality, [the probans is established as a reason].

"Invariable concomitance with the mere existence of the property to be proven" means that by means of the absence of the reason called "existence," which is the opposite of the reason called "non-existence," the probandum is established.
[§ 32. Examination of the Determination of Positive Concomitance (anvaya) in the Case of the Effect-Reason (kāryahetu):

Having thus established the determination of positive concomitance in the case of the essential-nature reason (svabhāvahetu) through the operation of a subverting proof (*bādhakapramāṇa*) against the contrary—which establishes identity (*tādātmya*)—the author, now explaining it for the effect-reason, says: "In the case of the effect-reason, the determination of positive concomitance" is the subject under discussion.

What, then, is this relation between cause and effect? Its establishment—that is, its cognition—is the determination of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) in the case of the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*). Demonstrating how the establishment of the causal relation occurs, he says "just as," and so forth.
The word "yathā" (as) has the sense of illustration.
The connection is that this smoke and so forth is perceived when this fire is perceived;
by this, he states the function of perception in establishing the relationship of cause and effect.

And it is not only perception that establishes the causal relation without doubt, but rather it does so when assisted by a prior non-perception; to demonstrate this, he says: "not perceived despite having reached the conditions for perceptibility.
If that smoke and so forth, while having reached the conditions for perceptibility, exists while other [conditions] are present...

When the conditions for perception are present, that which exists as a perceptible entity is not perceived prior to the proximity of the causal complex such as fire; however, when that very same causal complex [of fire, etc. is being perceived, its effect is established as being perceived.
However, it is not the case that [the object], while possessing a nature capable of being perceived, remains unperceived because of a deficiency in other conditions for perception;
rather, even though it is present in that location, it was previously unperceived due to not having reached the conditions for perception (*anupalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*).

And since it has reached the conditions for perception yet is not perceived, its non-identity with what existed before the presence of the causal complex of fire and so forth implies its arrival from elsewhere.
The production [of the effect] from a mat, a hut, or other such things present at that place and time, and its non-presence at that same place— this triad is thereby refuted.

And since the state of not being its effect would have to occur through these many modes, the suspicion that it is not its effect is dispelled by non-perception; thus, the causal relation—founded upon the perception that grasps the presence [of the effect] when [the cause] is present—is established beyond doubt.
Nor should it be suspected that smoke might arise from some invisible entity whose presence is restricted to the existence of fire, fuel, and so forth.
Because smoke conforms to the differences in fire, fuel, and so forth;

because when there is a difference in the fuel—such as sandalwood, aloe-wood, camphor, hair, or wool—it is observed that this [smoke] exhibits a corresponding difference; and because fire, which effects transformations in small or large amounts of fuel, possesses a corresponding nature;
furthermore, it is not logical for that which is invisible by nature to have a fixed presence whenever fire, fuel, and so forth are present.
Because there is no necessary connection (*pratibandha*).
Or, if there were a necessary connection, it would have to be either the state of being its effect (*tatkāryatā*) or the state of being its cause (*tatkāraṇatā*).
If it were its effect, [then...]
Smoke would not arise immediately after the contact of fire and fuel;
and because it follows the presence and absence of those very factors, its status as their effect is established.
And this is the same in the case of smoke as well.
Nor can fuel and such be the cause of that which is invisible by nature,
since we observe that fuel and so forth arise solely from their own causes, such as trees;
if one were to imagine their existence in that [invisible] state even there, the same response must be given.
If this objection is raised again, the same refutation applies and there would be an infinite regress.
By this, dependence on a single causal complex (*ekasāmagryadhīnatā*) is also answered.
Furthermore, it is precisely because smoke conforms to the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of that [fire] that fire should be postulated as its cause.
And that [reasoning] applies equally to fire and so forth as well.

If it is argued that fire and so forth should also be considered causes in that case, we say no; for when fire and so forth are present, there is no reason to postulate another thing as a cause when something else necessarily occurs.
For the conceptualization of a cause is based on the absence of the effect;
likewise, this applies to fire, fuel, and so forth, which do not exist when either one of them is absent.
Or rather, let there be causality for another thing as well, provided it is invariably present when that [effect] occurs.
However, the causality of fire and so forth is not thereby lost;
for if one were to act upon seeing smoke based on the certainty [of fire], there would be a discrepancy with reality.

Indeed, even though the diversity of the world is produced by the sovereign power of the karma of all sentient beings, those who act based on the observation of its effects do not fail to obtain what they seek simply because the observed causes have been discarded. Enough of this over-elaboration.

What, then, is the nature of this causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), which is based on perception aided by non-perception? He says: "Existence when that exists, and non-existence when that is absent.
For indeed, there is existence [of the effect] precisely when there is existence of that which is considered the cause;

and there is non-existence [of the effect] precisely when there is non-existence of that which is considered the cause—that is, when there is non-existence of that which is intended as the cause, there is non-existence of that which is intended as the effect.
That alone is the relation of cause and effect, and nothing else.
For if that [relation] were distinct from those two, it would either exist by its own nature as something not perceived in the form of cause and effect belonging to those two,
or else it would exist by its very nature as the essence of cause and effect themselves.

If the first position were true, then it would apply to every object, even to those things that stand in no causal relation to one another, because there would be no cause for such restriction; consequently, everything would be the effect of everything.
Furthermore, for that which by its own nature does not possess a certain form, there is no acquisition of that form even through conjunction with another.

For entities do not, upon abandoning their specific nature, assume a different form even when conjoined with something else; because this conjunction with another does not destroy their prior form, as there is no cause for destruction, as will be explained later.
Nor does it produce something unprecedented (*apūrva*), for that would entail the consequence of its being a different entity from them;
for when those [causes] have been accomplished, it is not logical for this [effect] to be unaccomplished or to have a different cause, since its nature would be that of those [causes].
For this distinction, or the cause of distinction, consists in the superposition of contradictory properties and the difference in causes.

Consequently, if there were no difference [between things], then— since there would be no other cause for distinction— the entire universe would become a single substance, and such other absurdities would follow.
For even a difference in appearance does not transcend the imposition of contradictory properties by way of mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*).
And consequently, since the two previous entities remain in that very same state, they do not acquire the nature of cause and effect even when associated with something else.
Now, as for the second alternative:
In that case, since those two are by their very nature related as cause and effect, how could another state [between them] not experience futility?
Furthermore, the cognitions of "cause" and "effect" are based solely on the fact that one arises when the other exists, and not on a distinct entity as their cause;
for such an entity, even if it met the conditions for perception, does not appear as a distinct form separate from the forms of cause and effect.
Even if one were to conceive of such a [relation], it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
If [the relation] has not reached the conditions for perception (*anupalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptatā*), how could there be cognitions of cause and effect based upon it?
For that [relation], being a distinct entity (*arthāntara*), does not bring about those cognitions by its mere existence alone.
Because it would follow that these two [the object and its absence] would arise at all times due to their being constantly present;

and since an unperceived qualifier cannot serve as the basis for a cognition qualified by itself in the qualified object, it is incorrect to claim that this [absence] has reached the condition of non-perception (anupalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptatā).
Furthermore, it is not logical that something which is actually seen should remain unperceived.
Because it is accepted that the cognitions of cause and effect are based upon that [inherence],

for it is not logical that a determination of something B should occur with respect to another thing A— which does not possess the cognition of B— if that basis [inherence] is not perceived; just as, for example, there is no determination of "one who has a staff" (daṇḍin) with respect to Devadatta when the staff is not perceived.
When the staff is not perceived,
a connection between a distinct entity and [the person] through either cause or effect is not tenable;
for if one were to postulate another connection, it would lead to an infinite regress.
If one accepts the relation of cause and effect, then existence [of the cause] would not be simultaneous with the cause and the effect.

Consequently, since it is absent at the time of the cause and the effect, how could it be the cause of the cognition of "cause" and "effect"? Furthermore, if one imagines that cognition based on them by mentally supplying two things that have already ceased, then the determination of causality would have only a conceptual object as its domain, not a real entity as its domain.

And since that [determination] is already accepted as being based on the presence or absence of a specific state, what is the point of postulating a different object? For if its object were merely imagined,
that determination would be purposeless, and furthermore, cause and effect cannot exist simultaneously.
For it is not produced by those two;
and how can there be a causal relationship between things that are produced individually? Furthermore, when it is produced by a cause, is it produced together with its own effect?
Now, what of the isolated [cause]? Is the isolated cause prior to its own effect,
or is it posterior?

If it [the cause] exists together with its own effect, then because both exist from something else entirely, there would be no mutual connection; thus, its status as being connected to the effect would be lost. Alternatively, if it exists alone prior to its own effect;

In that case, since the cause perishes immediately after producing that very [effect] due to its momentariness, how can it perform its own causal function? And if that function does not exist, how can it possess causality in dependence upon it? Furthermore, if that [causal function] is absent, how can a causal relation be produced by something that is not a cause?

Furthermore, if it were produced after having already performed its own function, then since it would have perished at the very time of performing that function, how could that which is non-existent produce an effect occurring at a subsequent time?
Moreover, the existence of that [relation] is what is called a "connection" (*sambandha*).
Or, if they produce that capacity for being produced by their very own nature when complete, what obstruction to their power is there regarding the effect,
such that it must be postulated elsewhere? Furthermore, if there were a dependence on the conjunction with another causal complex even in that case, it would lead to the fallacy of infinite regress.
Therefore, all the producers are indeed present;

and their causality is inferred by the absence of the effect when each one is removed. Thus he says: "Even though the other causes included within that causal complex (*sāmagrī*) are present as individual producers, because they manifest [the effect] individually, in the absence of this [one], [the effect does not arise]."
By the statement "it does not exist when that which is intended to be determined as the producer is absent," the object of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) has been stated.
However, the operation of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), as previously described, is devoid of non-apprehension and is connected with the grasping of existence when that [cause] exists.
And thus, by what means of proof is this causal relation established—the fact that the effect exists when the cause exists and is absent when the cause is absent?

Thus he says: "The causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is established by perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambhasādhana*)," meaning that its means of proof (*sādhana*) consists of a perception preceded by non-perception, which has the nature of a perception grasping other objects distinct from those [two]. As for that which was previously stated—that it is established by a perception dependent on non-perception—it should rather be called "established by non-perception and perception" (*anupalambhapratyakṣasādhana*), because its means of proof is a perception preceded by non-perception.

The establishment—that is, the ascertainment—of that causal relationship, which consists of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), is achieved through the aforementioned perception and non-perception; this is connected [to the statement] "in the case of the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*), there is the ascertainment of positive concomitance.

Now, one might object: the so-called "ascertainment of positive concomitance" is the determination that the effect, as it occurs everywhere, follows upon the existence of its own cause. How then can this alone be called the "establishment of the causal relationship"?

Anticipating this objection, [the author] says the following, demonstrating that this [concomitance] was stated in order to refute the opinion of those who hold it to be based on mere observation, and to show that it is not established by any other means, since the certainty of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is dependent upon the establishment of the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), and because one employs a metaphorical designation of the effect for the cause: "For only when there is a causal relationship... [is there concomitance] with respect to another thing.

That which is distinct from the probandum is one thing, whereas that which is non-distinct from it— because its identity is ascertained through the operation of a subverting proof (*bādhakapramāṇa*) regarding the contrary case— the ascertainment of its positive concomitance (*anvaya*) has already been stated previously; thus, the mention of "another object" (*arthāntara*) refers to the fact that such an ascertainment would belong to that very other object.
How so?

There is a certainty of positive concomitance (*anvayaniścaya*) in the form "wherever there is smoke, fire must necessarily be present," based on the rule that fire exists wherever [smoke] is. However, there is also a certainty of positive concomitance of taste with another object, such as color, even though no causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) exists between them.
Since that [smoke] depends on a single causal complex (*ekasāmagryadhīnatayā*), its deviation from its own cause is precisely mediated by that [complex]; thus, there is no fault.

Now, even if smoke is indeed the effect of fire, why is it that wherever that [smoke] is, fire must necessarily be present, such that the determination of positive concomitance (*anvayaniścaya*)—which is the basis for establishing the relation of cause and effect—is said to occur? To this, he says:

For it is only when there is the existence of fire—that is, when there is existence itself—because existence (*bhāva*) is the very fact of being present, that smoke possesses the state of being an effect.
Therefore, it is only when the relation of cause and effect exists that the aforementioned certainty of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) occurs.

For if, wherever there is smoke, fire were not necessarily present, then, because smoke would exist even in the absence of fire, its state of being an effect—defined by the characteristic of existing only when fire exists—would be lost.

[207] For the purpose of illustration— T. [208] Of those things such as fire and so forth, which consist of small or large quantities of fuel, [209] their effect is a substance whose nature is invisible.
[210] Even when speaking of the production of fuel and so forth from trees and the like, if one were to postulate that some invisible entity is the cause,
[211] then [212] it would be the invisible [cause] of the smoke.
He explains this sentence exactly as such, [noting] that it contains an implicit restriction (*avadhāraṇagarbha*): "[from fire]," and not,
on the other hand, from the existence of that which is considered to be a non-cause.
[216] Smoke—
[217] moreover, in the absence of that which is considered not to be its cause,
[218] it would either have to possess the conditions for perceptibility or else be the opposite of that.
Regarding the first, he says:
"Of that which does not appear as another form.
Regarding the second, he says: [220]
[221] When one is joined with punishment, even in the absence of the determination to punish, [the notion of "God" is superimposed]—T.
[222]—upon the two [entities].
[223] This occurs when there is the conceptualization of being the cause of the cognition of cause and effect.
The relationship between the conceptualization of cause and effect and that of a distinct entity.
[227] effect; [228] cause and effect; [229] in the causal complex.
[230] The manifestor—T.
[231] Thus, this is the occasion for the proof; that—T. [232] The ascertainment of positive concomitance.
[233] [§ 33. Explanation of the means for determining positive concomitance (*anvaya*) in the case of non-perception (*anupalabdhi*):

Now, he states the determination of positive concomitance in the case of non-perception: "In the case of non-perception as well—not only in the case of the essential nature (*svabhāva*) and the effect (*kārya*) reasons—" [T. 240a].
The determination of positive concomitance (*anvayaniścaya*) has been explained; however, the determination of positive concomitance is also stated in the case of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*).
What is its nature?

To this he says: since the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*)—namely, the conventional usage of "non-existent" (*asadvyavahāra*)—and its fitness (*yogyatā*) are what are to be proven, "fitness for that" (i.e., fitness for the conventional usage of "non-existent") is intended [as the probans].

The non-apprehension of that [object], which has reached the conditions for apprehensibility, consists in the apprehension of something other than it; this occurrence or activity—which does not depend on any further cause and pertains solely to that [other thing]—is the means of establishing, that is, the proof of, the conventional usage of "non-existent. This constitutes the determination of the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) in the case of non-apprehension.
But how, then, does the linguistic usage of "non-existent" (asad-vyavahāra) occur with respect to that alone?
To this he says: "Because of the demonstration of the absence of any other cause.

For when the linguistic usage of "non-existent" is [established] through nothing other than the aforementioned non-apprehension (anupalabdhi)—since [other factors] such as the absence of cognition, designation, or causal efficiency [do not apply]—[then it occurs with respect to that alone].
If it is being proved that "it is not a cause," then its occurrence is established in mere non-perception as previously described;
and by that, there is a certainty of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) in that non-perception.
Otherwise, if there were a suspicion of dependence on another cause, [the proof would fail].

Even when the aforementioned non-perception exists, the conventional usage of "non-existent" does not necessarily follow; how, then, could there be certainty regarding positive concomitance (*anvaya*)? Furthermore, the absence of other causes has been explained at length in the *Vādanyāya*, and should therefore be understood from that very source.

Alternatively, the cause for the conventional usage of "existent"—namely, the existence of that which meets the conditions for perceptibility—is distinct from the cause for the conventional usage of "non-existent."
Because it is distinct, non-existence is demonstrated therein through the non-perception of another cause; by whatever means of valid cognition this has been stated, by that very means,
since its impossibility is ascertained when the object exists, there is an ascertainment of the positive concomitance (anvaya) in non-perception.
And we shall demonstrate that [absence] when considering its exclusion from that [subject].
Thus, the determination of the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) for all three types of reasons has been stated by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

This is because, in the case of an essential reason (*svabhāvahetu*), the establishment of identity (*tādātmya*) is the basis [for the inference], due to the operation of a subverting cognition (*bādhakapramāṇa*) against the contrary.
Because, in the case of the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*), the causal relationship is established by means of perception and non-perception;

and because, in the case of non-perception (*anupalabdhi*), it serves as the cause for establishing the absence [of the object] by being the means of proof that establishes the absence of other possible causes.
And at that time—T.
[§ 34. Explanation of the means for ascertaining the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) of the effect and the essential nature.
Now, desiring to demonstrate that the ascertainment of negative concomitance for all three types of reasons is based upon their respective means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), he says:
"The ascertainment of negative concomitance, just like the ascertainment of positive concomitance (*anvaya*), is based upon its respective means of valid cognition."

Furthermore, it is stated that for both [types of reasons], the reason for the respective means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is not only the positive concomitance (*anvaya*), but also the ascertainment of the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).
What, then, is this?
It is the establishment of the absence [of the reason] in the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāve 'bhāvasiddhiḥ*).

To what extent are those two reasons—the one consisting of that [the cause] and the one consisting of that [the pervader]—provers of the probandum in the form of the cause and the pervader; and how is their absence established in the absence of the probandum?
By which means of valid cognition?
By the non-perception of the cause and the non-perception of the pervader.

In the case of an effect-reason (*kāryahetu*), the certainty of the absence [of the probandum] when the probandum is absent is established through the non-perception of the cause (*kāraṇānupalabdhi*).

In the case of an essential-reason (*svabhāvahetu*), it is established through the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*). But when do these two non-perceptions become the means of proving that [absence]?

When the relationship of cause and effect or pervader and pervaded has been established— specifically, when the causal relation is established through perception and non-perception— the non-perception of the cause serves as the proof for the absence [of the effect] in the case of the "effect-reason" (*kāryahetu*), because its existence is established through the operation of a subverting means of knowledge (*bādhakapramāṇa*) regarding the opposite, namely the absence [of the cause] when the probandum is absent. When the relationship of pervader and pervaded has been established, the non-perception of the pervader serves as the proof for the absence [of the pervaded] in the case of the "essential-reason" (*svabhāvahetu*), because its existence is established through the operation of a subverting means of knowledge regarding the opposite, namely the absence [of the pervader] when the probandum is absent.

By saying this, it is stated that in both cases, the determination of both positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) results precisely from the ascertainment of the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) characterized by identity (*tādātmya*) and causality (*tadutpatti*).
For this very reason, it was stated elsewhere: "Either from the relation of cause and effect," and so forth.
Of what kind?
"Having visible objects" means those two for which a visible object is the domain; that is how they are described.

If the cause and the pervader are such as have reached the conditions for perception (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*), then their non-perception establishes the absence [of the effect and the pervaded] in the absence of the probandum; this is the meaning.

But when is the qualification "having a perceptible object" required for those two? To this he says: "Of that whose object has been specified"—that is, whose object (the locus) characterized as a dissimilar instance (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) has been stated—when the demonstration of the absence [of the probandum] in the absence [of the reason] is being performed, why is the requirement of "having a perceptible object" still expected even there?
If this is argued, he says: "Non-apprehension," and so forth.

Otherwise, if the qualification of being a perceptible object (*dṛśyaviṣayatā*) is not required for the two types of non-apprehension, then one would be taking as a dissimilar example (*vaidharmyadṛṣṭānta*) an object that has reached the conditions for apprehension (*anupalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*).
In that case, since both the cause and the pervader would also be characterized by non-perception when they have reached the conditions for such perception,

how could the absence [of the effect or the pervaded] in the absence of the probandum be established by these two, given that the absence of a cause or a pervader characterized by non-perception cannot be established in some remote object, such as Mount Sumeru?
The intention is that the non-perception of the cause and the pervader (*kāraṇavyāpakānupalabdhi*) is itself unestablished.

Now, one might ask: "Even when demonstrating the absence of something whose object has not been specified, why is the qualification 'having a perceptible object' (*dṛśyaviṣayatā*) not required for the two types of non-perception? To this he says: "anuddiṣṭaviṣayam" means that the object—namely, the form of the example by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmyadṛṣṭānta*)—has not been specified.

Since the demonstration of the absence of the reason when the probandum is absent is established— even without the qualification of being "perceptible"— simply by establishing that necessary connection, therefore, in that case of proving the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) where the object is not explicitly indicated, the qualification of "perceptibility" for the two types of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) is neither required nor accepted.

For it is thus: even when speaking by means of a generality (*sāmānya*) that encompasses all things without exception, whatever has a nature that is necessarily connected to something else—by way of identity (*tādātmya*) or origination from it (*tadutpatti*)—will certainly not exist in the absence of that [connected thing], because otherwise it would follow that it lacks an intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*) or is causeless (*ahetukatva*). As it has been said:
"There is also an inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) with respect to the intrinsic nature, which follows upon the mere existence [of the thing]."
"In the absence of that [cause], there would be an absence of the self-nature [of the effect], because they are non-different.
Likewise: "The smoke is the effect of the fire, because it follows the properties of the effect.
If it were to exist even in the absence of that [fire], it would overstep its state of having a cause. (PV 3.33) Thus.
Therefore, in that case, the requirement for the object to be perceptible (*dṛśyaviṣayatā*) would be entirely useless; the point is that nothing follows from it.

By the phrase "when the mere establishment of the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) [is sufficient]," he demonstrates the impossibility of that [requirement] for those who do not describe the reason (*hetu*) as having a necessary connection, but instead claim negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) based on mere non-perception alone.

For instance: if there were no necessary connection, and all things devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhya*) were perceptible, then the absence of the means of proof (*sādhana*)—which has not been perceived among them—would be established.
Regarding this, Kumārila also says: "If,
after going to and returning from those places, an object is not perceived, then,
due to the absence of other causes [for its non-perception], it is understood to be non-existent."
[ŚVārthā- 38] Thus,
even though [the subject] is invisible due to its distance in space and so forth, since mere non-perception of the reason (*hetu*) is possible there,

this negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)— characterized by the absence of the probans (*sādhana*) wherever there is an absence of the probandum (*sādhya*) in its entirety— is doubtful; for such [non-perception] occurs only where...

Because it is expressed by the two distributive phrases— "where there is an absence of the probandum, there is an absence of the probans"— the ascertainment of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) has also been described as being based precisely on the aforementioned connection. Therefore, for those others who desire the establishment of positive concomitance as the basis for their demonstration, its non-existence has likewise been stated.
Because it is impossible for inferential cognizers to perceive all things possessing causes as being endowed with the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*),

and because the concomitance of the probandum across its entire range of locations and so forth must be established through a distributive repetition— namely, "wherever there is the reason, there is the probandum"—
the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is not established merely by repeatedly observing the coexistence of the probans (*sādhanadharma*) and the probandum in a few locations and so on.
Since there is no obstacle, such cases are frequently observed; yet, because the opposite is also possible, even for this [reason], [the following objection is raised]:
"But surely, even for those things that are not perceptible, there is non-perception among them;
therefore, from non-perception alone, the determination of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) occurs everywhere. To this, he says:
[236] In the case of the probandum (sādhya), [237] when there is an absence of the entire probandum, [238] characterized by the absence of the probans (sādhana),
whether it be visible or invisible.
[239] By means of a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) based on a necessary connection;
[240] mere observation—T.; [241] of the positive concomitance.
[242] Otherwise, however—[§ 35. Explanation of the means for ascertaining the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) in the case of non-perception (*anupalabdhi*):
Now, with reference to non-perception, he says: "The ascertainment of negative concomitance is stated in the case of non-perception"—this is the remainder of the sentence.
What is its nature?

To this he says: [it is] non-perception, which consists in the perception of that which is distinct from it, [occurring] when there exists something that has reached the conditions for perceptibility—namely, other conditions for apprehension being present—and which possesses a visible nature; [that is,] when there exists the form of the absence of the probandum.
That which is the non-existence of an existing thing, and that direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) which apprehends it, is shown to have the characteristic of its [the object's] absence;

it is "shown" (*darśana*) because by means of it [the absence] is made known (*pratyāyyate*). This is the indicative means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); the determination of the negative concomitance (*vyatireka-niścaya*) in the case of non-perception consists of that very nature.
And because it is the cause of that [determination], it is called a means of valid cognition in that way.
For if an entity that possesses a visible nature were not perceived even though it exists and the conditions for its perception are present, how could it have a visible nature?
Indeed, that which becomes directly perceptible when other conditions for perception are present is alone designated as having a visible nature.
Therefore, when such [conditions] are present, it must necessarily function through direct perception.
Otherwise, it would never be perceptible,
because there would be no distinction [between its states].
The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whatever has only a certain set of conditions as its cause necessarily occurs when those conditions are present;

for example, a sprout, which has only the causal complex of the seed and so forth as its cause. And perception, when an object is present, has only the attainment of the aforementioned characteristics of perceptibility as its cause. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).

By this means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), when there is non-perception of the essential nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*), the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)— characterized by the absence [of the probans] where the probandum is absent— is ascertained.
And this very means of valid cognition is also the cause for the ascertainment of positive concomitance (*anvaya*),
because by means of it alone, the absence [of the probans] is demonstrated in other instances where [the probandum] is not perceived.

However, regarding the non-perception of the cause (*kāraṇānupalabdhi*) and the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*), which will be discussed later, the very means for establishing the two types of necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is the basis for determining positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). Since that [means] has already been demonstrated in the case of the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*) and the essential-nature reason (*svabhāvahetu*), it is not stated separately. For instance: the absence of the cause and the pervader is necessarily accompanied by the absence of the effect and the pervaded; and when there is the exclusion (*vyatireka*) of the absence of the effect and the pervaded—characterized by their presence—the absence of the cause and the pervader is necessarily excluded as well.
Because of its existence;

otherwise, it would follow that the effect and the pervader would be causeless and devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). Therefore, there is nothing to be stated separately. [243] "Attainment of the conditions for perception" consists of the completeness of the other conditions for perception and a specific nature (*svabhāvaviśeṣa*). — [NB Pari- 2]
[244] Non-apprehension [is the reason for] proving non-existence;
[245] it is shown in order to demonstrate that [the object] cannot be established by any other means.
[246] — necessarily, such a... — T.
[247] when [248] the absence of the cause and the pervader is excluded.

[§ 36. Nomenclature of the three types of the reason. By this much of the text, it has been explained that "the reason is a property of the subject (pakṣadharma) which is pervaded by its part" (*tadaṃśena vyāptaḥ*). Now, in order to explain the statement "it is of three kinds," he says: "that which has this definition"—namely, that whose definition is "being a property of the subject and being pervaded by its part" (*pakṣadharmaḥ san yas tadaṃśena vyāptaḥ*)—is the reason.
It has these characteristics;
it is indeed threefold.
The explanation of the word "it" (saḥ) is "the cause" (hetuḥ).
The explanation of the phrase "only threefold" is "of exactly three types.
He names those reasons by their respective individual names: "essential nature," "effect," and "non-perception.
The word "and" (ca) serves to aggregate them as being reasons.
The word "iti" (thus), indicating completion, clarifies the sense of restriction alone;
for example— when some [property] such as sound is to be proven as impermanent, the presentation of "existence" (*sattva*) as a reason of essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
When a location possessing fire is to be proven, "smoke" is the presentation of the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*);

and regarding non-existence, the presentation of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) is: "the non-apprehension of that which has reached the conditions for apprehension," both with respect to the absence itself and to its conventional usage.
[§ 37. Demonstration of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the status of fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) for those outside the three types of valid reasons.]

Why, then, is the reason (hetu) only of three kinds? Anticipating this objection, [the author] states that since objects other than the three kinds of reasons are pervaded by the state of being pseudo-reasons (*hetvābhāsa*), which is the opposite of being a valid reason, the status of being a reason is necessarily restricted to these three alone; thus, he establishes the state of being a pseudo-reason for those things excluded from them, supported by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Showing this, he says: "Because the rule of inseparable connection (avinābhāva) applies only to these three types of reasons—namely, those called essential nature (svabhāva), effect (kārya), and non-perception (anupalabdhi)—the meaning is that there is no inseparable connection in objects other than these three types of reasons.

Consequently, because they lack inseparable connection, objects distinct from essential nature, effect, and non-perception are pseudo-reasons (hetvābhāsa), just like [the reason] "knowability" (prameyatva) and so forth; this is what is being stated.

Furthermore, the absence of inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) is understood through the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*), precisely because it is excluded from the three types of valid reasons; this is due to the absence of identity (*tādātmya*) and causality (*tadutpatti*), which are the two pervaders of inseparable connection.
[§ 38. Determination of Inseparable Connection: Now, what is this inseparable connection?

To whom does this belong, or how is it said to be restricted to this very [state]? To this he says: "The aforementioned non-pervasion of the pervader"—by virtue of being its cause and by virtue of being its very nature.

Wherever that which is pervaded—whether an effect (*kārya*) or an essential nature (*svabhāva*)—is present, there [the pervader] must necessarily exist; or rather, wherever the pervader—known as either a cause (*kāraṇa*) or an essential nature—is present, it exists only in that locus (*dharmin*) and not even in the absence of it. This pervasion (*vyāpti*) described as the relationship between the pervader and the pervaded is what is called "pervasion as stated" (*yathoktāvyāpti*).
Inseparable connection (avinābhāva).
Of what?
Of the property of the subject (pakṣadharma), that is, of the property belonging to the subject of the thesis (sādhyadharmin).
This kind of inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) does not exist elsewhere than in the three types of reasons as previously described;
for it is only here, in these three...

It exists in the threefold [reason], because of the presence of the two types of inseparable connection— identity and causality— and because these two possess the relationship of the pervaded and the pervader, just like "being produced" and "impermanence. Therefore, it is stated that [the reason] is restricted to this very threefold cause by way of its absence elsewhere.

Thus, by this [statement], the meaning of the phrase "the fallacious reasons (hetvābhāsa) are other than those" has been demonstrated along with its logical justification, namely, that there is a necessity of inseparable connection (avinābhāva-niyama).
Furthermore, it has already been stated previously how inseparable connection does not exist in anything other than the three types of valid reasons.
Alternatively, if a different object (*arthāntara*) is something other than its own-nature (*svabhāva*),
and that is also other than the effect— whether it be the cause or neither—

then it is also other than the aforementioned non-apprehension; that is, it is either mere non-apprehension or the apprehension of something else that is to be negated, whether that "other" is contradictory to it or not contradictory.

In that regard, as for another type of object (arthāntara): if it is an immediate effect, it cannot be characterized by those with limited vision through its distinction from other things; therefore, it lacks the status of a logical mark (aliṅgatva).

Even if one determines the distinction based on the observation of the effect, the determination of the property of the subject (pakṣadharmatā) occurring after the establishment of the probandum (sādhya), as well as the process of positive concomitance (anvaya), would be redundant.
Furthermore, even a remote effect is not a logical mark of its cause.
Because there is deviation due to the possibility of an intervening obstruction or deficiency. As it has been said:
"In regard to an effect that follows from the transformation of the potencies of the causal complex, there is inconclusiveness (anaikāntikatā), because an obstruction is possible. (PV 3.7)
Thus, in the case of an inference based on capability (*yogyatā*), there is no other [separate] logical mark (*liṅga*);
nor is it the case that neither exists,
because without a necessary connection (*apratibandha*), it would be impossible for it to be a means of cognition.
If it is asked, "How is the determination of the proximity of Rohiṇī derived from the cognition of the rising of Kṛttikā?"—

surely it has already been stated that even this [determination] is not tenable in the absence of a causal connection, because, due to the lack of any distinguishing factor, there would be the undesirable consequence of cognizing everything from everything. Therefore, some cause for the transition of the circle of constellations must be postulated through an interval of time.

Just as the non-disturbance of the elements [is used] to infer the rain that will occur at a later time, this must be conceived as arising from the mark of the effect (*kāryaliṅga*) through the inference of properties of the cause (*hetudharmanumāna*).
Even mere non-perception (*anupalabdhi*) is a cause for doubt,
because even when a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is absent, the non-existence of the object is not established.
How could even the apprehension of that which is to be negated establish its non-existence?
For it is impossible for an unerroneous apprehension to be absent.
However, the apprehension of a contradictory [thing] establishes the absence of the counter-positive.
However, since that contradiction is established precisely through the non-perception of others when it exists, it is non-perception itself that is being employed by way of that [contradiction].
Otherwise, because perception is not prohibited, the absence [of the object] would not be established.
Furthermore, the perception of what is not contradictory is inconclusive with respect to negation.
Because coexistence is possible among things that are not contradictory, and since no other mode is possible, inseparable connection (avinābhāva) does not exist elsewhere.
[2. Examination of the Essential Nature Reason (svabhāvahetu)]
[§ 1. Stating the definition of the essential reason (svabhāvahetu):
[249] That which is accepted as something other than the effect-reason (kāryahetu) is also that very same thing... the meaning is that it is indeed a different object (arthāntara).
[250] Because the effect is immediately subsequent to its cause.

[251] Now, regarding the fruit of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) and those capacities (*śakti*), he first states the definition of the essential nature as a reason (*svabhāvahetu*). Among those three types of reasons, the definition of the essential nature as a reason is stated first:
that by which something is established is the means of proof (*sādhana*).
That [subject] and that property constitute "its state" (tadbhāva);
that very thing is the mere presence of the probans-property (sādhanadharmabhāvamātra). The "concomitance" (anvaya) is of that [mere presence].

That which belongs to it— namely, to that property to be proven (sādhyadharma)— is the essential nature (svabhāva) as the reason (hetu), because of the metaphorical application of the whole to its part.
Since the property to be proven is what is explicitly heard [in the statement], it is understood that the essential nature of that very [property] is the reason.

But how is it that this [reason] has the same nature as the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*), given that it is perceived through differentiation? To this he says: "By means of that differentiation—which is caused by the distinction of limits (*avadhibheda*)—consisting in the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) from another non-existent [cause] and from another non-momentary [entity]. (S. 61b)

Although there is a difference between the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) and the probans-property (*sādhanadharma*), in reality— that is, from the perspective of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*)—
the very nature of the mark (*liṅgasvabhāva*) is itself the very nature of the property to be proven.
For instance, that which is excluded from what is non-existent is the very same as that which is excluded from the non-momentary (*akṣaṇika*).

Therefore, because there is no difference from a single substratum (*dharmin*), the property to be proven (*sādhya*) and the proving property (*sādhana-dharma*) would also, in the ultimate sense, not be distinct at all.
He says: "mutually... [Tibetan: *paraspara*].
[§ 2. The qualification "merely existing where the property to be proven exists" and so forth, for the purpose of refuting the opinions of others:

If, in reality, the property that serves as the means of proof (*sādhana-dharma*) is of the very same nature as the subject possessing the mark (*liṅgin*), then why is the property to be proven (*sādhya-dharma*) qualified by the phrase "that which is concomitant with the mere existence of the property that serves as the means of proof"?

For how could that which is the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of something not necessarily follow from that alone? Otherwise, there would be the consequence of it being formless or lacking that intrinsic nature. Therefore, he says: when the probandum-property (sādhyadharma), whose intrinsic nature is the reason (hetu), exists—that is, when the intrinsic nature of the reason exists—there is no deviation from the positive concomitance (anvaya) with respect to the mere existence of the proving-property (sādhanadharma).
Since there is no deviation (vyabhicāra) regarding that which is a positive concomitant (anvaya),
a qualification is appropriate only when such concomitance is possible and yet subject to deviation;
however, in this case, since there is only concomitance and no deviation at all, a qualification is indeed inappropriate.

Nevertheless, when defining the characteristic of the reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*), that qualification of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*)— namely, its following only the presence of the proving property (*sādhanadharma*) through the concomitance of that alone— is made with reference to the views of others, such as the Naiyāyikas, because of their divergent opinions;
it is not made with reference to our own view.

Demonstrating that very misconception of others, he says: "For the others—the Naiyāyikas and so forth—hold that [motion] has a cause distinct from the object; that is, it has as its cause an object other than the productive object, such as conjunction with a substance possessing velocity (*vega*). For they say thus: 'From conjunction with a substance possessing velocity, motions arise in the parts.'"
From those [atoms] comes the separation of parts;
from that, the destruction of their conjunction; and then the effect-substance (kāryadravya) produced by them also perishes.
Thus, the cause is a distinct entity.

Therefore, because it depends on a cause that is a different entity and is absent even when "producedness" (kṛtakatva) and so forth are present, it does not possess a positive concomitance (anvaya) with the mere existence of that [cause].

The existence (bhāva) of that producedness and so forth is its being (sattā); that alone is the "mere" (tanmātra). That which possesses this concomitance is the property to be proven (sādhyadharma), characterized by impermanence. They maintain that the nature (svabhāva) of producedness and so forth is even the opposite of that [impermanence].
Therefore, a qualification has been made;
and by that qualification, the author of the definition states that such destruction—which is caused by something else—is not of the nature [of the thing itself].
By means of the qualification, he indicates that being of the nature [of the thing] belongs only to that which exists by the mere presence of its own existence, and not to anything else.
Because it indicates this: [§ 3. When destruction caused by an external factor is the probandum, the reason "being produced" is inconclusive.
Likewise, he states that when that [destruction] caused by an external factor is the probandum, the reason—such as "being produced"—is inconclusive (*vyabhicāra*) and uncertain (*anaikāntika*).

An example of this is as follows: when destruction caused by a cause (*hetumati vināśe*) is the property to be proven (*sādhya*), the reason (*hetu*) "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) lacks the nature of that [destruction] and is thus non-concomitant (*avyabhicāra*). Now, one might object: since impermanence is accepted by others as distinct from the nature of being produced, it is certainly not desired [by them] that impermanence has the nature of being produced; so why is it said that "they accept a nature that is concomitant even with the mere absence of that [nature]"? The intention is as follows: even for those who accept the two properties called "being produced" and "impermanence" as distinct, there must necessarily be [the nature of] "coming into existence after not having existed," "ceasing to exist after having existed," and "having a non-abiding nature."

Otherwise, since there would be no distinction between producedness (*kṛtakatva*) and impermanence (*anityatva*) even in the case of the self (*ātman*) and so forth, both would exist [there too]. Therefore, let the relationship of probandum and probans (*sādhyasādhanabhāva*) belong to those very two— namely, "coming into being after not having existed" (*abhūtvā bhavanam*) and "ceasing to exist after having existed" (*bhūtvā abhavanam*), which constitute non-abidingness (*anavasthāyitvam*)— by means of the conceptual construction that manifests the distinction between producedness and impermanence arising through the power of perceiving them.
What is the use of postulating a distinct property (*dharma*)?

Even if one does so, since it is the entity itself that serves as the basis for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), it is that which must be considered by those seeking such efficiency. As it has been said:
"By those who do not deny the referents of words, through the distinction between the positions of existence and non-existence..."
For it is the object itself that is contemplated here, since the arising of the fruit is bound to it.
What is the use of various modifications for that which is incapable of purposeful action (arthakriyā) to those who seek it?
What is the use of examining the beauty or ugliness of a eunuch to a woman in love?

Thus, although entities are perceived and determined in some respect by a certain nature that excludes others, they remain undetermined in another respect—that is, by a nature that excludes what is not of that form—due to the presence of causes for error. Since these two aspects, the determined and the undetermined, are brought under a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) by means of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it is logical that "producedness" (*kṛtakatva*), which is itself the very nature of impermanence, serves as the logical mark (*liṅga*) with respect to destruction. It is established through inference, preceded by the ascertainment of the connection, based on a means of valid cognition other than the initial perception.

And thus, the very nature of destruction is what is intended by those [proponents] through the reason called "being produced" (kṛtakatva) according to the aforementioned logic and so forth. If that [destruction] were not invariably concomitant with that [property of being produced], its lack of identity with that nature would be stated by means of a qualification, on the grounds that it has a different cause.

It might be thought: "By means of being produced, destruction itself is directly inferred as possessing the cause; subsequently, impermanence is established as existence qualified by subsequent non-existence (pradhvaṃsābhāva), or as inherence (samavāya) in that [existence]."
For this very reason, there is no consequence of impermanence regarding the self and so forth.
We consider "destruction" to be the non-existence of an entity characterized by annihilation (*pradhvaṃsa*),
whereas "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) is the inherence (*samavāya*) of existence within its own cause.
That there is nothing undesirable in making known the non-existence of intrinsic nature (*asvabhāvatā*) through the qualification "destruction" [of that entity]—
this is incorrect.
Because such a destruction is contradictory to having a cause,
as the Master himself will state later;
and nothing at all follows from that which is inferred by him.
Because that [permanent entity] lacks the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā-sāmarthya*).
For those who, having understood the means of achieving pleasure and pain, desire to act accordingly, investigate something out of a practical intent and not out of mere addiction.
Therefore, by this very fact, one must infer that the nature of the entity is indeed unstable.
And that very [non-existence] must be conceived as having a cause;

otherwise, since the non-existence of destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*), which is distinct from an entity, would remain unchanged even when a hammer or similar instrument arises—being useless for its production—that entity would simply persist in its former state. How then could existence characterized by that [destruction], or the inherence (*samavāya*) with it, constitute impermanence?
Furthermore, if the existence and inherence— characterized by the non-existence of destruction produced by a hammer or other means— in an entity whose nature is immovable constitute its impermanence,
then why would this not apply to the self (*ātman*) and so forth as well? Thus, the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) remains exactly as it was.
Furthermore, even the inherence in its own cause does not establish "coming into being after not having existed" for one who does not accept it;
for it is precisely that existence (*sattā*) which comes into being after not having existed that is described as "being produced.

Moreover, since existence and inherence are accepted as eternal and thus devoid of any modification, it is not logical for prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and destructive non-existence (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*) to serve as qualifiers [of them], because they have not previously existed.
And when [the state of] being produced is admitted, let that very fact of being produced and the nature of instability itself be destruction.
What is the use of postulating a separate entity that is fruitless, lacks any means of valid cognition, and is contradicted by valid cognition?
Thus, even for others, the admission of the identity between being produced and destruction is inevitable.

Therefore, if destruction—characterized by non-abiding—is admitted to have a cause distinct from the object itself, then the fact that "being produced" (kṛtakatva) does not possess that nature is made known by the qualification;
for it is impossible for that which is unproduced when the former is produced, or which has a different cause, to have that as its nature.
Thus, with respect to that probandum, there is a deviation (vyabhicāra) of the property of being produced.
For instance: those things which depend upon other causes for their occurrence in a particular state do not necessarily exist there; as, for example, dye on cloth.

And since non-existence through destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*) depends upon other causes even among produced entities, this is the perception of a pervasion by the contradictory (*viruddhavyāptopalabdhi*).

Now, it might be argued that because the dyeing of a cloth has a limited cause, and because the presence of that cause depends upon its own specific conditions, and because the substrate [of the dye] is unstable due to the occurrence of adverse conditions, it is indeed logical that the dyeing is not necessarily destined to occur;
but this is not the case for destruction.
Because its causes are infinite, there must necessarily be the presence of at least one among them in things such as jars;
nor do any destroy the substratum of destruction prior to the presence of those causes,
on account of which destruction would not begin due to their absence.
[253] with respect to an entity [254] by means of its being produced and so forth [255] by means of its impermanence and so forth.

The meaning is that, having cognized some object, those desiring to attain or avoid the means of pleasure and pain respectively examine those means of pleasure and pain.

That is incorrect;
for although there are many causes of destruction, nevertheless, because their presence depends upon their own respective causes,
and because even when those causes are present, there is an infinity of opposing factors that obstruct their efficacy.
Since causes do not necessarily possess their fruits, it remains possible that something might not perish; thus, the deviation [of the reason] is not excluded. [Objection:
But if this dyeing of cloth were perceived everywhere, even though it is dependent [on other factors], then why would it not be necessary?
[Response: It would be so, if it were indeed perceived in that way.
But that [destruction] is also perceived otherwise.
If this is so, then one need not feel mental distress due to the suspicion of a change in nature regarding destruction, which is perceived everywhere.
Or rather, do you possess the light of knowledge that pervades the entire expanse of all things?
On what basis does one speak in this way? Or, even if such a state [of non-destruction] were possible, how could the operation of inference not incur futility regarding what is perceived?

Furthermore, even when one observes the destruction of certain things produced by causes, since there are instances where things whose birth depends on causes are seen otherwise, how could one—having conceived doubt—ascertain that such a state exists in those things remote in space, time, or nature?
Furthermore, this destruction, characterized by the non-existence of an entity even when it has been produced, would have to be eternal;
for if that destruction were to cease, it would follow that the entity must re-emerge.
Furthermore, no cause for its destruction is perceived, as is the case with things such as a jar. As it has been said:
"Just as causes for destruction are observed in the case of jars and the like, such a cause does not exist for destruction; how then could it arise without a cause?"
Thus, why is it not accepted that there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) by that very [reason] when the destruction of what is produced (*kṛtakatva*) is the property to be proven (*sādhya*)?
If it is argued that this is an invariable (*aikāntika*) property of entities (*bhāva*), from what, then, is this ascertained?
If it is argued that this is because no change in their state is perceived, we reply:
even if this non-perception exists, since it does not exclude the existence of the self and so forth, how can it exclude change in another case?

If it is argued that this is because [the absence of the reason] is apprehended through inference (*anumāna*), then one must ask: how does that very inference exclude the presence of the reason in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) if non-apprehension itself is not established there? Thus, this argument is trivial.
