although inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*) is the subject at hand, nevertheless, because some people understand through the very form of formal application (*prayogabhaṅgī*) due to the habit of observing such applications, and since this is possible even within inference for oneself, inference for others (*parārthānumāna*) is introduced here as a secondary topic.
And in order to explain this, he says: "The formulation of the statement that establishes the three characteristics of that essential reason (*svabhāvahetu*) is the *prayoga*.
He demonstrates that very point: "That which has a common property; the state of having that [property] is the *sādhya* (the probandum) by means of it..."
One [type of] application is by similarity (*sādharmya*); the other is by dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), which is the state of that which possesses a dissimilar property.
He states the examples for these two respectively: "For example, whatever exists..."
The word *yat* (whatever) in the phrase "whatever exists" (*yad yat sat*) primarily functions as a term of distribution;
likewise, the word *tat* (all that) in "all that" (*tat sarvam*) also primarily functions as a term of distribution.
Here, by the inclusion of the term "all" (*sarva*), there is a complete grasping of everything, thereby excluding any external pervasion (*bahirvyāpti*).
Regarding the phrase "just like jars and so forth":

for one who has established through valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) between existence and momentariness in the case of jars and the like, this statement of an example is intended to provide a reminder of that [connection] in that context, not to establish the probandum (*sādhya*),
because the probandum is not established by the mere presence of an example.
For it is not the case that because one thing exists in such a way, everything exists in that same way, as this would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
"And it is the word 'existent'" is the application of the property to the subject (*pakṣadharmopasaṃhāra*).

An example of the application of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-prayoga*) is "in the same way," and so forth. The word "tathā" (in the same way) signifies conjunction; and thus, the application by way of dissimilarity is illustrated.
Here too, the term "all" (*sarva*) should be connected by changing its case-ending: "in the absence of momentariness, the absence of existence would follow for everything.

Demonstrating the purpose of the inclusion of "all" in both formulations, he says: "In every locus (*dharmin*) possessing the property to be proven (*sādhanadharma*), and not merely in the locus of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadharmin*), there is the *upasaṃhāra*—that is, the bringing together or application—of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*)."

Therefore, the demonstration—that is, the presentation—of that pervasion (vyāpti), which consists in the form "the pervader exists there alone" and so forth, is the very definition of those two; thus they are described as such.
Consequently, those who, setting aside the subject of the thesis (sādhyadharmin), demonstrate external pervasion (bahirvyāpti)—

They— namely, those who argue that even if the probans (sādhana-dharma) is pervaded by the probandum (sādhya-dharma) in the subject of the example (dṛṣṭānta-dharmin), the establishment of the probandum is nonetheless untenable because it does not necessarily exist as such everywhere— are refuted;
for there is a pervasion of the probans by the probandum everywhere when the latter exists.
Why is that very same [instance] not shown, by which the external pervasion (*bahirvyāpti*) would be declared incapable?
For it is not the case that "He is dark-complexioned, because he is his son... [is a valid instance].

Even when the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of "son-ness" with "darkness" is demonstrated by means of a currently perceived son—outside of the probandum (*sādhya*)—the establishment of the probandum still occurs.

Therefore, it is precisely that pervasion which, established through universal inclusion (*sarvopasaṃhāra*) and based on a connection proven by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), is capable of establishing the probandum; that alone should be demonstrated for the sake of its recollection.
Furthermore, even when the pervasion is demonstrated through universal inclusion, the locus (*dharmin*) qualified by the property (*dharma*) is not cognized at that very moment.
For inference, which occurs subsequent to the demonstration of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), would then be a mere recollection (*smṛti*).

This is because such an inference is dependent upon the cognition of the probans (*sādhana*) as being inseparably connected (*avinābhūta*) with the probandum (*sādhya*) in the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*), and it is impossible for this to occur prior to that demonstration.

Furthermore, if the universal pervasion (*vyāpti*) were preceded by that [recollection], how could the subsequent inference—which has a particular object as its domain—be considered a recollection? Thus it is argued.
[275] The application— [276] he stated the application of the pride of application— [277] namely, "whatever exists," etc.
[278] Because of the cognition of the subject as qualified by the property to be proven [279],
[this occurs] in that [cognition] which is preceded by the presentation of the property residing in the subject [280].
[281] Because of the recollection of pervasion (*vyāpti*), [§ 5. Even in the formulation by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-prayoga*), the demonstration of pervasion is appropriate.
But surely:

It is logical that the formulation by way of similarity (sādharmya-prayoga) has the characteristic of demonstrating pervasion (vyāpti), because it demonstrates the necessary presence of the property to be proven (sādhya-dharma) when the property that serves as the proof (sādhana-dharma) exists; but how is this so for the formulation by way of dissimilarity (vaidharmya-prayoga)?
For in that case, only the absence of the reason when there is an absence of the probandum is stated,
but it is not said that when the reason is present, the probandum must necessarily be present.
This is not a fault.
For in this case, the absence of the reason in the absence of the probandum is not shown to be of a non-existent (tuccha) nature;
rather, the reason—such as existence (*sattva*) and so forth—is a property of a real entity (*vastudharma*).
How could the non-existence of that very self-nature itself constitute the essential form of the reason?
For this reason, the logical reason (hetu) must possess three characteristics;

however, in the formulation based on dissimilarity (vaidharmya-prayoga), the property of being subject to cessation when [the probandum] has ceased—which is an internal property of the reason itself—is demonstrated.

And when the property serving as the means of proof (sādhana-dharma) is of such a kind, the existence of the property to be proven (sādhya-dharma) is necessarily understood through that very [dissimilar instance].

Otherwise, since it would be impossible for that which has ceased to possess the property of cessation, it is not tenable that the formulation of dissimilar instances (*vaidharmya-prayoga*) has the demonstration of pervasion (*vyāpti*) as its defining characteristic; for that [dissimilar instance], being of the nature of a non-entity (*tuccha-rūpa*),
lacks the connection characterized by the indication of the pervasion of the reason.
[284] Of a sentient being (sattva)—
[285] in the case of a nature whose characteristic is the turning away from opposing factors [§ 6. The futility of the application of a proposition].

[Objection: "But in both types of formal argument, the statement of the thesis (*pratijñā*) has not been shown; how, then, can its meaning be understood? And yet, the employment of the means of proof (*sādhana*) is intended for the purpose of communicating that meaning. To this, he says: "In these two types of arguments, by the power of the mere statement of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) and its relation [to the probandum], the meaning of the thesis—which will be explained later—"

Since the probandum (*sādhya*), characterized as the collection of the property (*dharma*) and the locus (*dharmin*), is already cognized through the reason (*hetu*), the formal employment of the proposition (*pratijñā*) has not been shown. An opponent, failing to understand this capacity, says: "If the object of knowledge (*prameya*)—the probandum—is not presented by words, how could there be any cognition of it? How could there be a cognition of the meaning of the proposition? If you think thus, then at the time of inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*)...
If one understands by oneself without another person providing the instruction, who would be the one to point out the object of cognition (*prameya*)?
None at all.

Rather, one understands the object of cognition oneself through the perception of a probans (*sādhana-dharma*) that is inseparably connected (*avinābhūta*) with the probandum (*sādhya*). Likewise, in inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*), let there be understanding of that very object from that same [probans] alone; what is the use of stating the proposition (*pratijñā*)?

If there is no one at all to point out the object of cognition (*prameya*) at the time of one's own realization, how then does that realization occur? To this he says: for one who has perceived—having seen by means of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)—the smoke, which is the probans (*sādhana-dharma*), situated in a particular location within the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*), [realization occurs] by virtue of the force of ascertaining the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) of that smoke with the fire, which is the property to be proven (*sādhya-dharma*), through valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

When there is a recollection of the previously established pervasion—that is, the invariable concomitance (avinābhāva)—then by the power of that alone, specifically through the power of grasping the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) and grasping the pervasion, the cognition of the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñā*) in the form "fire is here" occurs, even without the formal employment of a proposition.
It might be thought: "Even in that case, something like an 'ear-demon' (*karṇapiśācikā*) tells him the object of knowledge (*prameya*. To this he says: "No."

And at that time, during the process of inference for one's own sake, no invisible being such as a *karṇapiśācika* (ear-demon) informs or tells this cognizer the object of cognition, saying, "There is fire here."
If you are a speaker of truth, you ought not to say this;
for we too, upon seeing smoke in a particular location, cognize fire by depending on the recollection of its pervasion (*vyāpti*) by fire.
Yet no one informs us, "Fire is here."
And since there is the cognition of that [object], it is likewise appropriate for the cognition of anything else as well.
If it is argued: "Even if no one points it out, one will nevertheless establish the object of cognition for oneself and then follow the logical mark (*liṅga*) to cognize it," [the response follows].
He says: Not only is there no one who informs [him], but even prior to the operation of the inferential mark (*liṅga*), he does not himself apprehend anything such as fire and so forth.
Why? If this is asked, it is because there is an absence of a cause for the cognition "fire is here" in the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as its reason.
For a three-featured reason (*trirūpa-hetu*) is the cause for the cognition of an imperceptible object; in its absence, how could that cognition occur?
If one were to say that such cognition occurs even without a logical mark (*liṅga*), then, given that cognition is desired [to be valid], the logical mark would be rendered useless.
Since its purpose is the comprehension of the object to be inferred (*anumeya*), how could it not be purposeless if that [object] were not comprehended through it?
And demonstrating the extreme stupidity of the opponent, he says: having himself, quite independently, established that "there is fire here."

How does he establish it independently? Since he establishes it spontaneously, without means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), for the sake of understanding that [object], and for the purpose of understanding the object of comprehension (*prameya*) established without a cause,
he subsequently pursues the mark (*liṅga*) as its cause— what kind of sequence or order is this in the process of understanding?
For instance—the sequence of the wise is that first there is the pursuit of the logical mark (*liṅga*), and from that follows the comprehension of the probandum (*sādhya*).
But this is an unprecedented inferer who resorts to the reverse of that; thus [the author] mocks him.

As it is said in the world: "Having shaved his head, he asks for the lunar mansion"—because this sequence is similar to that, one understands [the conclusion] by oneself through the very power of grasping the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) and recollecting the pervasion (*vyāpti*). And since that which establishes [the conclusion] has already been stated, there is no purpose whatsoever in the mention of the object of inference (*prameya*).
If, indeed, at the time of inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*), one understands the probandum (*sādhya*) by oneself alone, that is entirely reasonable,
because the logical mark (*liṅga*) is also understood there by oneself alone.
In inference for others (*parārthānumāna*), however, just as one understands the logical mark from another, so too must the object of cognition (*prameya*) be understood from another alone.

Therefore, the employment of the formal proposition (*pratijñā*) is indeed appropriate; thus he says: "Not only by oneself, but even by another—that is, when that object of cognition (*prameya*) is stated by an opponent debater—it likewise 'floats,' because that statement, by expressing a doubtful meaning, is not a factor for the ascertainment of the probandum (*sādhya*), since it does not, through a lineage [of reasoning], penetrate the profundity of the object of cognition."
Even so, because that which is unrelated to it is established as being based merely on the speaker's intention, [it remains] precisely above [the object].
If one asks, "Why does it float?"—it is because of a lack of utility; it has no utility whatsoever toward the cognition of the probandum (*sādhya*).
This means that [the thesis] is not stated because it is incapable of proving that [object].

Anticipating the objection that the opponent might sometimes state merely its utility, he says: "If it is thought that the utility of the statement of the proposition (*pratijñā*) consists in the presentation of the object of the reason—that is, the presentation of the *sādhya*, which is the object of the reason."
To this, he says: by that very same object;
the word "first" (tāvat) refers to the sequence.
If the object being presented were to possess meaningfulness, then its presentation would constitute the purpose of the statement of the thesis (*pratijñā*).
But what is the point, what is the purpose, of merely indicating the object (*viṣaya*)?
Is it not the case that the comprehension of the probandum (*sādhya*) and the comprehension of the application based on similarity (*sādharmyavat-prayoga*) are the purpose of indicating the object?
Therefore, such indication is the function of the statement of the proposition (*pratijñā*).

For instance, if the statement of the probandum were absent, when it is said, "Whatever is produced is impermanent," it would not be known whether this is an application based on similarity (*sādharmya*) or one based on dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*).

For in this case, both possibilities are suspected: that [the example] possesses similarity when proving impermanence by means of being produced, or that it possesses dissimilarity when proving non-producedness by means of permanence.
However, when the statement of the proposition "Sound is impermanent" or "it is non-produced" is present, both are understood without doubt.
Furthermore, there would be no cognition of a reason that is contradictory or inconclusive;
however, in a formal argument preceded by a thesis, such as "Sound is impermanent because it is produced," the status of the reason is indeed cognized.
"In [the argument] 'It is eternal, because it is produced,' there is contradiction;
in '[It is] preceded by effort, because it is produced,' there is inconclusiveness."
Furthermore, the three-fold nature of the reason (*hetu*) is not understood [independently], because it is established in relation to the probandum (*sādhya*).

When the statement of the proposition (*pratijñā*) is present, the subject of the probandum (*sādhyadharmin*) is called the "position" (*pakṣa*) through a metaphorical designation of the whole for its part; thus, the property of being produced (*kṛtakatva*), which exists therein, possesses the status of being a property of the position (*pakṣadharmatva*).

And since a "similar instance" (sapakṣa) is an object that is similar by virtue of the generality of the property to be proven (sādhyadharma), the presence [of the reason] in the similar instances means its existence in what is similar;

and since a "dissimilar instance" (asapakṣa) is that which is not a similar instance, the absence [of the reason] in the dissimilar instances would be understood as its non-existence even in that which lacks the property to be proven.

Anticipating this objection, he says: "If the cognition [produced] by the application of the similar instance (*sādharmyavat-prayoga*) and so forth is characterized by certainty regarding the probandum (*sādhya*),

and consists of the determination of its own nature, then— otherwise, since it would not occur without the statement of the proposition (*pratijñā*)— that which was stated [previously], namely that the similar instance serves for the sake of establishing the probandum..."

And since the presentation of the object is for the sake of knowing the application (*prayoga*) and so forth, all that would be appropriate only if it were explained that at the time of one's own inference (*svārthānumāna*), even without the statement of the proposition (*pratijñā*), there indeed occurs a cognition characterized by the establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*) through the apprehension of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) and the recollection of the [logical] connection. Thus it has been stated.
In the same way, it will also occur in inference for the sake of others.
Since this is so, therefore, when this proponent of the formulation of the thesis understands the probandum for himself,
then, upon his own comprehension of the probandum, the object is presented by means of the statement of the thesis.
Even without that [explicit statement], some person,
understanding through the power of the logical mark (*liṅga*) alone and ascertaining the probandum,
perceives us as petitioners when we are presenting our case; at that time, he seeks a price characterized by the employment of an unstated proposition (*apratyakta-pratijñā-prayoga*).
Like what? Like a Brāhmaṇa on a festival day.

Just as a Brāhmaṇa who maintains a chariot might eat at other times even without a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), yet on another occasion during a festival such as a Śrāddha, he says to a petitioner who is full of faith: "If you give me one coin for every *ghṛtapūra* (ghee-filled cake)..."
"Therefore, I eat, and not otherwise.
You are just like that.

Furthermore, as for what you say—that at the time of inference for the sake of others, just as the probans (*liṅga*) is not understood by the person to be convinced when it is not stated by another, so too is the probandum (*sādhya*)—[that is incorrect].

In that case, this would be logical if he, having ascertained even the logical mark (*liṅga*) merely through the opponent's words, were to understand the probandum (*sādhya*) in accordance with it; for if we too desire to bring about the cognition of another, why should we not also employ a thesis-statement (*pratijñā*) devoid of the statement of the logical mark?
Because our own words alone would serve as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for him.
Because the cognition of the object to be inferred arises from that very [inference] itself;
and this is not the case,
since [the cognition occurs] even from our words— not only at the time of inference for oneself, as the word "even" (api) implies, but also without our words.
However, even when our statement is set forth, he does not even apprehend the logical mark (*liṅga*) from our words;
how much less will he follow it for the sake of establishing the probandum (*sādhya*)?
Rather, if that logical mark is established for him by himself through some means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then our statement merely serves to produce a recollection (*smṛti*) regarding it.
At that time, one understands the probandum by following the mark (liṅga) which is established for oneself;
one does not even drink water merely because of our word.
Therefore, what is the difference between these two states, consisting respectively of the statement and non-statement of the proposition (*pratijñā*)?
There is none at all, because in both cases the realization of the probandum (*sādhya*) occurs solely through the power of the probans (*liṅga*) as established for oneself.
Consequently, in both inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*) and inference for others (*parārthānumāna*), there is reliance upon the probans as established for oneself.

Therefore, since there is no difference regarding the cognition of the probandum, the presentation of the thesis (*pratijñā*) is indeed useless even in inference for others (*parārthānumāna*). For if the logical mark (*liṅga*) itself were not stated here, and the proponent were to recall it by himself as something previously established, why then would he employ the statement of the thesis, which expresses a doubtful matter?
It might be thought: "Even if the statement of the proposition (*pratijñā*) has no utility for the establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*), let there be no employment of it for that purpose;

nevertheless, its inclusion remains necessary for the sake of knowing the formal application (*prayoga*) such as that which possesses similarity (*sādharmyavat*), because there is no cognition of it otherwise. To this, he says: "And it is observed that there is cognition of the formal application such as that possessing similarity even without the statement of the proposition."
Consequently, even the presentation of a thesis for that purpose is not appropriate.
How much less, then, can there be comprehension from an application based on similarity (*sādharmyavat-prayoga*) and so forth in the absence of a statement of the probandum (*sādhya*)?
To this he says: "From the mere statement of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) and its connection [with the probandum]."
He thinks thus: indeed, no one remains after merely stating "whatever is produced is impermanent," for such a person would be defeated simply due to the deficiency of the proof;
rather, one must necessarily apply the reason to the subject (dharmin).
In that regard, if one were to say, "And sound is produced," then there is the comprehension of an application by way of similarity (*sādharmyavat*);

if, however, one were to state, "And it is eternal," then there is [the comprehension] of one by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmyavat*). Thus, from the statement of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) preceded by the statement of the relation, the two types of formal application are understood.
Even reasons that are contradictory or inconclusive are not recognized merely by the statement of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*).
However, when the statement of the [logical] connection is also made, how could there be a lack of recognition?
For instance, when the statement of the property of the subject—"whatever is produced is impermanent"—is uttered, the reason is understood.
When that which is being enjoined pervades that which is being restated—
as in the statement "whatever is produced is eternal"— it is contradictory,
because there is a pervasion by the opposite.
In the demonstration that "whatever is produced is immediately preceded by effort," there is the determination of inconclusiveness due to deviation.

Furthermore, the three-fold character (*trairūpya*) of the reason is indeed understood, because at the time of demonstrating pervasion (*vyāpti*), the pervading property (*vyāpaka-dharma*) is apprehended as the probandum (*sādhya*).

And where the pervaded property (*vyāpyadharma*) is subsumed under a subject (*dharmin*), that [subject], being understood as qualified by the pervading property (*vyāpakadharma*), is the "thesis" (*pakṣa*) because it constitutes a part of the totality of the probandum (*sādhyasamudāya*). Furthermore, that locus upon which the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the subsumed pervaded property is demonstrated is recognized as the "similar instance" (*sapakṣa*), an object similar by virtue of the generality of the property to be proven; thus, there is its presence in the similar instance (*sapakṣe sattvam*).

And by implication, wherever the cessation of the pervader is determined to entail the cessation of the pervaded, that is the "non-similar instance" (asapakṣa); thus, non-existence in the non-similar instance is also ascertained.
This is so provided there is some purpose in knowing the subject (pakṣa) and the other factors as well.
However, for those engaged in worldly discourse, the comprehension of an imperceptible object does not depend upon conventions such as the "subject" (*pakṣa*) and so forth.

For instance, in the world, the actual state of things is such that when something is observed in one place, it indicates another thing where there is an invariable connection (*pratibandha*) between them— provided one knows that connection—
and this process does not depend upon grasping conventions regarding the subject and the rest.
In that regard, let the authors of treatises formulate definitions according to their own conventions or otherwise, as they please, for the purpose of understanding the nature of the tradition;
however, at the time of practical usage, following such [definitions] is of no utility whatsoever.
However, it is precisely that form of the indicator as described—which is established by convention—that is useful for those engaged in practical discourse.

If that [form] is understood, the establishment of the probandum is accomplished by that alone; therefore, even if one is unaware of the conventions regarding the subject (*pakṣa*), the similar instances (*sapakṣa*), and so forth, nothing is lost.

For this very reason, the venerable Teacher stated: "The observation of an effect that is inseparable [from the probandum] is inference for one who knows it"—thereby demonstrating that the mere form of the indicator is independent of conventions such as the subject.
However, since some people there proclaim even non-existent defects due to their own intellectual failings, what can we say to them?

Therefore, for the sake of understanding the application of the *sādharmyavat* [inference] and so forth, the statement of the proposition (*pratijñā*) consists merely in the statement of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) and its connection [to the probandum].
Since comprehension occurs in the manner already described, the statement of a thesis (*pratijñā*) is improper; what utility, then, does it have? None at all.

Furthermore, this proponent, having bypassed the very sequence by which he himself has understood the object of inference (*anumeya*), resorts to a different sequence for the sake of convincing others; thus, by way of deceiving others, he is perceived as nothing but a rogue.
Demonstrating that he is not one who acts out of mere faith, he says: "Just as [one's own] certainty," and so forth.

Just as the production of certainty has been accomplished for oneself, in that very same way, the means (*sādhana*) is taught by those devoted to the welfare of others for the sake of producing certainty in others as well.

In this regard, since this principle holds true, even without the speaker himself presenting the object of cognition (prameya) through a statement that serves as a means of demonstration at the time of his own inference, he— while establishing the object of cognition for another who is in a state of doubt or the like— makes the other understand the very same object of cognition that he himself has realized.

Regarding the unprecedented [position]: at the time of one's own comprehension, one resorts to a sequence or means different from that which was previously experienced for the comprehension of the object of knowledge (*prameya*). What, then, is the reason for resorting to this alternative sequence here?
Nothing at all, except for the purpose of deluding others.

For instance: if the sequence of one's own realization is the basis for understanding, why abandon that and resort to another sequence? How could you have realized it by means of that [other sequence]?
Since this is so, there is no purpose whatsoever in stating the object of cognition (*prameya*), which is the probandum (*sādhya*), by means of what is called the thesis (*pratijñā*).
Why?
Because, as the conclusion states: "even otherwise" (*anyathāpi*), that is, even without that [statement], there occurs comprehension (*pratipatti*), meaning the realization of the probandum.
[286] He will establish—T.
[287] The mark—[§ 7. The non-membership of the application, conclusion, and so forth, in the syllogism as a means of proof.]

Having thus removed the thesis from the proof-statement, he says— extending the very same logic already stated— in order to remove other elements such as the application (*upanaya*) and the conclusion (*nigamana*) imagined by others from the proof-statement: "By this [logic], namely the principle that 'understanding arises even otherwise,' the application, the conclusion, and so forth (the inclusion of 'and so forth' referring to doubt, desire to know, etc.), have been answered and rejected."

In this context, the definitions of these two are as follows: "The application (*upanaya*) is the conclusion 'it is so' or 'it is not so,' depending on the example" [NSū 1.1.38], and "the conclusion (*nigamana*) is the restatement of the proposition (*pratijñā*)" [NSū 1.1.39].
As for the proposition, its definition is: "The proposition is the statement of what is to be proven" [NSū 1.1.33].

By the phrase "by this," he demonstrates exactly this: because the cognition of the probandum (*sādhya*) does not arise—i.e., its production is impossible—merely through the statement of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) and the relation [with the probandum], and thus lacking the application (*upanaya*) and so forth.
Here, the author of the *Uddyota* says: first of all, the thesis (*pratijñā*) must necessarily be stated for the purpose of indicating the object [of inference].
Since the world first examines the object to be cut and so forth,
and only thereafter employs the instrument such as an axe;

likewise, as long as the reason— whose capacity has been observed in the example— is not applied to the subject (dharmin) by means of the application (upanaya), how can there be any cognition of the probandum?
And by this, the meaning of the reflective cognition (*pratyavamarśapratyaya*) observed in inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*) is demonstrated.
For instance: in inference for oneself, one first perceives smoke in a location;
thereafter, one recollects the pervasion (*vyāpti*), thinking, "In whatever place I have seen smoke, there I have also seen fire."
Then one reflects again, "And here there is smoke"; that purpose of reflection is expressed by the *upanaya* (application) in an inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*).
Furthermore, the *nigamana* (conclusion) must also necessarily be stated.
For although it was previously stated that "sound is impermanent," certainty regarding this had not yet arisen;
now, however, the matter established by the force of valid cognition is concluded by this [conclusion] for the sake of its firm conviction.
Furthermore, by this [statement], the operation of all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is subsumed;
for the scripture (*āgama*) is the thesis (*pratijñā*),
and the reason (*hetu*) is inference (*anumāna*).

The example (*dṛṣṭānta*), perception (*pratyakṣa*), analogy (*upamāna*), and application (*upanaya*)—the operation of this entire fourfold set of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is concluded by the conclusion (*nigamana*). How, then, could this [conclusion] not be fruitful?
Anticipating this objection, he says: "Abandoning the passion for the *ḍiṇḍikas*—the *ḍiṇḍikas* being naked teachers—they [the conclusions] are fruitless above..."

Being preoccupied with writing names above [the lines], they are like those who, when another speaks, think: "I must certainly state something against him, even if it is improper and useless. Abandoning such misplaced persistence, close your eyes, withdraw external distractions, and consider this for a moment: what is achieved by merely stating the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) and its connection?
Is there cognition of the probandum through the statement or not?

For, to whatever extent we admit that only so much of the matter is to be expressed in an inference for others (*parārthānumāna*), to that same extent—neither less nor more—is it the cause of cognition even in an inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*). What contradiction of its capacity is there in this case?
For this reason, one would not even produce a cognition in the case of inference for others;
since cognition occurs when the existence [of the object] is understood, what is the use of this proliferation consisting of the thesis, application, and conclusion?

For instance, even in the formal employment of the proposition (*pratijñā*), the application (*upanaya*), and the conclusion (*nigamana*), if the probans (*sādhana-dharma*) were not pervaded by its own probandum (*sādhya*) as ascertained by valid cognition, or if it did not exist in the subject of the probandum (*sādhyadharmin*), then these [members] would certainly not function as causes for comprehension.

However, when that [pervasion and presence] is possible, then even in the absence of the proposition and so forth—as in the case of inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*)—comprehension is not prevented because the essential form of the indicator (*gamaka-rūpa*) is complete. Therefore, why this insistence on an irrelevant point?

For it is not logical that the ascertainment of the probandum (*sādhya*) should result from the mere statement of the proponent regarding the property of the means of proof (*sādhanadharma*), if that property lacks the capacity to imply the probandum;
for that would entail the consequence of the futility of adducing the reason (*hetu*).
Or, if that [reason] possesses the capacity to imply it, then the statement of the proposition (*pratijñā*) is likewise [redundant].

As for what was stated—that "the thesis (pratijñā) is for the purpose of indicating the object"—the author of the treatise himself has provided the answer: he who employs a proof does so only after having determined the object, thinking, "By means of this proof, I shall establish a cognition regarding this probandum. Thus, there is no transgression of worldly convention.

Otherwise, if the cognition of the probandum (*sādhya*) arises from the proof (*sādhana*), then that very proof must be defined as the object (*karman*). How, in the absence of such an object, could the establishment of the probandum in inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*) be dependent upon a proof?
Furthermore, how could one who has established the relationship between fire and smoke in the mind think, "Where is the fire? Where is the fire?"?

Thus, one seeks fire in a certain location and apprehends the fire merely from the sight of smoke; how, then, could there be a reflective cognition (*pratyavamarśapratyaya*) in the case of inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*)? If, on the other hand, that [fire] was sometimes seen there, and its inclusion [in the inference] is for the sake of another (*parārtha*), then why is the occasional consumption of curds and so forth not also included, since one might have apprehended fire from smoke even after having eaten curds?

Furthermore, regarding the statement that "the thesis (*pratijñā*) is scripture (*āgama*)," if the speech of the proponent himself were the scripture, then since the probandum would be established from that alone, the employment of the reason (*hetu*) and other members would be purposeless. Alternatively, if the thesis is called scripture because the meaning of the thesis is recited in scripture, [then...]
In that case, since it is not stated in any scripture that "there is fire in this place," how can the proposition (pratijñā) possess the status of scripture (āgama)? Furthermore,
it is also incorrect to say that "the reason (hetu) is inference" (anumāna),
for the reason is not merely the property of being present in the subject (pakṣadharmatva).
Because it possesses three forms [of cognition],
and because not every instance of an example (dṛṣṭānta) is perceptual (pratyakṣa), how could an "example" be "perception"?
Furthermore, analogy (upamāna) is not even a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
How could its function be subsumed by the conclusion (*nigamana*)?

Furthermore, if the reason whose capacity has been observed in the example must necessarily be applied to the subject (*dharmin*), then let that alone be the application (*upanaya*); what is the use of stating the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) as "because of being produced"?
That [application] itself will both subsume the reason whose capacity has been observed and demonstrate its presence in the subject; therefore, nothing is achieved by the [conclusion].

Therefore, since the initial employment of the proposition (*pratijñā*) is not even accepted there, how could its repetition constitute a conclusion (*nigamana*)? Thus he says: "Therefore, it is established that in a statement of proof (*sādhanavākya*), this much alone—the mere expression of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) and its connection [with the probandum]—is superior as the formal employment, and not that which consists of five members (*pañcāvayava*). [288] Proposition, etc.
[289] Of the reason; [290] when there is the possibility of pervasion and so forth; [291] the state of being a cause for cognition.
[292] Because it would follow that the introduction [of the reason] is useless; [293] the proof—
[294] seeing a place with smoke— T.
[295] Regarding inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*) [§ 8],
there is no fixed rule for the sequence of the statement of the reason (*hetu*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) within a syllogism (*nyāyavākya*).

In this context, regarding the proof-statement (*sādhanavākya*), not only is the employment of the thesis (*pratijñā*) and so forth inappropriate when accepted by another (*paropagata*), but there is also no fixed rule of sequence such as "the reason must be stated first and the example afterwards."
Nor is there anyone [who objects] here.

Why? Because whether the reason (*hetu*) comes first and the pervasion (*vyāpti*) afterwards, or the pervasion comes first and the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) is applied afterwards, it remains a means of cognition (*gamaka*) nonetheless.
[§ 9. Refutation of the Threefold Application of the Reason] But is it not said that its application is twofold?
For the Naiyāyikas maintain that the reason (*hetu*) is threefold: positive (*anvayin*), negative (*vyatirekin*), and both positive and negative (*anvayavyatirekin*).

Therefore, its formulation is threefold—by way of similarity, by way of dissimilarity, and by way of both similarity and dissimilarity—and this must be stated. To this he says: even when stating the [logical] connection, not only is a fixed order of sequence not appropriate, but there is also no difference in meaning between the two cases, because the three characteristics are present in both.
Therefore, every reason is indeed both positive (*anvayin*) and negative (*vyatirekin*); the point is that there is no such thing as a reason that is exclusively positive or exclusively negative.
Consequently, how could there be a threefold classification of formal application (*prayoga*)?
Thus he thinks.
Why, then, is there no difference in meaning?

If this is asked, he says: because in both cases—whether through similarity (*sādharmya*) or dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) in the formal argument (*prayoga*)—despite their being of the nature of affirmation and negation respectively...

Although a difference between the properties (*dharma*) is perceived, nevertheless, it is precisely the state of the probans (*sādhana-dharma*) being of the same nature as the probandum (*sādhya-svabhāvatā*) that is made manifest through the applications of similarity (*sādharmya*) and dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*).
Now, in the application of similarity, the existence of the probandum follows upon the existence of the reason (*hetu-bhāve*).
And in the case of dissimilarity (vaidharmya), the absence of the reason in the absence of the probandum is understood from the word [of the statement],
not identity (tādātmya). So why is it said, "because it manifests that very existence"?
Therefore, he says: "For not," and so forth.

If, in the formulation based on similarity (*sādharmya-prayoga*), the existence of that [probandum] were not implied by the existence of the [probans], then why would there be the existence of the probandum necessarily and invariably when the probans exists, even though the probans does not have that as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)?
Let it be, for all we know, merely occasional.

When the reason exists, the necessary concomitance (*ekāntabhāva*) of the probandum with it—expressed as "whatever is produced is impermanent"—is stated through the application of positive concomitance (*sādharmyaprayoga*).
Since this [concomitance] is not possible for that which is not a different entity without identity (*tādātmya*), it implies that [identity] by the force of the argument.
To the question, "How is it that the existence of another thing is not necessarily [present] when something exists that does not have its nature? he says: "Because of being produced," and so forth.

If, even in the absence of being immediately following effort (*prayatnānantarīyakatva*), the state of being produced (*kṛtakatva*) exists, then it lacks that intrinsic nature (*atatsvabhāvatva*); this same situation applies to impermanence (*anityatva*) as well.

Consequently, due to the lack of identity (*tādātmya*), there would be no positive concomitance (*anvaya*) of being immediately following effort with impermanence, nor would there be its cessation upon the cessation of the latter. How, then, could the one be understood from the other?
This is not a fault;

for since identity (*tādātmya*) exists there, positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*) are unimpeded with respect to the mere states of impermanence and being produced. However, it was stated that this [fire] lacks identity with respect to the mere state of being produced. Now, one might object: "Even when fire ceases, the cessation of smoke—which does not have that as its nature—is observed, and yet there is positive concomitance. To this, he says: "Of the effect" (*kāryasya*).
For the basis of positive and negative concomitance is the necessary connection (pratibandha),
because pervasion (vyāpti) consists of those two; in the absence of that [connection], those two [concomitances] would also be absent.

In that case, since smoke is a distinct entity from fire, there exists a connection characterized by its origination from that [fire], which serves as the basis for positive and negative concomitance; thus, those two [concomitances] may exist.
However, where those two are said to belong to what is not a distinct entity, the intention is that there must necessarily be identity (*tādātmya*).

An example of this is as follows: when these very two—being produced (*kṛtakatva*) and being immediately subsequent to effort (*prayatnānantarīyakatva*)—are reversed, there is no negation of one upon the negation of the other.
Exclusion of others (*anyanivṛtti*)— of the form: "That which is not immediately preceded by effort is also not produced"—

is such that, because this is so, there is necessarily the presence of the probandum when the reason exists, according to the definitions of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).

And since the absence of the reason is necessarily concomitant with the absence of the probandum, even a single [reason]— whether employed by way of similarity (*sādharmya*) or dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*)— implies the second; therefore,
because the three characteristics (*trairūpya*) are cognized in both cases, there is no need for a second verbal expression.

Regarding the statement "for the sake of another," even though the relationship [between the reason and the probandum] is being expressed, it is only the formulation (*prayoga*) that differs—whether by way of affirmation (*vidhimukha*) or negation (*pratiṣedhamukha*)—but not the meaning itself. Therefore, its establishment is twofold through formulation:
by way of similarity (*sādharmya*) and by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*).
However, it is not [differentiated] by similarity and dissimilarity themselves.

Because its meaning is revealed by either one alone, every logical reason is in reality both positive and negative; there is no such thing as a purely positive or purely negative reason. Concluding this, he says: "Thus, in a single proof-statement, it is not [expressed] either by way of the positive concomitance or by way of the negative concomitance."

The formulation of both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) is intended as their direct presentation by means of words; for there would be futility in making known what is already understood, as there is no purpose in communicating what has already been realized.
Clarifying that very realization of the other [concomitance] through the force of the meaning, he says: "By virtue of having that as its nature," and so forth.

If the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) of the reason with the probandum is established by virtue of its having that [probandum] as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), then for that very reason, its absence when that [probandum] is absent is also necessarily established;
for it is impossible for that which has that as its intrinsic nature to exist in the absence of that [probandum], since it would thereby lack selfhood (*nairātmya*).

Likewise, when the absence of the reason is established upon the absence of the probandum by virtue of its having that as its intrinsic nature, then for that very reason, the positive concomitance of the reason with the probandum is also established.

However, by those who explain it thus: "In a formulation based on similarity (*sādharmya*), the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is employed for the purpose of demonstrating a restriction— namely, that the absence of the reason (*hetu*) must occur only in the absence of the [property to be proven] in the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*),

and not elsewhere, lest there be the consequence of its absence in other dissimilar instances or in contradictory instances, and lest there be the consequence of exclusion from the contradictory alone."

That [interpretation] of its meaning is also untenable. Why? Because not only is the absence of that [property] the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), but even something else that is contradictory or possesses another property is the counter-example; for it is not merely that which does not serve as the locus of the intended property.
Or rather, it is only through the contradiction characterized by non-coexistence (*sahānavasthāna*) that something is a counter-example (*vipakṣa*),

and not through the characteristic of being established by mutual exclusion (*parasparaparihārasthita*). This is because the property of "producedness" (*kṛtakatva*) and so forth occurs in an object that possesses other properties such as impermanence and selflessness.
There would be the consequence of the absence of a logical reason (*hetu*).

Furthermore, when heat (*auṣṇya*) is to be proven, since fire is defined by its characteristic of heat, it would follow that fire is excluded from what is cold—which is indeed contradictory—rather than from anything else that is neither hot nor cold. Consequently, fire would not necessarily grasp [the property of] heat;
this would be its fault.

Regarding this, the Teacher said: "If the status of being a counter-example (vipakṣa) is desired for one [instance], then let it be desired for its very absence alone, and not for something contradictory or anything else;
for that [absence] exists elsewhere too—in things that do not serve as the locus for the property intended to be proven, as well as in things that are contradictory."
But for us, who accept all three types of counter-examples (*vipakṣa*),
the intended meaning is that there is no other [example] which does not serve as a substratum for the property in question; this is the sense of "exclusive existence" (*ekāntabhāva*).
Because impermanence exists even in the absence of being immediately subsequent to an effort,
[there is no pervasion between] the probandum and the reason.

but not from the intrinsic nature of all constituent factors.

[§ 10. The Proof of the Momentariness of the Nature of Sentient Beings:

If, in the case of a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*), the basis for the probandum being the very nature of the probans consists in positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), then this is expressed through either the positive or the negative formulation of the syllogism, whether characterized by similarity (*sādharmya*) or dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*).

When the implication of the other is stated by way of implying identity (*tādātmya*), then their being of that very nature (*tatsvabhāvatā*)—established by valid cognition—is the basis for that [implication], and not something perceived merely through words; with this intention, he says: "How is this...
and so forth, [explaining] "by which" means by the perishable nature of the existent.

The meaning is that the reason characterized by existence (*sattva*) has momentariness as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Furthermore, the intention of the questioner is this: here, existing things are of two kinds—produced things such as jars, and unproduced things such as space. Among these, those which are unproduced are eternal because they possess the characteristic of eternity, according to the Vaiśeṣika sūtra: "That which exists and is without cause is eternal" (VaiSū 4.1.1). Since they possess the characteristic of eternity, they are certainly not non-eternal; how much less could they be momentary?
Thus, there is no such thing as the momentary nature of a real entity (*sattva*).

Furthermore, even for those things that exist and are produced, since their destruction follows the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) with hammers and other such causes, destruction possesses a cause; therefore, in the absence of that cause...

Since destruction follows from that which is produced, even for an existent thing (*satva*), the nature of momentariness does not exist at all; thus, there is no possibility of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).
Furthermore, destruction must necessarily follow the positive and negative concomitance of causes such as a staff and so forth.
Because it is observed as such; for indeed—destruction does not enter into a state of association with pots and the like.

Furthermore, even elsewhere, it is accepted by the followers of the Sugata that the very conformity to positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) is the basis for the conventional usage of "having a cause."
"In that case, since this [logical connection] exists here as well, why is the conventional usage of that term not applied? [The opponent replies:

"But surely, by one who establishes the certainty of positive concomitance (*anvaya*), the fact of its being of that very nature was already demonstrated previously through the operation of subverting evidence (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*), based on such statements as: 'The certainty of positive concomitance also [occurs] in the case of an essential reason (*svabhāva-hetu*)'.
So how can there be any occasion for this prima facie objection?"

True; however, by the former teachers, when momentariness was to be proven for that which is produced (*kṛtaka*), it was stated—by means of a *prasaṅga*—that since opponents necessarily admit that produced things must have a cause-based destruction at their end, the proof of the impossibility of such a cause serves as the subverting evidence (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) against the contrary [position of eternal duration], thereby establishing identity (*tādātmya*) with respect to destruction. This was stated specifically regarding the characteristic of being produced.
This is presented as a prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) in order to demonstrate that existence (*sattva*) leads to the nature of that [specific thing] and not to anything else,

and also to elaborate upon what was previously stated— that the definition of "contradiction with causal efficiency" applies to all that exists— by means of the mere fact of being a real entity (*vastu*).
However, existence characterized by being uncreated is simply impossible.

Because a restriction of place, time, and intrinsic nature is impossible without a determining cause, the former teachers did not exert effort toward establishing its identity as that [nature], since its permanence—on account of the deficiency of even one of its factors—is like that of an existent which lacks a cause (as stated in Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 4.1.1: "That which exists and is without cause is eternal"). Thus, there is no possibility of its being eternal.
The author of the treatise, however, [argues] generally that all existence possesses a momentary nature;
and furthermore, even for that which has the characteristic of being produced,

and even for an entity remote in space, time, or intrinsic nature, its identity with that [momentariness] follows from the very state of things, by virtue of the contradiction with causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).

The opponent himself will demonstrate that destruction, which is necessarily admitted by the other [party], cannot be causeless because there would be no distinction [between things], resulting in the absurdity that everything perishes as soon as it has arisen. [336] [326] [327] The opponent alone.

[§ 11. An Examination of the Nature of Existence in Order to Refute Destruction with a Cause:

In this regard, the former masters have stated: "For everything that exists which is produced, there is necessarily at the end a destruction caused by a cause. Regarding that which is asserted by others, [the author] begins to demonstrate its independence [from causes] by stating:
"Because a cause for destruction is untenable."
If, then, there is no cause for destruction, from what does that inevitable destruction of those produced things arise?
For it is not logical that any intrinsic nature (svabhāva) should be accidental; thus he says: "by its very nature."
The word *bhāva* signifies a cause in the sense that "from this, an effect arises. Therefore,
things (*bhāvas*) arise within themselves from their own causes as perishable— that is, having a nature of perishing— and as non-abiding, like mustard seeds on the point of a needle.

For these entities that possess the characteristic of being produced and have arisen from their own causes, there is no production of destruction from anything else, such as an impact or the like. Why? Because that impact, fire-contact, and so forth—which are accepted as the causes of destruction—lack the capacity [to produce it].
For instance, at the time of contact with fire and so on, we perceive a triad.
That very same wood and so forth is the object of destruction; it becomes another state such as charcoal,
and its non-existence, characterized by the cessation of the wood and so forth, is of a void nature.

Beyond this, one need not consider any further operation of causes such as contact with fire; for regarding the nature of things, it is nowhere logical to attribute causal efficacy to a cause of destruction.
This is because a cause of destruction does not produce in a thing—such as fuel—which has arisen from its own causes with a stable form, a nature characterized by instability.
Why? Because that fuel and so forth are produced from their own causes alone.
For there can be no alteration in what has been produced with a stable nature; its very essence cannot be made otherwise.
Because if it were to arise later from another cause, it would follow that it is a different entity;
because it is impossible for that very same thing to undergo change;
and because it is impossible to conceive of the operation of a cause upon it [at that point].

Alternatively, when the triad is examined: as for that which is to be destroyed, such as wood and the like, the cause of destruction—namely, contact with fire and so forth—does not produce its very nature (svabhāva), because it has already arisen from its own causes;
thus, there is the state of having an unstable nature (asthirasvabhāvatā).
[338] There is no becoming otherwise for that which has not ceased; [339] a stable self;
[340] the state of being wood.
[§ 12. Examination of Kumārila’s Position on the Nature of the Other Entity (bhāvāntarasvabhāva):

Kumārila, however, maintains that it is not the very nature of the entity itself that is produced by contact with fire and so forth; rather, it is the non-existence through destruction (pradhvaṃsābhāva) of the fuel and so on.
And this [non-existence] is simply another subsequent entity, such as charcoal, which is devoid of the form of the fuel and so forth. As it has been said:
"The non-existence of milk in curd is characterized as non-existence through destruction" (ŚV,
Abhāva 3). And it is not at all contradictory to accept that such a form of non-existence possesses a cause.
And thus someone has said: "An entity devoid of any other entity is here considered a non-entity, like a non-perception; why then does that [non-entity] not arise from a cause?"
Refuting this view of the followers of Kumārila, he says: "Nor even... and so forth.
If the subsequent non-existence were merely another entity consisting of an effect, then [factors such as] contact with fire would be operative in the production of charcoal and the like.

This is indeed our desired position; however, if the production of a different state [of the fuel] were admitted, then since fire and the like would have no activity with respect to the fuel and so forth, the fuel and the rest would remain exactly as they were.

Consequently, just as there was the perception of the fuel and so forth prior to contact with fire, and a distinct purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) produced by it, so too there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of that same perception and so forth occurring even when charcoal and other products have arisen.

[Objection: But if the non-existence of destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*) is the nature of another entity (*bhāvāntara*), then when that [destruction] arises, fuel and so forth would have been destroyed; since they are then non-existent, how could there be the consequence of their being perceived in such a way? [Response: True. However, he thinks as follows: lest all other things, such as fuel or even a cow, likewise become non-existent, one must state the basis for establishing the destruction of charcoal and the like. Thus, the destruction of fuel and so forth is established by the arising of another entity, namely charcoal and the like. It is not that fuel and so forth do not exist at all; rather, they are said to be "destroyed" because they have undergone a transformation into another state. Therefore, the consequence of their perception does not follow. Furthermore, this is not a case of mere non-existence (*abhāvamātra*); rather, the destruction of fuel and so forth is established through the production of another entity, such as ash. Consequently, the objection that "if destruction were a positive entity, the world would be eternal" is refuted. This is because the world is impermanent due to the continuity of change (*anyathātva*). For example, just as milk becomes curd, gold becomes ornaments, and clay becomes pots, so too does fuel become ash. In this way, the world is impermanent because it undergoes transformation, yet it is not non-existent, because it exists in the form of another entity. Thus, the position is maintained. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the opponent’s view—that "the destruction of fuel and so forth is established by the non-existence of fuel and so forth"—is rejected. For if destruction were merely non-existence, then since non-existence is eternal, fuel and so forth would never cease to exist. Therefore, the destruction of fuel and so forth is established by the arising of another entity, such as ash. Hence, the world is impermanent because of its transformation, and it is not non-existent because it exists as another entity. This is the intended meaning.
