If you argue that "when that [fuel] exists, there is the cessation of that [fire]," oh,
what eloquence! For, since you do not accept that cessation has the nature of a non-entity (tuccha), you are merely calling that very other entity, such as the embers and so forth, "cessation."

Thus, this point is established: when there is the state of being charcoal and so forth, because of that state of being charcoal and so forth, the destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) of the wood and so forth is the charcoal and so forth.
Nor is there [simply] the existence of that [wood] while there is the state of being charcoal and so forth, because it is impossible for something to be a cause with respect to itself.

If it is argued that its nature is that of destruction because it arises from fire and so forth, and because the state of being charcoal and so forth occurs through the crushing of the fuel and so forth; [Response: ... [The text continues with the refutation of this argument].
What is this so-called "annihilation" (upamarda)?
If it were cessation, that would be characterized simply by the charcoal and so forth, and thus it would not differ from the previous state.
Therefore, wood and the like cease of their own accord.
However, it is more appropriate to hold that embers and so forth arise from fire and the like;
otherwise, why would it not follow that wood and other such things are likewise perceived [as arising]?

Furthermore, if non-existence as destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*) were a distinct entity, then for those things such as lamps or cognitions—which perish without having undergone any transformation—what distinct entity would their destruction be?
If it is argued that they too take as their objective support non-manifestation (*avyaktatā*), the personal existence (*ātmabhāva*), and transformation (*vikāra*) itself as destruction (*dhvaṃsa*),
we say no; for there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the existence of a non-manifest state that is a positive entity (*bhāvarūpa*) in the case of a lamp and the like.

For if "unmanifestness" (*avyaktatā*) were the attainment of the state of being a potentiality (*śakti*), then since the nature of a potentiality is inferred from the observation of its effect, how could lamps and the like be conceived as existing in the form of a potentiality in the absence of that effect?
Alternatively, if unmanifestness were the attainment of a nature devoid of the capacity for perception (*upalabdhi-yogyatā-vikalātmatā*),
even in this case there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for their existence in such a state.
The wise do not respect words that lack authoritative proof.
Since the self does not exist, how could there be the existence, modification, or transformation of cognition and the other faculties?
Because a refutation has already been established elsewhere, it is not discussed here; enough of this digression.
It might be thought: "Because fuel and the like are covered by another entity such as charcoal, their perception and so forth do not occur. To this he says: "Nor even," and so on.

It is also not tenable that another nature constitutes an obstruction for something else, such as fuel; for while that fuel remains in its original state with its form unaltered, an obstruction is impossible—not only because perception and the like would be precluded, but because the obstruction itself could not exist.
[341] — its non-existence is accepted — ŚlV [342] the lamp — [343] cognition.
[344] effects— [345] would be postulated— as having the nature of a self. [346] Selfhood.
[§ 13. Examination of the position that [destruction] is both an entity and a non-entity:

Not only is neither the intrinsic nature of an entity nor another entity produced by a cause of destruction, but even the non-existence of an entity is not produced; thus he says, "Nor... and so forth.
If one asks, "Why?"—

If one accepts that non-existence is an effect by means of a positive injunction (*vidhi*)— that is, through exclusion (*paryudāsa*) as something other than the intended existence— then does it consist of the very nature of fuel and so forth,
or is it a different entity?
For this cannot avoid the dilemma of being either distinct or non-distinct.
And the same fault has already been stated in that regard.

Now, it might be argued: "This [negation], being of the nature of a non-implicative negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*) and having the form of a mere void (*tuccharūpa*), is admitted to be produced by fire and so forth;
and since fuel and the like lack intrinsic nature (*naiḥsvābhāvya*) when that [negation] exists, how can there be any occasion for the aforementioned fault?"

And that [destruction] must necessarily be an effect of that [cause], such as fire, because it conforms to the presence and absence of that [cause]; for even in other cases, the linguistic convention regarding its existence is based upon that. As it has been said:
"When an existing entity has come within the range of cognition, it is not perceived while that [cause] is present.
How could an entity that perishes not have destruction as its effect?"
Just as an entity that did not previously exist comes into being through causes, so too, having come into existence, it does not continue to exist through causes. [349]
Thus [it is said].
Therefore he says: "The negation of existence," and so forth.

This is the intended meaning: if destruction were merely the passing away of a thing, consisting of a void (tuccha) that does not involve contact with another positive entity (bhāva), then the operation of causal factors (kāraka-vyāpāra) would not be possible therein, because [such an operation] pertains to that which has the nature of coming into being (bhavana-dharmin).

If it is argued that there is no contradiction in its being an effect because it arises from that [cause], since even that [cause] is admitted to come into existence after not having existed; we say no. For a thing whose nature is to come into existence attains the state of being an entity, and thus its status as a non-entity is lost.
Since that which "comes into being" is considered a "thing" (*bhāva*), there is no other ground for the application of the term "thing" even in the case of a sprout and so forth.
If it is argued that this ground is "the capacity for causal efficiency" (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*), [we reply:]...
If it is devoid of all causal capacity, how then can it be an object of cognition?
For that which is not a cause cannot be an object of cognition,
as this would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga).
Furthermore, how can there be an understanding of the causality, or even the reality, of that which is not an object [of cognition], such that it is said:
"That entity is indeed of the nature of a void"?
Or, if it does produce cognition, how is it not connected by way of causal efficiency (*sāmarthya*)?
If you ask, "How can that which is not the object of the cognition 'it exists' be an entity (*bhāva*)?",
then how can it also have the status of being an effect?
If it is argued that [the effect] exists because of its own cause, then how is it that it lacks the status of being an object for the cognition of existence? For instance:
if it exists because of its own cause...
It would be perceived as "existent," and so forth;
for the wise say that what exists is "existent. Yet it neither exists nor comes to be.

If it is argued that the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) is some distinction among the referents of words such as "existence" (*bhāva*) and "non-existence" (*asan*), [we reply: no, for that [distinction] exists only by way of having non-existence as its nature. If this is said, [we reply: no.
Because it is contradictory:
since that which does not exist is called "non-existence," how can it be designated as "existing"?
If you argue that it is not an entity because it does not appear within its own cognition in any established form, [we reply:]...
If it is argued that there would follow the consequence of the non-existence of the eyes and so forth, which are entirely beyond the senses,
because they appear in the form of causes for cognition— [we reply: no,
because this [cognition] also appears in the form of something that possesses an existent nature.
And how can there be a connection between the exclusion of all forms (*sarvarūpaviveka*) and existence (*bhūti*)? For existence is indeed the emergence of something in some form;
for this [exclusion] as well, it is identical in its appearance as an object of cognition and as having that [existence] as its causal nature.
Furthermore, it is impossible for that which is causeless to be an object of cognition.
For us, however, cognitions of non-existence are indeed devoid of an object, as they arise from the maturation of their own latent predispositions (*vāsanā*).
Moreover, if non-existence were itself an existing entity, how could the negation by way of exclusion (*paryudāsa*) be distinguished from the absolute negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*)?

If it is argued that it is distinguished by exclusion (*paryudāsa*) through the affirmation of a non-existent form, we say no; for a non-existent form is contradictory to coming into being (*bhavana*). Indeed, "it comes into being" is connected with *bhūti*, which is existence (*sattā*).
In that case, how could there be a positive injunction (*vidhāna*) of something possessing a real nature (*sadrūpa*)?
For the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) would have to be exclusively a preclusion (*paryudāsa*),
because in all instances an injunction is primary.
Or rather, it might not exist at all.
For if something were to be excluded from anything, then it would be touched by that which is distinct from it through the process of exclusion;
and that is not the case.
When it is said that "cessation occurs everywhere," this is because some other entity is being enjoined;
likewise, by this [statement], only another entity would have been expressed,
not the distinction between those two.
Moreover, in the case of non-discrimination (*aviveka*), there can be no exclusion (*paryudāsa*);
it would also result in the mention of something irrelevant,
because while the cessation of existence (*bhāva*) is the subject at hand, what is being enjoined is simply another entity that is non-existent in nature.
Nor does it have the nature of non-existence in its own form (*svarūpa*), because for that which is non-existent even in its own form, there is a contradiction with being an effect.

As for being non-existent in the form of another (*pararūpa*), every entity whatsoever has that nature; thus, there would be no distinction between this [pot] and others such as a jar. Or, let this non-existence be distinct from fire and so forth; even so, why [does it not arise] when those [causes] are present?
Why are wood and the like not perceived?

For if it were so—that is, because fire and the like have already fulfilled their purpose in another action—then fuel and the like would continue to be perceived as before, even after [the fire] has ceased from them.
By that very suppression...
If it is argued that [the destruction] arises from destruction, how can there be its sublation?
Certainly not by means of a subsequent non-existence (pradhvaṃsābhāva).
Because it does not exist at the time when the fuel exists;
nor by fire and the like,
since their operation is admitted to consist solely in the manifestation of destruction.
Furthermore, the non-existence through destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*) that has arisen does not destroy fuel and so forth,
because that would entail the consequence of simultaneity; and even if destruction were to effect the annihilation, the threefold dilemma remains exactly as it was.
Furthermore, this leads to an infinite regress.
If it is argued that cessation is simply that very destruction of fuel and so forth produced by fire and the like, and therefore its non-perception follows from this, [we reply: no.
How could one thing be the cessation of another? For that would lead to an over-extension of the principle.
Furthermore, if this [self] were possessed of causes, why does it not undergo a differentiation of its own nature according to the differentiation of those causes?

Even sprouts of rice, barley, and so forth, while experiencing a difference in their own nature that is absolutely distinct due solely to a difference in their causes, are determined by direct perception itself.
However, destruction—which is characterized merely as the passing away and does not depend on contact with any other entity—is not like this;

for even when there is a difference in its causes, such as striking or contact with fire, it appears within its own cognition as having a single form, owing to its nature as a mere non-entity (*tuccharūpa*).
For we do not perceive any form there other than the emptiness of existence;
and since this has been examined in detail in the *Kṣaṇabhaṅgasiddhi*, let it rest for now.
Therefore, at the time of contact with fire and so forth, nothing happens to that [entity]; rather, it is simply correct to maintain that it no longer exists.
For this [entity] is not said to have "perished" by virtue of becoming something else; rather, because it itself was unstable by nature, it is called "perished.
Consequently, neither its non-existence nor anything else comes into being.

And likewise, since there is no such thing as something possessing the nature of coming into being (*bhavana-dharman*), fire-contact and the like cannot produce an entity that is already in the process of becoming; thus, for fire-contact and so forth, there would be a mere negation of action.
This being the case, fire-contact and the like do not act as agents; and since that which is not an agent is not a cause, there is therefore no cause whatsoever for destruction—namely, fire.

[348] The existence [349] of fire and so forth is [350] the ground for the application of the term "existence. If non-existence also possesses causal efficacy (*sāmarthya*), then it would possess the nature of existence; if it does not, then [the author] says:
[351] Of general terms such as "existent" (*sann iti*);
[352] by means of the eyes and so forth;
[353] Brahmins and so forth (first marginal note).
The kṣatriya— [in the case of the second dual]—
is that which is to be excluded from the void-like form.
[§14. The impossibility of a cause for destruction even on account of its pointlessness:
Not only is a cause for destruction impossible due to lack of efficacy, but it is also impossible due to its pointlessness.

He says this very thing: if [a thing] is perishable by its own nature—that is, having the habit of perishing, unable to remain stable within itself, like a mustard seed on the point of a needle—then for it there is no need for causes of destruction.
Why?
Because of that very nature; because of its very nature of instability.
For indeed, effort toward making a mustard seed stay upon the point of a needle would not be fruitful if it were impossible for it to stay there by its very nature.
In this very context, he demonstrates the pervasion (*vyāpti*) with the words "for whoever," etc.
Furthermore, when that state exists—that is, when it possesses that intrinsic nature—it does not depend on another cause from the cause that produced it.
The passage beginning with "For illumination and so forth" provides an explanation of the example.
By means of a proof that establishes identity (*tādātmya*), it demonstrates the pervasion (*vyāpti*) through the fact that being of that nature does not depend on any other cause:
for whatever is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of something, if that intrinsic nature were to lack identity with it while depending on another cause, [it would be contradictory].
For if that which has arisen from its own cause were to lack that very nature, it would follow that selflessness (nairātmya) is itself devoid of intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāvatā).

Just like luminosity and so forth, it does not, however, require another cause for its subsequent state of being of that nature—that is, for its nature as having the property of non-abiding; this is the fruit of valid cognition (pramāṇaphala). If it has the property of non-abiding, that is, if it has a perishable nature (naśvarasvabhāva), [then it follows].
"A thing is produced by its own causes as an intrinsic nature" is the application of the property to the subject (*pakṣadharmopasaṃhāra*).
This is an observation of what is pervaded by the contradictory (*viruddhavyāptopalabdhi*),
because dependence on other causes and independence [from them] are characterized by mutual exclusion.

Because of contradiction, and because its nature as such is pervaded by the non-dependence upon any other cause; [§15. Dispelling the fault of inconclusiveness regarding the reason proving inherent perishability].
Anticipating an opportunity for an opponent’s objection here, he says: "Like seeds, etc. (8.16), and so forth.
He analyzes this very point with the words "It might be so," etc., stating that [the causes] do not produce [the effect] alone.

If one asks why, it is because even seeds and the like— which possess the nature of producing sprouts and so forth— depend upon water, earth, and other factors distinct from their own causes for that causal capacity.
Furthermore, since they do not require any other cause for that state [of destruction], there is no inconclusiveness [in the reason].

Similarly, the case of fuel and so forth—the subject of the analogy—is that even though it has been produced from its own causes as having a perishable nature, it would possess that very perishability at the time of its destruction; this is the application of the example.
Thus, there is no inconclusiveness, as in the case of seeds and the like.
Why is this so? Because that which has the nature of producing a sprout and so forth—namely, the seed and the like—produces the sprout and so forth;

and because, in its being of that very nature, it does not depend on any other cause. Furthermore, that which, while depending on soil and other factors, does not produce [the result] when in a state such as being inside a granary, lacks that nature; that is to say, it lacks the nature of producing a sprout and so forth.
In that case, since the reason characterized as "having that nature" (tadātmatā) does not exist at all, there is no inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*) on its account.
[§16. Due to sublation by perception, identity is not established through recognition.
Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that by the very perception of recognition, the seed and so forth are observed to possess a single, identical nature?"
In that case, from where does this distinction— characterized by having the nature of producing or not having the nature of producing— arise,
such that there would be no inconclusiveness?
Furthermore, recognition is not invalid.

In this regard, because it possesses the defining characteristics of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)— such as being a cognition of an object not previously known— and because it arises from the contact of the sense faculties with an existing object, recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) is indeed direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Furthermore, there is no means of knowledge more authoritative than direct perception.

Anticipating the objection that this [inference] would be invalid because its object is sublated by the establishment of a difference [between the two states], he says: "For this very reason"— that is, precisely because of the contradictory properties of being a producer and a non-producer— "a real difference," meaning a difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), between "those two states"— namely, the states of being a producer and a non-producer— of the seed and so forth, must be ascertained and determined.

For just as a rice seed is understood through direct perception to have the nature of producing that [rice] sprout— because when it exists, the production of a rice sprout is observed— and a barley seed is understood to lack that nature— because when it exists, no rice sprout is perceived, being apprehended by a direct perception that grasps the barley seed as distinct from it;

likewise, why is it not determined here, in these two states, that the rice seed has the nature of producing its own sprout or not producing it, solely by the power of direct perception grasping those states as distinct from or non-distinct from the sprout?
If it is argued that while a difference between the two states is indeed accepted, there is no difference in the possessor of those states, we say: no.
For that would entail the undesirable consequence that the possessor of the states would appear in perception by way of another form distinct from the forms of the states.
Indeed, it is not logical for something to be perceptible if it does not appear in its own cognition as distinguished from the form of what is not itself.

If it is argued that since there is no difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) between the state (*avasthā*) and that which possesses the state (*avasthātṛ*), how can there be an appearance under a different form?

Well then, for one whose distinct form has not been acquired from the states, non-difference from the self is not tenable when there is a difference in the states—just as in the case of the states themselves.
Consequently, for this [self] which experiences a difference in its own essence just like the states, how can it possess the status of being the substratum (*avasthātṛ*)?

If it is argued that there is no fault because, even though there is a difference in states, the entity remains of an undifferentiated nature and is established as such, and because some kind of difference exists [between them], then: if this very self is placed before us and it is said, "This is the substratum of the states, and these are the states," then there is indeed a difference between the substratum and its states; in that case, to say "in some way" (*kathañcit*) is merely a word in the air.
Consequently, even when it is perceived directly, the consequence that it must appear as a distinct form differentiated from the nature of non-self does not cease.
Or, if there were non-difference from that [non-self] nature; [357]
If it is argued that, just as there is the consequence of difference for the substratum [of states],
so too there is the consequence of non-difference for the states;
or, if it is argued that even those two possess difference and non-difference in some respect.
In that case, for those two—the state and the possessor of the state—which possess difference, some other form must be admitted as the cause of their partial non-difference.
And likewise, that [other form] must also have a partial difference from them;

otherwise, because it would be absolutely non-different from them due to having a single nature, it would follow that the state and the possessor of the state are respectively absolutely different and non-different from one another.
If there were some kind of difference in the form itself, then another form would be the basis for that, and yet another for that as well;
thus, an infinite number of forms would necessarily result for each single entity.
And we do not experience a perception that manifests an infinite number of forms.
And how, not experiencing [these states], could we deceive ourselves by imagining them through mere conceptualization?

Therefore, because that which has reached the conditions for perception is not perceived when distinguished from the nature of its states, and because it would follow that it possesses an infinite number of forms, the substrate of the states—which possesses both difference and non-difference in some respect—is simply non-existent;
furthermore, those states possess a distinction in their intrinsic natures as being productive or non-productive.

Since things are understood through direct perception itself, how could recognition—which determines their identity—be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) when it experiences contradiction from that very [perception]?

For, even though seeds and the like possess the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of producing sprouts and so forth, if they were to depend on other causes for that very essence, then the previous reason would become inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). Or, let there be some persisting entity; [nevertheless...]
This very point establishes the difference between those two as well.
For instance, the phrase "of those two states—the productive and the non-productive" is a locative dual.

Thus, the meaning is this: there is a difference, that is, a diversity of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-nānātva*), in the entity characterized as the subject (*dharmin*) between its productive state and its non-productive state; for this very reason.
Precisely because its nature as producing or not producing [a cognition] is determined by perception,
a conventional usage characterized by certainty must be established therein,
since the object is seen to be characterized by the superimposition of contradictory properties.
Nor can it be argued that only the states possess the nature of producing the sprout and so forth, while the substratum (the entity itself) does not;
for that would entail the non-existence of the substratum, characterized as it is by a total absence of all causal capacity.

Therefore, the recognition of entities as having a single form contradicts the evidence of perception—which establishes the distinction between the natures of being a producer and a non-producer at earlier and later times—and is thus sublated by experience.

How indeed could it be a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*)? If that which appears [in consciousness]—possessing an undifferentiated form—is unreal, then even for one who experiences a state arising from the sense faculties, there would be an absence of being born from the contact with an existent object (*satsamprayogaja*); consequently, how could it have the status of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), like the cognitions of those suffering from ophthalmia and the like? Furthermore, apart from the nature based on causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), there exists no other ultimate intrinsic nature (*paramārthataḥ svabhāva*) for seeds and so forth.
Since the realization of which would constitute recognition as a valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa)—
given that ultimate reality is characterized by the capacity for causal efficiency (arthakriyāsāmarthya)—

therefore, this determination of identity (tattvādhyavasāya) must be understood as purely erroneous, based solely on the production of a subsequent similar state, like the case of hair, plantain stalks, or pillars, for those whose hearts are captivated by mere similarity of form.

Therefore, although there is indeed a moment-by-moment difference in existent things, it is not perceived by the ignorant. However, when there arises the production of a dissimilar subsequent state due to the occurrence of adverse conditions, then the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) that determines its identity does not rely upon its actual existence.
Nor is there any other similarity [between the two moments] than the fact that they produce a single conceptual cognition (*parāmarśapratyaya*) of the same form.

Furthermore, although there is no difference in their being distinct entities, by virtue of their own causes and due to the influence of their specific nature (*prakṛti*), only some— and not others— perform a purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) characterized either by a single uniform conceptual cognition or by the cognition of an object and so forth; this has been explained in detail by the author of the treatise in the *Pramāṇavārttika*, and thus it is not elaborated upon here.

[358] Otherwise, absolute difference and non-difference would result in a separate entity.

[361] Direct perception; [362] form, light, and so forth.
[§ 17. Furthermore, because recognition is sublated by inference, a stable existence is not established on its basis.]

And in order to demonstrate that one must necessarily understand the aforementioned difference between the states of being a producer and a non-producer regarding seeds and so forth, he states an inference that subverts their non-difference: because there is no alteration in the nature of entities such as seeds—which is the very nature that produces its own effect—when those [conditions] are present. [8]

[21] Because it is impossible for that which has the nature of a non-producer to ever become a producer, there would follow the consequence that a thing possessing the nature of producing a sprout and so forth would produce its own effect even earlier— during its stay in the granary and such— just as it does later when the causes such as water are present.
For instance, even when water and other conditions are present, the seed and so forth perform their function by means of their very own nature alone.
Not by means of another's form;
and if that intrinsic nature (svabhāva) which produces its effect at that time also existed previously, [then it would have produced it then as well].
In the recognition "this is that very same thing," because there is a determination of the non-difference from its former nature of the causal essence present before one, [the opponent asks]:
"What follows from this? Why should it not produce that effect even previously?
The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whatever has the nature of producing something at a certain time, that necessarily produces it at that time.
Because it is contradictory for that which is not a producer to have the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of being a producer;
or else, because anything else would also incur the status of having that same intrinsic nature—
just as, for example, that very seed and so forth [become producers] at the time of the proximity of water and other conditions.

Furthermore, even in states such as being within a granary, this seed and so forth is established by recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) as having precisely the nature of producing its own effect; thus, there follows the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of it being a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
Yet, it does not produce [the effect].
Therefore, it does not have that nature of production.

The application by way of contrapositive (*viparyaya-prayoga*): Whatever, at whatever time, does not produce the effect that is to be brought about by its nature of producing it, does not have that nature of producing it at that time; for example, a *kodrava* seed which does not produce the effect to be brought about by its nature of producing a rice sprout.

Furthermore, prior to the proximity of causes such as water, the seed and so forth do not produce their own effect—which is brought about by the nature of producing that effect—due to the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*). Therefore, how can recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), since it experiences sublation even by inference?
[Objection: But surely, since the inference being sublated by this [recognition] lacks validity, how can it possess the power of sublation?
Since its status as a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) is not established, how could there be sublation?
Nor is there any mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*),
for this inference does not become a valid means of cognition simply because recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) is not a valid means of cognition.
However, this is due to the obstruction of its own probandum;
and that [obstruction] is ascertained by the force of a subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) in the case of the contrary. [363] And [the phrase] "of rice and so forth" — T.
[364] By means of recognition [365] the reply [§ 18.
Refutation of the superiority of perception over inference].
If it is argued that there is no means of valid cognition more authoritative than perception, we say: no;
for the status of recognition as perception is not established.
We do not claim that this [recognition], being of the nature of perception, is sublated by inference.
And what constitutes the superiority of perception (*pratyakṣa*)?

For it is called a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because it does not exist when its object is absent; and this is the same for inference (*anumāna*) as well, since it is produced by a mark (*liṅga*) that is invariably connected to the object. Thus, there is no distinction between them.

Furthermore, if recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) were a valid cognition even while falling into contradiction with inference, then why would the cognition of a blue flower and others—which perceives their identity due to the similarity of their forms—not also be a valid cognition?

For the distinction inferred from the observation of effects such as flowers and fruits does not experience that state through direct perception. Furthermore, the detailed refutation of the validity of recognition has already been established in the *Kṣaṇabhaṅgasiddhi*; let this matter rest for now.

Since, in the manner thus described, there is a real difference (*vastubheda*) between the states of being a producer and a non-producer in the case of seeds and the like, therefore, that other specific state (*avasthāviśeṣa*) following which the production of effects such as sprouts occurs—
That very [seed] possesses the nature of producing a sprout,
because the nature of producing that [sprout] is inferred from the observation of the effect.
If, then, that very [seed] possesses the nature of producing a sprout,

Since the preceding distinct states do not possess the nature of producing that [effect], how can they be designated as its causes, or why would those seeking a sprout take them up? To this he says: "But the preceding ones" refers to the specific states existing during the time of abiding in the granary and so forth, which [lead to] the final specific state that is the cause of the sprout.
The causes [are so called] because, through a succession of specific qualities imparted by other conditions, the effect arises from them;
therefore, they are designated as "causes" by way of metaphorical usage, and they are taken up by those seeking the sprout.
For the production of that which has such a nature, such as the seed, does not depend on any other cause.
And that which does not produce [an effect] while depending [on other conditions] does not possess the nature of producing it.
Therefore, the conclusion is that there is no inconclusiveness (*anaikānta*) regarding the reason "because of having that nature," as in the case of seeds and so forth.

Thus, when recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) is asserted by others as a means of valid cognition (*pratyakṣapramāṇa*) for the sake of establishing stability, we demonstrate its inconclusiveness by means of examples such as seeds.

At that time, because it is sublated by both perception and inference in the manner already stated, its identity [with the seed] does not exist; how, then, could there be oneness among entities from which non-absolutism (*anekānta*) might follow? This has been established. However, when others assert as a reason that seeds and so forth possess a single nature across prior and subsequent times because they are recognized through recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), [the following applies]:
In that case, this reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddha*).

Nor does it subsist anywhere within the subject (*pakṣa*), as he says: "Because unity is absent in things (*bhāva*) which we maintain to be momentary (*kṣaṇika*). This is the connection [of the argument].
[366] *Girikāntaka*-... *kanni*...?
[§19. Removal of the fault of inconclusiveness (anaikānta) regarding the argument "because they have that as their intrinsic nature" (tatsvabhāvatvāt):

Now, even for one for whom entities are momentary, although seeds and the like lack identity from moment to moment, because no distinction is perceived, all of them—even those whose intrinsic nature is to produce [the sprout]—would depend upon water and other conditions with respect to that production, just like the final moment.

Anticipating the objection that this remains inconclusive (*anaikāntikatva*), he says: "There is no inconclusiveness even with respect to momentary things, because of their arising from various successive conditions. Since momentary things arise at every moment from distinct and successive conditions, they possess different capacities; thus, like the final moment, they lack the nature of being producers [of a single effect]. How then could there be a non-differentiated nature for those whose births are conditioned by a diversity of causes?
For it is not logical that there should be an undifferentiated nature when specific differences are not perceived, even though the births are produced by a variety of causal factors.
Because if they did not conform to the distinctions among causes, it would follow that they are causeless;

as he will state: "Although conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), which possess distinct potencies at every moment through their conjunction with successive conditions, appear to be of identical form due to some degree of similarity, nevertheless, their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is indeed distinct."
"Therefore, something is the cause of something else.

Regarding the statement, "Because it produces that which has such an intrinsic nature," the opponent speaks in order to demonstrate its inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*): "Those [factors] such as the seed, soil, and so forth, being 'final'—that is, occurring at the end—are each individually capable of producing the sprout; for an effect does not arise from causes taken in fragments."
If you maintain that [causes] produce [the effect] individually, why do they not each produce it on their own?

Consequently, among these [causes], only one certain one would produce the sprout, while the others, though possessing that same nature, would not produce it; thus, the argument "because of producing that nature" is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

The opponent thinks: "In the same way, even seeds and so forth in states such as being inside a granary, although they possess the nature of producing sprouts and so on, will not produce them; thus, the inconclusiveness (*anekānta*) remains exactly as it was. To this, he says: "Since you think thus, and because the opponent has stated it by means of a general term, he replies with a general answer: (1) they certainly do produce [them]; (2) in this regard, regarding the production of their own effect, there is no possibility of a change in state (*anyathābhāva*), nor should non-productivity be suspected."
Why? Because intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is non-deviant.
For if they did not produce [an effect], they would not possess the very nature of production.
Since they are accepted as having that nature, they necessarily produce [the effect].
And thus, how can there be an inconclusive [reason]? This is the sense.

[§ 20. Having raised the objection that if an effect is produced by the capacity of one alone, others would be of no use, this is the rebuttal thereof: If the final [causes] were to produce [the effect] individually, then since the effect would be produced by one alone, the utility of the others would be rendered objectless.

Thinking that there is indeed no production [of the effect], the opponent says: "While those final auxiliary causes— being simultaneous in their operation, possessing a capable nature, and being admitted as fit for the performance of that effect— are present, what is the use of another [cause], since the effect has already been produced by one alone?"
Not at all anyone [does so].
Why then is it said that "they indeed produce"?
He answers this: "Indeed not"—there is certainly no such thing as acting with foresight, that is, acting with prior deliberation, on the part of entities such as seeds and the like.

For, because they act with foresight, others might withdraw after reflecting: "Since even one among us is capable of producing this effect, what is there for us to do here? Thus, adopting an attitude of indifference, they would not exert themselves toward the production of that effect.
Because those entities such as seeds and so forth possess operations devoid of intentionality— operations empty of deliberation— they all participate in the production of a single effect;
and with respect to an effect whose nature is to come into being, their operation consists solely in their prior existence.

For if the operation were indeed something entirely distinct from the active entity, then since the effect would arise from that [operation] alone, the status of being an agent would be lost to the possessor of the operation.
If it is argued that "this is its operation, and therefore it possesses the status of an agent," then surely,
because the application of the operation is metaphorically attributed to that which does not actually contribute to the effect, its ultimate status as an agent would be forfeited.
And what is its connection with its operation? If it is inherence (*samavāya*), no;
for that has already been refuted.

Furthermore, if [an entity] possesses activity through inherence (*samavāya*), then it would follow that even another entity which is not conducive to that effect would possess that state [of activity], because inherence—which is the cause of the cognition "it is here"—is uniform everywhere due to its oneness.
If it is argued that there is no such over-extension (atiprasaṅga) because the activity of that [effect] is produced only by that which is intended and is itself active; [we reply:]...
But surely, it is said that its production therein occurs precisely because of inherence (*samavāya*);
and that [inherence] is the same everywhere.
Why then does it not produce the effect itself by means of that very exertion through which it produces the operation?
That by which an intervention is resorted to;
and how this [cause] produces an operation merely by its own presence and not by another operation,
because that would lead to the fallacy of infinite regress.
Likewise, it has already been stated that the effect [arises] from that very same [cause].

Therefore, the operation of the cause consists precisely in the prior existence of the effect when that effect is yet to come into being. And since that [prior existence] belongs to all [causes], they are all designated as being "active" in the production of the effect.
That effect also arises from all [causes] together, because the existence of that [effect] follows precisely from the existence of all [the causes].
For there is no other birth for an effect apart from the very existence of what is considered its cause.
If it were otherwise, since the causal operation would occur in that [cause] alone, the production of the effect by them [all together] would be impossible.
And therefore, even though the causes are present, how could there be its existence or perception?
If it is argued that this is because it produces an arising related to those [causes], we say no;
for it is impossible for that which is non-existent to enter into a relationship with them.
Alternatively, if existence were inherent in itself (*svata eva sattve*), then the purpose of birth would be untenable.
Furthermore, since the self (*ātman*) which is perceived at the time of birth must have existed previously as well, it would follow that it should have been perceived then too;
if it existed in another form, it could not be said to exist [as that same self].

Since the distinction between entities is characterized by the distinction between their forms, that which has the nature of perception must be non-existent prior to its arising, because it is not perceived. Therefore, how could it have a connection with arising?
Therefore, since the effect itself, having previously not existed, comes into being through the state of the cause, its birth is indeed from that [cause]; thus, it is produced from all [the causes].

If it is argued: "But since even a single one has the capacity to produce it, the operation of the others—characterized by their mere presence—is entirely redundant; therefore, the existence of the others there is not logically consistent," he says: "[It arises] from its own cause, characterized as the totality of earth, seed, water, and so forth."

Transformation (*pariṇāma*) is the production of a subsequent moment that possesses a specific quality conducive to the arising of the effect and has had an excellence (*atiśaya*) imparted to it at every moment. Therefore, those things which possess the property of proximity (*upanidhi*), meaning their presence at the location of the effect, being thus situated at the location of the effect, do not deserve censure—[namely: "Since even a single one of you is capable of producing this effect, why are you all present here?"
Thus, they do not deserve further questioning.
For it is not possible for even a single one of them to exist there without the presence of the others.
Why? Because "it has that as its nature" (*tatprakṛti*); this is an expression emphasizing the state of being (*bhāvapradhāna*).

Since each individual capable [cause] has as its nature that which is produced through the transformation of a totality (sāmagrī) consisting of earth, seed, water, and so forth, how could there be the occurrence of it in isolation? This is because the various distinct causes denoted by the term "totality" initiate other specific, capable particular characteristics (sva-lakṣaṇa).

Consequently, because an excellence is being added at every moment, there arises a production [of the effect]; and because isolated [causes] lack the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) for producing that [effect], since they possess an intrinsic nature produced through connection with other conditions, the cause is incapable of producing [the effect]. This point will be clarified in various places as the occasion arises.

Therefore, whatever entity has a nature produced by a specific causal complex (*sāmagrī*), that entity cannot occur even if one [factor] is absent due to the deficiency of a cause; thus, the coexistence of those things born from a single complex is necessary. Since the effect exists only when all of them exist, all of them indeed produce it. Thus, there is no inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*) regarding the statement "because of the production of that nature.
Revealing the intention with which he asked, "Why do those final [causes], being capable, not produce [the effect]?", he says: "Being capable," and so forth.
The proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādin*) also demonstrates the intention behind his statement that "[they] indeed produce [the cognition]," by saying "not,
in that very case," and so forth.
He explains this very point with the words "of that very [cognition]," and so forth.

The intended meaning is this: "This is capable here; this is incapable"—this is determined through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), which are established by perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*), because there is no other cause for such determination.

Furthermore, since those positive and negative concomitances (*anvaya-vyatireka*) are observed in relation to one and the same effect, and not with respect to various different ones, they are understood to be capable of producing that single effect alone; thus, there is no production of various other things.
Now, when those [causes] are seen producing [the effect], are they of a nature to produce it at that very moment, or were they already so even previously?
Regarding this, there is a dispute:

since they possess that same nature even prior [to the production], there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of their being produced even before, just as they are after; thus, a difference at every moment is asserted.
This explains the phrase "they would cease."
