[§ 21. By those who accept that a difference in the effect arises from a difference in the cause—the Kṣapaṇakas and Jaiminīyas—there is the raising of the charge of inconclusiveness (anaikāntya).
Furthermore, the Kṣapaṇakas and Jaiminīyas, raising the charge of inconclusiveness in another way, say: "It is distinct."
When a single effect characterized as consciousness arises from multiple cooperative causes— such as the eye and so forth— which possess mutually exclusive natures and act simultaneously,

then since there are many causes of distinct natures while the effect is a single entity of non-distinct nature, there would be no differentiation in the effect resulting from the differentiation of the causes.
Therefore, the eye and the other [senses] should not be accepted as the producers of a single effect through their own distinct natures;
rather, one must admit that they possess a common nature (*sāmānya*) which is non-distinct and produces that single effect, by means of which they generate the non-distinct effect.
And that [nature] produces the effect only when they are in a state of completeness (*samagrāvasthā*), not when they are in a state of separation (*vyagrāvasthā*).
Nor does its absence follow from the absence of each individual [cause],
because it is contradictory for that which has the nature of a universal (sāmānyātman) to ever be non-existent;
nor, at that time, does it possess a nature that is non-productive.

Because it would follow that there is a distinction between its states when all [causes] are present and when they are not, even though it possesses the same form whether it is a producer (*janaka*) or a non-producer (*ajanaka*).
And thus, there would be a loss of its nature as a universal (*sāmānya*). Therefore, when this [entity] exists in the presence of the complete set of causes, such as the eye and so forth—

"The form that is the producer exists even when each [of the other factors] is absent, yet it does not produce; therefore, because production occurs from its own nature, your argument is inconclusive.
[§ 22. The proponent of the established doctrine offers a rebuttal:
The proponent of the established doctrine says: No.
"According to their respective [causes]," and so forth.
He thinks as follows: "What, then, is this cause intended by you?
Is it each individual [organ], such as the eye and so on?"
That is incorrect; for an effect has as its intrinsic nature that which is produced by a causal complex (*sāmagrī*), and it is that very complex which constitutes the cause.

Now, since in that state each individual member of what is designated by the term "causal complex" (sāmagrī) is admitted to possess the nature of producing [the effect], the eye and so forth are individually causes.
If this is so, what is this restriction that because something arises from many, it must be produced by many? For there is no subverting proof (bādhaka-pramāṇa) against the opposite case.
From where is it determined that the effect is produced by only one?
If it is argued that [the effect arises] because it exists when that [cause] exists, this is equally true in the case of multiple [causes] as well.
As it has been said: "Those [causes] which are capable of producing that very single [effect] are not capable of producing another; thus, there is no production of something else."
Nor does it follow that from a plurality [of causes] a plurality [of effects] arises;
for, according to us, unlike your view, it is not the case that the cause itself assumes the nature of the effect,
whereby the effect would become manifold due to the manifoldness of its transformation.

However, the unprecedented (apūrva) exists only in certain [entities]; and since it exists only when there is a plurality of entities, it is called their effect— so how could there be the consequence of its being manifold?

As for that undifferentiated nature which is said to be the producer, since it exists even when [the other causes] are present alone and because its intrinsic nature is to produce that effect, it would follow that the effect must be produced from it; or else, since there is no difference in it when others are present, it would not produce it even then.
Therefore, those specific factors in whose presence or absence the effect is seen to exist or not exist are themselves the producers; so how can there be any inconclusiveness?
Now, if it is argued that "there would be no difference in the effect due to a difference in the cause" by relying on the causal totality (*sāmagrī*),
that is not so; for,

according to each respective totality, through the distinction of its own specific nature and the application of its particularities, there occurs [the production] of that effect characterized as consciousness.

The "particulars" (viśeṣāḥ) are the distinct intrinsic natures (svabhāvāḥ) differentiated by the diversity of their causal complexes (sāmagrī). Through their application—that is, by means of those applications which are the operations of the diverse causal complexes—there are produced particular intrinsic natures of effects; because these are non-confused, they possess a nature that is mutually excluded from one another.

Since effects possess distinct forms precisely because of the difference in their causal complexes (*sāmagrī*), how could there not be a difference in the effect resulting from a difference in the cause? To illustrate: one causal complex, characterized by mental attention (*manaskāra*), its excellence (*sādguṇya*), and so forth, gives rise solely to conceptual cognition (*vikalpavijñāna*).
Another [type of consciousness] is characterized solely by mental attention (*manaskāra*) and the sense faculties (*indriya*);
from that, the deluded sensory consciousnesses arise.
Yet another consists of the object, the sense faculty, and mental attention.

Furthermore, since non-erroneous cognition arises [from these], there is indeed a distinction among effects produced by distinct causal complexes (*sāmagrī*), because their specific natures as effects do not overlap. Thus, due to the difference in causes characterized by their respective causal complexes, there is certainly a distinction among effects. Now, one might object: when cognition arises from the object, the sense faculty, and mental attention, how can there be no confusion, given that the objective domain of their utility is one and the same?
Since such a commingling is accepted, there is no fault.
As it has been said in that very same context: "Because of the capacity [of the cause] in that single instance," and so forth.
If that is so, how then do they possess the status of being its producers?
If the effect does not differ because of that difference [in the causes],
then how indeed do the complete [causes] possess the capacity to produce their respective effects, such that in the absence of those [specific causes], that [effect] would not occur?
For their capacity to produce is established precisely by the fact that something arises only when they are present.
In that regard, when there is the existence of one or many [causes], it is said that they possess the capacity to produce one or many [effects].
Beauty,
place, time, and so forth [are among these causes].
[395] Even in the absence of an external object, there is internal conceptual construction; [396] for example, the cognition of water in a mirage.
[§ 23. Explanation of the occurrence of difference even among effects produced by the same causal complex.]

Now, if multiple things arise from a single causal complex (*sāmagrī*), let there be a distinction between them and those produced by other causal complexes; but how is there a distinction among them *mutually*?
For it is held that entities possess this or that form based on their being produced from causes that possess this or that form.

In that regard, when consciousness arises from the eye, visible form, and mental attention, since the moments of the eye and the visible form also exist at that time, they would—because they are produced from causes non-different from those of the consciousness—either possess the nature of consciousness, or conversely, the consciousness would possess the nature of those two; how could such a consequence not follow? And it has been said:
"Entities possessing this or that nature are born from causes possessing this or that nature."
"Is that form and so forth non-cognition, since it arises from causes not distinct from those of cognition?
This is not a fault,
because they are utilized as its efficient and material causes through their respective distinctions in intrinsic nature.
For attention (*manaskāra*) is the appropriating cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) of consciousness;
however, in the case of the eye, it is the cooperative cause (*sahakāri-kāraṇa*) for the arising of that which is capable of producing its own consciousness.
The same should be stated accordingly for the other [faculties] as well.

Therefore, the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) that produces a moment of the eye is of one kind, while that which produces consciousness and so forth is of another; it is precisely due to this difference between them that there is a difference among the effects.

This might be argued: "Since positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) are followed by all [factors] through the moments of the eye and so forth, from where does this distinction arise—that here, in the state of being the material cause (*upādāna*), there is a distinction? [The answer is: because of the presence of a distinction [in the nature of the causes].
Why is it not employed elsewhere, but rather as a cooperative cause (*sahakāribhāva*)?
Because [the nature of] being of the form of consciousness and so forth either conforms or does not conform, and because there is respectively deviation or non-deviation from that state.
For instance: consciousness imitates the cognitive nature of mental attention (*manaskāra*), not the state of being dull or impaired as it might be in the case of the eye and other [senses].
The same should be understood for other cases as well.
Furthermore, since consciousness exists exclusively by necessity, the operation belongs to the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) and not to the eye or other [faculties].

Moreover, regarding the arising of a subsequent moment of the eye, it is the previously existing eye that serves as the cause for its own cognition’s capacity, and not the immediately preceding condition. The same should be said for such form (*rūpa*) as well.

Therefore, even though there is a difference in states, that which serves as the basis for a cognition that apprehends a single form, and which is the cause for the production of effects falling within its own continuum, is the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*).
That which serves as the basis for the arising of a particularity in another continuum, depending upon its prior state, is the cooperative cause (*sahakāri-kāraṇa*).

And this is the nature of entities, inherited through a succession of their own causes, by which they produce one effect that serves as the basis for the establishment of its own continuum, and another that serves as the basis for the designation of a different continuum; thus,
due to the production of internal distinctions within that very causal complex (*sāmagrī*), the moments of visual consciousness, form, and so forth [arise] from one another.
The difference in character is not contradictory;
[the author] states the answer regarding that pleasure and so forth in the following verse (PV 398).
[399] When the effect exists— [400] arising immediately after the moment [of the cause]—
[401] there is an activity by necessity; such is the connection.
[§ 24. Even when there is multiplicity of causes, the effect is single; yet when there is a difference in the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), there is a difference in the effect.

Therefore, if it were the case that "due to the difference of causes"—that is, due to the multiplicity of causes—there is a difference or multiplicity of the effect, then, because of the absence of a necessary connection (*pratibandha*), the argument would be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). And since that [multiplicity of the effect] is not admitted, there is no flaw whatsoever.

Now, if the distinction of a cause characterized by its causal complex (*sāmagrī*)—that is, its difference from other complexes—is said to be the distinction of the effect, meaning that the effect possesses a nature distinct from those things which are not its causes, then, since that [distinct nature] exists here, how could it be that there is no distinction of the effect due to the distinction of the cause?
With this intention, [the author] says: "It is not the case that there would be no distinction of the effect due to the distinction of the cause."
Why?
Because it was stated [earlier], "according to their respective [natures]," and so forth.
Demonstrating that both of these are observed in practice through valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding effects, he says: "Just as," and so forth.

For instance, although a jar arises from a lump of clay and other factors, it does not possess a manifold nature despite the multiplicity of its causes; nor does it possess an identical intrinsic nature with things produced by a different causal complex. This is the meaning of the example.
In this regard, he first demonstrates the difference from that which is produced by a different causal complex, starting with the words "from a lump of clay," and so forth.

In this case, the lump of clay, the potter, and the string— possessing distinct natures and joined with other auxiliary causes— produce effects characterized as bricks and so forth that have natures different from those produced by other factors; yet when combined, they produce an effect consisting of a jar that is indeed dissimilar to those [other effects].

For instance, a lump of clay independent of a potter and other such factors is observed to produce, by way of being its material cause (*upādāna*), an effect consisting of clay that is distinct from trees and the like produced by other causes;
yet, when accompanied by the potter and others, it produces a jar consisting of that very same substance.

Furthermore, through the specific qualities imparted by those causes, it acts with a nature distinct from the mere lump of clay, and thus produces an effect—such as a brick—that is indeed different from the product of the lump alone.

In the same way, even a potter and so forth, when accompanied by other material causes (*upādāna*) acting as auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*), produce an effect that is distinct [from them]; that is, together with a lump of clay, they generate an effect consisting of a jar, which possesses specific qualities imparted by those causes.
This is the collective meaning.

In this regard, the nature of the jar that is distinct from the lump of clay arises from trees and the like—which do not possess the nature of clay because they have other material causes (*upādānakāraṇa*)—and it arises from the potter, who functions as a cooperative cause (*sahakāribhāva*) by imparting a specific excellence to the clay-lump as its material cause. Thus, for that very jar, which exists as clay by virtue of having the clay-lump as its material cause, there is a particular configuration (*saṃsthānaviśeṣa*), such as the form of a broad base and belly; and by virtue of having that [configuration] as its nature, it is distinguished from others.

For those for whom the lump of clay, together with other auxiliary causes, is the material cause (*upādāna*) of bricks and so forth, its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is distinct from them. Because of the specific difference imparted by the causes—the lump of clay and the potter—as stated in the Sūtra, that very jar, which consists of a particular shape of clay, possesses the nature of being produced by both the lump of clay and the potter; thus, the jar is endowed with their respective forms, and these two [causes] are characterized by the specific qualities imparted by the thread-like [auxiliary] causes.

Because its nature is distinct— that is, differentiated and severed— from the wheel and other factors by virtue of having an essence different from their state of independence, the jar produced by the three aforementioned causes arises with a nature that is indeed distinct from each of those other single effects as well as from the effects of two [causes]; thus, it is due to the difference in the causal complex (*sāmagrī*).
Effects are indeed distinct from one another, possessing mutually non-confounded natures; thus, the non-confusion of the specific effects resulting from their respective applications is established.
This is because [the effect] conforms to the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of the various causes inherent in each individual state, and because it does not arise piecemeal.

Furthermore, although [the effect] is produced by each [cause] individually, in reality, when other causes of the same genus as each [individual cause] are present, that particularity which was not observed is seen upon the presence of the others; therefore, it is said: "This is produced by that."
This is analyzed by those who contemplate reality (*tattvacintaka*).

For those seeking a specific effect undertake the acquisition of multiple causes for the sake of bringing about a causal totality (*sāmagrī*) capable of producing the desired effect through a succession of effects in which each mutually provides assistance.

Since it is thus from a difference in causal totalities that distinct effects arise—characterized as either a jar undivided from its parts such as bricks and wheels, or a jar divided from them—it is therefore so, in the manner described.
From a potter devoid of a lump of clay—that is, from one included within another causal complex—no effect whatsoever possesses the nature of clay;
for it is only that [potter] whose self is assisted by the cause, the lump of clay, who serves as the specific cause for that [effect].
It does not arise from clay alone.

Because a specific configuration that is external to that causal complex is the cause of an effect consisting of a specific configuration of clay, precisely by virtue of being assisted by the potter's material cause;
for [otherwise] there would be a lack of distinction within the causal complex.
The explanation of the scriptural fragment beginning with "no" is as follows: "[405] When there is multiplicity of causes, there is unity of the effect;
and due to the difference in the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), there is a difference in the effect."
[406] Of the lump of clay and the potter;
[407] by means of the employment and activities of those causes, those specific intrinsic natures (svabhāvaviśeṣa) which are the effects— of these, [408] of the jar...
The connection is that those who contemplate reality discern that "this is produced by that," through the discrimination of clay and so forth.

[§ 25. The Unity of the Effect despite the Multiplicity of Auxiliaries. Having thus demonstrated, by way of example, that the effect differs according to the difference in the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), he now says—demonstrating that even when there is multiplicity of auxiliaries, the effect lacks a manifold nature: "And it is not the case that those two, the clay and the potter, when joined together and having their natures assisted by one another's material cause (*upādāna*)," and so forth.

That specific capacity (*śaktiviśeṣa*), which is a distinct fitness arising from a state accompanied by other conditions— despite the fact that its object is different from the object of other states— just as it is distinct from those others,
so too there is no distinction [between them] by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Even in terms of its own nature (*svarūpa*), there is no plurality nor a manifold essence in the effect.

The specific quality (*viśe�sa*) produced by those two—consisting of the clay and the particular configuration—is itself distinct from what is produced by other causal complexes; thus, this is its differentiation.
But how is it known that "it has no differentiation even by way of its own nature, just as it does not have it from others"? To this, he says: "Of the clay and the configuration," and so forth.
For if the distinction between the clay and the pot— which exists in those respective states and consists of a specific configuration of clay that is the object of a specific capacity—

were to differ from it in its own nature (svarūpataḥ) as it does from anything else, then, because the clay and the configuration would not be of one another's nature due to the absence of mutual identity, the clay would not appear through that specific configuration which is its cause.
Nor does a particular configuration exist by way of the nature of clay,
as it does with respect to other forms.
For that which is not the intrinsic nature of something does not appear in the cognition apprehending itself under that identity.
Just as [a cognition] possesses color and taste;
or rather, it is logical that knowledge, arising through the efficacy of an object that lacks such a form, should conform to that form,
because otherwise the consequence of its being erroneous would follow, and consequently there would be no determination of the object by virtue of that [knowledge].
Therefore, since clay and its configuration possess a single nature, it is not the case that the multiplicity of causes necessarily entails a multiplicity of natures in the effect;

for, although the cooperative causes such as the eye and so forth have distinct intrinsic natures, there is no contradiction in their producing a single effect, and thus they perform a common, singular action by virtue of having a single form.
Or, it might be argued that they perform a common effect by means of distinct forms.
This, however, is said to be the state of being a producer of a single effect with respect to a single causal complex (*sāmagrī*).
But in ultimate reality, because those included within that complex also initiate another moment of their own kind, they are parts of a different complex.

Furthermore, just as there is no single effect produced by a single cause, so too there is no single effect produced by multiple causes; thus, even if one accepts that the multiplicity of effects follows from the multiplicity of causes, there is no inconsistency.
Consequently, if one attempts to prove multiplicity based on a single effect, the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) remains doubtful.
If the proof were made in a general sense, there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established; therefore,
it is a negative inference (*vyatirekin*) whose object is a specific capacity.
[§ 26. Refutation of the position that there is both difference and non-difference between substance and mode, as accepted by the Ahrīka and others:

But surely, even if clay and its particular configuration possess a single intrinsic nature, the Ahrīkas and others maintain their difference on the basis of distinctions such as number; how then can this serve as an example for the unity of that which is produced by multiple conditions?

For in all cases, a distinction between substance (*dravya*) and mode (*paryāya*) is maintained on the basis of differences in number, name, definition, and function, while non-distinction is maintained on the basis of non-difference in place, time, and intrinsic nature, just as in the case of a jar and its color and other qualities.
To illustrate: "The jar is one; color and the rest are many"—this is the difference in number.
The distinction between designations is as follows: "the jar" and "color and so forth.
That which is characterized by persistence is eternal like a substance, whereas the particulars characterized by exclusion are momentary.
However, for the Jaiminīya, there are some [entities] that persist over time; thus, there is a difference in their definition.

Furthermore, the fetching of water is performed by means of a jar, whereas the coloring of an object is performed by means of its color and other qualities; thus, there is a difference in their function.

Thus, in all cases, there is a difference between substance and mode in terms of number and so forth, but non-difference in terms of location and so forth. Therefore, because clay and its configuration are in some sense distinct, the effect produced by both the clay and the potter is indeed manifold.
However, just as there is unity [in that effect], so too it is produced from those two as a single, non-distinct essence.
"That which has multiple causes is necessarily multiple;
moreover, that which is single has only a single cause, because it is produced from a non-different form by its auxiliary conditions (sahakārins); thus there is no deviation [in the rule].
This is incorrect.

If one does not admit a difference by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), then difference cannot be established otherwise, because it would follow that a single effect does not arise from multiple causes. Alternatively, if one does admit a difference by way of intrinsic nature, then since clay and its shape are not identical to one another, it would be difficult to avoid the consequence that those two do not appear through their respective specific intrinsic natures of being clay and being a shape.
For if there were no difference by way of intrinsic nature between the property (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*), [the distinction between them would be untenable].
There is no difference [in the object] even due to differences in number and so forth;
for numbers and the like, even when they differ, being of a different nature, are not capable of subverting the non-difference that constitutes its own essence.
To begin with, the difference in number is incapable [of doing so].
Because we observe the usage of the plural even for a single substance—
as in "the teachers" (*guravaḥ*)—
and because the plural ending is not invariably absent, it is not the case that color and other qualities (*rūpādayaḥ*) are the cause [of the plural designation] here.
For if [the word] "heavy" (guru) were to have as its objective cause (nimitta) the [individual] characteristics such as form (rūpa) and so forth, it would never take the singular number.
If it is argued that only the possible nature of the substratum (dharmirūpa) is intended to be expressed, we say no;
for if it were intended as a single entity, there would follow the consequence that neither "entirety" (kārtsnya) nor "heaviness" (gaurava) could be perceived.

Furthermore, since the term "rice grains" (*vrīhayaḥ*) expresses a genus (*jāti*) and does not denote the substratum (*dharmin*) nor its properties such as color and so forth, it provides no answer at all.

Moreover, because a real entity (*vastu*) which possesses both forms is denoted by the word "heavy" (*guru*), how could there be an intention to express the form of the substratum—which is possible [in that context]—as a unity?

Consequently, since the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) seen in the expression "one heavy thing" (*eko guruḥ*) is not observed, synonyms (*paryāya*) would also have to fall within the scope of the singular number.
And since these [categories] differ only in their modes of expression,
how can a difference be established through a difference in number?
Furthermore, even names are based on conventional designation.
If its occurrence depends on desire, how can there be a difference in the object [denoted] from that?
Since we observe a difference in designations even for a single thing— as in "Indra," "Śakra," and "Purandara"— how can this [desire] be the cause of a real difference?
If it is argued that even here a distinction of powers is understood from the acts of ruling (*indana*), being able (*śakana*), and splitting (*dāraṇa*), we say no;
for it is the whole [the Lord] who is the agent of these effects.
Indeed, it is not the power itself that rules, is able, or splits.
What then?
It is also the nature of the substratum (dharmin),
because those two are admitted to have a single intrinsic nature (ekasvabhāva).
Furthermore, because one does not observe grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with words such as "capable" (*śaknoti*) which denote that [same object],
it is not reasonable to assume a metaphorical usage (*upacāra*) on the grounds that the object is the referent of an unerring cognition.
And what need be said regarding those synonyms for which there is not even a slight correspondence in meaning?
The difference in characteristics (*lakṣaṇabheda*) is also not a valid reason, because it is unestablished (*asiddhatvāt*).

For no single entity (*bhāva*) is established anywhere as being concomitant (*anvayin*). To explain: substance (*dravya*) is not asserted by the shameless [Vaiśeṣikas] to be eternal by way of being immutable and permanent (*kūṭasthanityatā*).
Because its permanence is admitted through transformation (*pariṇāmanityatā*).
And that [transformation] occurs by way of the continuous succession of preceding and succeeding moments;
for there is no annihilation of this [continuum] in its own form, as there is in the case of its various modalities (*paryāya*).
It is accepted that only the modes (*paryāya*) cease by way of their modal form, but not the substance (*dravya*), which is therefore held to be eternal.

However, this kind of immutable eternity is not possible for a substance, because a substance distinct from its modes is unestablished; for such a substance, which meets the conditions for perception, is not observed apart from those modes.
The conceit of a "substance" (dravya) belongs only to those of dull intellect regarding these modes (paryāya), which possess identical forms and perform identical functions;
it is not perceived as something distinct from them.
Furthermore, for us, the distinction between effects is simply unproven.
Because certain things, such as form and so forth, alone perform that causal function;
nevertheless, it is stated even while making this concession: for an effect is of two kinds—occurring at a different time and occurring at the same time.
In that case, there would first have to exist a basis for differentiation;
however, such a thing is not possible here because the property (dharma) and the substratum (dharmin) are simultaneous.
Furthermore, [the reason] "being simultaneous" is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) regarding a difference in effects.
Because it is possible for cloths and other such things to undergo differentiated transformation;
for cloths and the like are observed to perform multiple functions while undergoing differentiated transformations,
yet they do not differ in their nature as substrata (*dharmī*).
And because there is no contradiction in one [entity] performing multiple functions;

for in this case, it is not the cause itself that attains the nature of the effect, such that— were the single causal entity to assume the form of a single effect— it would, due to the absence of any other form, be unable to assume the nature of any other effect.
However, that which is a novel effect (apūrva) is precisely that which comes into being previously non-existent when some thing exists;

in that regard, when the object, sense faculty, and attention— whose distinct natures have been imparted through mutual dependence— are present, and there occurs a specific moment distinct from others, the admission of multiple causal operations follows because each of them conforms to the presence and absence of that [effect].
There is no contradiction,
because even in the case of a single action, the very fact that it is permeated by the existence of that [nature] is the basis;
and that [basis] remains the same even in the case of multiple actions.
But surely, since the effect characterized as consciousness occurs in their proximity, their very nature as producers of that [consciousness] is determined,
because a cause exists in the form of a producer in relation to the nature of its effect.
Therefore, how could there be the possibility of any other effect from those [atoms], each of which has the nature of producing consciousness?
Or, if that were the case, they would possess the intrinsic nature of producing something other than that;
and consequently, they would not produce consciousness at all, because their intrinsic nature would be to produce something else.
This is not a fault,
because they possess a nature that performs multiple functions. For instance— in that state— each one consists in the production of a specific moment of its own kind as well as other moments.

Because their existence is observed to be immediately followed by that [effect], it is precisely the nature of producing consciousness that is established; thus, its nature of not producing is excluded, since that alone is the counter-correlative (pratiyogin), and not the nature of producing anything else.
Furthermore, this does not entail that they possess a manifold nature (anekātmatā).
Because a single unique essence (*ātmaniśaya*) is the cause of multiple effects,
an entity— though expressed by multiple words based on its exclusion from the opposite (*viparyayavyāvṛtti*) in relation to other things— does not thereby acquire a manifold nature,
since it is that very same distinct, singular essence which is so designated.
For example, [the statement] "form is visible and possesses resistance" (*sanidarśanaṃ sapratigham*);
for in this case, the words are not based on a difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*),
because otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of a lack of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).
If it is argued that there is no fault because those things which have that [single cause] as their basis exist together in one place;
or if it is argued that even in the case of dependence, how could a single thing not produce multiple effects, since it is employed through its very manifold nature—[we reply: No, [it is not so]. No.
For otherwise, the defect of the absence of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) would persist as before.
Nor do we perceive through direct perception (*adhyakṣa*) a difference in the nature of blue and other such qualities;
nor can a difference in nature be inferred solely from a difference in their effects.
Because there is no obstruction [to their coexistence],
and because there is no means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) to apprehend such [an obstruction];
for even in the case of entities that have multiple effects, such as lamps and the like, they are perceived by direct perception (pratyakṣa) as having a single nature.
Furthermore, in that case as well, there would be no subverting evidence against the contrary [position].

Moreover, if one does not admit that a single entity performs multiple functions, then this observed regularity—attested by valid cognition—that specific qualities such as color, taste, odor, and tangibility necessarily coexist in certain instances would not exist;
for it is impossible for those things which have distinct causes to be subject to a rule of coexistence.
For even those things caused by that [single cause], whose births depend upon that very same cause, it is impossible for them to have a fixed concomitance.
If it is argued that there is a rule of coexistence in one place because they share the nature of a single substratum (*dharmī*), we say no;
for it remains to be examined how a single thing can possess multiple natures.

Furthermore, for one who experiences a single nature within the manifold, multiplicity is difficult to avoid; otherwise, how could there not be an absolute distinction between the property (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*)?
For instance, it is with reference to that very essence (*ātman*) that this is established as "this is the substratum" and "these are its attributes."
If there were a difference between them, then there would be only difference;
thus, even for multiple [causes], there would be no production of a single effect.

For it is not logical that the object, the sense faculty, and mental attention—without depending on the assistance provided by their mutual contribution as material causes (*upādāna*)—should simultaneously initiate a single effect.
Furthermore, nothing whatsoever produces anything by itself;
consequently, the very relationship of cause and effect would perish everywhere,
because a single [cause] lacks both multiple and single effects, and because there is no other possible mode [of causation].
Nor is the universe entirely without cause,
because there is a restriction regarding place, time, and nature.
Therefore, for things that arise dependent upon the same causal complex (*sāmagrī*), there is either a restriction on their coexistence or a restriction on their performance of a single effect.

And thus, how could a single entity not have multiple effects when it simultaneously assists its own momentary state and the other material cause? Consequently, how could one imagine a distinction based on the difference of effects?
Furthermore, how is one not insane who, while asserting that substances and their modes possess a single nature, yet rejects the fact that a single thing can have multiple effects?

Otherwise, it would follow that it lacks intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*). Furthermore, if substances and modes were of a single intrinsic nature, then the difference between their effects would be based solely on a single entity; thus, one who asserts a distinction based on the difference of effects is clearly shameless and deserves to be ignored.

[416] [they are distinguished] by number and so forth.

Even the objection raised by the Vaiśeṣika—that it is illogical for a single thing to produce multiple effects—is not tenable.]

Even the Vaiśeṣika, who asserts that a single substance is the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of substances, qualities, and actions, and that a single action is the efficient cause (*nimitta*) of conjunction, disjunction, and latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), is struck down by the very wrath of his own tenets when he rejects the notion that a single thing performs multiple effects.
Nor is a difference in potency (*śaktibheda*) the basis for this [distinction].
Since these powers are independent of that single auxiliary cause, how could they be restricted to a specific substratum,
rather than pervading all individuals without exception? Therefore,
precisely because of this excellence of its own nature (*ātma-atiśaya*), which assists numerous powers, it likewise performs numerous effects.
Thus, enough with this overly prolix discussion;
[let us consider] the specific distinction of the [mental] application in its entirety.
[442] Of a single—T.
[443] substance [§ 28. Refutation of the claim that non-difference in place, time, and intrinsic nature establishes non-difference].
Furthermore, the non-difference that is asserted on the grounds of the non-difference of place, time, and intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is likewise untenable.
To explain: even if place and time are non-different, color, taste, smell, and touch are differentiated by way of their modal forms (*paryāya*); therefore, how can non-difference be established?
As for intrinsic nature, if it consists of both persistence (*anuvṛtti*) and exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) for each of the two—substance and mode—individually; [then...]
In that case, there would be two distinct entities, like a jar and a cloth, rather than a single entity possessing two forms; how, then, could non-difference be established?
Furthermore, it is not logical for persistence and exclusion to be the very nature of a thing.
Because those two depend upon the persisting and the receding [respectively],
one must therefore state that the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the persisting and the receding is something other than those two;
it is not the case that their very persistence and recession constitute their intrinsic nature.
For memory is not the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of the rememberer.

Furthermore, if both persistence (anuvṛtti) and exclusion (vyāvṛtti) were its intrinsic nature, then a distinction between the intrinsic natures would have to be stated due to their differing characteristics.
If it is argued that the nature of clay and so forth constitutes the intrinsic nature—
If it is argued that "non-difference" here refers to similarity,
then that is possible only where there is difference, because similarity has as its locus things that are similar.

Consequently, there would be only two distinct entities, rather than a single entity possessing two forms. Now, if it is accepted that identity consists in the absence of a second form— that is, non-difference— then how can there be duality of form?
For here, by the word "form" (rūpa), intrinsic nature (svabhāva) is denoted. And if that [nature] is one, how can there be a twofold form?
For it is a contradiction to say that there is both a single intrinsic nature and a twofold form.
Furthermore, if unity is not accepted by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*),
how then can that which is manifold be called "one"?
It cannot be so called, first of all, because of being produced from a single cause.
Because a difference in causes is established everywhere through the distinction between the material cause (*upādāna*), the efficient cause (*nimitta*), and the instrumental cause (*kāraṇa*);
nor [is it established] by virtue of producing a single effect,

since even for a single [cause], a distinction between effects consisting of differentiated transformation (*vibhakta-pariṇāma*) and undifferentiated transformation (*avibhakta-pariṇāma*) is admitted.
Nor is there identity on the grounds of being denoted by the same designation, because even a single entity can possess multiple synonyms. Furthermore,

since everything is capable of being denoted by the same term— given that it is impossible for the same designation to denote both what has been produced and what has not been produced— and because the objects differ due to a difference in capacity, this has been stated in response to one who asserts a difference in objects based on such designations.
Nor is it one because it is the object of a single consciousness, for even in a single instance, multiple cognitions may arise.
For example, many people gaze upon the rising of the moon; how then is its oneness admitted?
Furthermore, since it is possible for many things, such as blue, yellow, and so forth, to be the objects of a single cognition, it would follow that they are one and the same.
Thus, the claim that a single entity possesses a dual nature does not cohere in any way whatsoever.
Consciousness, however, arising as a reflection of blue, is designated as distinct by way of its exclusion from the appearance of yellow and so forth;
yet, in reality, it does not possess two forms.
Alternatively, because substance and mode are intermingled, it is said to have two forms due to its variegated nature, like Narasimha.
That is incorrect,
because the variegated nature of the Man-Lion (Narasimha) is not established;
for he is indeed a composite form consisting of a collection of many atoms.
Furthermore, those atoms do not individually possess the form of Narasiṃha; rather,
its upper portion is the form of a lion, while its lower portion is the form of a man.
Furthermore, that very same thing would be a different genus from both the man and the lion,
rather than being a variegated form; for it is a variegated form that is called "śabala."
"Vicitratā" means having diverse intrinsic natures (*nānāsvabhāvatā*).
And how can there be unity when there is diversity of intrinsic nature?

Thus, this is merely a delusion of the dull-witted, caused by the observation of a single conventional designation—such as "army"—based on seeing a single effect among many things, even though they are actually manifold.
Thus, first of all, space, time, and intrinsic nature are individually shown to lack causal efficacy in establishing [the object's] unity.
Furthermore, even when combined, they are shown to be inconclusive through various arguments.

For instance: modes (paryāya) possess non-different space, time, and intrinsic nature, yet they differ in the form of their modes; and since the negation of both property (dharma) and substratum (dharmin) has already been stated, the doctrine of "both" is impossible.
