For the object of words is not at all the form of a real entity that appears in sensory cognition;
so by what means could there be a distinction [of the object] based on a difference in designations? (2)

It is so because of such statements as "being solely directed toward the ultimate reality" (paramārthaikatānatva), and because [an object] does not appear in the cognition of one whose eyes are not engaged with the word. (3)
Just as in the case of [perceiving] an object, those words have a conceptualized domain;
if that distinction of the conceptualized were to arise from a difference in names, [it would be like this]. (4)
There might be some distinction of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), but never any [distinction] regarding the entity (*vastu*) itself.
Nor is a distinction of number considered anything other than a distinction of verbal expression. (5)

Therefore, even from that [statement], there might somehow be a distinction regarding the imagined [nature] alone—as in the verse beginning "For those for whom words are under the power of things" (PV 3.64)—but not regarding the real thing itself. // 6 //
Difference itself would dissolve, because it is not distinct from that [unity]. (19)
If non-difference is not abandoned, then difference would be merely a product of conceptual construction;
or, if that [conceptual construction] were not unreal, there would be falsity regarding non-difference. (20)
Since the existence of one thing among those whose natures consist of mutual exclusion is caused by the non-existence of the other, therefore a single entity cannot possess two forms. (21)

If its difference from those two is also [established] by them, and if that which is the substratum and the property, and that which is other than them, are differentiated by that very same nature; // 43 //

If, on the other hand, even in that case, a difference distinct from them is postulated for the sake of establishing their non-difference, then the same undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) as before would follow.
"And in this way, that [configuration] would possess the status of being the substratum (dharmin), because the other two [the universal and the particular] are dependent upon it.
Here, having raised the objection from the perspective of the Vaiśeṣika school, he says: "It is something entirely different," and so forth.
For "configuration" (saṃsthāna) is said to be the arrangement of parts (avayava-sanniveśa).
And since it is characterized by conjunction, it is of the nature of a quality (*guṇa*).
Therefore, it is distinct from the clay substance (*mṛd-dravya*), because substance and quality possess unmixed natures.

Consequently, if the potter’s activity is said to pertain to the specific configuration of the lump of clay while the clay itself constitutes the essence of that lump, [then the potter's role concerns the quality].
"In that case, because the two are absolutely distinct and because there is a multiplicity of causes, it follows that there must be a multiplicity of effects.
The proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntin) says: "This has already been addressed.

The refutation regarding the difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) between clay and its configuration was stated [previously] in such passages as "because clay and its configuration are not identical to one another," and so forth; therefore, the configuration is not something other than the substance of the clay.

Therefore, by means of the potter— who possesses an excellence derived from the material cause (the lump of clay) and acts as a cooperative condition for that effect-moment— and by means of the lump of clay— which is assisted by that material cause and acts as a cooperative condition for that effect-moment— each one individually produces the entire effect consisting of the clay and its configuration; thus, even though there is a multiplicity of causes, there is no multiplicity in this [effect].

Right here he states the reason for the reinforcement: "Moreover," and so forth. If that configuration residing in the jar were distinct from the clay, then why would the potter not produce it separately?
For there is no necessity that things which are distinct must not be separated.

And the potter is understood, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), to be the cause of that configuration which consists of qualities; thus, he exists separately from that effect.
The opponent says: "{1} Of the quality," and so forth.

"{2} That which resides in substance (*dravya-āśrayin*), possesses no further qualities (*aguṇavat*), and is not a cause in conjunctions and disjunctions, being independent [of them]" (VaiSū 1.1.16)—from this definition of a quality, it follows that a quality is always dependent upon a substance.
How could that [earth] ever be separated from it?
Anticipating this objection from the Buddhist side, the Vaiśeṣika himself says: "In its configuration," and so forth.

If, by its very nature, that earth-substance (*mṛd-dravya*)—which is the substratum of that configuration consisting of qualities—is of the nature of a substrate because of such statements as "it possesses action and possesses qualities" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 1.1.15), then...
Or rather, why does such a configuration, which consists essentially of being placed upon the potsherds, depend at that time upon the activity of the potter?
Why does it not arise by itself?— such is the intention of the objector.
Anticipating such an objection, the Vaiśeṣika states the refutation: "No, because from that," and so forth.

That which is the clay substance and that which is the configuration consisting of the broad base, belly, and so on—the relationship between these two, characterized as that of substratum and superstratum—[is what is meant by "from that"].
In this regard, since both of these possess that capacity which they acquire from the potter, they depend upon the potter;

he states the fault in the case of non-dependence on the potter as follows: otherwise, if there were no dependence on the potter regarding the mutual capacity for connection between those two, then the clay lump would, by its very nature, possess the capacity for connection with such a shape.

And since that being so, there exists a *dharmatā* (intrinsic nature) of the very substance characterized by its fitness for connection with that configuration; therefore, even prior to the presence of the potter, there would have to be a connection with a specific configuration, because the substance and the configuration possess a nature that conforms to their respective effects—[§ 31.
Establishing the non-difference of substance and quality].
The proponent of the final view (siddhāntavādin) says: "In this way," and so forth.
If [the clay] indeed depends upon the potter for its mutual capacity for connection, then it follows that this capacity of the clay-substance arises from the potter.
Furthermore, there is no difference—that is, no diversity—in the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of these two: the clay-substance and its capacity.

For if that were the case, then the separation of fitness from the substance would follow as before. Now, if one were to argue that even fitness is not established separately because it is dependent upon the fit [substance], then, lest its inclusion [in the substance] occur even prior [to its production] simply by virtue of being a property of the thing, one must accept that there is another fitness for the connection with the substance, which arises from the potter for that [initial] fitness.
That [non-existence] also must not be accepted as having a nature distinct from the substance, because it would follow that it could be separated [from it].
Or, if the consequence of its being separable is raised again, the same rebuttal applies to it,
and the same answer follows once more.
Thus, because of the consequence of an infinite regress, one must necessarily admit that the nature of the potsherd-substance and its suitability [for that function] are non-different.
What is established when this is the case?
To this he says: "There exists, indeed," and so forth.

Since the substance of the potsherd, which is capable of entering into a specific relation of conjunction, is produced by both the lump of clay and the potter, it follows that even though it possesses a single intrinsic nature, it can nonetheless possess specific qualities imparted by multiple conditions; thus, our own position is established.
And so, why this excessive insistence of ours on proving that clay and its configuration possess a single nature?
If, by relying even on functional capacity (*yogyatā*), it is established that there is no consequence of multiplicity for an effect— despite being produced by multiple conditions— due to its unity,
then there is no purpose whatsoever here in refuting the doctrine of substance (*dravya*) and quality (*guṇa*).
The intention is that this has already been refuted elsewhere.

Furthermore, by the use of the term "insistence" (*nirbandha*), it is established through the following reasoning that these two are indeed identical: because clay and shape are not of the nature of one another, it would follow that they would not appear as distinct from their respective specific natures of shape and clay.
Thus, their oneness is proven.

He explains that even though other arguments (*yuktyantara*) are possible, no insistence (*nirbandha*) characterized by their explicit statement is made, because the point at hand (*prakṛtasiddhi*) can be established otherwise as well. Thus, it is established. [474] — T.
[§ 32. Summary of the distinction of effects due to the distinction of causal complexes, and the unity of the effect despite the distinction of causes:

Having thus demonstrated that there is a distinction from those produced by other causal complexes due to the distinction of the complex itself, and that the unity of the effect is not contradictory even when the auxiliary factors are manifold, he says, in conclusion: "Therefore..."
"Cooperating causes," and so forth:
by which— namely, when there is an accumulation of other conditions, that incomplete causal complex becomes a different complex,
and that [new complex] produces a distinct effect altogether, which is different from the effect produced by the previous complex.

Furthermore, although the co-operating factors (sahakārin) that are the objects of the designation "single causal complex" (ekasāmagrī) are manifold, there is no contradiction in multiple things performing a single action;
and since a single effect is observed to follow the positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) of those [factors], their unity is established by way of their intrinsic nature (svabhāva).
For this reason, the conditions (pratyaya) that possess the nature of co-operation and are included within a single causal complex [are distinguished] from other causal complexes.

They do not have the same object of cognition (*upayoga*), for those things whose objects of cognition are not identical with that of a single cognition [do not arise from the same cause]; this is because it is understood through the force of logic that they possess different objects of cognition only in relation to other causal complexes (*sāmagrī*).

By this, that which was previously raised as an alternative—namely, "if by the word 'cause' the causal complex is meant, then since there is indeed a difference [in the effect] due to the difference in that [complex], as compared to those produced by a different complex, why is it said [that there is no difference]?"—is refuted.
"—there would be no difference [in the effect] due to a difference in the causes. This conclusion, demonstrated by the example, has been summarized.

Now, if by the word "cause" (*kāraṇa*) one refers to the auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*) that constitute the domain of the designation "assemblage" (*sāmagrī*), then a difference in the effect characterized by multiplicity is certainly not admitted on account of a difference in those [causes] characterized by multiplicity, because there is no contradiction in multiple [factors] performing a single action.

And because one observes the production of the manifold from the single, he concludes by demonstrating the identity of the clay and its configuration: "Even though the nature of the effect— consisting of the clay and its configuration— is one," that is, even in the absence of plurality, "in reality" (vastutaḥ),
from the perspective of ultimate truth (paramārthataḥ), "even though" the clay and the configuration appear as if distinct within the conceptualizing mind (kalpanābuddhi).

Having thus established in the example that the difference among effects arises from a difference in their causal complexes (*sāmagrī*), and not from a plurality of effects due to a difference in the cognitions directed toward a single complex, [the author] applies this to the present case of the eye and so forth, saying: "Just as in this example, there is a difference in causes—a difference in the causal complexes—characterized by a triad of complexes consisting of the potter, the deficient lump of clay, and the additional thread together with them; [and this occurs] 'among the distinct [effects]'..."

Regarding various natures— that is, specific instances characterized as a pot that is undivided from its constituent parts such as bricks, or a pot that is divided from them— it follows from their distinct utility that they do not have a single effect,

but rather have distinct effects. In the same manner, when consciousness arises from the eye and other [senses], one should infer that because the causes characterized as causal complexes (sāmagrī) differ due to other complexes, they produce multiple effects.
Explaining this very point, he says: "For instance," and so forth.

That causal complex (*sāmagrī*) which is devoid of the eye, characterized by consciousness known as the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*), and dependent upon other conditions—from that [complex], the nature of awareness (*bodharūpatā*) is perceived as being derived from it (*tadupādeyatvena*), whether it be conceptual or otherwise; that same [nature of awareness] belongs to visual consciousness as well.
Of that very visual consciousness— of what kind?—
which exists as having the nature of apprehension, which is arising, and which at that very moment is restricted to that single effect [of the visual faculty], [it arises] from the visual faculty.

Due to its proximity— specifically, the assistance provided by the immediately preceding condition (samanantarapratyaya) as an appropriating cause— there arises from that [consciousness] a specific determination toward the apprehension of form,
which is to say, a specific determination toward the aspect of form,
being thus distinguished from the aspects of sound and so forth.
Because it is produced by the totality of causes consisting of the eye together with the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*),
the cognition possesses a form similar to that object— derived from the object, the superior immediately preceding condition, and the sense faculty—

and not merely a manifestation of form like a deluded cognition; thus, it is demonstrated that the effect is precisely the totality characterized by the object, the sense faculty, and mental attention.
Other effects produced by one or two [causes] should be inferred for oneself.
In this regard, although the effect characterized as visual consciousness is in fact non-different [from its causes], there are the causes— namely, the object, the sense faculty, and attention.
From their own individual natures, these [cognitions], being distinct from those [objects] that do not produce them, possess specific characteristics such as the nature of awareness;
thus, even though they are of a single essence, they are designated as plural in relation to what does not produce them.
Since this is so, therefore, even when there is a difference in causes—

just as there is no difference despite the difference in conditions included within a single causal complex (sāmagrī)— there is likewise no non-difference despite the difference in causes characterized by distinct complexes, because the specific effect produced by another complex is a distinct effect.

Therefore, that which is said—[T. 283a] "If the effect remains undifferentiated despite the difference among the auxiliary causes (sahakārin), let it likewise remain undifferentiated despite the difference in the causal complexes (sāmagrī); but if it is differentiated due to the difference in the causal complexes, why is it not also differentiated by the difference among the auxiliary causes, since there is no distinction [in the logic]?"—is thereby refuted.

For it is thus: due to the mutual approach and so forth, based on specific conditions (*pratyaya-viśeṣa*), and because of the mutual assistance of the continua of the auxiliary causes directed toward a single effect, there arises from those auxiliaries—which possess restricted capacities—a single [effect].

However, as for another causal complex (*sāmagryantara*), the production of a different effect occurs from other causes that possess distinct intrinsic natures (*svabhāva-bheda*) based on their capacity to bring about that other effect. Thus, how could there be [a contradiction]? This is because it has been demonstrated [above]. [475]—T.
[476] Regarding the objects — T.
[477] Just so — T.
[478] Because of the governing context — T.
[479] Thus, produced from that—T. [480] Therefore, in relation to the producer—T. [481] The effect is not produced—T.
[§ 33. Being a producer is itself being a substratum, not being a supporter.
But surely, every effect has a substratum, just as derived matter (upādāyarūpa) does;
for it is maintained by you that when that [derived matter] arises from the primary elements (bhūta), it takes those very [elements] as its support.

Likewise, other effects such as consciousness and so forth must also depend upon some cause. And for that cause, its status as a generator comes first, while its status as a substratum for the effect comes later.

"Production does not [occur], because that which has such a nature is produced from that"—thus, the inconclusiveness (*anekānta*) remains exactly as before. To this he says: "These very things are those aforementioned distinctions of causal power (*kāraṇa-śakti-bheda*), the specific powers of causes.
Of what sort are they? They are those whose own [powers]—the distinctions of causal power characterized as auxiliary conditions (*sahakārin*)—arise from another totality (*sāmagryantara*)."

Regarding the production of that specific effect, those whose power is "unobstructible"— meaning it is impossible to obstruct or hinder it— exist by virtue of that state of having unobstructible power; being thus necessarily endowed with the power to produce the effect and being fully engaged,
they constitute the causal totality (*sāmagrī*) for some single effect produced by a single condition.
Since everything arises from the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) alone due to the absence [of any other cause], the nature of the effect of that complex is said to be the basis for its own persistence.
Why, then, is its power unimpeded?
Because of momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*).
For the power of a momentary thing cannot be obstructed;
because by the time an obstructor is active in producing another nature, the momentary thing has already ceased after having performed its own effect.
But how, then, is it logical for a cause that is not simultaneous [with its effect] to be a support?
To this he says: "For instance," and so forth.

Because that effect characterized as consciousness has a unique nature—distinct from those [causes] such as the eye when taken collectively, and distinct from anything else that does not produce it—since the effect is not produced in fragments, [it is unitary by virtue of its cognitive form].
Since the whole arises from each individual part, it is born as one;
therefore, those parts are called its supports.
For indeed, there is no benefactor other than that which produces [the effect].
Moreover, that which provides no assistance cannot be a substratum, because that would lead to an over-extension [of the definition].
Therefore, the status of being a substratum for that which exists at a different time is not contradictory.

As for the claim that the derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) of the primary elements (*bhūta*) serves as their support (*pratyāśrayatva*), that too is simply its being the producer (*janakatva*) of its own location; it is not the case that something which was previously a producer later becomes a sustainer (*sthāpaka*), whereby there would be an inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) argument.
[The support of the means of proof—T.]
[483] It relies on something else entirely as its basis—T.
[484] Its intrinsic nature—T. [485] Because it is non-existent anywhere at all—T.
[486] — relying upon the interval — T.
[487] the state of being an occurrence — T.
[488] it becomes the cause for establishing — T.
[§ 34. The production of an excellence is not "auxiliary causality" (sahakāritva), but rather the performance of a single purpose.
Furthermore, suspecting that the opponent might raise the objection of "inconclusiveness" (anaikāntika) by arguing that [the cause] produces that very nature [of the effect] in another way, he says:

"In those whose powers are unobstructed, there is no obstruction"—that is, for those whose power is such that it has no obstruction, which is to say, no impediment; this is their state of having unobstructed power.
And because it has no subsequent effect:
for those things which, having arisen, produce their effect after a lapse of time, there might indeed be an obstruction of their power;
but not so for those which produce their effect immediately after arising.
By this, he states the absence of any impairment for those things that perish moment by moment.
He also states their lack of any benefactor—namely, "in those to which no excellence can be imparted.
And he expresses that quality of being incapable of having excellence imparted to them in the phrase "in those that are momentary."
For it is not possible to impart a distinction to momentary things, because that which imparts the distinction must coexist with them or arise immediately after them,
and at that time, the former has already ceased.

In such conditions as these, what is the meaning of "mutual cooperation" (*sahakāra*) by virtue of which they are called "cooperators"? Is it not already established that there is an absence of cooperation precisely because no excellence (*viśeṣa*) can be imparted [to them]? Why, then, is it said "in those whose power is unobstructed"?
For indeed, there is nothing that obstructs their power.
It is called "cooperative.
True;
however, this was said for the purpose of making it known that [the cause] is in every respect incapable of acting upon it.
Furthermore, he rejects the notion that auxiliary causes (sahakārin) provide assistance by removing obstacles to a capacity;
therefore, since auxiliaries that impart a specific excellence (atiśaya) are impossible for momentary things, their productivity is dependent solely upon their own causes.
And such [productivity] exists at all times.

And [the opponent] thinks that [the argument] is indeed inconclusive (*anekānta*), because [causes] do not produce [the effect] alone, since they produce that which has such a nature (i.e., the nature of producing).

He refutes this: "Certainly not; the production of an excellence (*atiśaya*) is not what constitutes 'cooperation' (*sahakriyā*), for if it were, there would be no auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*) due to the absence of such an excellence.
But where is it that the production of an excellence by the conditions does not occur?"
In all cases;
for nowhere is a cooperative action (*sahakriyā*), characterized by the production of an excellence (*atiśaya*) among co-arising factors, possible. What, then, is cooperative action?
Thus he says: "The performance of a single purpose" means the accomplishment of one effect by many;
the word "even" (*api*) is used in the sense of possibility.
By the force of logic alone, we conceive of cooperation everywhere as being of this very kind, and not otherwise.

An example here is as follows: "the causal complex of the final [moment], which is the cause of the immediate effect such as the sprout, by means of the totality of conditions" (*pratyayasāmagryā*). This refers to the appropriation (*upādāna*) [of that complex].
[§ 35. Only the performance of a single effect is primary cooperation; the other is secondary. It might be argued: "This cooperation is merely figurative;

rather, the production of an excellence (*atiśaya*) is the primary [form of cooperation]. To this he says: That alone—characterized by the production of a single effect—is primary cooperation, not that characterized by the production of an excellence.
This is because that [cause] itself is secondary;
this will be explained further below. Why is this so? He says: because that very [cause], being distinct, is the cause with respect to the intended effect.
Furthermore, the designation "cooperative cause" (sahakārī) applies only to that which is a cause, not to that which is not a cause;
for all things are called "cooperative" when they exist simultaneously,
and it is precisely the final collection of causes that is of such a nature.

Just as the final [cause] possesses the state of being a cooperative cause (*sahakāritva*) for the production of a single effect, so too should it be understood that the preceding collection of causes—which initiates each subsequent, distinct moment—is likewise a cooperative cause; this is because the final [cause] is cited merely as an illustration.
Therefore, every effect, such as a sprout or the like, or whatever is characterized by specific qualities, is produced by multiple conditions.

In all cases, the state of being a cooperative cause (*sahakāritva*) for a collection of causes that produces effects by accumulating or diminishing them consists precisely in the performance of a single purposeful action, not in the production of a specific excellence (*atiśaya*).
This might be argued: "Even in that case, let the state of being a cooperative cause consist in the production of a specific excellence, characterized as the performance of a single purpose."
To this he says: "And in that final moment, because it is impossible to produce a distinction, even the production of an excellence does not constitute auxiliary causality.
Why is it impossible to produce a distinction? To this he says: "Because there is no differentiation of a single, partless intrinsic nature."

For in that case, there is no distinction such as, "this part, which has not had an excellence produced in it, was born from its own causes, whereas this one has had an excellence produced by the auxiliary factors.
Even if such a distinction were indeed absent, [the objection remains].
But why is a distinction not made?

To this he says: because the arising of a distinction is characterized by the production of another intrinsic nature (svabhāva), and how could there be the establishment of another intrinsic nature in that which is partless?
It might be thought: "Let the ultimate particular (*antyaviśeṣa*) have a distinct nature itself. To this, he says: "If it were another entity," and so forth.
If the particular were characterized as another entity, then its status as ultimate would be lost.
Let it be lost.
If it is asked, "What is the fault?
[the answer is: consequently, because of its infinity, it would not be a direct cause.

Since this is so, there is no production of a specific quality (*viśeṣa*) in the primary cause from the auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*); therefore, the very performance of a single purposeful action (*ekārthakriyā*) constitutes the state of being an auxiliary.
Now, one might object: "If no specific quality (*viśeṣa*) arises from the auxiliary causes, then their capacity to produce an effect is not tenable. To this he says: "They are capable," and so forth.

For if they were produced as inherently incapable, then the arising of capacity from the auxiliary causes would have to be admitted. However, those final conditions arise together, being inherently capable by their very nature, and they do not delay for even a single moment.
Since those [causes] are restricted to a single moment, there is no prior, posterior, or separate existence apart from that moment;

and since the effect arises immediately after them and not at a later time, in such cases, cooperation consists solely in the performance of a single purposeful action, rather than being characterized by the production of an excellence (*atiśaya*).
This is because it is contradictory for causal capacity to exist [in a cause] by its very nature [if it were to produce an excellence].

Thinking that the very arising of a capable [entity] is untenable because there is no mutual agreement [regarding its existence], the opponent says: "From where does the capable [entity] arise? and so forth.
The proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādin) replies: "From its own causes. However, with reference to the views of others, it was stated: "By its own nature" (svabhāvataḥ).

For the opponent indeed maintains that the capacity of a cause—which has already arisen—comes from its auxiliary conditions; thus, the statement "by way of its own nature" (*svabhāvataḥ*) is intended to refute that view.
However, nothing whatsoever is produced by way of its own nature.
Because that would entail the consequence of being causeless;
for those births which directly depend upon them.
[493] Indeed, for one who produces—T. [494] for the sake of negating that—T.
[§ 36. The establishment of the restriction regarding the performance of a single purpose among momentary things.]
The restriction of momentary things to a single causal efficiency is itself untenable,
because even isolated moments are seen to be similar to the final moment.
For instance, they are distinguished by perception and non-perception according to whether "this is of such a form" or "it is not so."
In that regard, earth and the other factors are exactly as they are perceived when in proximity with other conditions, even when they are alone.
Therefore, just as when accompanied by others, even when alone they would each initiate their own respective subsequent moment capable of producing a sprout;
thus, because that which possesses the nature of producing a sprout and the like would not produce it when alone, [the opponent argues] "because that which has such a nature produces [its effect]."

Thinking that [the principle of] non-absolutism (*anekānta*) alone [is true], the opponent says: "Why do those causes, such as earth and seed, bring about this [seed] which is capable [of producing a sprout] only upon the proximity of another condition (*pratyaya*),
and not when they are alone?"
If it is argued that [causes] always occur only in combination, he replies: "At some time, in some instance, they may also be otherwise; they may even exist alone.

For instance, it is observed in certain cases that internal and external factors, when accompanied by certain others for a particular effect, produce that very same effect even when devoid of those companions. What fault is there if they are capable of producing [the effect] while existing alone?
If this is argued, he says: Furthermore, since even individual [factors] can be capable producers, not only a plurality but even a single factor—

such as soil, seed, and so forth— could produce an effect such as a sprout when it has arisen in a certain place and time, provided that its own nature necessarily possesses the capacity for production.
The opponent argues that [the seed] does not produce [the sprout] alone, even though its own nature is present; therefore, there is an inconclusive reason (*anaikāntika*).
Anticipating this, he says: "By successive [factors]," and so forth.

By various other factors—such as the granary, the effort of the person who removes it, the basket, the act of throwing it [into the field], the carrying of it to the field, and the scattering [of the seeds].

Because of that conjunction with conditions, [entities] possess distinct powers at every moment; they never possess a single power existing across prior and subsequent times. For even when there is a difference in causes—characterized by the conjunction with various successive conditions—if there were no difference in power, it would follow that they are causeless.
Furthermore, in other cases as well, such as the seeds of rice and barley, the difference in power is invariably based on a difference in causes.
Although conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), being produced by causes coming together and combining, continue as a continuum and exist through that succession,

they may— due to some degree of similarity in color, shape, or any other manner characterized by the production of a cognition that grasps them as having a single form— be perceived as "having the same nature" (*sarūpa*), meaning they appear similar because their forms are identical.

Even though they are recognized as the same, the nature of these seeds and so forth is indeed distinct and dissimilar— not identical by virtue of recognition, nor of uniform form— just like artificial and non-artificial gems, pearls, and the like, because their causal complexes (sāmagrī) are characterized by the conjunction of various different conditions.
Since this is so, by virtue of having a distinct nature, or rather, by virtue of having distinct potencies, or by virtue of being produced by various successive causal complexes...
Through the establishment of moments, only a specific thing such as an earth-seed is the cause of a specific effect such as a sprout,
or of that which is capable of producing it; not everything is the cause of everything.

And thus, for disjoined factors such as soil, seeds, and so forth, there is simply no nature of producing a sprout, nor a nature of producing a capable moment; because that which produces possesses that nature, whereas that which does not produce lacks that nature.
Therefore, there is no inconclusiveness (anaikāntika) in this regard, since whatever possesses a certain nature arises from its own causes as being exactly of that kind.
Furthermore, it would not be inconclusive [to argue] that it does not depend on another cause for its existence;

however, because recognition— which has similarity as its object— is sublated by the fact that its nature possesses distinct potencies inferred from the difference in causal complexes (*sāmagrī*), it lacks validity,
and thus similarity is not established for things that perish moment by moment.

Previously, by the passage beginning with "For this very reason, the difference between these two states must be determined as a real entity" [S. 116b], recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) having identity as its object was refuted;
now, however, the distinction is that [recognition] has similarity of nature as its object.

[§ 37. Explanation of the Determination of the Relation of Cause and Effect among Momentary Entities:

It has been stated that "only a certain thing is the cause of a certain other thing. Regarding this, in order to demonstrate—even though it is possible to determine—what is the cause of what, [the author] says "In that regard," etc., beginning with "In that regard" (*tatra*), meaning:
in those momentary entities which, at every instant, possess a nature of causal capacity.
"Non-obstruction" (*avyavadhāna*) means that which is not obstructed;

"non-obstruction and so forth" (*avyavadhānādi*) refers to a location where those qualities such as being too distant or too near are absent. That which has such a location is "one whose location is non-obstructed and so forth" (*avyavadhānādideśa*).

"Form, sense-faculty, and so forth" (*rūpendriyādi*) refers to form, the sense-faculty, and the mental attention (*manaskāra*) and other factors. That which is characterized by this collection of causes is what is called the "causal complex" (*kāraṇakalāpa*), defined as the totality of conditions (*sāmagrī*).
This collection of causes— consisting of the form, the sense faculty, and so forth, along with a location that is not obstructed— is the cause capable of producing consciousness, and nothing else;
for it exists only when that [collection] exists,
and it is absent even when other things are present.
And because the distinction between the capable and the incapable is based solely on this [proximity],
there is the mutual approach and mutual drawing near of those [factors] such as the sense faculties;
by the inclusion of the word "etcetera," the removal of obstructions [is also implied].
Because it is impossible [for such a thing to exist], as it would depend upon a causal complex (*sāmagrī*).

Having thus demonstrated this faultless determination of the relationship between cause and effect regarding internal phenomena, he says "by this principle," etc., in order to extend [this rule] to other cases as well.
This principle which has just been stated regarding the determination of the relationship between cause and effect is to be seen everywhere else as well.
Because of the statement "in all cases," he says "at every moment" and so forth, lest there be a cognition [of such restriction] even in non-momentary things.

Those powers which, occurring at each and every moment, follow upon various distinct natures, in those cases this specific determination of the performance of a single purpose by auxiliary factors is to be observed;
however, it does not apply even to those entities which others imagine to have a stable, unitary nature.
The term "single" (*eka*) is used because stability (*sthairya*) might otherwise be designated even on the basis of a continuum (*santāna*).
The term "stable" (*sthirā*) is used because unity (*ekatva*) exists even in a single moment (*kṣaṇa*).
It is "uninterrupted" (*avyavadhīyamānā*). [499] T.
[500] Why, moreover, is it not accepted that [the capacity for] performing a single purposeful action exists in things that are stable and possess a single intrinsic nature?
Thus he says: "intrinsic nature," and so forth.
Granted that an entity might not exist by itself;
however, a change in the intrinsic nature of a thing is not possible through its own self.
Furthermore, if a stable entity possesses a nature capable of producing an effect, then its non-activity is untenable, and thus it would produce [the effect] at all times.
On the other hand, if its nature is incapable, then even in that case, activity is untenable.
The sense is that one should never act at all;
for it is not possible that one acts at some times and does not act at others.
Consequently, if non-momentary things possess a nature capable of performing that causal function, they must be of a single, identical form in both their associated and unassociated states.
If even individual [causes] were to perform that same function, how could there be a possibility of "cooperation," characterized by the restriction to a single joint effect?
To this, the opponent replies: "Accompanied by another," and so forth.
Even if a non-momentary entity possesses a nature capable [of producing an effect] even when alone, nevertheless, it produces [the effect] only when accompanied by others, not when alone.
For this too is its nature: namely, that "its own effect must be produced by it when accompanied by others, and not by it alone, even though it possesses a capable nature.
The proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādin) says: "What [is the status] of the one that is alone? and so forth.

The question arises from one who considers that an entity must perform its own function only in conjunction with others and not alone; this is logical only if the nature of the solitary entity is incapable, and not otherwise.
The opponent, however, without understanding this intention, says: "It is capable. [He means:
Even for a non-momentary entity acting alone, its very nature is indeed capable; otherwise, its non-momentariness itself would be lost.
The proponent of the established tenet (siddhāntavādin) asks: "What does it not do?

For there is no non-action on the part of that which is capable, as is the case in the state of being combined; thus, by one who desires action only when combined, it must be admitted that the isolated [cause] possesses an incapable nature.
Now, if it is thought that even if the head of the isolated [cause] were cut off, it still would not act, to this he says: "not acting," and so forth.
For capacity is to be inferred from its effect; and since there is never at any time the production of an effect by the isolated [cause], how can its capacity be postulated?
There is no such rule that that which has a capable nature must necessarily produce an effect.
Thinking that "it is seen otherwise as well," the opponent says, "the weavers and so forth," and so on.
The proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntin), being patient, replies, "one whose nature is play," and so on.
The "beloved of the gods" (devānāmpriya) is either honest or a fool; because he has been raised in comfort, his very nature is one of amusement.
Playing is the characteristic of a child; by analogy with that, he demonstrates a deficiency in wisdom,
specifically a lack of application toward the treatises due to being raised in luxury.

For one who is unpracticed and of poor intellect, because his nature is forgetful, even though a task has been performed, he causes it to be done again and again; thus, he causes it to be remedied repeatedly.
Where, then, has this been explained?
To this he says: "For instance," and so forth.
This has already been thoroughly examined under the heading [501], "The argument is inconclusive, like a seed and so forth.

Thus, having established that since a non-momentary entity possesses a capable nature, it is contradictory for that which is combined to have the nature of performing an action while that which is alone does not, he concludes by saying: "Therefore, for that which has such a nature—namely, one capable of performing an action—it is impossible for it to be otherwise... [502]... [503]... [504].

Because there is never an absence of capacity, the production of the effect— which is the very nature of that subject possessing the property of causal efficiency— is unavoidable in the state of association, just as it is in its final state;
for it is precisely this [subject] that performs the single effect.
[503] — its activity — T. [504] — not even any non-existence — T. [§ 39. Refutation of the capacity that constitutes the intrinsic nature of entities as accepted by the Mīmāṃsakas.]
It might be thought: "This non-momentary entity is simply incapable by itself; therefore, it does not act alone, but its capacity arises from its auxiliaries in the state of association."

Therefore, since it acts only when conjoined [with other causes], he says: "In the final state, when capacity arises—of what kind [is that entity] which was previously incapable? This refers to the case where its nature is held by the Mīmāṃsakas and others to be such that this capacity is produced in it.
For they do not admit any difference in essential nature (*svabhāva*) between the entity and its capacity.
They maintain that even if there is some difference between them, they are perceived precisely as having that same intrinsic nature (*tatsvabhāva*).
That very production of something unprecedented is indeed the production of a previously non-existent entity, which consists in the capacity for that specific intrinsic nature.
For it is not logical that, while possessing a single intrinsic nature, the capacity itself should arise as something new while the thing remains incapable.

Because it would follow that there is a difference in the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of those two, since the superimposition of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmādhyāsa*) is the defining characteristic of difference.
If it is asked: "But how can the production and non-production of the capacity and its possessor, which are indeed being perceived, as well as their single intrinsic nature, be denied?"—we reply: No.
Because it is cognized by a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*);
otherwise, you, who follow cognition, would not be able to deny even such things as a double moon.
If it is argued that they are denied because a subverting means of knowledge (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) exists, [we reply:]...

In this case as well, why are the mutually contradictory and subverting [states] of the arising and non-arising of a single-natured entity not accepted? Furthermore, how could one perceive the distinction— whereby a subject (*dharmin*) such as a diamond or a stone, which remains established, has produced a capacity of that very nature— if there were no appearance of a difference between the prior and subsequent times?

If it is argued that because the non-arising or the simultaneous arising of effects such as consciousness would otherwise follow, one must conclude that this capacity— which previously did not exist when the eye and other factors were present— arises and is sequential; then, if this is so, the recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) produced through the two times, earlier and later, which functions with a single form, cannot be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), even though it apprehends a stone or similar object devoid of the appearance of any new capacity, since it is sublated by inference or presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*).
Thus, it would be accepted [as follows]:

since there is a contradiction in the identity of nature between arising and non-arising, only that which is capable arises as something unprecedented; and why is it not admitted that the delusion of oneness among those of limited vision—caused by the perception of similar subsequent states—is like the case of hair, nails, and so forth, which have been cut and grown back again?
[505] Of those very things, whose capacity is devoid of [the state of being] unaccompanied— [506]— and which has never before been experienced— [507].
[§ 40. Refutation of the Naiyāyika-accepted capacity (*sāmarthya*) consisting in the nature of an entity:

Now, the Naiyāyikas and others might think: "If capacity is defined solely as the proximity of auxiliary conditions (*sahakāri-pratyaya*), then it does not possess that [entity's] intrinsic nature (*atatsvabhāva*); thus, there is no consequence of the production of something previously non-existent. To this, he says: "If capacity is held to be of a nature other than that [of the entity]..."
That entity, such as a seed and so forth, being as it was before, does not become an agent even afterwards because it has not abandoned its own nature.
Why?

Because the Naiyāyikas maintain that "capacity" (sāmarthya) is the name for a distinct entity characterized by the proximity of auxiliary conditions (sahakāri-pratyaya), and that this very [entity] is what is expressed by the term "excellence" (atiśaya).
For it is precisely from that [momentary cause] that the production of the effect occurs, by virtue of being conditioned by its existence.

If those auxiliary conditions were also non-momentary, this same undesirable consequence would remain unavoidable even in their case; therefore, for one who accepts that cooperation is characterized by the restriction to the performance of a single purposeful action, momentariness alone must be admitted.

Furthermore, in order to refute the restriction of non-momentary entities to the performance of a single causal function, he states the reason for the accumulation [of arguments], beginning with "Moreover" (*api ca*): Why does that non-momentary entity, which is asserted to produce its own effect when all auxiliary conditions are present, produce it only at that very time?
For by whatever cause it performs that causal action at that time—namely, by virtue of having the nature of performing that effect—it would have performed it even earlier, since its nature is stable;
therefore, how could there be for it a restriction to the performance of a single effect? This is the intended meaning.

Thinking that no other logical justification needs to be sought, since things are seen exactly as they appear, and that this principle is everywhere unimpeded, Kumārila said: "It is seen performing [the action]," and so forth.
Because I saw him performing the effect at that very moment, by the force of that observation, we say that he performs it.
What is the point of stating this other argument?

Since he was not seen performing that action previously, the restriction regarding the performance of a single causal function (*ekārthakriyā*) is established even for non-momentary things. For an entity produces its effect by virtue of having the nature of producing it, and not by the power of being perceived, since it performs its own effect even when unperceived. Thus, this response is irrelevant; mocking this, he says:
"Aha! What great power! and so forth.
This is the manifestation of your great power, O Being of Great Majesty, because of this:

even though entities are devoid of the nature of performing an action—if entities were to produce an effect simply by virtue of having the nature of performing an action, then why was this very [point] not stated as the answer?

Since it has been demonstrated that the production of effects is superior [to other modes of action], how could it not possess great power, given that by its mere nature—that is, by its mere existence—it employs itself in various types of operations?
Nor do I have any intolerance toward this point; however, if indeed some cause were somehow disregarded...

Or, if [the object] were to transcend the range of vision of this venerable person—[the word] "atrabhavataḥ" being a term of respect—then "hanta" expresses a manifestation of dejection; [it means]: "Alas, its nature is non-productive; this is what it is—a thing whose nature is non-productive, and therefore its continuity would be severed. This thought of ours torments the mind.
The opponent says: "Indeed, we do not," and so forth.
We certainly do not claim that entities devoid of the nature of cause and effect perform their causal functions merely by virtue of our perception;
rather, those entities possess that causal nature by their very own essence.
Then they perform their own respective functions.
Observing them, we simply recognize that "these possess the nature of agents.
For the function of seeing consists in the cognition of an object as it actually exists.
"Not in the activity whose intrinsic nature is ignorance.
To this, the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādin) says: "True."
This too is the case:
do we perceive this as a reasonable statement out of a fondness for logic,
or does Your Honor, having somehow uttered something reasonable despite being constantly devoid of reasonable speech, ask this question out of a sense of satisfaction— what is it?

Thus he says: "The intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of those entities is characterized by the performance of an effect—that is, the property of producing an effect; for that reason, it is true that there would be no lapse into indifference, no neutrality, or non-activity on the part of those whose auxiliary conditions (*sahakāri-pratyaya*) are all present and complete, were they not to produce the effect—this statement of yours is also logical."

However, this must be asked: does that nature which possesses the property of non-delayed action arise for them at that very moment—the final state when they are complete—immediately before the effect is produced;
or rather, did it exist even previously, even during those states when they were mutually separated?

In that case, if it has arisen at that very moment with that nature, it is simply a new production; if it does not have that nature, then it is not an agent at all. Fearing the previously mentioned faults, the opponent says: "It existed.
Why? Because it is both "fallen away" (*pracyuta*) and "arisen" (*utpanna*), hence "fallen away and arisen" (*pracyutotpanna*).

The refutation of that [position] is as follows: for those entities whose intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is unchanging, unarisen, stable, and unitary, it is contradictory for an intrinsic nature that was perceived at some time not to exist [later], because if an intrinsic nature seen once were not to exist at another time, it would follow that it is something else. This is because such a thing could not occur in stable entities whose prior and posterior forms are neither fallen away nor arisen;
rather, it occurs only in momentary things, for an intrinsic nature seen at one time would not exist at another time, since in that case it would be different.
It does not occur in stable entities whose prior and posterior forms are neither fallen away nor arisen.

Here he says: "Then what now? and so forth. It might be thought: "This sentence of ours is not at all similar to that one. To this he says: "Or who [is there]... and so forth. If this [sentence] were not equal to that one, then prior to the state of all the auxiliary causes—

Furthermore, the meaning of this statement— "this [entity] has the nature of non-delayed action (*akṣepakriyāsvabhāva*), that is, the nature of performing its effect without delay, yet it does not produce the effect"— must be explained. The Naiyāyikas, however, maintain that the determination of whether entities have the nature of being causal (*kāraka*) or non-causal (*akāraka*) depends upon the presence or absence of auxiliary conditions (*sahakārin*).
It does not exist by way of its own nature;

therefore, even though it possesses a single, stable nature that is neither fallen away nor newly arisen, it does not have the nature of producing its own effect even previously, but rather [it produces it] only when all auxiliary conditions are present.
Anticipating that objection, he says: "sahitaḥ" (endowed), and so forth.
He refutes this with: "anyas tarhi" (then it must be something else), and so forth. [The opponent argues:
"Granted that the nature of the endowed [cause] is to produce its own effect..."
And since that which is solitary possesses a nature contrary to those [two], from what does its "otherness" arise?
To this, he says: "Because of a difference in intrinsic nature," and so forth.
For the very difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is the defining characteristic of the difference between entities (*bhāva*).
If that [nature] differs by virtue of being of a form that produces or does not produce its effects, how could there not be a difference between entities, as in the case of rice and barley seeds?

For there is no entity other than its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), such that it would not differ even when that [nature] differs, for that would entail the consequence of being devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*).

But has it not been said that, because the states of being a producer or a non-producer by their own nature are absent, and because they depend on the presence of other conditions, the forms of being a producer or a non-producer do not exist; so how can there be the consequence of a difference in entities even when that [nature] differs?

"Because its nature is characterized by a distinction that does not depend on anything else," for this reason he says: "For indeed, even in association... and so forth. This response of yours would be applicable if that entity which is intended as the "other" auxiliary were to become an agent in its own form when it is present, rather than in its own essential nature;
but this is not the case.
For if that were the case in an ultimate sense, he alone would be the supreme agent;
however, in that situation, the designation of agency would be nothing but a construction of conceptual imagination (*kalpanā*).
And that which conforms to conceptual imagination is not capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).
For a young boy is not appointed to the act of cooking simply because he is metaphorically designated as "fire.

Consequently, an effect would not depend upon that [boy], who provides no assistance; thus, it would either arise from those auxiliary causes alone even when they lack [the fire], or else it would not arise from them either.
If even those [factors] were agents by way of another's form, they would themselves be non-agents; therefore,

since all things are thus non-agents in their own right, they would also be non-agents by way of another's form, resulting in the total abolition of agency in every respect, such that nothing whatsoever could arise from anything.

Therefore, since an entity produces its own effect by its very nature (*svarūpa*) and not by another form (*pararūpa*), there is no room for this [objection]. Consequently, the principle that "the one [entity] is accompanied [by others] while the other is alone" remains entirely unshakable.
Now, if that nature by which this [entity] is a producer exists at all times—both in the state of being accompanied and in the state of being unaccompanied—then that nature...

Furthermore, for this entity of stable nature, that very same capacity to produce its own effect—which exists even prior to its state of association—is precisely what constitutes its nature of non-delayed action during its state of association; therefore, there can be no cessation of the production of the effect under any circumstances.

Alternatively, an opponent might say: "This [entity] was produced by its own causes with a nature of producing its own effect only in dependence upon other conditions; thus, when alone, it does not act."
Furthermore, there is no difference in its intrinsic nature between its state when combined with others and its state when not;
for its nature of producing its own effect while depending on other conditions exists at all times. Therefore, he says: "For even in the state of combination," and so forth.

Since its agency consists in its own essential form, and since that form exists even prior [to the presence of other conditions], and since dependence on other conditions is untenable—given that there is no excellence (*atiśaya*) acquired by the self from them, and because such dependence is characterized by the notion of being assisted (*upakāra*).
Otherwise, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*);

for since the production of its own effect by the entity alone is unavoidable, how could there not be a difference [between the entity] when it is acting and when it is in an associated state? This is the intended meaning.
Furthermore, the claim that "its nature is to produce its own effect in dependence on other conditions" refers to the form [of the entity] as characterized by another [associated] form.
The meaning is this: its status as a causal factor (*kārakatva*) is characterized by the presence of other conditions at a specific time, and not prior to that.
Consequently, by asserting that its nature is to perform an action only occasionally and not at all times, how can it be said that its nature of producing an effect exists at all times?
Surely, in this way, a difference in its very nature (*svabhāvabheda*) between those two times—that [time when it acts] and other times—would be established.

Therefore, it is established that for non-momentary entities, there is no such thing as "cooperation" characterized by the restriction to a single causal function. The opponent, seeking to show that the fault is equal for both sides, says: "Even for one who... and so forth; this is easy to understand. [He asks: "Even if they are indeed momentary, why does [the same fault] not apply?"

Thus he says: "It has been stated in this regard that the activity of that which is not separate from its auxiliaries belongs to those very final conditions (*antya-pratyaya*) which, by their own nature, arise together as momentary entities, for which there is no prior, posterior, or separate existence."

How could that which exists in a single moment—that which is by nature restricted to occurring in only the final moment—be otherwise? Could it exist before the final moment, after it, or separately from it? And that which becomes otherwise is precisely what exists in the final moment; having its own nature assisted by a continuum of cooperating causes, it possesses the property of acting without delay. Therefore, this reductio ad absurdum raised against the non-momentary position does not apply to the momentary position; for how could it apply there?
"Of the agent and the non-agent," and so forth.

The "agent" is the last [term], and the "non-agent" is other than that; their intrinsic nature (svabhāva), though distinct, is spoken of as a unity because the distinction is not intended to be expressed.
Likewise, regarding the agent...
That which is the penultimate cause,
and that which is the cause even of a non-agent— distinct from those, yet spoken of as a unity through the intention to express non-difference—
is so stated because there is a contradiction between the two natures of the agent and the non-agent within a single substratum (dharmin).

Likewise, regarding the two causes that produce those two intrinsic natures—one producing the nature of an agent and the other producing the nature of a non-agent—there is also a contradiction between them in a single substratum, provided they are distinct.

Since the non-agent nature produced by the cause that produces the nature of a non-agent is distinct [from the agent nature], it is not the case that "that which exists is the very same thing that does not exist"; thus, this undesirable consequence does not follow.
