[§ 41. Refutation of the view that only the effect depends upon auxiliary causes:
But another has postulated a different restriction regarding the performance of a single purpose by things of a stable nature; he presents that [view] with the words, "He who thinks," and so forth.
For the very nature of an entity is always such that its property is to act without delay.
But it is not as some assert— that the determination of the causal nature of things depends upon the presence of auxiliary conditions, and not on their own account.

Since it is impossible for that which is inherently a non-agent to become an agent through the form of another—lest the established order of causal factors (*kāraka*) be utterly destroyed—an entity of such a nature would never depend upon association for the performance of its own effect; for otherwise, one thing would be associated while another would be solitary, due to a difference in their natures as agent or non-agent. If it is asked: "If that is indeed always of such a nature, why does it not produce the effect at all times?"

Since the effect has a nature that depends on other conditions, even though it remains as a producer when those [conditions] are present, it does not arise from the cause alone; therefore, in this case, the fault lies solely with the effect itself.
Since that [entity],
although existing as a sole producer, requires other conditions, therefore—
because its effect arises only from those [conditions] combined with it— the non-momentary entities possess the nature of cooperation, characterized by the performance of a single purposeful action.
"Is it even possible?

The proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādin), demonstrating that this [opponent] has not escaped the previous fault, says: "Even for one who speaks thus, how can that entity intended to be eternal act alone? For it is stated: 'Its very nature is such that it possesses the property of non-delayed action.'"
Furthermore, an effect arises only from [factors] acting in combination, because of the statement: "Its nature is to be produced by a causal totality (*sāmagrī*).
Therefore, it does not arise from [factors] alone; thus, the contradiction previously stated remains as it was. To explain: if—
If its nature is one of non-delayed action (*akṣepakriyā*), then it must necessarily perform its effect; if it does not necessarily perform it, how can it have the nature of non-delayed action?

Since the nature of non-delayed action is understood from the observation of the effect occurring without delay, and not otherwise, the author says "not alone," etc., anticipating the opponent's objection.
"I did not say that [the agent] acts alone; rather, I said that its nature is to act without delay.
To this, he replies: "How then," and so forth.
If it is not accepted that [the agent] acts alone, how can it be described as having a nature of acting without delay?
If it is stated in that way, then surely this very point is illuminated—that is, expressed—by these words:
what is it?
That "it indeed acts."
For that alone has the nature of unimpeded activity which necessarily acts; how, then, could that which does not necessarily act possess such a nature?
As for what was said—"This is the fault of the effect itself, in that [it...]"—[the response follows].
The claim that "while existing as a producer, it requires other conditions" is also untenable;
for how could this non-momentary entity, being capable even when alone, disregard another condition that is required for its effect? It certainly would not.
And what could be done by one that does not disregard it?
He said: "Disregarding and setting aside other conditions, one would forcibly and by sheer violence produce this effect.
If that were so, what benefit would there be for it?"

If this is argued, he says: For in this way, by one who acts forcibly toward his own effect while disregarding another—even though he is capable as a solitary entity—that capacity of his which belongs to him alone is shown, that is, made manifest.
Otherwise, because he would act only in conjunction with another and never act alone, others would have the notion: "This one is not capable even when solitary."
In that case, how could this [cause] shine forth as if its power were eclipsed?
Therefore, it is incorrect to say that an effect depends upon other conditions.
Demonstrating that the contradiction remains exactly the same even when considering the effect, he says: "kāryaparam" and so forth.
By asserting that an effect depends on something else, you state that it does not arise from a cause alone;
yet by saying "that [cause], even when alone, is capable," you assert that the effect arises from that [cause] alone.
And these two [positions] pertain to one and the same effect.
Therefore, how could production and non-production—two mutually contradictory states—occur in a single substratum (dharmin) called an effect, arising from one and the same cause?

Since the superimposition of contradictory properties is the very definition of difference, you who assert these two in a single entity speak like one saying, "She is both a mother and a barren woman. Thus, you do not escape the previously mentioned fault.

Since even while speaking thus he asserts what is contradictory and does not perceive it, therefore this proponent of non-momentariness— his vital points being pierced and tormented by the "dart of envy," which is characterized by indignation at the faultlessness and the attainment of flawlessness by those who maintain the position of momentariness because it is irreproachable— is one whose vital points are pierced by the dart of envy (*īrṣyā-śalya-vitudyamāna-marma*).

Thinking that this wretched man, due to his disturbed state of mind, does not perceive even the contradictory nature of his speech and thus wails and cries out in a distressed, agitated, and incoherent manner— therefore, because there is no regard for the words of one with a disturbed mind, and because pointing out such faults would only produce further suffering, being like pouring salt on a wound— one should maintain equanimity toward him.
Thus, it is fitting for those who are wise and rich in compassion [to speak thus].

Therefore, having demonstrated that in non-momentary things, the nature of cooperation—defined as the restriction to the performance of a single effect—is in no way possible, he concludes by saying: "Therefore, this..."
And so forth.

For those things which, being of a stable nature, can exist even separately—that is, for those non-momentary entities—it is impossible to establish a rule of cooperation (*sahakāritva*), because they could potentially produce an effect individually and alone. Therefore, this definition of "performing a single purposeful action" (*ekārthakriyā*) [does not apply to them].
Cooperation belongs only to those things that are momentary.

This is because such things—whose nature is to arise from the transformation of their own causes and to depend on one another—are produced by a single totality (*sāmagrī*) consisting of mutual substantial causes (*upādāna*) and cooperative conditions (*sahakāri-pratyaya*), and cannot exist separately.
[523] The activity of dependence—T.
[524] Dharma — T. [525] -prasāva — T. [526] Bhajeta — T.
[527] Certainly—T.
[§ 42. Only in the case of momentariness is the nature of cooperation as the performance of a single purpose established.

Now, is it not observed that cooperation among entities also consists in the production of an excellence (*atiśaya*)? Why was it stated previously [528]: "In all cases, the production of an excellence is not what constitutes cooperation"?
If one asks, "What then? Is it not simply the performance of a single purpose by many? to this he says: "But where [there is assistance] by way of the continuum," and so forth.
Everywhere, cooperation is characterized solely by the performance of a single purpose; nowhere is the production of an excellence possible.

However, where there is assistance by way of the continuum—through the generation of successive moments that are increasingly more distinguished than the preceding ones from their respective prior conditions—

Entities function as cooperative causes (*sahakārin*) in bringing about a specific effect—just as fire, water, and so forth act in the production of boiled rice from rice grains and the like, or as earth and other factors act in the production of sprouts and the like from seeds and the like. In this regard, the "cooperation" (*sahakriyā*) of conditions (*pratyaya*) in the production of a particular quality is what is spoken of in common worldly usage. Based on the continuum (*santāna*), an effect called a "continuum"—characterized by a second or subsequent moment distinguished from the preceding moments—is produced.

Thus, because of the determination of identity between the preceding and succeeding moments, one might think, "This is an excellence of that very same thing," and thus [attribute it] to a substratum of substance;
however, this is merely figurative and not ultimate.
Rather, when subsequent distinctions arise from preceding moments—which possess properties brought about by the transformation of their own causes—[the excellence belongs to the stream itself].

In that case, from the ultimate perspective, the very definition of cooperation for the preceding collection of causes is their performance of a single purposeful action; thus, there is no flaw whatsoever.
Why, then, is it not accepted that an excellence (*atiśaya*) is produced by depending upon a substance (*dravya*)?
Because no specific quality (*viśeṣa*) arises in a momentary substance or entity, since that [quality] consists in its existence in the immediately succeeding moment.
If, then, no specific quality arises in a momentary substance such as rice, then let it not exist even in the subsequent moment.
Therefore, just as momentary things, even though they do not obtain any mutual distinction from one another, act only when conjoined and not individually, so too do non-momentary things.
Consequently, their state of cooperation will consist precisely in this: the performance of a single purposeful action (*ekārthakriyā*).
Nor can it be said that "whatever is the nature of something which was previously non-productive, that remains so even later.

For instance, when one has entered a dark room from a bright place, the sense organ is observed to produce the cognition of an object even though it did not do so [previously]. As it has been said: "For those who have just entered [a dark] inner chamber from the heat..."
Furthermore, objects are not perceived by the sense organs because they do not appear [to them].
[ŚV Pratyakṣa 126].
Therefore, he says: "For not [from rice, etc.]," and so forth.
Since proximity is equivalent to non-proximity when no specific transformation occurs, even in the presence of fire and other factors, cooked rice would not be produced from rice and the like.

Likewise, for one who has entered a dark room from a bright light, if the sense faculty does not gradually acquire an excellence (*atiśaya*) from its own auxiliary factors, then it would not produce the cognition of an object afterwards any more than it did before.
Therefore, when an effect that was previously impossible is observed in a certain case, that effect is indeed distinct from that [cause].
Just as the seed of *kodrava* is distinct from the seed of *śāli*, so too is that which produces an effect characterized by excellence (sātiśaya) distinct from that which lacks it;

thus, it has been demonstrated that where an effect arises from auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*) in a sequence, the so-called "auxiliary nature" characterized by the production of an excellence is merely figurative (*aupacārika*), whereas the primary (*mukhya*) auxiliary nature is indeed defined solely by the performance of a single purposeful action (*ekārthakriyā*). This applies even in that case.

But where the auxiliary causes produce the effect by mere proximity of the object without delay, is there also in that case the production of an excellence (*atiśaya*) based on a continuum (*santāna*)?

To this he says: "In those that act without delay," and so forth. For in the case of those [causes] such as the sense organs which, being produced from their own causes, are located in a place without intervention and act without hesitation, no production of a specific quality (*viśeṣa*) through mutual interaction is possible.
It was stated previously that "[they are] momentary.
If there is no production of a distinction, then how can things devoid of distinction serve as causes for cognition?
To this, he says: "In that regard, by their respective conditions—those which belong to each [cognition] individually," [and so forth].

Those things which have arisen from the absence of mutual approach, intervention, and so forth, and which reside in a location that is suitable—by virtue of being neither too near nor too distant—and which possess an abiding state in such an unobstructed place, attain the status of causes for cognition simply by the fact that their own nature has been produced; that is, they exist as the very production of their own nature. Along with this production of their own nature, they function as causes.
In that case, what is the point of seeking a mutual production of distinction?

For if they were not produced from their own causes as possessing a specific state— characterized by being situated in a suitable location and so forth— which is capable of generating their own effects due to factors such as mutual proximity,
then one might seek a mutual production of distinction among them.

But this is not the case when such things arise from their own causes alone; for this reason, in that context— regarding those sense organs and so forth which act without delay— their primary state of cooperation consists precisely in the performance of a single purposeful action, whereas the secondary state, characterized by the production of an excellence based upon a causal continuum, is merely figurative.
Now, why is the state of being a cooperative cause (*sahakāritva*) not established as characterized by the production of a specific excellence (*viśeṣa*)?

For that too must indeed be established because it is well-known in the world. To this he says: "But in a case where, regarding an effect, the cooperative causes do not attain the status of a condition merely by occurring in proximity without intervention, as is the case with the sense organs and so forth..."

However, producing at every moment a specific excellence that is conducive to the arising of the intended effect, the causal continuum— characterized by the occurrence of successive moments— requires other auxiliary conditions in order to attain its own internal excellence when the effect, which occurs after a lapse of time, is to be produced.
But the causal moment is not simultaneous with that [effect].

Therefore, from those other causes, having obtained a different intrinsic nature characterized by a succession of specific qualities conducive to the production of the effect, the continuum—which is conceptually grasped as a unity—is spoken of in common worldly usage.

However, in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), even there, each preceding collection of conditions is restricted to a particular distinguished moment that is conducive to the production of each subsequent effect; thus, the definition of a single functional activity (*ekārthakriyā*) is established.
In this way, they experience cooperation.
But how, then, do they acquire another intrinsic nature?
Since they bring about their effect in a gradual sequence, he says: "In that regard, by their own nature," and so forth.

In that causal continuum, those causes which are called material causes (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) and those conditions (*pratyaya*) designated as cooperative causes (*sahakārin*), the first moments of their occurrence—by virtue of not depending on a cause for their destruction—arise by their own nature (*svarasataḥ*).

When cessation has occurred, from those very first moments which are ceasing by their own inherent nature, there arises a moment distinguished by a specific quality conducive to the production of an effect; from those [moments] arise third moments possessing even more conducive qualities, and from those, fourth moments possessing the most conducive qualities.

Thus, up until the point where an infinite collection of causes, possessing extreme excellence, has arisen, there is the production of the effect; in this way, from the auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*), there is the acquisition of a different nature (*svabhāvāntara*), and the production of the effect occurs with delay. Regarding this, an opponent objects: [The term] "auxiliary factor" (*sahakārin*) [derives] from a cause characterized by acting together (*saha-karaṇa-śīla*).
The singular number is used in the sense of a genus (*jāti*).

When it is intended that an effect, such as a sprout, arises from a cause characterized by the final moment of the causal complex— which has acquired a specific quality (*viśeṣa*) in the manner just described— then [it refers to] that very first specific quality which is conducive to the production of the effect.

It is maintained that [the cause] which gradually increases is the producer of the effect; however, the production of that very [cause] would not occur, because those moments occurring in the first instant do not acquire mutual distinction, due to their lack of differentiation and because such [distinction] is not admitted.
If it is argued that "even though they have not acquired mutual distinction, they will initiate a distinction conducive to the production of the effect," he says:

The intention is that if the production of a particularity conducive to the arising of an effect— such as a sprout— is desired from non-distinct [causes] and from those that are mutually non-distinct, then the effect would never arise,
because there is an absence of particularity.
Consequently, the auxiliary causes would produce the effect while remaining entirely independent of the production of mutual distinctions from one another.

If it is asked, "What is established by this being so?", he says: "Therefore, even though they are momentary, [the causes] perform their own effect without depending at all on the production of mutual distinctions."

They perform a single function characterized by a specific restriction, and thus they attain the status of being cooperative causes. For that reason, even non-momentary things could possess causality, and there would be no production of an excellence of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvātiśaya*) from those things to be depended upon. Thus, the proponent of non-momentariness brings his own position into parity with the momentary view. As he says:
113.27 [529] each preceding moment—T.
[530] is divided—T.
[531] Because of the dependence on momentariness—T. Who would be commended for speaking thus, unless there were a lack of shame?
For everything arises from ignorance; that [ignorance] is the same even regarding momentary things.
In no way can specific causes for those conditions be established, because,
like eternal things, moments are indistinguishable from one another.

Thus [it may be argued]. In this regard, one might think: "Even at the first moment, the earth, seed, and so forth are present as having produced specific qualities (*viśeṣa*) from one another—by which [principle] there is a connection between each thing and that with which it is related, even if it is situated at a distance;
for according to the maxim, 'even those existing in distant places stand in the relation of cause and effect'. Anticipating this objection, he says: "Now, by the auxiliary cause," and so forth.

Even if the auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*) are devoid of mutual contact, they assist one another by the very nature of things; thus, for the sake of producing a specific quality conducive to the arising of the effect through the auxiliary cause, it would follow that only that which has already acquired a specific quality (*viśeṣa*) could be present at the time of contact.
If this were the case, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
For instance—even when that particularity arises, another particularity produced by a cooperative cause must be admitted;
and likewise, even for the arising of that [second particularity], yet another must be admitted.

Now, if it is not the case that the cooperative causes produce another particularity in one another as the cause for a particularity conducive to the production of the effect, [then the following ensues].
Because they are capable [of producing their effect] by their very nature (*svabhāvataḥ*), he says: "And not," and so forth.

For the auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*), such as soil, seeds, and so on, do not possess a state of perpetual capability at all times for the production of that specific excellence (*viśeṣa*) which is conducive to the arising of the effect; nor is there anything constantly adhering to or perpetually bound to them by virtue of such a state of capability.

There might be a specific quality (*viśeṣa*) in these [factors] such as the soil and the seed that produces a particularity conducive to the arising of the effect; by this, the objection—"If a particularity were produced from what is not itself particularized, then the effect would likewise [arise from the non-particularized]"—would also be refuted.
Why is this so? He says: "Because it is the means for that," and so forth.

Because the manifestation of the effect is observed when these—such as the soil, seed, and so forth—are present in their proper conditions (*upāya*), and because the non-production of the effect is observed when they are absent—that is, when their mutual contact ceases—if these factors were always in a state capable of producing the specific qualities conducive to the arising of the effect, then that specific quality would also always exist.

Consequently, the effect, which arises through that succession, would never fail to arise; thus, the production and non-production of the effect would not correspond to the presence and absence of those conditions.
Therefore, the auxiliary causes are not always in a state capable of producing the specific qualities conducive to the arising of the effect;

for, since an auxiliary cause existing separately cannot— out of fear of infinite regress— confer a produced distinction upon it, and because such a distinction is neither accepted nor logically tenable for those factors that exist at the very first moment of contact with one another.

For that reason, the first distinction—that which is conducive to the production of the effect—is not produced from the auxiliary causes for things such as soil and seeds, which are themselves unassisted and simultaneous [with those causes];
yet it is maintained that this [distinction] is indeed produced.
Therefore, because there is no difference between all the moments occurring in the state of separation and those in the state of totality, [the objection does not hold].
Even though it possesses the nature of producing that [effect], it does not produce it [at all times] because it produces it only when in a state of completeness;

just as momentary things possess a cooperative capacity characterized by a specific determination toward a single purposeful action, so too will it be for those of stable nature. Thus, the proponent of non-momentariness, having exhausted all other means, like a sick man, highly prizes this very point of similarity.
The proponent of the final position (siddhāntavādī), mocking the opponent with a witty turn of phrase, says: "As for us, however, [it is] not [a matter of] again and again," and so forth.
If, even when spoken repeatedly, the world attains an understanding of the principle (nyāya), then we shall speak even a hundred times;
how much more so two or three times?

For those such as we who are engaged in the welfare of others, there is no weariness in repeating a point again and again. And when the author of a treatise, speaking in this manner, clarifies that very same meaning through a different approach at some point, those who seek to avoid the charge of redundancy are merely exerting themselves in vain for no purpose.
If there is no agitation, then alas, let it be said; to this he replies: "Not merely from the production of a particularity," and so forth.
In reality, the status of being a cooperative cause for auxiliaries is never possible anywhere through the mere production of a particularity;

because, since that [particularity] is absent in seeds and the like existing at the first moment, there would be a lack of cooperation when it comes to producing a particularity conducive to the arising of the effect.
However, it is precisely the performance of a single purposeful action that is conceived— on the basis of the aforementioned arguments— as the ultimate co-operation of auxiliary factors.
And since this [performance] certainly exists for those things that possess the initial contact, why would they not be auxiliaries?
The opponent says: Even that single purposeful action would not occur for those things that are devoid of mutual distinction.

If, however, it is admitted that even for those devoid of mutual distinction there is that single purposeful action, then—since the capacity to produce it is accepted in each individual thing in that state—it would occur separately as well, just as it occurs in that state.
For instance—even in that state, they act without any distinction from one another;
why then would their individual performance of that specific action not also follow? Indeed, there is no difference whatsoever between these [atoms] in their combined and uncombined states.

If you say, "Let it be so; what is the harm?"—that is, if you think that when there is the consequence of the distinctness of the specific quality conducive to the production of the effect, then the effect such as a sprout, which by nature comes into being from that specific quality, would also possess that specific quality [even] from a mere auxiliary cause alone; [then we reply:]...
Here too, the entire response has already been stated.
For it is said that entities, being momentary, are indeed without distinction between their aggregated and non-aggregated states. To this we ask:
is this [alleged difference] based merely on some superficial distinction, or rather on a distinction that produces a specific quality conducive to the arising of an effect?
If the first alternative is intended, that is incorrect;
for no state devoid of particularity whatsoever is possible, since there always exists a particularity arising from its connection with various successive conditions.
For nothing is ever exclusively one and the same,
since there exist, as the case may be, the shadow, sunlight, wind, cold, and so forth of its substratum;
nor, even in their absence, is that [object] exactly the same.
This is due to the difference in causes.
However, this much may be granted: that a certain specific factor is conducive to a particular effect, but not every factor is so for every effect.
Showing that this has already been stated previously, he says: "at every moment by various other conditions."

"Although mental formations (*saṃskāra*), which possess distinct capacities at every moment due to their connection with various successive conditions, are perceived as having similar forms because of some degree of uniformity, nevertheless their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is indeed distinct; therefore, only a specific [formation] is the cause of a specific [result]. [537]
"Because in momentary entities, due to the arising of one after another, there is an absence of unity"—this has been stated here very concisely.
And thus, in the phrase "for us, however, there is no repeated statement," the inclusion of the word "again" twice is appropriate.
Furthermore, the manner in which a specific distinction arises within the continuum of an entity has also been explained.

"In that case, since there is the cessation of the preceding moment by its own inherent nature (*svarasataḥ*), there is the production of a specific [subsequent] moment from those very [preceding moments]; thus, there is the production of a distinction.

Now, if it is intended—based on a distinction that produces a specific quality conducive to the arising of the effect—that those things which undergo the first contact are mutually indistinguishable from one another, as previously stated, that too is incorrect.

For what kind of things are the earth, seed, and so forth, which produce the specific quality conducive to the arising of the effect? They are those that occur in immediate succession, being devoid of any intervention or the like.
Because its existence occurs only when that [other cause] exists, and because the determination of what is a producer is based solely on this much;

and since those [causes] of such a kind do not exist at all times, how could they—when separate—initiate a specific excellence conducive to the production of the effect, such that the performance of the effect would follow even from them alone? He demonstrates this: "those whose locations are suitable are 'suitable-located' (*yogyadeśāḥ*)."
The state of being that [proximity] is "suitability of place" (yogyadeśatā);

those whose beginning is this—namely, the various states such as "uninterrupted spatial proximity" and so forth—are described as such; and these are both those [states] and the various states themselves, thus they are so described.

Those specific states that arise in soil, seeds, and so forth— such as being in a suitable location or being in an unobstructed location— are characterized by the capacity to produce effects defined by particularities conducive to the arising of the result.
Since seeds and the like are not always of such a nature, how could they produce such specific effects even when separate?

This too has already been stated previously, because of the statement: "In that regard, the collection of form, sense-faculties, and so forth, which exists in a location free from obstruction and other such conditions, is the cause capable of producing consciousness";
and because that [statement] was merely an illustration.

In this case as well, it is indeed understood that the collection of factors such as the earth and the seed, existing in a location characterized by non-intervention and so forth, is the cause capable of producing the specific quality conducive to the arising of the effect.
And such a specific quality does not exist at all times,
because of the absence of the cause that produces it.
Because that specific condition (*pratyayaviśeṣa*), which consists precisely in their mutual approach and so forth, is the cause of that [effect];

this too has already been stated previously. Thus he says: "And regarding the production of those [causes], which possess distinctions conducive to the arising of the effect, that from which they arise—that too has been stated more than once: 'That specific condition which is the basis for their mutual approach and so forth...'"
"That cause is capable of producing that [effect]"—thus it is said.

Likewise, by the statement: "Those [factors] which, through their respective conditions, have come to reside in suitable locations and so forth by way of mutual proximity and support, attain the status of being causes for cognition simultaneously with the completion of their own nature."
Since this is also understood here,
even if there is no distinction among these [causes] due to their mutual impossibility,
by whom can that which is produced by its own cause be prevented?

Nor can there be an expectation of mutual [contribution] among entities that have already acquired their specific qualities from their own causes alone, since it would be untenable to maintain that they lack specific qualities derived from one another.

Furthermore, although each of those conditions—which produce the specific qualities conducive to the arising of the effect—possesses individual capacity, the production of the effect cannot occur in fragments; rather, the whole must be produced by each one individually.

Just as there is no activity for isolated factors—because a specific agent is absent and because each individual member of the complex, such as the soil, seed, and so forth, lacks efficacy when separate—this has also been stated more than once: "And since these do not exist prior, nor posterior, nor separately, even though they are capable, they lack the state of existing prior, posterior, or separately. [S. 132b]
Because of such statements as, "defects do not adhere," and so forth; therefore,

since one does not admit that such a specific quality— which would depend solely upon its own material cause— is possible for isolated [atoms], how could there even be an effect by way of initiating a specific quality conducive to the production of an effect?

But whence is this arbitrary rule obtained—that the sprout and other effects produce a succession of specific qualities conducive to the production of the effect through mutual cooperation, whereas [the seed] produces the quality conducive to the production of the effect merely by arriving at a location free from obstructions and the like? To this he says: "And because there is a twofoldness of effects, it is therefore divided in this way.
How is there a twofoldness of effects?

Therefore, he says: a single effect consists of that whose nature is an arising characterized by a succession of moments—each moment being more distinguished than the last—produced immediately by the auxiliary causes in locations such as those without intervention; these [moments] are defined as specific qualities (viśeṣa) which, in relation to their prior state, consist in a distinct state of being.

And another [type] is the opposite of that, which arises by the mere presence of auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*) and does not depend on a succession of specific qualities (*viśeṣaparamparā*) produced by one another.
An example of this is like a sprout and so forth; by the inclusion of "and so forth," examples such as cooked rice are also intended.
Likewise, that faculty which has the nature of acting without delay— just like consciousness and so forth—
is qualified by this [term] in order to exclude a faculty that has entered a dark inner chamber from its luminous state.
If it is asked, "Why is this so? it is because of the difference in the intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) of cause and effect.
For some effects have an intrinsic nature produced solely by the presence of the causal complex (*kāraṇasāmagrī*), while others depend upon its transformation (*pariṇāma*).

A certain cause also possesses, by its very nature, the capacity to produce its effect through its mere presence, arising from its own causes alone; it does not depend, in the production of its own effect, upon a succession of specific qualities produced by mutual interaction.
Another cause, however, has a nature contrary to that.
Just as a certain thing has the nature of producing a rice sprout while another is its opposite,

and the rice sprout has the nature of being produced by that [rice] seed rather than having the nature of being produced by seeds such as barley, the intrinsic natures of entities— which arise through the power of their own causes and are established by valid cognition— cannot be subjected to questioning.
However, regarding those things which are established by valid cognition as having the nature of producing a certain effect, the following inquiry arises: do they always possess that nature,
or only at that specific time?

In that case, if it were always of that same nature, then just as later, it would follow that it must perform its function even earlier; therefore, thinkers who investigate reality declare that for things such as the seeds of rice and barley, there is a difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) between the causal and non-causal states by virtue of their acting through another form. Furthermore, the recognition of identity based on the production of similar subsequent moments—such as in the case of hair and nails that have been cut off and grown back again—is not contradictory here. Thus, there is no contradiction.
And since there is a twofold nature of effects due to the difference in the intrinsic natures of those causes and effects, when this [twofold nature] exists,
that cause which depends upon the mutual assistance of their respective continua from the cooperating factors such as soil and seed—

The effect of that [cause], such as the sprout and so forth, which has reached its final state, has as its cause for production a specific quality (*viśeṣa*)— which consists in the existence of a distinguished second moment immediately following the first moment— that is conducive to the arising of the effect.
This initial [quality] does not arise from a mutual modification produced among those cooperating causes (*sahakārin*) that have undergone their first contact with one another.
This occurs precisely because of the dependence on mutual approach and so forth, due to a specific causal condition; for it exists through that.

From that first particularity—which is conducive to the production of the effect—there arise, starting from that point, those particularities characterized by the increasingly superior subsequent moments produced by the auxiliary causes that have acquired their own particularities from other sources upon their occurrence in the first moment. These are "born from that," meaning they are born from the particularities produced by the auxiliaries.

Why? Because that first particular has that [cause] as its material cause (*prakṛti*); because it acquires particulars favorable to itself through auxiliary causes (*sahakārī*)—which depend on mutual proximity and so forth and arise from specific conditions (*pratyaya*)—and because those subsequent particulars have a nature produced by the generation of particulars conducive to the production of effects brought about by those auxiliaries, without depending on mutual assistance.
Since this is so, the previously mentioned infinite regress (*anavasthā*) does not occur.

Now, if it is argued that even a seed or the like situated in a granary must be assisted by a cooperative cause such as soil, and that the soil and so forth must likewise be assisted by that [seed] with a produced particularity, then there would indeed be an infinite regress—this is not so, because we do not accept that kind of [mutual assistance].
Rather, we accept a particularity in this case arising from human effort and the like, which is the cause for scattering [the seed] in a field;
this consists in the immediate contact between the moist earth and the seed, which produces a particularity conducive to the material cause of the effect.

Regarding this, as for what was stated by the opponent: "Just as earth, seeds, and so forth, when participating in their first conjunction, produce a particularity conducive to the production of an effect without depending on a particularity produced by one another;
likewise, even entities that possess a stable nature will come into being restricted to that single effect, independent of any particularity produced by one another."
Accepting that [position], he says: "In that case, even if it is non-momentary," and so forth.
If even a non-momentary entity produces an effect just as a momentary one does, let it indeed do so;
no one prevents it.

However, if that nature by which it performs an action is such that its character is to perform that action without delay—meaning it is a dharma whose very disposition is to act dependently—then, because a separate state is possible, it would follow that even in isolation, and not only when combined, it would be capable of performing that action; this has been stated many times.

But as for one that does not possess that nature—that is, one lacking the nature of acting without delay—even then, in the state of being combined, it remains non-productive just as before, since agency in the form of another nature was already refuted previously.

Thus, having refuted the co-operativeness of non-momentary entities—both by way of performing a single purposeful action and by way of producing a specific result—the author concludes, saying "Therefore," and so forth.

Since both types of co-operativeness are untenable, there is no co-operator whatsoever for a non-momentary entity; consequently, it would produce its own effect even when alone. What, then, is the point of asserting that a non-momentary cause depends upon co-operative conditions?
Showing that this is logical, he says: "But for the most part," and so forth.

For one who maintains the doctrine of a permanent cause, if that cause produces its effect by depending on other conditions, then it is evident that there must necessarily arise a different intrinsic nature (*svabhāvāntara*) in that permanent cause which acts while depending on other conditions.
It is not said that there is dependence for that which is non-functional and does not experience functionality;

because it is observed that, for the most part— that is, as a general rule— a continuum of entities (*bhāvasantāna*) residing in, or existing within, that collection or conjunction of auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*), having acquired specific qualities produced by those auxiliary conditions, performs its own effect.
138.1} Therefore, it is analyzed in this way like a seed and so forth;
and the inclusion of the term "generally" (prāyas) is for the purpose of excluding the collection of sense faculties and so on that act as projectors.
This is because the logic applicable to that [momentary case] cannot be conceived in any way for non-momentary things, since their existence as distinct entities is impossible;
however, the arising of a different causal nature later on for that which was previously non-causal is not contradictory.
For it is not logical that the very same non-causal thing should possess a causal nature as its own essence, but it is not illogical for it to possess one that is not its own essence.
For this very reason, there is the apprehension of another intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
In that case, one must simply accept that the nature which is not an agent is subject to cessation through its own inherent tendency (*svarasanirodha*).
Consequently, everything is well-established.

Now, suppose it is thought: "The production of a different causal nature (*kāraka-svabhāva*) is admitted [only] if the permanent cause did not possess the causal nature even previously; however, since that [nature] exists even previously, its dependence on other conditions and its production from them has already been explained. To this, he says: "Of the causal agent," and so forth.
For if the causal nature existed even prior to the state of completeness [of conditions], then its non-activity would be illogical.
Even in the state of aggregation, it acts precisely by virtue of its own nature,
since agency in the form of another has already been refuted;
nor does it act [as such].
Therefore, that nature did not exist in it previously.
And if it were not produced even by other conditions, why would it depend on them in vain?

[§ 43. Conclusion of the Discussion on Causeless Destruction:

Thus, regarding the statement "because it is produced with that very nature," which was stated to avoid the charge of inconclusiveness—that "whatever has a certain nature, being produced from its own cause, becomes exactly like that and does not depend on any other cause for that state"—it is as follows:
When non-absolutism (anekānta) has been presented through another mode, [the opponent], desiring to refute it, stated "by means of the conjunction with successive conditions" and so forth.

Having completed that incidental discussion—which was undertaken to demonstrate how the nature of cause and effect, which exists in momentary things by a certain logic, is impossible in non-momentary things—the author, returning to the main subject, says: "Therefore, whatever is of such a nature," and so on.

If there is no need for causes of destruction for an entity whose nature is not to endure, then there will be such a need for an entity whose nature is to endure; to this he says: "Even for that which has the nature of endurance," and so forth.
For even for that which has the nature of endurance, there is indeed no purpose whatsoever served by causes of destruction.
For that stable intrinsic nature which has arisen from its own causes cannot be altered by anything else, because it would entail the loss of its unstable character; indeed,
while entities may well cease to exist of their own accord, those that truly exist do not abandon their own intrinsic nature.

Now, if it is maintained that even for that which has the nature of stability (*sthitidharman*) there is the occurrence of change (*anyathātva*), then upon the occurrence of change, its very nature as something stable would no longer exist;
for it is impossible for a nature that is identical to the entity and lacks stability to arise later while having been absent previously.
Indeed, for that which is of such a nature, [change] cannot occur in that [state].

It has been stated that "the superimposition of contradictory properties is the defining characteristic of difference," because if [an entity] were present, its non-existence at some time would be untenable, as that would entail the consequence of it not having that nature.
And this being the case, the former alternative remains: that an entity is by its very nature characterized by non-abiding.
And regarding that first alternative, the refutation has already been stated: namely, that the cause of destruction is redundant.
Alternatively, if this entity is indeed of a stable nature, its state of instability arises only later, in the absence of a cause of destruction.

Otherwise, cessation would be impossible; therefore, he says: That which is a change—characterized by the state of having the property of non-duration—of that which previously possessed the property of duration due to a cause of destruction, is another, distinct nature from its prior nature produced by its own causes. Since this [new nature] arises subsequently and has a different cause, how could it be the nature of that [original entity]?
If it is argued that this is because it appears as having that nature,
then such an appearance would occur due to similarity for one whose distinction from the other is unperceived, provided that it arises from another while its prior nature still exists;
otherwise, how could the contradiction be avoided?
If it is argued that there is another intrinsic nature (svabhāva),
how can that which is another intrinsic nature belong to it?
For it is not logical for one thing to be the intrinsic nature of another.
Because it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Why should that other intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) not belong to it as well?
To this he says: "Because of the difference in intrinsic nature," and so forth.
"Let it be; what is the fault if that is indeed another entity by virtue of having a different nature?

To this he says: "And thus, since it is another entity, the previous state—which was produced from its own causes as something possessing the property of stability—is established in a state characterized by non-falling away, while a new nature is being produced by the cause of destruction."

It does not possess the property of cessation, because the cause of destruction is occupied with the production of another entity; thus, for that which has the nature of persistence, cessation is not a transformation into something else.
For it is not logical that when another entity, such as a mallet, comes into being, there should be the cessation of the other.
Because it would lead to an over-extension [of the argument].
Furthermore, it has already been stated that [the effect] arises precisely through the destruction of that [cause].
But is it not indeed observed that, for copper and the like which possess a solid nature, there occurs the arising of another nature, such as liquidity, due to a cause of destruction such as fire?

And since the preceding [argument] does not establish that there is a state of falling away (pracyutidharmatā), he says: by this— namely, what was just mentioned— the production of a different intrinsic nature, such as liquidity or solidity, in copper, gold, and so forth (the word "and so forth" including liquids and the like) due to fire, cold, wind, and so on, is refuted and rejected for copper and other substances that possess a fixed form.
Because the fault is equal [in both cases].
How, then, is the arising of another intrinsic nature (svabhāvāntara) possible, and how is the non-existence of the former—while it remains with the property of non-decay—logical?

To this he says: "In that case as well, in copper and so forth which possess a solid form and the like, because the previous form, such as solidity or liquidity, has ceased through its own inherent nature (svarasa), since there is no connection with a cause of destruction."

When destruction occurs—due to fire and so forth (the phrase "and so forth" including the sprinkling of water, cold air, and the like)—that which possesses a solid form, such as copper, naturally ceases to exist because of an excellence produced in the material cause (*upādāna*) through the specific conditions (*pratyaya*) based on the mutual proximity of the auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*). Precisely from that material cause, due to the particularity produced by the material cause and the auxiliary causes such as fire, there arises something entirely different and distinct, namely a nature characterized by liquidity or solidity; for the mention of "liquidity" is merely an illustration.
[It is not that] what has arisen is simply the previous form of copper or the like, which was stable as solid or liquid, that has merely transformed into the nature of being liquid or solid.

To this, the opponent says: Who has stated that "for that which exists with the property of stability, there is the arising of a nature of non-stability due to a cause of destruction, and from that, destruction"?
For it is on that basis that you say such things as, "and that which is a change from another state is a different intrinsic nature."
However, it is stability itself that is produced by its own causes; its unstable nature does not arise from a cause of destruction.
How is this known—that it is produced by its own causes as something whose very nature is stable?
Because it persists when a cause of destruction, such as fire, is absent.
If a thing were produced from its own cause as having the nature of not abiding by way of its own-being (*svabhāva*), then it would not abide even when that [cause] is absent.

However, for that which has the nature of abiding by way of its own-being, another specific nature is determined by its very causes, namely: "destruction occurs spontaneously from something else, such as a contradictory factor like fire.
In the phrase "from something else" (*parasmāt*), the ablative case is used with the elision of the suffix *lyap*; the meaning is "in dependence upon another" (*param apekṣya*).
This [thing] has arisen with its own nature determined by its very causes, such that it must itself cease upon encountering its opposite. As it has been said:
"That is its very nature, by which it ceases upon encountering [the contrary]."
"As with others, [the cause] of the contradictory is the stream [of the effect], such as a hammer and so forth.
Now, one might object: "If its destruction occurs by itself upon the proximity of a contradictory factor, it follows that it is causeless;

and for that which is causeless, a restriction of place, time, and nature is not logical. To this he says: "And indeed, what is called 'destruction' is not a separate nature from the thing that perishes."
Since this would entail the aforementioned fault,
however, destruction is simply the departure from existence;
and because that [departure] lacks intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*), its possession of a cause is not at all tenable.
For that [non-existence] does not belong to it;
rather, it simply does not exist by itself.
Therefore, since there is no existent thing, for what is causality admitted?

The proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādin) says: This does not transcend the two alternatives just mentioned. What are these two alternatives? They are: "Is the entity eternal? and so forth.

[306a] But surely, for one who accepts the nature of persisting for a period of time, there is no room at all for the conceptualization of permanence? No; even by accepting that, permanence itself is accepted.
For instance—if this thing, which has the nature of persisting for a year, is produced by its own causes, then upon the completion of that year...

Whatever nature it has at the time of its initial arising, which possesses the property of persisting for a year— by virtue of which it remains for that year— is the very same [nature] at the end of that period;
therefore, it would continue to remain for another year.
Even at its end, because it does not abandon the inherent nature of the property of persisting for the first year, there is the consequence that it would persist for subsequent years;
thus, even if one accepts the property of persisting for a period of time, permanence itself is accepted, and so the conceptualization of permanence is difficult to avoid.

Furthermore, because of the acceptance that it ceases of its own accord when the cause of destruction is present, there is the conceptualization of impermanence, which is the conceptualization of a perishable nature.

For instance: since this entity perishes by itself upon the presence of what is considered the cause of destruction, its very nature—given that the nature of an entity is uniform—is that of something perishing immediately upon arising;
consequently, how could it be possible for it to have the property of persisting for another moment of time?

When such an alternative has been proposed, if one accepts the subsequent alternative, its persistence over time is precisely what is severed; thus, he must accept the alternative of permanence itself.
In that case, by accepting its own destruction upon the proximity of a cause of destruction, he asserts that it first exists as permanent and later becomes impermanent, having a perishable nature.
And by speaking in this way, he asserts two distinct states of being.
The particle *ca* (and) refers to what will be stated hereafter.
Of what nature are the two entities? They are such that their two intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*)—the eternal and the non-eternal—are distinct.
He who asserts the subsequent destruction of that very same eternal nature previously accepted as eternal, has in fact declared its destruction at every moment;

for otherwise, according to the reasoning stated above, destruction would be impossible even later. If, on the other hand, its destruction does not occur at every moment, then since that [destruction] is likewise impossible later, he has effectively asserted its non-destruction at all times; thus, with respect to the nature previously intended to be eternal, there is no cause for destruction.
[The opponent claims: "It is indeed incapable and thus does nothing at all.

[The author replies: "But surely the capacity of the cause of destruction has not been admitted by the opponent, since he maintains that destruction occurs spontaneously upon the presence of a contradictory factor? [The author replies: "No;
for precisely because of this, it would follow that destruction is dependent upon that [contradictory factor]."
Otherwise, why would this [cause] be required if it were ineffective?
For the state of being a cause is characterized by dependence.
If it is argued that one's own causes are at fault here, in that they compel it to depend on them even though it is ineffective; [we reply: ...
What, then, is this misplaced insistence on their part that they apply them in such a manner?
Therefore, it is only when there is a dependence upon the effect to be assisted that causes, being applied, appear appropriate;
otherwise, even those things which are of the nature of effects would not respect such an application.
And how can something that is ineffective be called a "contradictory" factor?
For it has no distinction whatsoever from that which is considered non-contradictory; thus, this [objection] is trivial.
As for what was also said: "Just as for other proponents of momentariness, even though a hammer or the like is ineffective, it is nonetheless required..."

[The opponent claims: "Just as the stream of jars and so forth ceases, so too for us, an entity persists for a period of time. This too is said out of ignorance of our own system; for for us, there is no such thing as a "stream" distinct from the moments that could cease upon the proximity of a hammer or other such causes, which would otherwise be ineffective.
For only moments exist;
and they do not depend on hammers or other such causes for their own cessation, because they cease by their very own nature.

However, as for their cessation— which is characterized by the occurrence of potsherds and so forth through a process of exclusion (*paryudāsa-vṛtti*)— and in the presence of which there arises the conventional usage "the jar and so forth have ceased" because the cause of delusion (consisting in the appearance of a similar subsequent state) has been removed for people who are attached to unity:
in that case, there is no lack of efficacy whatsoever on the part of the mallet and other such instruments.
Because they exist only when that [cause] exists;

for, due to a specific condition— namely, the mutual proximity and so forth of the swift mallet and other auxiliary causes with the momentary jar— an excellence arises, and since the potsherds and so forth possess the nature of coming into being, they have that [jar-moment] as their inherent nature for producing them.
Desiring to avoid the consequence that two intrinsic natures would follow, the opponent says: "Not prior," and so forth.
Why is this?
Because it possesses a single intrinsic nature.
Since that which has a single nature at all times must necessarily be eternal, it is impossible for it to later possess a nature of impermanence.

To this, the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādin) replies: "If that entity is eternally of a permanent nature by its very essence, never entering into or undergoing destruction, how can it be said to have perished?"

Why? Because between that intrinsic nature and its destruction—namely, the state of being eternal for the former and the state of being non-eternal for the latter—there is no identity of form, since they are mutually exclusive by their very nature.
Concluding, he says: "Since, therefore, destruction is not at all tenable for things whose nature is stability, it follows that when this [destruction] exists..."

If it is maintained by others that destruction is necessarily inherent in that which exists as a produced entity, then [the entity] perishes by way of its own nature of destruction and does not remain; thus it is "destruction" (*vināśa*).
The suffix *ghañ* is used here in the sense of the agent, according to the rule of frequent usage (*bahulavacana*).

That which has such a nature must exist as a produced entity (*kṛtakarūpa*) arising from its own causes, because it possesses that very nature of destruction characterized by non-abiding; otherwise, it would be impossible for destruction—which is necessarily entailed—to occur in those things that are produced by nature.
If you say, "Let it be so," [we reply:]...

He says: Even so, although [the entity] has the nature of perishing by itself—just as when it has the nature of not perishing—it was already stated during the presentation of the first alternative that a cause of destruction is useless because a change in nature is impossible; thus, we do not say it again.
Therefore, the passage beginning with "by which" and so forth is easy to understand.

Thus, having established—by means of both incapacity and futility—that the existence characterized by being produced does not depend upon destruction for its cause, and that such dependence is logically inconsistent, [the author], demonstrating how this very point functions as a subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) in the case of the contrary, says: "Therefore, destruction... and so forth.
The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: Whatever is independent with respect to a certain state is necessarily restricted to that state.
For example, the final causal complex is restricted to the production of its own effect.

And a produced entity, being independent regarding its destruction—because it is connected with a destruction that is necessarily occurring—is likewise [restricted] by others [to destruction]. This is an application of a *svabhāvahetu* (essential reason) in the form of a *prasaṅga* (reductio ad absurdum), which serves as a subverting proof (*bādhaka*) in the case of the contrapositive.

Therefore, since destruction is necessarily concomitant with that [existence], and because destruction is not occasional, it follows that whatever entity possesses the characteristic of being produced perishes immediately after its arising; such an entity is perishable, having a nature that is subject to destruction. Furthermore, upon the cessation of the property to be proven—namely, perishability—the existence characterized by being produced also ceases.

Thus, when a being (*sattva*) possesses the characteristic of being produced (*kṛtalakṣaṇa*), the establishment of its momentariness through positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*) is accomplished; for, independently, the identity between "being produced" and "momentariness" is established, and consequently, their respective positive and negative concomitances are also ascertained. Therefore, with respect to the former teachers, since there is no such thing as an unproduced existent, that [space] cannot be eternal simply because it lacks the definition of eternity—namely, "that which exists and is without cause" (VaiSū 4.1.1).

As for that which exists and possesses origination, it has been established by the aforementioned reasoning that others necessarily accept it as perishable, and thus it does not persist for any length of time.
