[§ 44. Demonstration of the pervasion of identity between existence and momentariness in general.]

But when it is stated in general that "whatever exists is necessarily momentary," without regard for the distinction between existence characterized as produced and unproduced— speaking with full confidence and without relying on the opponent's own admission that even for the produced, destruction is inevitable— then the very fact that everything is independent with respect to destruction is not established.

For those things, such as jars and the like, whose destruction is observed while they exist, it is logical that they are independent [of a cause for destruction] because no such cause is applicable to them.

However, as for those such as mountains which are obstructed by distance and the like, and whose entry into destruction is not observed, there is necessarily an absence of any basis for accepting their perishability.

Even in the final moment, since it is impossible to say that this [entity], while perishing, is independent with respect to destruction— because there is no distinction [between moments] such that it would necessarily possess that state even at the beginning— it is dependent upon its own nature. Thus, the independence with respect to destruction is unestablished, for even unproduced things such as space and so forth are dependent upon a perishable nature.
Perceiving that the perishable nature of an existent thing cannot be established independently— since the positive and negative concomitances (*anvaya-vyatireka*) which are its basis are impossible—

and considering that at that time only the subverting proof characterized by the contradiction with causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) can be stated as establishing identity (*tādātmya*), he raises the prima facie objection (*pūrvapakṣa*) and says: "If [the thing] were perishable by its very nature..."

Even by the reasoning already stated, among things such as jars whose destruction is directly perceived, there might be something—such as a mountain hidden by distance or other factors—whose destruction is unperceived;

or even something unconditioned (*akṛtaka*), such as space (*ākāśa*), which, though existing as a positive entity (*sad-rūpa*), might not have that nature—that is, it might possess a non-destructible nature. The word "even" (*api*) [indicates this possibility].
This is raised as a doubt because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes its nature as perishable;

consequently, since it would depend upon a perishable nature, its independence from such a nature is unestablished. Therefore, by virtue of that, the fact that momentariness—the probandum—is of the very nature of existence (*sattva-svabhāvatva*) remains unestablished, and thus the basis for that [inference] is undermined.
"Nor is there establishment through positive and negative concomitance.

What, then, is the basis for this suspicion, by which someone might suspect that even something which does not have that nature [could produce it]? He says: "For everything is not the nature of everything," because entities are seen to possess diverse natures—some are resistant (*sapratigha*), while others are non-resistant (*apratigha*).
Likewise, there may be things whose natures are blue, non-blue, and so forth;
similarly, some might be perishable while others are suspected of having an imperishable nature—this is the doubt raised by the opponent (*pūrvapakṣa*). [Reply:
No—it should not be suspected that "some might even have a nature other than that," for...

For if it were to exist in such a manner, it would be non-momentary; and if that were the case, it would follow that it lacks substantial reality (avastutva). So how could there even be a suspicion that it does not have that [momentary] nature as its essence? Furthermore, why does the consequence of lacking substantial reality follow from non-momentariness?
Since the establishment of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) for a sentient being follows from its nature of momentariness, he says: "For power... and so forth.
[561] *Anitya-viprakṛṣṭaḥ* — T.
[563] By virtue of being independent of space, [564] jars, cloths, and so forth [565] [arise].
[566] Consciousness and the other [aggregates], [567] because it would follow that they are not real entities.
[§ 45. Existence is precisely the capacity for causal efficiency.]
And that [existence] belongs only to momentary things.
He thinks as follows: first of all, this must be investigated here—what is the characteristic of existence that is appropriate for entities?
In that regard, it cannot be characterized by connection with "being" (*sattā*), because such a definition would be over-narrow (*avyāpti*).
Because it is absent in universals (*sāmānya*) and the like, or because it would be over-extended (*ativyāpti*) since it would also exist in cases such as the son of a barren woman;
for if it is asked, "How can there be a connection with existence (*sattā*) for the son of a barren woman and the like, given their non-existence?"—we say: no.
Because of mutual dependence:
since their non-existence follows precisely from the absence of connection with existence, and that absence of connection follows from their non-existence.
Furthermore, if the connection with existence belongs only to things that already exist, then another definition of existence must be stated, and the connection with existence would be redundant.

If it is argued that because those [entities] lack the capacity for any causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), they are devoid of connection with existence (*sattā*) precisely due to the non-existence of that very thing;

then, in that case, since only that which is endowed with the capacity for causal efficiency possesses a connection with existence, it follows that the capacity for causal efficiency itself is the definition of an entity. Thus, the connection with existence is redundant.
And thus it is so.

Otherwise, how could universals (sāmānya) and the like possess existence as their own nature (svarūpa)? For the capacity for causal efficiency (arthakriyāsāmarthya) exists in all things; therefore, that alone is the defining characteristic of an entity (bhāvalakṣaṇa).
The statement that "existence is characterized by origination, destruction, and persistence" (Tattvārtha-sūtra 5.29) is also untenable,
because origination and destruction are contradictory to persistence, and thus cannot coexist within a single substratum (*dharmin*).
If it is argued that there is production and destruction in one sense and permanence in another sense,

then since permanence is not as [the entity] is produced and destroyed, and production and destruction are not as [the entity] is permanent, a single entity possessing the characteristics as described would be impossible.

Since no other characteristic of an existent (bhāvalakṣaṇa) is possible, and because [the opponent] admits that even a capacity (śakti) ultimately produces its own cognition, otherwise the systematic arrangement of the six categories and so forth would be untenable— it is that very [capacity] which is the characteristic of an existent;
conversely, the absence of all capacities is the characteristic of a non-existent.
The inclusion of the term "all" is for the purpose of refuting the notion that non-existence consists in the absence of causal capacity in all other things;
for whatever lacks causal capacity toward anything whatsoever is said to be absolutely non-existent.

Since existence is defined solely by causal capacity, if this were to belong to a non-momentary entity, then existence would not be established as having a momentary nature. Consequently, how could there be positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka)?

If this is argued, he says: "Nor does a non-momentary entity possess efficacy toward any effect, even one characterized as cognition; how then could it have existence defined by that [efficacy], as would be the case for the past and so forth?
For if that were so, the momentary nature of existence would not be established.
Now, since efficacy is beyond the senses and because there is no fixed rule regarding the commencement of effects by causes, how can there be an absence of that [efficacy]?

Since for that which is momentary, existence—which is being negated by non-existence characterized by the absence of all causal capacity—is necessarily experienced as having a momentary nature, whereby positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) would obtain; therefore, he says: "By succession and simultaneity," and so forth.
It is not at all the case that the absence of all causal capacity in the non-momentary is stated on the basis of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) or from the absence of an effect.
But [it is not so], because of the absence of that which pervades it.
To explain: the performance of an effect is pervaded by either succession or simultaneity, since there is no other possible mode.

Therefore, since those two—which pervade the capacity to produce an effect—are incompatible with non-momentariness, that [capacity] which is pervaded by them must cease [in the case of a non-momentary thing].

The cessation of even the capacity for causal activity implies non-existence, which is characterized by the absence of all capacities; this non-perception of the pervader (vyāpakānupalabdhi) draws [the concept of existence] toward momentariness, because two contradictory properties cannot coexist in one place.

Consequently, existence, being excluded from non-momentary things, remains only in momentary things and thus experiences their very nature—thereby establishing the pervasion (*vyāpti*) in the form of positive and negative concomitance: "whatever is existent is necessarily momentary."
Certainty arises.

But is it not said that, because no other mode is possible, an effect such as a sprout and so forth is produced by a seed and so forth only through either succession or simultaneity? Yet, from what is that very absence of another mode established for the nature of the effect?
If another mode [of existence] were to meet the conditions for perception (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*), how could there be absolute impossibility?

There would merely be a negation of its presence in a particular place and so forth. If, however, it does not meet the conditions for perception, there is no certainty regarding non-existence in the case of remote objects; thus, how can its absence be established?

Therefore, since causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) can occur through other modes, even if succession and simultaneity are excluded, there is no exclusion of the capacity for causal efficiency. Consequently, how could there be a definition of "devoid of all capacity" when things are non-momentary, such that positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*) between existence and momentariness would be established? No;
for there is no fault in either case.
For instance—succession (*krama*) means a sequence, the isolation of the sprout and so forth from other effects;
simultaneity (*yaugapadya*) is its coexistence with other effects such as the seed;
and a different mode (*prakārāntara*) is the sprout’s becoming otherwise even in the absence of those two states.

And when that nature of the sprout and so forth—whether conjoined with other things or existing alone—is ascertained by direct perception to be non-existent, then its very nature, which meets the conditions for apprehension, is not perceived as being excluded from both sequential and simultaneous existence.

Since the object is perceptible, once its conjunction with others or its isolation has been removed, direct perception arises manifesting a location and so forth devoid of it; thus, because the non-apprehension of its nature occurs, the conventional usage characterized by the determination of non-existence and so on proceeds.

And regarding that state of being such as a sprout and so forth, when its exclusion from existing outside of two states is negated—whether it exists in some place and time, or in another place and so on, or sequentially, or even if the other state exists—there is no [other possibility] whatsoever.
Since the absence of any other mode is established by direct perception itself (*pratyakṣata eva*), how could causal efficiency (*arthakriyāśakti*) not be pervaded by succession and simultaneity?

However, the author of the treatise will state later, extending the argument by saying "likewise by this [same means] succession, non-succession, and so forth," that the establishment of the absence of other modes occurs through direct perception alone.

Even though other modes [of existence] meet the conditions for non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi-lakṣaṇaprāpta*), the establishment of their absence follows precisely from the fact that succession (*krama*) and simultaneity (*yaugapadya*) are mutually exclusive.

For instance, since things that are mutually exclusive entail the affirmation of one through the negation of the other, if the latter were not negated, there would be a contradiction between affirmation and negation; thus, how could a third mode—which consists in the negation of both—possibly exist?

The formal argument (*prayoga*) here is as follows: Wherever there is the determination of one alternative through the exclusion of another alternative, there is no possibility of a third alternative; for example, when yellow is determined as the non-blue alternative through the exclusion of the blue alternative.
And there is the determination of one of the two alternatives—succession or simultaneity—through the exclusion of the other alternative.
When an object in the form of cause and effect is not made the object of a mode that is being excluded, there is the perception of a contradiction (*viruddhopalabdhi*),
and there is the establishment of what is other than that excluded mode;
for these two— characterized as "being outside of that" and "identity with that"— are defined by their mutual exclusion, consisting respectively in the forms of "otherness" and "identity."
Nor should one suspect an infinite regress here due to the apprehension of further subverting arguments, because this is merely a recollection of a contradiction already established previously.

In cases of the perception of the contradictory (*viruddhopalabdhi*), having demonstrated the presence of the reason (*hetu*) in an external locus (*bahirddharmiṇi*), it is precisely the proof of contradiction that constitutes the subverting factor (*bādhaka*);
and this exists here as well.

Therefore, since two contradictories cannot coexist in one place, there is a certainty regarding the absence of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*), just as in the case of cold and hot touch, or existence and non-existence. So how can there be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*)?
In that regard, a non-momentary entity does not produce effects sequentially, because it remains unchanged from its non-productive state.
Furthermore, dependence upon auxiliary causes (sahakārin) cannot be proposed, as both types of auxiliary causality are untenable;
for it would follow that all effects must be produced at the very same time as the single act [of production].
Because the nature of that agent exists at that very time;
nor [can it act] simultaneously, because that would contradict perception and other means of valid cognition, and because it would entail the consequence of that action occurring again.
If it is argued that [the agent does not act] because [the action] has already been performed, we say no; for the capacity [to act] has not departed.
Otherwise, the action would have occurred even previously, since there is no difference in the nature of the non-agent.

If it is argued that this is because what has already been done cannot be done again, then there follows the consequence of a distinction within a single effect based on its being either possible or impossible to perform, as in the case of the seeds of rice, *kodrava* grain, and so forth.

Furthermore, since he is eternal and performs actions simultaneously, then because he exists even prior to that [action], the consequence is that the action would have to occur at that very time; and since he existed even earlier than that, it would follow that it never occurs simultaneously [with anything else].

Action would [have to] exist; and since an agent who performs [actions] simultaneously at one time could not possess the capacity for all purposeful actions at another time—characterized by a lack of such capacity—how is it not momentariness?
Or, if action is admitted, it must necessarily be according to the position of succession.
And the fault in that case has already been stated.

Thus, since the non-existence of the sense bases such as the eye would follow if they were non-momentary, existence occurs only in momentariness; therefore, because it is established that whatever exists possesses a perishable nature—namely, "whatever exists is necessarily momentary"—the pervasion (vyāpti) in the form of positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) is established.

[569] of another kind; [570] of that which is prescribed; [571] having become the basis for the suffix ṇa—T.
[572] Because the other is established by way of being excluded; [573] because there is no other [alternative];
[574] because it contradicts direct perception.

[576] T. adds here: "In the *Vivaraṇa* composed by Brāhmaṇācata, this is the first chapter: the Section on the Reason of Essential Nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
[§ 1. The Establishment of the Relation of Cause and Effect]"

Thus, having established the determination of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) as the basis for proving identity (*tādātmya*) in the case of an essential reason (*svabhāva-hetu*),

and since the cause of proving the relation of causality (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) in the case of an effect-reason (*kārya-hetu*)— namely, that [concomitance] and its basis, which consists of perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*)— has already been shown previously, [the author now addresses] another source of error held by opponents regarding that [causal relation], in order to remove it from that subject.

Showing this, he says: when the object to be understood (*gamya*) is a distinct entity (*arthāntara*), namely a separate thing (*vastu*), the reason (*hetu*) is an effect (*kāryahetu*); but when it is not a distinct entity, the reason is an essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
Why, then, is only the effect the reason when the object is a distinct entity? He says: "Because of non-deviation" (*avyabhicārāt*); [it is] the effect.

For indeed, [the effect] does not deviate from another object (arthāntara), nor anything else, as was stated previously; therefore, when another object is to be understood through the power of conjunction, the effect alone is called the logical reason (hetu). And as for the objection raised by the opponent—that there would follow the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of a relationship of signifier and signified in every respect—as stated by the Teacher with the words "na ca kenacit" and so forth, [this is refuted].

Anticipating that an opponent might perhaps raise this objection even here regarding the "effect-reason" (*kāryahetu*), he says: "The relation of cause and effect," and so forth. For if the effect is stated as the reason, then its capacity to make [the object] known would be by virtue of the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*). And that being the case, it would follow that the relationship between the signified and the signifier (*gamyagamakabhāva*) obtains in every respect.
Just as the general properties of fire are cognizable, its specific properties—such as being produced from grass or wood—would also have to be cognizable.
Likewise, just as the specific properties of smoke are indicative, its general properties—such as substantiality (dravyatva) and earthiness (pārthivatva)—would also have to be indicators.
Why? Because there would be no relationship of producer and produced in any respect whatsoever.
For the relationship between the produced and the producer is called the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*).
And this [relation] exists between fire and smoke not even partially, but in every respect.

To explain: just as fire is the producer by way of general properties (*sāmānyadharma*) such as fire-ness, substantiality, and existence, so too is it the producer by way of specific properties (*viśeṣadharma*) such as being made of grass or being made of leaves.

And just as smoke is produced by its own specific properties necessarily restricted to it, such as being smoke and being pale, so too is it produced by general properties such as existence (*sattva*) and substantiality (*dravyatva*).
Consequently, just as there is a cause-and-effect relationship between those two, so too does a relationship of indicator and indicated (*gamyagamakabhāva*) necessarily follow.
"The objection of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that 'this [the sign] is the basis for that [the signified] alone.
To this he replies: There is no relationship of producer and produced in every respect; and if that is so, how could there be such a relationship of the signifier and the signified?
If one asks 'Why?'—"

In the absence of that—that is, in the absence of those specific properties such as being produced from grass or leaves—smoke in its mere form arises; thus, because there is no such restriction of its origination (*tadutpattiniyama*) for the self [of smoke] with respect to those specific properties, how could it be so?

Likewise, in the absence of that—that is, in the absence of fire—the general property of substantiality (*dravyatva*) and so forth arises; since there is no such restriction of its origination in the form of "this [substantiality] arises only from fire," how could it be so? From what [source] then?

Is the relationship between the produced and the producer [established] in every respect? For if it were so, the relationship between the signified and the signifier would also have to exist in every respect.
Indeed, in the absence of a necessary rule of "arising from that" (*tadutpatti*), it is not logical to establish the relationship between the produced and the producer.
Since this is so, therefore the effect, such as smoke and the like, [is pervaded] by as many inherent natures as there are, such as "smokeness" and so forth;
the third case ending here is used in the sense of a characteristic (itthambhūtalakṣaṇā). It is "inseparable" (*avinābhāvi*), meaning it does not exist without [the probans].

"Without which does it not exist?"—this also connects with the phrase "by as many intrinsic natures as there are in the cause. It is understood that those intrinsic natures residing in the effect do not exist as a cause without those [intrinsic natures] residing in the cause; thus, it is by means of these [latter] that those [former] are [the cause].
Where is it invariably concomitant?
In the cause—that is, with respect to the cause; another meaning is that the locative case here denotes the substratum (*ādhārasaptamī*).

Now, the effect is the indicator (*gamaka*) and the logical reason (*hetu*) for those general properties residing in the cause—such as fire-ness, substantiality, and so forth—as many as exist, with which [the effect] is invariably concomitant.

Why is this so? He says: "Because of the rule of being its effect. This is because there exists a rule of the form "that [effect] is the effect of those very general properties residing in the cause. For the effect never deviates from those general properties at any time.

Having thus defined the aspect residing in the cause by means of the subsequent term, he defines the aspect residing in the effect by means of the preceding term, saying: "And by those very [properties]," and so forth.
The effect, too, through its own inherent properties, makes known the properties residing in the cause;
for instance, the specific forms such as the state of being smoke or the pale color of the leaves that arise in the interim cannot exist without those general properties residing in the cause.
Here too, the phrase "because of the necessity of being its effect" is to be understood.
This is because those very specific properties residing in the effect are necessarily effects in relation to the general properties residing in the cause.
Indeed, those specific properties residing in the effect never occur at any time without the general properties residing in the cause.

Consequently, the restriction that these [effects] alone possess the nature of being effects applies, and not to others— such as substanceness (*dravyatva*) and so forth— which exist even without the general properties residing in their causes.
Thus, in this way, it is only the general properties of the cause that are inferable, not its specific properties.
Even in the case of an effect, only its specific properties (*viśeṣadharma*) are indicators, not its general properties (*sāmānyadharma*),
because of the restriction that it must be an effect of that [cause].
As for those [properties] of the cause...
Those specific properties (*viśeṣadharma*) for which there is no necessary rule that they are the effects of that [cause] are not indicators;

and as for those general properties (*sāmānyadharma*) of the effect, such as substantiality (*dravyatva*) and so forth, they too lack the capacity to indicate precisely because there is no necessary rule that they are its effects. Thus, if the capacity to indicate is based on the relationship of cause and effect, how can there be an indicator-indicated relationship in any absolute sense?
Would it not follow [as a consequence] for others as well? — No; that which existed previously... [Tibetan: T.]
[579] It is possible—T.
[580] —by one who does not seek [it]—T.
[581] with pale leaves—T.
[§ 2. Even if the relationship of producer and produced exists in every respect, the relationship of the signified and the signifier is not likewise.
Anticipating the objection that this would result in an undesirable consequence for the opponent, he says: "In part," and so forth.

For if it is maintained—on the basis of the necessity of being an effect—that only the general properties (*sāmānyadharma*) of the cause are to be signified, and only the specific properties (*viśeṣadharma*) of the effect are to be signifiers;
In that case, it follows that there is a relationship of producer and produced only in part:

the general properties (*sāmānyadharma*) alone of the cause would be the producers, not the specific properties (*viśeṣadharma*); and likewise, the specific properties alone of the effect would be the produced, not the general properties.

In every respect, the relationship of producer and produced is intended; thus, there is a contradiction with one's own tenet. He resolves this: "There is no consequence of a producer-produced relationship by way of parts, because the entity is partless and that [relationship] is accepted as existing in its entirety."
Because the relationship of indicator and indicated is also accepted in every respect, he says:
"produced by that," and so forth.
For if the particularity produced in the effect by those specific properties residing in the causes can be apprehended, [then the inference is possible].
In that case, because it is accepted that the specific properties residing in the cause are what is to be known when there is the apprehension of the specific property produced by it;

and likewise, because it is accepted that the universals residing in the effect— such as substanceness (dravyatva) and so forth— which have particularity (viśeṣa), such as smokeness (dhūmatva) and so forth, as their limiting adjuncts (upādhi) or qualifiers, are the means of cognition (gamaka).

For instance: when there is the perception of the smoke of *aguru* resin, there indeed occurs the inference of its fire; and by means of the qualification "smokeness," there is an inference of fire through [the universal] "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) and so forth.

It is not the case that because the relationship of produced and producer exists in every respect, the relationship of the signified and the signifier (*gamya-gamaka-bhāva*) must likewise exist in that same way, since that [latter relationship] depends upon cognition.
For it is thus: a logical mark (*liṅga*) does not function as a means of cognition by its mere existence, because it is a communicator (*jñāpaka*).
Indeed, a communicator makes known the object to be communicated only when it depends upon its own ascertainment, and not otherwise.
How then is it said: "In the absence of that, because there is no necessity of its arising"?

If one were to accept the relationship between producer and produced in every respect, then in the absence of that [cause], the existence [of the effect] would simply not exist; therefore, he says: "unqualified," and so forth.

For if one takes up merely the effect in its unqualified state—devoid of the apprehension of the specific qualities produced by that [cause] and lacking the qualification of a specific logical mark (liṅga)—[then the aforementioned fault follows].
Or, if one intends to refer to substance and so forth in a general sense, then because smoke exists even in the absence of specific qualities belonging to its cause,

and because properties such as "substance-ness" (dravyatva) which are not distinguished from that [smoke] exist even in the absence of fire, there would be a deviation (vyabhicāra). Therefore, in every respect,
the relationship of produced and producer (janyajanakabhāva) is not accepted.
And because of that absence, there is the relationship between the signified and the signifier;
however, this is not the case when a specific distinction is intended,
since in that instance there is no deviation.

For instance— if indeed smoke in general exists even in the absence of specific qualities such as being produced from grass or leaves, yet its specific quality produced by those [causes] is not [present],
and if that [specificity] can be apprehended, [then inference is possible].
In that case, the particularity (*viśeṣa*) is indeed cognizable, because only that which is ascertained can function as a logical mark (*liṅga*).

Likewise, although the mere state of being a substance (*dravyatva*) or existence (*sattva*) may occur even in the absence of fire, it is not of the nature of smoke; therefore, since that which is qualified by such [smoke] is non-deviant, its capacity to signify is not precluded.
[582] Because it depends on an indicator—T.
[§ 3. Dispelling the doubt that the cognition of the causal relation is extremely difficult to attain.]

Anticipating an objection from an opponent here, he says: even though some smoke or the like may at some time arise from some fire or the like, every such smoke is of that same kind—of the same genus—as that which was once seen arising from fire; it has an origin from exactly that sort of thing from which that single instance was seen to arise.
From what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is it determined that "birth is of such a kind," such that it is said:
"In the case of the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*), positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) are based on the establishment of the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*)"?

For instance, even if by means of perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*) it is understood that a certain smoke is the effect of a causal complex consisting of fire and so forth—does this much suffice to establish that another [smoke] of the same kind is also the effect of that same [causal complex]?
Because perception and non-perception, which are based on that [object], have no operation there;
for let it be that those two have an operation only upon that very object, and thus it alone possesses the status of being its effect— what then follows for anything else?
By what means could its birth from such [a cause] occur?
For in this way, since it has been observed that a certain manifestation of smoke is produced by fire and so forth, why is that same [causal status] not accepted for a jar and other things as well?
Because there is no distinction [between them] in terms of being other [than themselves].

If it is asked, "What fault is there in that case?"—[the answer is: since, in that situation, there is an absence of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there is no certainty regarding such a mode of origination; and because of the suspicion that [the smoke] might originate even from something not of that nature, the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of such smoke and so forth with fire and so forth is not established.
Thus, on what basis does the effect-reason (kāryahetu) possess the capacity for proof?

For it is not the case that one must establish the positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) of that very same smoke— which was apprehended through perception and non-perception as being produced by a specific fire restricted to a particular place, time, and state—
because such [a specific smoke] is impossible in other places and so forth.
What then?

Since it is precisely such a universal nature (*sāmānyātman*) that serves as the logical mark (*liṅga*), and since there remains the suspicion that it could arise even from something not of that nature, how could there be a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) or negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) with such a thing? As it has been said:
"Because of the differences in state, place, and time, the potencies differ among various things. [T. 315b]
"The cognition of entities through inference is extremely difficult to obtain" (Vākya-kārikā 1.32).
To this, the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādin) replies: "No, because they do not arise from that," and so forth.

He thinks as follows: although here, at one time, the nature of smoke and so forth has been ascertained through perception and non-perception as being produced by a causal complex such as fire, the possibility that such a thing might arise even from what is not of that nature is still suspected, because it is distinct from what was previously observed. In this regard, just as a particular instance of smoke produced by a causal complex such as fire—once ascertained—is distinct from another particular instance of smoke that is of the same kind even if it arises from something else (due to the manifold powers of entities), [so too is the case in question].

—it might be suspected that this could happen; likewise, that [effect] too, having been ascertained once to be produced by a causal complex such as fire and so forth, remains exactly like that in relation to anything other than those [causes].
In that case, if the birth of such a thing were to arise from something else that is not of that nature, then for that which possesses such an intrinsic nature (svabhāva) [the following would apply]:
It follows that even for smoke whose nature is observed to be produced by a causal complex such as fire and so forth, fire and its causal complex are not the cause;
for such a nature would have a nature produced by causes distinct from the causal complex of fire and so forth.
Consequently, since the causal complex of fire and so forth is not the cause, that which was [produced] by me once—
Consequently, that smoke which was previously observed would not exist either;
for whatever does not have something as its cause is never produced from it even once,
because that would entail the consequence of it being causeless.
Regarding the term *atadbhāvinaḥ*: by the word *tat*, the intended cause such as fire (*agni*) and so forth is grasped;
*atat* means that which is not that, namely something different from it, dissimilar to it, such as the head of Śakra (*śakramūrdhan*) and the like.

Therefore, for that which has the nature of not arising from something else—that is, for such a thing characterized by those marks, namely smoke—if it were to arise even once from the absence of fire or other such causes, there would be a contradiction with its very existence. Yet, such a thing does indeed arise from a causal complex consisting of fire and so forth; therefore, it is understood through perception and non-perception occurring just once that such a specific nature has precisely such a cause.
Thus, whence can there be any suspicion of deviation?

Therefore, since smoke of such a kind as has been observed once to arise from the causal complex of fire and so forth is by its very nature produced by that [complex], it exists only from such [a cause]; hence, the certainty of positive and negative concomitance—that "wherever there is smoke, there is the causal complex of fire and so forth"—is established.

Alternatively, it is explained otherwise: here, the establishment of the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) was previously stated to be based on perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*), in order to demonstrate the positive and negative concomitances (*anvayavyatireka*) that are based upon it;
however, that is incorrect.
For instance, in the case of a certain initial smoke which arises immediately after the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) of fire and so forth, at the time of its first production—

Even when there is the existence—that is, the production—from some causal complex such as fire and so forth, every [subsequent smoke] is of that same kind as the smoke existing in the first moment; for it is perceived through direct perception itself as being non-different from its preceding moment.
"Born from such a cause" means that the first moment of smoke is born from a cause characterized by a specific causal complex of fire, fuel, and so forth.
"How can it be said that its birth is from such a kind of cause—that is, that it has a birth of such a kind? For there is no absence of smoke and so forth in that case.

And thus, since smoke is seen to arise from something other than that from which it was previously observed, there would be a lack of confidence in all cases. To this, the proponent of inference replies: "And likewise, smoke arises even from what is not fire."

"If you think that because the existence of Śakra’s head and so forth is not incompatible with its [the fire's] existence, there is no positive or negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) between fire and smoke—this is the doubt raised by the opponent.
As it has been said:
"If things were momentary, how could their modes of being have a dependent occurrence anywhere?"
The moment of smoke produced by the first moment of smoke is of such a nature that it produces only another first moment of smoke, namely the second moment of smoke, and not the third and so forth.
This same principle should be stated everywhere, including for the third moment onwards and for sprouts and other phenomena.
But from what cause does this distinction arise?

If this is argued, he says: because it is impossible for that which does not arise from that— that is, for smoke whose nature is not fire, fuel, and so forth, and which is indistinguishable from its first moment— to ever be absent even once, even for a single time, due to the absence of that causal complex consisting of fire and the rest.

For just as the second moment is similar in relation to the first, so too is the first similar in relation to that [second]; thus, because there is no distinction in their similarity, if such a thing were to exist without fire, then such a thing would not have the nature of being produced by fire, and it would therefore never arise from it even once. Or, if it does arise, since its very nature as being produced by that [fire] is manifested by its being "such," how could it arise from something of a different kind?

Therefore, since that which arises from something of a different nature is itself of a different nature, there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*). This is due to the well-established nature of the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*). — *Vākya*... [fragmentary text]
If this is argued— [587] then [it would follow that it is] not like that—
[588] thus it is refuted.
Therefore—[T.
590]—if one desires to [T.
591]—it would not be as it is—[T.]
[592] By virtue of the difference in the power of their causes—T.
[§ 4. Even though the smokes produced by different causes are not actually such [i.e., identical], there is the misconception that they are such because of their similarity.
Now, since all moments of smoke are useful for causal functions such as scratching the throat, inducing tears, or blackening the eyes, how could it be that they do not possess such a nature? [593]
No, for that causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) as well—whose nature is conditioned by the distinction between moments—lacks such [permanence], and thus the same fault applies there too.
If it is asked, "How then does the conventional usage of 'smoke' occur everywhere in the world? [the answer is:

it is due to the force of a conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*) of oneness based on the production of subsequent similar [moments], since conventional usage is impossible with respect to [discrete] moments.
If it is asked, "When there is similarity, why is there not identity?
[the answer is: because that which is similar is other than that which is identical.
For instance, a *gavaya* is similar to a cow, but it is not identical to it.
For another [object] is indeed similar to it;
even though in the ultimate sense it is not similar, how could the conceit of similarity that arises in those of dull intellect be prevented?
For instance, even the determination of reality cannot be prevented from occurring in what is not that [reality] by those of limited vision.
How much more so, then, the determination that it is exactly like that? As it has been said:
"When a continuum arises elsewhere with similar color and shape, people have the notion of that [object] in what is not that; how much more so when it occurs within a single continuum?"

But those who contemplate reality maintain that things possess such-and-such a nature due to the distinction between causes of such-and-such a kind, and not because they possess a uniform nature. Therefore, if something of such-and-such a nature were to arise even from what is not of such-and-such a nature, then its nature would be produced by that [cause]; consequently, for that which does not arise from that [cause], there could never be an occurrence from it even once. Establishing this very point, he says: "In mutual dependence," and so forth.
For, in relation to the cause, the effect has the nature of being produced, and in relation to the effect, the cause has the nature of producing.
Indeed, that from which something is seen to arise has the nature of producing that [effect].
And it is understood that the other is its producer;
otherwise, it would be impossible for the one to arise from the other, and impossible for the other to produce it.
If this is indeed the case, what is established regarding the subject at hand?

To this he says: "In that case," when this very principle holds, if smoke—such as that which is produced by the causal complex of fire and so forth in the first moment—is of the same nature as that which exists in the second and subsequent moments, then by virtue of its being of a nature that produces [fire] from the causal collection consisting of fire, fuel, and so on, [it follows that it is not different from the first moment].
It would arise from another [cause] distinct from that which has been determined—namely, from the first moment of smoke produced by the causal complex of fire, fuel, and so forth.

In that case, such a nature of smoke would not have as its produced nature (*tajjanya-svabhāva*) that which is produced by the causal complex of fire and so forth; rather, it would be produced solely by smoke itself. Consequently, even once, it would not [arise] from that causal complex of fire and so forth.
It could not be so;

for if such a nature were to arise from something else, it would possess a nature produced by that [other thing], and not a nature produced by fire and the like. How, then, would its occasional arising from that [fire] be logical?
Here is the illustration: "like other things" (*arthāntaravat*).

For just as another thing, which is not admitted to be produced by that [cause], arises from something else and thus does not possess the nature of being produced by that [cause]—that is, it does not possess the nature of being produced by the causal complex of fire and so forth—and therefore does not arise from it even once;
likewise, smoke of such a kind [is also like this]. Therefore, it is understood that when it arises from that [fire], it is of a different nature altogether.

It might be thought: "Even though this [smoke] has a nature not produced by that [fire], it is forcibly produced as such by the causal complex of fire and so forth; what fault is there on the part of poor wretch?

To this he says: "Nor indeed" (nāpi)—meaning not only would it not arise from that because its own nature is not produced by it, but the causal complex of fire and so forth also would not produce such smoke as exists in the second and subsequent moments.
Why?
Because it does not have the nature of producing that [effect].

For if such a thing were to arise from something else, then that very thing would possess the nature of producing it, and not the causal complex consisting of fire and so forth; thus, how could that which lacks the nature of producing it bring it about?
An illustration of this is as follows: "like another causal complex.
Just as another causal complex—which is not admitted to have the nature of producing that [effect]—does not produce it, so too is the causal complex of fire and so forth.
For indeed, that [complex] proceeds precisely by following its own inherent nature.
Then, from where would that [effect] arise through the power of the causal totality?

[§ 5. Regarding the production of such-and-such by such-and-such causes, the effect also possesses the nature of being such-and-such:

It might be thought that even though smoke has a nature produced by a causal complex such as fire and so forth, it is "such-and-such" (tādṛśa); and although it has a nature produced by smoke, just as that very same smoke exists as having both a nature produced by fuel and a nature produced by fire.
In that case, even such smoke, by virtue of having a nature produced by both causal complexes, would arise from both; therefore, he says:

"And it is not at all logical—that is, consistent with reason—that such smoke should have a nature produced both by that [fire] and by what is not that, namely, produced by the causal complex of fire and so forth, and produced by smoke."
Why? Because it has a single nature;
for there is no difference in such a form of smoke.
Indeed, even when there is a difference in time, its such-like nature does not differ.

For if there were a difference [in nature] such that one thing arose from another of a different kind, dispute would be impossible; for if that [thing] were produced by causes of both similar and dissimilar kinds, then it would necessarily possess both a similar and a dissimilar nature. Demonstrating this very point, he says: "Smoke and non-smoke," and so forth.

By the word "smoke" (dhūma), such a nature as is produced by a causal complex consisting of fire and so forth is intended; by the word "non-smoke" (adhūma), a different kind [of smoke] produced from other causes is meant. And it should be understood that their respective natures—being of such or not-such a kind—are due precisely to their being produced by such or not-such causes, according to the principle to be stated hereafter.

Therefore, because fire possesses the characteristic of smoke, it has a nature that produces both smoke and non-smoke; since it has a nature that produces such and non-such [effects], as it comes into being in such and non-such ways, its nature would be both smoke and non-smoke, and thus it would possess such and non-such natures.
Why then would it be of such a nature alone?
Why is this so? He says: "Of the natures of effects," and so forth.

For those natures of effects which are mutually incompatible are produced by the natures of causal complexes that are themselves mutually distinct; they are not inherent, because that would entail the consequence of being causeless.
Therefore, smoke arising from such and non-such [causes] would necessarily possess such and non-such natures.

It might be thought: "In the case of having such-and-such or not-such-and-such an intrinsic nature, there is no dependence on such-and-such or not-such-and-such causes, because causes are required only for the mere production of effects. To this he says: [601] "And because, if there were no dependence on causes—meaning, if there were no dependence on such-and-such or not-such-and-such causes regarding the state of having such-and-such or not-such-and-such a form—it would follow that such-and-suchness is causeless (*ahetukatva*)."

For there is no other kind of origination for things of such and such a nature apart from their coming into being after not having existed, wherein there could be a dependence on that [cause] even for those things which are independent of causes of such and such a nature.
Therefore, by the word "origination," it is precisely the state of having such and such a nature that is expressed.
In that case, if one accepts dependence on a cause, how could there not be dependence on a cause regarding the state of being such and such?

Therefore, since the causal complexes (*sāmagrī*) themselves possess such-and-such or not-such-and-such characteristics, there is a distinction among effects based on their possessing such-and-such or not-such-and-such intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*); how, then, could that which is of one nature arise from something of a different nature?

As for what was said—that "just as a single smoke is produced by fire and fuel, though they are of different characteristics, so too a single-characterized effect will arise from a different causal complex, even if it is of different characteristics"—that is incorrect.

For we do not deny that things which are distinct can be productive; indeed, even though they are mutually distinct, those factors—whose nature is determined by the specific conditions of the transformation of their own causes and who are restricted to that particular state—produce that single effect.

However, because there is a restriction on the nature of the produced and the producer through mutual dependence, it is said that such an effect arises only from such [causes] and not from something else, since the latter lacks the nature to produce that specific result.
Because even in the absence of that [cause], if it were to arise from something else, there would be no necessity regarding its production;
and if there is no necessity, the relationship of cause and effect is untenable.
However, if—like fire assisted by fuel as its material cause—it were restricted to that state, being assisted by that very material cause like fuel [is to fire].

If even a dissimilar instance of smoke or the like were to produce a similar instance of smoke, and this were understood through perception and non-perception, then—who would not accept that it too is a producer of such [an effect], given its necessity of having the nature of producing it, just like fire and other causes?

However, since there is no necessity of the nature of being produced and being a producer between those two when they are dissimilar, how could there be the relation of cause and effect? Thus, for a dissimilar thing arising from a different kind of cause, there would be a state of causelessness.

Since this is so, therefore that specific causal complex consisting of fire, fuel, and so forth must be understood as the producer of the first smoke, and not anything else; and that smoke must be understood as the first smoke produced by that specific causal complex of fire and so forth, and not anything else. Thus, because there is a restriction of the nature of the produced and the producer in the form of cause and effect according to the principle stated above, whatever is the cause of something [is its specific cause].

At one time, it was established through both perception and non-perception that the production of such an effect does not arise from a cause of a different kind— that is, from a cause of a dissimilar nature—
nor is the production of a dissimilar effect prevented from arising from such a cause. Thus,
having demonstrated that the nature of such and dissimilar effects is produced by such and dissimilar causes, he concludes:

He said: Therefore, whatever effect is observed and ascertained through perception and non-perception from a particular cause at one time, that effect does not deviate from it; such an effect does not arise from something of a different nature.
For this reason, once the causal relationship is established in this manner, a cause of that specific kind produces only an effect of that specific kind.
When this certainty has been established, the pervasion of the effect by its cause—in the form of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)—is proven by the aforementioned reasoning:

that there is no production from what is of a different class. One who does not understand this point—that there is no production from a cause of a different kind from the observed cause—and who, thinking that the intended meaning here is merely "the effect is not produced from a cause of a different class," raises an objection:
He says: "But surely, it is observed that some effect arises even from a cause of a different class (*vijātīya*);

how then could there not be a contradiction with observation for the claim that 'there is no arising from a different class'? To explain how this is so, he says: "For example, from cow-dung and so forth—the word 'and so forth' including horns, moonstones, and the like—arises the water-lily (*śālūka*) and so forth—the word 'and so forth' including water from a reed-pond and the like."
For instance: the production of a lotus from cow dung, of an arrow from a horn, and of water from a moonstone [is observed].
Yet, cow dung and the like are not non-homogeneous (*vijātīya*) with respect to the lotus and so forth; why then is it said that "there is no production from the non-homogeneous"?
The proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntin*), demonstrating the opponent's error, says: "There is no production from the non-homogeneous."
For the intended meaning here is that whatever is seen to arise from a certain cause does not arise from anything of a different nature than that [cause],
and not merely that it does not arise from something of a different genus from its effect.
And there is no deviation in that case.

Thus it is said: for indeed, the very nature of cow-dung and so forth is the primary cause of such things as the water-lily (*śālūka*) and the like, because it is the cause of the first moment—the initial beginning—of the continuum of the water-lily and so forth; thus, it is the cause of the beginning of the continuum of the water-lily and the like.
There is no difference in cause, nor does anything arise from something of a different nature, because at that initial stage everything arises with cow dung and other such things as its causes.

However, when there is a continuous occurrence characterized by the arising of successive moments caused by preceding moments in a stream—such as in the case of an arrow—then existence arises from the arrow.
Thus, for that which arises from horns and the like in a stream and so forth, it is not of the same nature as the arrow and such; and for that which... [S. 154b]

The existence of things such as arrows arises from their respective preceding causes, but not from things like horns; thus, because such a thing cannot possibly arise from a cause of a different class from its observed cause, the certainty of the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*) is established.
This remains so even when lotuses and the like are accepted as being based on their own preceding species within an beginningless continuum.
Even then, showing that there is no deviation (vyabhicāra) because such a nature is absent even when certain things like cow-dung exist, he says:
"And it exists," etc.
[This refers to] that series of lotus roots (*śālūka*) for which cow-dung and so forth are the cause, and that [series] which always has its own kind as its cause; of these two...

There is indeed a difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāvabheda*) between two lotus roots—one born from cow dung and the other from something else—even though there is no difference in their form (*rūpa*).
If it is asked, "How can there be a difference in appearance when the form is identical? [the author] replies: "For not... and so forth.

Because the mere identity of form is not the cause for things being of that same nature—that is, for their similarity—since, due to the similarity of form between two lotuses, one born from cow dung and the other from elsewhere, they would have to be of that same nature and there could be no difference in genus;
why is this so? To this he says: "Even for those whose forms are non-different," and so forth.

For even among those certain things which possess a common form, a difference in genus is observed based on some distinction other than that form; therefore, the similarity of form [is not the cause].
Thus, this is the basis for their being of one kind;
for instance, even when there is a similarity of form, a distinction is sometimes observed between two flowers, as in the case of two sun-flowers, one blue and the other not.
In some cases, it is like the two types of *karkoṭaka* plants, one barren and the other fruit-bearing;

in some cases, like the two types of *trapuṣa* plants, one sapless and the other flavorful; and in some cases, like the two types of *campaka* trees, one produced from a tree and the other from something else, distinguished by their fragrance.
In some cases, due to their power, it is as if two *harītakī* fruits have lost their capacity for touch and utility;

therefore, although the recognition "this is that very same thing" based on the similarity of form establishes a commonality between the two lotus roots (*śālūka*) born from cow-dung and other sources, nevertheless, because they are produced by distinct causal complexes (*sāmagrī*), [they remain different].
Only a difference in genus (jāti) is to be understood, not identity of genus;
for that very reason, recognition is erroneous, and thus the "suchness" (tādṛśatva) imagined by it is unreal.
[598] Smoke would not be smoke—T. [599] From that which is not smoke, smoke-born—T. [600] ...would not exist—T.
—regard is intended; therefore—T.
[602] in the arising [603] —the non-similar—T.
Because a rule is observed when there is an absence of a causal complex other than smoke—
this is the example.
[607] Therein — T.
[608] Born from the *utpala* — T. [609] Arisen from reeds — T.
[610] "The existence of something different from a horn and so forth"—T.
[611] "Connected with its own genus"—T.
{p. 162.1} [§ 6. Faults in the case of a non-distinct effect being produced by a distinct causal complex.]

If, however, in the case of water-lilies (*śālūka*) produced from cow dung and other such things, or smoke produced from fire and other such things, their very same nature were to exist despite being based on distinct causal complexes (*sāmagrī*) due to the force of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), what fault would there be? To this, he says: "Otherwise, indeed," and so forth.

For if, indeed, that causal complex which is accompanied by conditions characterized by its own kind, as well as that which is independent of its own kind— such as the cow-dung and so forth for the lotus (*śālūka*) and the like, or for smoke that which is characterized by fire, fuel, and so forth, or that which has the nature of Śakra’s head and so forth and consists of smoke and the like— if from such a diverse causal complex an undifferentiated effect of exactly the same kind, such as smoke or a lotus, were to arise; [then there would be no distinction].

In that case, it would follow that the difference and non-difference, or the distinctness and non-distinctness, of the effect— whether characterized as belonging to the same class or a different class— would not depend on the difference and non-difference, or the distinctness and non-distinctness, of the cause in its form as a causal totality; consequently, the difference and non-difference of the entire universe, the aggregate of all entities, would be without cause, [existing merely as] belonging to the same class or a different class.

Therefore, wherever the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is of a different character, even if there is some similarity due to certain commonalities, the effect remains of a fundamentally different genus (*vijātīya*).
Now, one might object: "Even when there is a difference in the causal complexes of smoke and fuel, the learned do not admit a difference in the genus (*jāti*) of the smoke."
This is not a fault, because the exclusion of what does not possess that nature (*atadrūpaparāvṛtti*) is equal in both cases;
for even though there are subtle internal distinctions of genus based on the difference between moments, the exclusion of heterogeneous things based on the coarse continuum is identical.

Just as the universal "cow" is established based on the exclusion of non-cows despite the internal distinctions between sub-species such as the brindled cow (*śābaleya*) and others, so too, among all cows—that is, all instances of smoke—there is a similarity in their being the basis for a single uniform cognition, even though there is a difference in the moments that serve as their material causes (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) and which establish them as belonging to a single continuum.
If it is asked, "How can this be so for the first instance arising from fuel?", the answer is: "It is not so."

For instance, the smokes of those substances indeed imitate the specific varieties of agallochum, camphor, sandalwood, and so forth; and the smokes of those substances likewise imitate the specific wicks made from drugs that relieve coughs and asthma. Yet, their distinctness as belonging to different classes does not arise from a difference in form.
For the properties of being of the same class (*sajātīya*) or of a different class (*vijātīya*) are not based on the identity or difference of forms (*ākāra*).
Indeed, rice sprouts and the like do not imitate the form of their seeds and so forth;
nor do they possess the state of belonging to that same class as non-rice and the like.
They do not experience [the distinction] based on exclusion.

Therefore, fuel itself—possessing specific qualities imparted by auxiliary conditions such as fire—is what produces such an effect as smoke, which has a different form from charcoal and so forth. Enough with this excessive proliferation.

Now, if indeed no difference in the effect arises despite a difference in the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), then since that [effect] is absent even when there is a difference in the cause, let it be admitted that it is causeless (*ahetuka*).
But what follows from this non-difference, such that the causelessness of both is asserted? To this he says: "For instance," and so forth.
For when, despite a difference in the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), no difference arises in the effect, its causelessness is established.

For when a cause exists, it is in no way possible for that which does not exist to possess causality. Therefore, even that non-difference of the effect [which you claim], since it arises from two distinct causal complexes (*sāmagrī*), is itself non-existent insofar as there is no actual non-difference;
how, then, can it possess causality?
For just as that which does not exist when a cause is present cannot possess causality, how could that which exists even when a cause is absent possess causality?
If it is argued that this is not so because the distinction between causes is itself based on non-distinction [of the effect],
then this distinction would never find a footing anywhere.

Even in the case of rice, *kodrava* grain, and so forth, there is no distinction in their causes; for if one were to postulate a cause without a specific basis, there would be no difference [between them].
Furthermore, since the non-difference of appearance is merely observed due to some cause of error, even though there is an ultimate difference [between things], it might be argued:
"For that which arises from something of a different nature..."
He desires that difference and non-difference be accepted as causeless; for he maintains that only entities themselves possess causes. Therefore, he says: "And distinct from those," and so forth.
Indeed, there is no nature of entities whatsoever apart from difference and non-difference which could possess a cause even when those two are causeless.
For if that [nature] were other than those two, it would follow that there is no relationship such that "these two, difference and non-difference, belong to this [nature]."
Because there would be the fault of infinite regress (*anavasthā*) in postulating a relation with something other than that [entity],

and because even in the case of non-difference, since difference and non-difference as well as the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the entity abide only within themselves, how could there be relatedness in the absence of mutual benefit? Furthermore, if one postulates such benefit, and it is maintained that the intrinsic nature of the entity has arisen from its own causes alone and is neither different nor non-different from anything else, [then the problem remains].

In that case, even if those two [difference and non-difference] exist, since there is no alteration of its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), how could the intrinsic nature of an entity (*bhāvasvabhāva*) possess both difference and non-difference?

Alternatively, if it were to be understood that the intrinsic nature possesses difference and non-difference by virtue of a difference and non-difference that are distinct from it, then if those two [distinct factors] themselves are different, the intrinsic nature of the entity remains exactly as it was; thus, there could be neither difference nor non-difference of it in terms of its own form (*svarūpa*) from anything whatsoever.

Furthermore, if one again postulates difference and non-difference based on that [nature], the intrinsic nature of the entity remains in that same state; thus, there would be either a lack of change or an infinite regress regarding difference and non-difference.
Alternatively, if they are non-different, it would follow that the very intrinsic nature of the entity is being produced by difference and non-difference.

Because it is impossible for that [entity] to be produced by means of another form; and because if it were to arise later from a different cause, it would follow that it is something other than that [original entity];
nor is the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of an existing thing produced.
Because that [nature] is established by its own causes alone;

or, if one imagines that the intrinsic nature of an entity arises from its own causes as something whose essence is both distinct and non-distinct, then distinction and non-distinction— which possess mutual exclusion— would be redundant,
since the cognitions of distinction and non-distinction would also be established from that very same source.

Therefore, since difference and non-difference—as conceived by the Vaiśeṣikas and others, consisting respectively of particularity (*viśeṣa*) and generality (*sāmānya*)—are untenable, it follows that the very nature of an entity (*bhāvasvabhāva*) alone is what is expressed by the terms "difference" and "non-difference. If those two were causeless, it would follow that the nature of the entity itself is causeless. Consequently, because entities would be causeless, they would either exist eternally or not exist at all.
For if things were without cause, their existence would have to occur at all times if it ever occurred at any time;
or else, their non-existence would also have to occur at all times if it ever occurred at any time.
However, it is illogical for existence to be merely occasional.
What is the reason?
Because if that which is depended upon were causeless, nothing at all would exist;
for it is by depending on it that there is dependence upon that which is to be depended upon.
It is logical that things which exist when a cause is present and do not exist when it is absent are occasional— that is, they arise at certain times— and not otherwise.
Therefore, one must not accept the production of an effect that lacks the characteristics [of its cause] from a cause that possesses different characteristics.
Because, according to the reasoning already stated, it would follow that things are causeless and so forth;

furthermore, he states another fault regarding the production of a non-distinct effect from a distinct causal complex: "And there would be no established distinction among the specific means of accomplishment, such as clay and threads, for the various things to be accomplished, such as jars and cloth."

In the world, the practical application (niyoga) whereby one who seeks a jar employs only a lump of clay and not threads, while one who seeks a cloth employs only threads and not a lump of clay, and so forth, would not be possible.
Why? He says: because of the powers (śaktayaḥ)—characterized as specific internal excellences (ātmātiśaya)—belonging to the causes, that is, the causal complexes (sāmagrī).
Regarding specific determination (*pratiniyama*): because only a particular causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is employed for a particular effect and not another for something else—
since only certain materials such as clay are taken up for the production of a specific object such as a jar, and not other dissimilar materials such as threads— for what reason is this so?
If this is asked:
it is because that very material cause, such as clay, possesses the capacity and suitability for that [effect], such as a jar, whereas another cause, such as thread, lacks that capacity for it.
Why does that [specific cause] alone possess the capacity for that [effect] and not another?

Therefore, he says: because there is a distinction—due to their having the nature of producing that [effect], such as a jar, from clay and so forth, and from threads and so forth; due to their having another nature, namely the nature of not producing a jar and so forth; and because they are different, being of a distinct state of being.
For indeed, the state of having the nature of producing or not producing that [effect] is not something other than the very form of the clay, the threads, and so forth.

But when it is not admitted that there is a specific restriction of capacity even among causal complexes (*sāmagrī*) that are mutually distinct— since it is accepted that a non-distinct effect can arise even from what is distinct— then, even from a cause such as Indra’s head, which is distinct from the causal complex characterized by fire, fuel, and so forth (which has the nature of producing smoke and the like) despite being distinct from that which has the nature of producing smoke, [the effect would arise] by way of the momentary basis.

Or, when the production of smoke and so forth—specifically that smoke which is produced by a causal complex (*sāmagrī*) consisting of fire, fuel, and so on, and which possesses those characteristics—is intended, there would be no restriction (*pratiniyama*) regarding its generative capacity; that is, there would be no restriction on the capacity to produce the specific effect intended, such as smoke.
Consequently, any arbitrary effect could arise from any arbitrary cause.
It is not the case that everything would arise from everything exactly as it is seen; rather, the meaning is that everything would arise from everything.
Therefore, one must admit a specific restriction of causal capacities among causes.

Therefore, even if a result produced by a dissimilar causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is perceived as having a similar form due to some degree of resemblance, its nature remains entirely different; thus, it is established that everything of such a kind is born from a cause of that same kind. It might be argued: "Even though the causal complex is dissimilar, its power to produce an effect characterized by those [specific] features is identical; therefore, the effect will possess those characteristics. And because this occurs only in certain cases, there is no occasion for the fault previously stated. To this, he says:
"But when there is equality in the power to produce that [effect]," and so forth.

First, the refutation already stated in the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*)—namely, "and smoke does not have a nature that is both produced by that [fire] and not produced by that"—applies here as well. Even while granting this point, he says: for such is the fuel, which undergoes a modification induced by fire acting as its auxiliary cause.

If the capacity— the specific excellence of its own nature— of smoke as a cause for the distinction of smoke [arises] from its own particularity, and if that very same capacity exists in the head of Śakra or in smoke, characterized by the excellence of its own nature as the power to produce an effect indistinguishable from the smoke produced by that causal complex (*sāmagrī*),
then, given the identity of that capacity, it would simply be fire, fuel, and so forth, stated under a different name.
Because it is impossible for that which is distinct from it to possess an excellence of nature distinct from it;
for that alone is fire which, imparting a transformation to the fuel,
produces smoke, and that alone is the fuel which, having its transformation imparted by fire, [produces] smoke.
It imitates its own kind.

And if you also accept this regarding the head of Śakra and so forth, then there would be a dispute merely over names, since the designation is made in that way while accepting no difference in the object; because it is so, the effect, such as smoke and the like, is observed.

At one time, when fuel and other such causes have been ascertained through perception and non-perception to possess a nature excluded from what is not that [cause], they do not deviate—whether with respect to the continuum or with respect to the moment—nor do they arise from anything else distinct from those [causes]. Thus, in the case of the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*), the determination of positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*) is established. [628]
{p. 167.1} [4. Examination of the Reason of Non-apprehension /] [§ 1.
Definition of the Nature of Non-apprehension, preceded by the Presentation of Divergent Views /] [612] Of a single genus—T.
[613] The connection is that it is the object of a single mental continuum (*ekasantāna*). [614] Its effect is the essence of that— T.
[615] And because it is produced by causes—T.
[616] —of everything—T.
[617] even of the cause—T.
[618] — due to non-difference — T.
[619] — such is the form — T.
[620] — by its own nature — T.
[621] Of difference and non-difference;
[622] of difference and non-difference;
[623] of difference and non-difference.
[624] At times — T.
[625] Regarding the seen and the unseen as they are — T.
[626] The cause of the difference in intrinsic nature — T.

[627] Or from the head of Śakra, etc.—T. [628] T. adds: In the *Hetubindu-prakaraṇa* composed by the Brahmin Ācārya Arcaṭa, this is the second chapter, concerning the effect as a logical reason (*kāryahetu*).
Thus, regarding the effect as a reason, since it has been observed that whenever X occurs, Y occurs, through repeated direct perception and non-perception, for all such cases...

It has been demonstrated that birth occurs only from such a cause and not from one of a different kind; thus, when the existence of even a single individual effect is observed to arise from some specific cause, the establishment of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) through pervasion (*vyāpti*) is secured.

However, regarding non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) as previously described—which is based on demonstrating the absence of any other causal factor—there is no disagreement concerning its positive and negative concomitances.
However, regarding its very nature, others disagree.

For instance, some, such as Īśvarasena and others, maintain that non-apprehension is merely the absence of apprehension, and that it serves as a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for establishing non-existence—which is of the nature of a simple negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*).
Others, however, [hold that it is] the non-transformation into the form of the cognition whose object is the thing to be negated.

The Mīmāṃsakas assert that the cognition of another object— either as the non-modification of the self into the form of the object of the knowledge of that which is to be negated, or simply as the consciousness directed toward an object other than that— is the means of cognizing absence (*abhāva*), and thus constitutes a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) beyond perception and inference;
for a cognition directed toward another object does not consist of perception or inference.
It apprehends non-existence, because its object is the aspect of existence, whereas the aspect of non-existence is distinct from that.

However, in the case of the non-existent portion (*abhāvāṃśa*), that which produces the cognition "it does not exist" acquires the name of the means of valid cognition for its absence (*tadabhāvapramāṇa*), just as the sense faculty acquires the name of perception (*pratyakṣa*) by virtue of generating the apprehension of its own object.

Likewise, others state that non-apprehension—characterized either as the presence of another thing (*anyabhāva*) or as the cognition thereof—is a means of proving only the absence [of an object], and not the linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*) regarding its absence; for once the absence is established through the mark (*liṅga*) of non-apprehension, the application of that convention follows of its own accord.
The Naiyāyikas, however, maintain that it is the very cognition "it does not exist"—a perception occurring immediately after the cognition that apprehends the bare location and so forth.

They do not declare that non-existence, which is of the nature of a mere void, has a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) consisting of a determinative act; rather, if that very [cognition] regarding the negandum, such as a jar, is expressed by the term "non-apprehension" (*anupalabdhi*), there is no contradiction whatsoever.

Thus, since the cognitions of opponents have diverged regarding non-apprehension, he says the following—first demonstrating the essential nature of non-apprehension—in order to refute them: "of that which has reached the conditions for apprehension..."
And so forth.

"Attainment of the conditions for perception" (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpti*) means the completeness of the other conditions for perception, which are designated as the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) and the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*).

And there is the specific nature of the objective condition (*ālambanapratyaya*).
