This nature has been explained by the author of the treatise elsewhere for the purpose of refuting the misconception of the Naiyāyikas, who hold that "that which exists, when other conditions for perception are present, becomes directly perceived. For they [the Naiyāyikas] maintain, by the term "attainment of the conditions for perception" (*anupalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpti*), that the properties of substances are magnitude (*mahattva*), consisting of multiple constituent substances (*anekadravyavattva*), and color-form (*rūpa*).
Because of its magnitude— according to the statement, "Perception [occurs] due to having multiple substances and due to color" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra IV.1.6)—
and because of such a statement,

they declare that the non-perception of something that has reached the conditions for perception is possible even when the object exists; thus, it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) for establishing the conventional usage of non-existence (*asadvyavahāra*).
For even in the case of the visual ray (*raśmi*), its magnitude, its being composed of multiple substances, and its color do not serve as causes for its perception;
yet, despite such non-perception, it is not possible to apply the conventional designation of "non-existent" to it.
As the author of the *Bhāṣya* said: "[It is not so] for that which is perceived through inference..."

"Non-perception through direct perception (*pratyakṣato 'nupalabdhi*) is the reason for non-existence" [Durveka: this refers to the author of the *Nyāyabhāṣya*, Pakṣilasvāmin, as noted in HBṬĀ 382.23].

Since the eye is indeed a sense organ, like the skin and so forth, it must—according to the opponent—act by reaching its object; thus, the visual ray is established through inference. How then can its non-perception through direct perception serve as the basis for the conventional usage of its non-existence?
"How could one establish [it]?

Thus, the Naiyāyikas claim that the non-perception of something that has reached the conditions for perceptibility (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) regarding the conventional usage of non-existence (*asadvyavahāra*). To refute this, the author of the treatise stated [the following], by demonstrating the true nature of "having reached the conditions for perceptibility" (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpti*).

For when the completeness of other conditions for perception and the specific nature [of the object] as previously described are called "attainment of the conditions for perception" (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpti*), rather than [merely] its largeness and so forth, then how could there be any occasion for deviation?
Because that [deviation] is impossible when the thing exists.
Indeed, largeness and so forth, precisely because they are impossible [in certain cases], cannot be designated by the term "attainment of the conditions for perception."
For a substance distinct from form and the other [sensory objects] does not appear in its own cognition through any other aspect that distinguishes it from the appearance of those [objects].
Nor can that which does not so appear experience perceptibility by means of an aspect that distinguishes it from what is not its own nature, for that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Therefore, how could there be the possibility of largeness and so forth for that which is non-existent? Nor is it possible for that which is not large by its own nature to become large even through a connection with [largeness].
Furthermore, if it were perceived under another form, how could the cognition apprehending it be non-erroneous?
Therefore, neither magnitude nor color is the perceiver of the substance;
for if those too were grasped by their own intrinsic nature, the substance itself would remain entirely beyond perception.
Furthermore, since the form of the substance is not perceived as distinct from them, they do not possess such a capacity for apprehension.
Furthermore, neither magnitude nor color is admitted to exist at the time of the substance's arising,
because a substance is held to be the inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa) of its qualities;
and since it attains that state only once its own self has been acquired, the substance is indeed devoid of qualities in the first moment.

Furthermore, in its second moment, this [entity] neither abandons its prior form nor does another form manifest, such that— having previously not attained the status of a substratum— it might acquire the status of a substratum through the obstruction by qualities such as magnitude (*mahattva*).
Furthermore, that which does not produce an effect cannot be a substratum;
and if it were a producer, it would necessarily be momentary, because for that which is non-momentary, there is a contradiction with causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). Therefore:
How could there be the possibility of an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), given that it is designated as such only because it produces an effect that emerges from itself?

This is not possible either in the case of momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*) or in the case of non-momentariness (*akṣaṇikatva*); for if there were no substratum (*ādhāra*) previously, there could be no absence of a substratum later.

Precisely because an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) is impossible, even the state of possessing multiple substances (*anekadravyavattva*) is impossible; for that alone is so designated which has multiple substances existing as its inherent causes in the form of originators. And since there is an absence of substance, there is no possession of multiple substances. Furthermore, even if magnitude (*mahattva*) and so forth were present, this [perceptibility] characterized by being reached by perception is not what we accept.
However,

the author of the treatise demonstrated that the non-perception of that which has reached the conditions for perceptibility (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*), when intended as such, is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) for establishing the conventional usage of non-existence; for it is the non-perception of that which has reached the conditions for perceptibility [which is required].

The non-perception of something other than the object to be negated—whether it be its cause or its pervader—is both a reason for [establishing] non-existence and a reason for the conventional usage of non-existence regarding the effect or the pervaded.

However, the non-perception of the object to be negated itself, provided it meets the conditions for perceptibility (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*), is shown by the word "or" (*vā*) to be solely a reason for the conventional usage of non-existence. As for that which...

The non-apprehension of that which has reached the conditions for apprehension (*anupalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*)—characterized by the cessation of perception and inference—is a cause for doubt, because even when the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) have ceased, the non-existence of the object is not established.
However, it should be understood that due to the absence of the causal conditions [for its apprehension], it is a cause for the negation of the conventional usage of "existent" (*sadvyavahāra*).
[629] Its non-cognition... T.
[630] For those possessing the eye of mental attention toward light, [631] there is also the lineage of the author of the *Nyāyasūtrabhāṣya*.
[632] Here, the *Nyāyasūtra* states: "The non-perception by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of that which is being inferred is not a reason for its non-existence."
[The editor notes: A passage of this form has been extracted as a statement of the author of the *Bhāṣya*— it is found [at NSū 3.1.36],
[beginning with] "by greatness" (*mahattvena*), [and] "having cast down" (*pracya-*) [633–634].
[635] — This is also accepted by you yourselves.
[§ 2. Refutation of Īśvarasena, Kumārila, and others, in order to clarify one's own preferred non-apprehension.
In that regard, first, as for those who maintain that non-apprehension is merely the absence of apprehension (*upalabdhyabhāvamātra*):
Or, as stated in the verse, "Cognition [occurs] with respect to another object" (ŚV, Abhāvapariccheda 11d), it is simply the cognition of an object other than that [negated thing].

In order to exclude that [misconception], and to demonstrate non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) characterized by the properties of the knower and the known, [the author], first showing that apprehension (*upalabdhi*) is of two kinds, says: "In this statement of non-apprehension, that apprehension which is heard [as] having the nature of an action..."
When that [perception] is considered as residing in the agent, then, since it is being regarded as a property of the agent who perceives,
the cognition of that [agent]— which is the cognition of the one perceiving— is called "perception" (*upalabdhi*).
And the complex of the intellect, the sense-faculties, and the body, which is comprised within the preceding moment, is said to be the producer of that perception.
For instance—it is asserted by others that the agent is either the producer or the substratum of perception.

However, it is not possible for anything other than the sense-faculties and so forth to possess the quality of being a producer; because the conventional usage of the relation between cause and effect is based upon positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), and such positive and negative concomitance do not occur in anything other than the sense-faculties and so forth, since perception necessarily occurs when the sense-faculties and so forth are present. If...

If, even when the sense faculties and other factors are present, perception does not arise at times, then the non-production of the effect despite the presence of all other causes indicates a deficiency in some other cause; thus, one might postulate a cause distinct from those already mentioned.
But this is not the case.
How, then, could the self be accepted as the instrumental cause for the arising of that [cognition]?
Because it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). As it has been said:
"When X exists, Y necessarily arises; yet if one imagines something other than that [X] to be its cause..."
"Because that would be the cause, there would be an infinite regress of causes in all cases" (PV I 26).
Since being a substratum (*āśrayatva*) also belongs only to that which produces, that too is not possible for the self (*ātman*).
If it is argued that it is a substratum because it stabilizes [the mind], we say no.
Because stability is absent if things are momentary, and because even if they were non-momentary, they would persist by not perishing of their own accord;

for indeed, it is the very non-perishing of perception that is called "stability," not the absence of falling. This is because, according to the established doctrine of others, "falling occurs due to weight, in the absence of conjunction" (VSū V.1.7), and perception lacks such weight.
If it is argued that [the object] is the substratum because of inherence (*samavāya*), [we reply:
surely that [inherence] is also held to exist only between things that stand in the relation of the supported and the supporter.
And for perception, which by its nature does not fall, there is no need for a substratum whatsoever.
Furthermore, if [the self] were the substratum by virtue of inherence (*samavāya*), it would follow that anything else could also be its substratum, because inherence is common to all selves,
since you accept it as being one.
Furthermore, because causal efficiency is incompatible with both successive and simultaneous action, this self lacks existence; therefore, how could it possess the capacity to produce anything,
or to serve as a substratum?
Thus, enough with this grinding of what has already been ground.

Having thus demonstrated positive apprehension (*upalabdhi*), he now demonstrates negative apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), saying: "Therefore, non-apprehension is a cognition consisting of knowledge that is distinct from the cognition of [the object] itself, having as its object another thing (*vastvantara*).
But how can apprehension itself be called non-apprehension?
Thus he says: "the intended," and so forth.

Just as in the section concerning what may and may not be eaten, because of its being other than the intended edible food, it is said that "the village cock is not to be eaten"—even though it is indeed edible, it is so stated because it is other than that [intended] edible food. And just as in the context of what may and may not be touched, because of its being other than the intended touchable object, it is said that "the Caṇḍāla and others are not to be touched"—even though they are indeed touchable, they are so stated because they are other than that [intended] touchable object.
In the same way, perception itself should be understood as non-perception.
If it is asked, "Since the negative particle (*nañ*) has negation as its object, how can it have existence as its object?", he replies: "By way of exclusion (*paryudāsa*)."

By way of *paryudāsa*— that is, by excluding the meaning of that which is to be negated— the negative particle (*nañ*) has as its object an existent entity (*bhāva*), because it functions toward a qualified meaning while retaining its own negation. Where the affirmation is primary, the negation is understood through implication, the subject of the affirmation is not expressed by its own word, and there is syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*), in that case the function is *paryudāsa*.

Furthermore, the predominance of the affirmation (*vidhi*) is established because the sentence "the perception of another occurs through the non-perception of the intended object" prescribes the perception of another; thus, the negation of the perception of the intended object is understood solely by the force of that prescription of the perception of another.

Since it would be impossible to prescribe another in relation to something if the perception of the intended object were not excluded, the subject of the affirmation is not expressed by its own word together with the negative particle (*nañ*).
What then?

By relying on the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) function of the word "other" (*anya*), the word "other" itself is employed in the sentence; thus, "an apprehension that is other [than the apprehension of the object]" is what is meant by "non-apprehension.

Furthermore, since the negative particle (*nañ*) has syntactic force (*sāmarthya*) with a nominal stem (*subanta*) and not with a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*), there is a single unified sentence: "non-apprehension is an absence of apprehension" (*na upalabdhir anupalabdhiḥ*).
Furthermore, *prasajyapratiṣedha* (absolute negation) should be understood as the opposite of this [relative negation].

For in that case, the negation is primary, while the affirmation is understood by implication; there is a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*), and the element subject to negation is connected with the negative particle (*nañ*) itself.

Having thus explained non-apprehension characterized as a property of the knower (*jñātṛdharma*), he says—beginning with "when [it] has the property of being apprehended"—in order to demonstrate non-apprehension characterized as a property of the object known (*jñeyadharma*).

When the property of an object being perceived is intended with respect to the action residing in the agent (karmasthakriyā), then perception should be understood as having the nature of the object (*viṣayasvabhāva*).
What is the nature of this object?
To this he says: "its own object," and so forth.

The nature of an object, characterized by its capacity to produce a cognition whose content is that very object—such as a jar which is to be negated—is what is expressed by the term "perception" (upalabdhi).
If perception is the nature of the object, how can it be characterized as a capacity?
For indeed, capacity is a property (dharma).
And since there is indeed a distinction between the property (dharma) and the property-possessor (dharmin), he says: "of capacity," and so forth.
For capacity, in the ultimate sense, is of the very nature of existence (*bhāva*) itself and does not differ from the essential nature of the thing;
otherwise, the existent would not be capable at all.
Furthermore, the relation "this belongs to that" would not exist in reality;
as for the conceptualization of a relation, it has already been stated that this leads to an infinite regress.
Thus, having established that apprehension is a property of the object, he says "therefore, another... and so forth, in order to establish the same for non-apprehension as well.

Therefore, that which is other than the object to be negated—such as a jar—which is capable of producing a cognition of its own object, is precisely that which is capable of producing a [cognition of its] perception;
it is not of a contrary nature, such as the form of a place devoid of a jar. That very thing is what is expressed here by the term "non-perception" (*anupalabdhi*).
Indicating the same logic as before, he says "as previously [stated]."
"Because it is distinct from the apprehension of the intended object, it functions as an exclusion (*paryudāsa*), like 'that which is not to be eaten' or 'that which is not to be touched.

But how is it that this negative particle (*nañ*), being a general term functioning in the sense of another meaning, [denotes] through the function of exclusion the state of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhitva*) of the place devoid of the jar, or rather of the cognition itself devoid of the jar; and why does it not [apply] without distinction to all things denoted by the word 'other'?"
Therefore, he says: "Wherein," meaning in which place, time, or state characterized by non-interruption and so forth;
and when which [object], such as a location or a form, is being perceived, [there is] that other thing which necessarily and invariably [is perceived].

When there is the perception of an object such as the color of a jar, that object—the color of the jar and so forth—is conjoined with that [other factor], namely, conjoined with that specific location, color, and so on.
If it is asked, "How is there the necessary perception of the other [factor] when one is being perceived? the answer is: because there is no difference in their respective capacities (*yogyatā*).
For the capacity to produce a cognition of their own respective objects is equal for both a spatial location (*pradeśa*) and a jar (*ghaṭa*).

When the form of the spatial location— being free from obstructions, distance, and so forth— imparts its own aspect (*svākāra*) to the cognition, then the form of the jar likewise imparts its own aspect to that very same cognition in exactly that manner.
If indeed its capacity is equal to that [of the object], how can there be a connection between them when they are established in their own respective natures?
To this he says: "Because of the connection in a single cognition.
For in a single cognition, both of those are connected by way of their own forms, not directly.
That cognition, arising in the form of two objects, demonstrates their connection within itself.
But why must that cognition necessarily possess the form of two objects, such that the connection between them occurs by means of the cognition?
To this, he says: "When those two exist," and so forth.
If these two, which possess an identical capacity for manifestation, were both existent, then there would certainly not be a cognition restricted to a single form.
Why? Because it is impossible.
For this possibility does not exist: that only one of two things possessing an identical capacity for manifestation should appear, and not the other.
For instance: since the capacity [to produce cognition] is undifferentiated, who would not project their own form therein?
Furthermore, there is the established experience of the simultaneous appearance of multiple [objects];
and those who speak in contradiction to experience do not become persons whose words are to be heeded by the wise.
If it is argued that the misconception of simultaneity arises because the operation is rapid, we say no;

for in the absence of a subverting cognition (*bādhakapratyaya*), it is illogical to assume an error, as this would lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that such a state would apply everywhere.
This is simply the nature of the instrument (*karaṇadharma*): that it produces the action in only a single object, not in many.

If it is argued that the sense organ is the instrument and therefore cannot be the cause for multiple cognitions, then how is it that a lamp or similar object produces cognitions in many people located in different places?
If it is argued that there is no fault because of the difference in agents (the perceivers); [we reply:]...
If, then, because the agent is one, the action is also one and resides in multiple objects, how is it that statements such as "the property of the instrument" do not collapse?
Furthermore, among entities that perish moment by moment, a relationship of agent, instrument, and so forth, or any action at all, is not logically tenable from the perspective of ultimate reality.

Furthermore, in an effect that conforms to the positive and negative concomitance of all its causal factors (*kāraṇa*), there is no excellence (*atiśaya*) belonging to any one of them by virtue of which one might postulate, "this is the agent" or "this is the instrument," and so forth.
Therefore, how could there be the possibility of a cognition restricted to a single form arising from two [causes] whose capacities are undifferentiated?
Thus, the co-occurrence within a single cognition is established.
Furthermore, this very [fact] is the logical mark (*liṅga*) for having a nature of equal fitness (*tulyayogyatārūpatva*).
For, in the absence of a nature of equal fitness, it is impossible for two things—such as color and taste—to appear simultaneously in a cognition produced by a single sense organ.

In this regard, for those followers of the Sugata who hold the view that "even when many [objects] are included within a single sense-field, only a single sensory cognition arises," there is indeed a primary conjunction with a single cognition.

However, those who describe it thus: "Even in that case, distinct cognitions arise for each object, caused by a single sense-organ and occurring at the same time, because there is no difference in the capacity of the objects present simultaneously to produce their own cognitions; for this very reason, these cognitions arise as being determined by the world as a unity"—[T. 646]... [they hold that there is only a secondary conjunction].

Because they are produced by a single sense-faculty and have a single objective basis (*āyatana*), their designation as "one" at a single time is metaphorical (*aupacārika*) in common worldly usage, due to such conventional determination.
If it is argued that, because of its association with a single cognition, the negative particle (*nañ*) might generally indicate everything else associated with it, he says:
"Therefore," and so forth.
Since, due to the non-distinction of their capacity (*yogyatā*) in the manner described, there is a conjunction of both [terms] within a single cognition, therefore,
those two things which possess that non-distinct form of capacity are, for that very reason, conjoined in a single cognition. Consequently,

the "otherness" (*anyatva*) intended here in this section on non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) is precisely the mutual dependence between those two things of such a nature, and not a dependence upon all other objects.

In common worldly usage, however, if "otherness" (*anyatva*) expressed by the negative particle (*nañ*) is sometimes said to depend on another entity that is not specifically differentiated, by resorting to the logic of pervasion (*vyāpti*), even so, that [type of otherness] is not accepted here.

This is because proximity (*pratyāsatti*) is relied upon; specifically, a proximity characterized by co-occurrence within a single cognition (*ekajñānasaṃsarga*) is resorted to, and no other. This is because we are engaged in an investigation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); otherwise, non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) would indeed be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
It may be so;
therefore, those who investigate reality should adopt such a form of difference as is the basis for the non-deviation of non-perception.
And that [form] is exactly as has been stated—this is the intended meaning.
Thus, having established otherness in dependence upon the association with a single cognition, he states "that alone," etc., demonstrating non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*).

When that very same location is "alone" in relation to the aforementioned jar, it is called "other" than that; at that time, either the cognition of the location as devoid of the jar is non-apprehension.
It is not, however, as Īśvarasena maintains, that non-apprehension is merely the absence of apprehension.
Because of the fault that will be stated later;

or rather, it is the nature of the location as distinct from the jar, and not the cognition itself as being distinct from it, as Kumārila said: "Or the cognition regarding another object" (ŚV, Abhāvapariccheda 11d).

For just as a cognition whose object is another thing, being experienced, depends upon the recollection of its counter-positive (pratiyogin) to serve as the basis for the linguistic usage of its absence, so too does the location devoid of that thing.

To explain: for a certain cognizer, the knowledge of non-existence arises in this way—"Since I experience only a cognition having the form of the bare location and not even the form of a jar, therefore there is no jar here."
For some, however, [the inference] is as follows: "Since this place is seen alone and not accompanied by a jar, therefore there is no jar here.
Therefore, since both possess equal capacity for the production of the cognition of non-existence, it is logical to establish both as non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*).

In that regard, when that [non-existence] is a cognition, non-apprehension is characterized as a property of the knower (*jñātṛdharma*), with respect to an action residing in the agent; when it is that [non-existence] itself as an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), it is characterized as a property of the object of knowledge (*jñeyadharma*), with respect to an action residing in the object.
Having thus established non-apprehension by way of exclusion (*paryudāsa*), he says "its non-existence," etc., showing its probandum:

even when a location or the like—which is devoid of all other things that have met the conditions for apprehension—is being perceived, there occurs a recollection of a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) such as a jar due to desire and so forth; it is the non-existence, or the conventional usage of non-existence, of that [counter-correlate] which is [the probandum].
The non-perception of the cause and the non-perception of the pervader establish both absence and the conventional usage of absence;
however, the non-perception of the essential nature establishes only the conventional usage of absence.
And the conventional usage of absence is characterized by the operation of cognition and verbal designation.

In this context, there is the cognition in the form "there is no jar here," the verbal expression denoting such an object, and the activity characterized by coming and going in that place by one who is free from doubt. Having raised the objection that this provides an opportunity for the arguments of Īśvarasena and Kumārila, and having already refuted their views while establishing the final system (*siddhānta*), [the author] speaks again specifically to refute their position: {p. 175.1} Here, anticipating the opportunity for the words of Īśvarasena and Kumārila, and although their views have already been rejected while establishing the settled doctrine, he speaks again for the sake of explicitly refuting their position.
"How is it that there is 'the existence of another'? and so forth.

For Īśvarasena thinks: because non-perception (*anupalabdhi*) is distinguished from the two types of reasons—effect (*kārya*) and essential nature (*svabhāva*), which are positive entities—it must necessarily be negative in nature;
otherwise, its distinction [from them] would be entirely purposeless.

And you describe the non-apprehension of another thing—such as a location distinct from that which is to be negated—or of the cognition thereof, as being of a positive nature; therefore, it must be that the existence of another is itself its non-existence, by virtue of which this is asserted.
But this is not tenable.
"Because existence and non-existence are contradictory, their identity is untenable.

Kumārila also thinks thus: "This twofold non-apprehension, characterized by the properties of the knower and the known, which you describe as being of the nature of non-existence—let it be the means for the cognition of non-existence;
however, how can that very thing—the existence or positive aspect of another object distinct from the negated thing, or of a cognition other than the cognition of the negated thing—be non-existence?"
How could there be a non-existent portion (abhāvāṃśa) of that which is to be negated, or of the cognition thereof?
It is not at all tenable,
because the existent and non-existent portions are distinct by virtue of being properties (dharma).

Even though there is no difference between the two in terms of their underlying substratum (*dharmin*), the distinction between their apprehension and non-apprehension is established through their emergence and suppression. As it has been said:
"For although we maintain that there is no difference in the substratum, a difference between the two properties (*dharma*) is admitted;
due to their nature of emerging and being suppressed, their apprehension is accordingly determined. (ŚV, Abhāva 20)

Thus, showing that this objection has already been answered, he says: "The answer to this challenge has already been stated; namely, how through the function of exclusion (paryudāsa) and in relation to something else, that which is to be negated or its cognition is expected, such that the object distinct from it, or its cognition, is called 'non-existence' (abhāva) and 'non-apprehension' (anupalabdhi). This is the reply of Īśvarasena.
For the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) is not exclusively a non-implicative negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*), but also includes an implicative exclusion (*paryudāsa*).
Therefore, there is no contradiction in the fact that the existence of another thing has the nature of a non-existence;
furthermore, how the existence of another thing can also have the nature of a non-implicative negation will be explained later.
However, the separate treatment of non-apprehension from the reason of essential identity is due to the intention of the cognizer.
For in the case of the reason of essential identity, the cognizer is intent upon the apprehension of a real entity;
whereas in the case of non-apprehension, he is intent upon the apprehension of absence.

From the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthatas*), however, it is precisely the fitness of the location for the conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) of the absence of the object to be negated that is established as a real entity (*vastubhūta*). Thus, the non-perception of the nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*) is not distinct from the nature-reason (*svabhāvahetu*). As for what Īśvarasena maintains—that "non-perception is merely the negation [of an object] without regard for its connection with another thing"—the author, refuting that, says: "It is not mere negation," and so forth.
Why? He says: "Because the proof of that is unestablished," and so forth.

For it is not established that non-existence— which is characterized by the absence of all causal capacity— can function as a means of proof (*sādhana*) or serve as a cause for establishment (*siddhihetu*),
because that which consists in the absence of all capacity is incompatible with such a role.
Alternatively, if it were a cause, how could it not possess causal capacity?
Or would it have the nature of a positive entity (*bhāva*)?
Since a real thing (*vastu*) is characterized by causal efficacy (*sāmarthya*),

and since a non-entity (*abhāva*) does not depend on auxiliary causes and cannot have any excellence added to it, there would follow the undesirable consequence that the cognition "it does not exist" would be produced eternally.
Consequently, because it would lack a means of proof (*sādhaka*), the very conventional usage of "non-existence" (*abhāvavyavahāra*) could not be established.
Alternatively, no proof whatsoever could be established for that non-perception (*upalabdhyabhāva*) which consists of a simple negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*).
For, being itself a non-existence, it would have to be proven by another non-perception.
That [object] too would require another [cognition], leading to an infinite regress.
Furthermore, unlike a sense faculty, that which is not itself cognized cannot be the cause for the cognition of its negation;
for since it would be constantly present, and thus independent of auxiliary factors, there would follow the undesirable consequence of that [negation-cognition] arising at all times.
And these two points— namely, "How can there be the non-existence of anything,
or its apprehension, or the cause of apprehension?
And how can there be the apprehension of that [non-existence]?"— he himself will elaborate upon in this very context.
Kumārila also states the following reply: "Of that [entity], which has a nature unconnected with another entity acting as its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*);
for it does not have a uniform nature that is connected by its very essence with other entities.
For if that were the case, even the aspect of non-existence would never be established anywhere."

He thinks: "Let there be the establishment of the very existence of such a thing, which is the establishment of the positive aspect (*bhāvāṃśa*) itself; let this be the establishment of the non-existence of another counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), that is, the establishment of the negative aspect (*abhāvāṃśa*) as you intend it, because the positive aspect itself can logically function as the negative aspect.
For instance, even the negative aspect is designated as "non-existence" precisely by virtue of its being unmixed with the nature of other things (*pararūpa*).
Otherwise, that would be impossible.

And since that [cognition] is the same with respect to the positive aspect as well, let that very thing be the non-existence itself, because its cause is the same; what is the use of postulating a separate aspect of non-existence?
For this very reason, there is the qualification "of that which has an unmixed form."

Since it is thus, therefore even "the existence of another" (*anyabhāva*)— which is the existence of another entity and which you consider to be the positive aspect (*bhāvāṃśa*)— is designated by us as "non-existence" (*abhāva*), not merely the negative aspect (*abhāvāṃśa*) according to your view. Consequently, it is entirely consistent that the positive aspect possesses the nature of non-existence.
"Nothing is contradicted.

This was said [by the opponent] in order to refute what was stated [by us]: "By means of the non-apprehension of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*), characterized by the knower and the known, it is only the conventional usage of absence (*abhāvavyavahāra*) that is established, not absence itself";
and also what was stated: "Non-apprehension is not a mere negation."

Because its proof is not established, [the author] says "characterized by the existence of another," etc., in order to show the proof for this [statement] from the second explanation: "non-apprehension is merely a negation.
He thinks as follows: for the world first understands the absence of a jar precisely from the perception of a bare location.

Either by means of the cognition of the mere location (*pradeśa*) or by the realization of the absence of the cognition of a jar, one proceeds to the conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) of the absence of the jar. Thus, in accordance with worldly consensus, non-existence (*abhāva*)— characterized as the existence of that which is other than the object to be negated (i.e., the location) or as the existence of the cognition thereof (i.e., the cognition of the negated object)— is itself [established] through a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), namely, sensory perception (*indriyapratyakṣa*) or self-reflexive perception (*svasaṃvedanapratyakṣa*).
And that [non-perception], being established, is sufficient to prove the absence of a jar both directly and indirectly, respectively;
and it is likewise proper to establish the conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) of the absence of a jar. Even with such an establishment, there is no detriment whatsoever to our own position.

For instance: even by way of a traditional lineage, that which is established through your accepted non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) is indeed established as such; thus, even when demonstrating the proof of that [non-apprehension] while treating negation alone as non-apprehension, this is the intended meaning:
just as for you, non-apprehension is twofold, consisting of the nature of the apprehender and the apprehended, and characterized as a positive entity (*bhāvarūpa*).

In the same way, for me as well, the absence of the perception of the characteristics of both the knower and the object of knowledge will likewise be twofold, designated as "non-perception. Among these, by means of the existence of another thing characterized as an object of knowledge—which is established through direct perception—the absence of the object to be negated, consisting in the absence of the perception of the characteristics of the object of knowledge, will be established under the designation of "non-perception. And by means of the existence of another thing characterized as a property of the knower—consisting in the cognition of the bare locus and established through self-awareness—the property of the knower, consisting in the absence of the cognition of the object to be negated, will be established under the name of "non-perception."
It will be established; and thus, how could there be an infinite regress by which the proof would remain unestablished?

In that regard, "characterized by the existence of another" refers to the place, which is a positive entity distinct from the object of negation and the cognition thereof, and is devoid of that object of negation.
That non-existence, which consists of that [non-cognition]— being distinct from the intended positive entity, from the negatable positive entity, and from the cognition of that [entity]—

is accepted by you as being non-apprehension; and since it is established by its own nature through the means of valid cognition, namely through sensory perception and self-awareness, it brings about the conventional usage of the non-existence of that negatable object.

Whether one establishes that which is characterized by the occurrence of cognition and its designation, or whether it is established through the establishment of the non-existence— characterized as the presence of something else— of that aforementioned [object],

such that the non-existence of that [object] or the non-existence of the cognition of it is thereby established; even if this is what is intended, there is no distinction whatsoever between the non-apprehension favored by you and the non-apprehension favored by us.
Then why is our view rejected?

Is it not the case that, when this is accepted, there is indeed a distinction: non-apprehension characterized by the presence of another would establish the conventional usage of the absence of the other indirectly, whereas the other [kind of non-apprehension] would do so directly? To this he says: there is no such distinction by which [non-apprehension] would [differ]. By means of which distinction... non-apprehension [would differ]?

There would be a contradiction [only] if the conventional usage of non-existence were established by means of that [absence] which we accept—namely, as having the nature of a positive entity (bhāvarūpā) yet devoid of contact with any real object;
for any other specific [kind of absence], even if it exists, is equivalent to non-existence because it lacks the power to sublate [the object].
As for what was said—"there follows the consequence that the conventional usage of non-existence cannot be established due to the absence of a means of proof for it"—[that is not a fault].
That too is incorrect,
because that very "presence of another" (anyabhāva) which you intend— consisting of a ground distinct from the object to be negated— and the perception having that as its object,
are asserted by you to be "non-perception" (*anupalabdhi*), whereas for us, it is the absence of the object to be negated that constitutes non-perception.
And why is the non-existence of that perception not accepted as a probans (*liṅga*) for proof?
For if that were the case, it would conform to worldly convention.

Furthermore, why is it said that the very establishment of the two kinds of non-existence constitutes the establishment of that absence, and that there exists no other [result] to be established by it? This is for the purpose of refuting our own position.
The prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that [the existence of the Self] is intended to be something transcendent to the world.

To this, he replies: Since there is no other entity because of non-separate establishment (*apṛthaksiddhi*), and since there is no absence of that [other entity] because of the absence of separate establishment, how can there be the relation of sign and signified (*liṅgaliṅgitā*)?
Likewise, due to the absence of a connection between the existence of another entity and its absence, there is no relation of sign and signified.

First, explaining the first reason, he says: "The existence of another thing (*anyabhāva*), which consists of a location devoid of that [object], is not a probans (*liṅga*) for the absence of the object to be negated;
furthermore, it will be stated later that 'the perception of that [object] is also not a means of establishing its absence.
The word *tāvat* is used precisely for this purpose."

Why is the existence of another thing not a means of proof? To this he says: when, upon the establishment—that is, the cognition—of one thing, there is no establishment and no cognition of another thing, that first thing becomes the *liṅga* (probans) of that second thing; such is the rule regarding the probans and the probandum (*liṅgaliṅgin*).
An example of this is: "like smoke and fire.

For instance, when fire is not perceived at the time of perceiving smoke, then the relationship of indicator and indicated (liṅga-liṅgibhāva) exists between the two; but it does not exist when the fire is being perceived at the very same time as the perception of smoke.
If this is so, what follows from it?

To this he says: the existence (*bhāva*), that is, the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), of one thing—by the very establishment of that, and by the very cognition of that, the non-existence (*abhāva*) of that [other thing], namely the negandum, is established and cognized; for the existence of another thing is itself of the nature of the non-existence of that [first thing], since the establishment of the former is precisely characterized as the establishment of the latter.

The Naiyāyikas, however, maintain: "For the absence of that which is to be negated consists in a non-implicative negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*), which is of the nature of a mere void (*tuccharūpa*). How could such an absence possess the nature of the existence of something else? Because existence and non-existence are contradictory.
Therefore, how could the establishment of the absence of that [object] occur simply through the establishment of the existence of something else?"

Therefore, he says: of that "state of being other than that" (tadanyabhāva), which is characterized as a location (pradeśa) and whose nature is unconnected with—that is, devoid of—the object to be negated such as a jar, [and] which is solitary, meaning its nature is empty of the object to be negated.
By this, he states that even the solitary location consists of a non-presuppositional negation (prasajyapratiṣedha).

If it is asked, "How can the nature of an entity be its insubstantiality (*tuccharūpatā*), given the contradiction?"—it is not so, because even that [negation] is insubstantial in its other form (*pararūpeṇa*).

For just as a non-implicative negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*)—which does not involve contact with another positive entity, appears in the conceptualization of emptiness, and is insubstantial by virtue of being devoid of the form of the object to be negated—is insubstantial in its own form due to the absence of that [positive] form; [so too is the entity].
Likewise, the existence of that other thing (tadanyabhāva) is also a form dissociated from the object of negation.
Therefore, how could its state of being non-substantial (tuccharūpatā) with respect to the object of negation be contradictory?
For this [existence] would be non-substantial in its own nature (svarūpeṇa), but not in the nature of another (pararūpeṇa).
Otherwise, how could this [entity] have the nature of being the absence of another, or how could there be the absence of that other in it?
For that which does not consist of the nature of the absence of something else is indeed that very thing,
just like its own essential nature.
Consequently, it would follow that the entire world possesses the nature of one another.
Therefore, all entities are devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) by way of the form of others, even though they possess form by way of their own nature; thus, this is faultless.
What, then, is the difference between a simple negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*) and a preclusive negation (*paryudāsa*)?
Nothing at all; rather, in common worldly usage, that which is a mere non-existence (abhāva-mātra) without depending on another form is called "negation by exclusion" (prasajya-pratiṣedha).
However, that which depends on another form—namely, being empty of the form of another—is called "negation by limitation" (paryudāsa).
It is not the case, however, that the other form does not consist of the voidness of the form of another.
Moreover, a different form is indeed experienced through the emptiness of that [original] form;
how then could it not have the nature of a non-implicative negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*) by way of another form?
If it is argued that the cognition of that [negated object] arises from it by implication (*sāmarthya*);
This is because there can be no capacity for cognition without a cause.

For if there were an absence of identity (*tādātmya*), then cognition would occur only if the non-presuppositional negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*) were the cause of that which is excluded (*paryudasta*); it could not be otherwise.
That which establishes the nature of the object of negation as being of the form of a mere void is the reality (*tattva*) of that [object] whose form is unmingled with anything else.

The means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is that very thing which has the nature of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), and not the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arising at a subsequent time, such as "there is no jar here. This is because the latter, being a grasping of what has already been grasped, is a form of memory and thus lacks the status of a valid cognition; for it establishes the absence—which is the exclusion (*vyavaccheda*)—of another thing, such as a jar, which is non-existent there, by means of grasping that very location as consisting of the absence of that jar.

For this location is of two kinds: that which has a form not in contact with a jar, being distinct from it by virtue of its exclusion from the jar, and that which possesses a jar, as well as the bare [ground] whose status as a substratum for the jar has not been apprehended.

When that [location] is grasped by perception through its distinction from the jar, both its difference from the jar and its absence of the jar are indeed grasped; thus, it is not for the sake of establishing the non-confusion of entities.
Furthermore, another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) would have to be sought for the purpose [of establishing] "this does not exist here.
This will be explained in detail later; let it rest for now.

Since the non-existence of that [object] is established by the aforementioned reasoning through the very establishment of the existence of something else, therefore the existence of something else is not the logical mark (*liṅga*) for the absence of the object to be negated.

Explaining the second reason, he says: "And because of the absence of a relationship. There is no relationship whatsoever between the existence of another thing and its own absence; therefore, how could there be the status of sign and signified? When is this said? [It is said] when one considers that the non-existence of a jar is established through the perception of the ground alone. For even if the ground is perceived, the non-existence of the jar is not established until the cognition of the non-existence of the jar arises. And since the cognition of the non-existence of the jar does not arise from the mere perception of the ground, it must be admitted that the non-existence of the jar is established by means of the cognition of the ground. Thus, the non-existence of the jar is established by means of the cognition of the ground, and not merely by the ground itself. Therefore, the cognition of the ground is the cause of the establishment of the non-existence of the jar, and the ground is not. Consequently, the ground is not the probans (liṅga) for the non-existence of the jar. Furthermore, the cognition of the ground is not the probans for the non-existence of the jar, because it is not invariably concomitant with it. For the cognition of the ground exists even when the jar is present. And since the cognition of the ground is not invariably concomitant with the non-existence of the jar, it cannot be the probans for it. Moreover, the cognition of the ground is not the probans for the non-existence of the jar, because it is not the object of that cognition. For the cognition of the ground has the ground as its object, not the non-existence of the jar. And since the cognition of the ground does not have the non-existence of the jar as its object, it cannot be the probans for it. Furthermore, the cognition of the ground is not the probans for the non-existence of the jar, because it is not the cause of the determination of that non-existence. For the determination of the non-existence of the jar arises from the cognition of the non-existence of the jar, not from the cognition of the ground. And since the cognition of the ground is not the cause of the determination of the non-existence of the jar, it cannot be the probans for it. Therefore, the cognition of the ground is not the probans for the non-existence of the jar. Nor is the ground the probans for the non-existence of the jar, because it is not invariably concomitant with it. For the ground exists even when the jar is present. And since the ground is not invariably concomitant with the non-existence of the jar, it cannot be the probans for it. Furthermore, the ground is not the probans for the non-existence of the jar, because it is not the object of that cognition. For the ground is the object of the cognition of the ground, not of the cognition of the non-existence of the jar. And since the ground is not the object of the cognition of the non-existence of the jar, it cannot be the probans for it. Moreover, the ground is not the probans for the non-existence of the jar, because it is not the cause of the determination of that non-existence. For the determination of the non-existence of the jar arises from the cognition of the non-existence of the jar, not from the cognition of the ground. And since the ground is not the cause of the determination of the non-existence of the jar, it cannot be the probans for it. Therefore, the ground is not the probans for the non-existence of the jar. Consequently, the non-existence of the jar is not established by means of the ground, but rather by the cognition of the ground. And since the non-existence of the jar is established by means of the cognition of the ground, the cognition of the ground is the cause of the establishment of the non-existence of the jar, and the ground is not. Therefore, the ground is not the probans for the non-existence of the jar. Furthermore, the cognition of the ground is not the probans for the non-existence of the jar, because it is not invariably concomitant with it. For the cognition of the ground exists even when the jar is present. And since the cognition of the ground is not invariably concomitant with the non-existence of the jar, it cannot be the probans for it. Moreover, the cognition of the ground is not the probans for the non-existence of the jar, because it is not the object of that cognition. For the cognition of the ground has the ground as its object, not the non-existence of the jar. And since the cognition of the ground does not have the non-existence of the jar as its object, it cannot be the probans for it. Furthermore, the cognition of the ground is not the probans for the non-existence of the jar, because it is not the cause of the determination of that non-existence. For the determination of the non-existence of the jar arises from the cognition of the non-existence of the jar, not from the cognition of the ground. And since the cognition of the ground is not the cause of the determination of the non-existence of the jar, it cannot be the probans for it. Therefore, the cognition of the ground is not the probans for the non-existence of the jar. Nor is the ground the probans for the non-existence of the jar, because it is not invariably concomitant with it. For the ground exists even when the jar is present. And since the ground is not invariably concomitant with the non-existence of the jar, it cannot be the probans for it. Furthermore, the ground is not the probans for the non-existence of the jar, because it is not the object of that cognition. For the ground is the object of the cognition of the ground, not of the cognition of the non-existence of the jar. And since the ground is not the object of the cognition of the non-existence of the jar, it cannot be the probans for it. Moreover, the ground is not the probans for the non-existence of the jar, because it is not the cause of the determination of that non-existence. For the determination of the non-existence of the jar arises from the cognition of the non-existence of the jar, not from the cognition of the ground. And since the ground is not the cause of the determination of the non-existence of the jar, it cannot be the probans for it. Therefore, the ground is not the probans for the non-existence of the jar. Consequently, the non-existence of the jar is not established by means of the ground, but rather by the cognition of the ground. And since the non-existence of the jar is established by means of the cognition of the ground, the cognition of the ground is the cause of the establishment of the non-existence of the jar, and the ground is not. Therefore, the ground is not the probans for the non-existence of the jar. Furthermore, the cognition of the ground is not the probans for the non-existence of the jar, because it is not invariably concomitant with it. For the cognition of the ground exists even when the jar is present. And since the cognition of the ground is not invariably concomitant with the non-existence of the jar, it cannot be the probans for it. Moreover, the cognition of the ground is not the probans for the non-existence of the jar, because it is not the object of that cognition. For the cognition of the ground has the ground as its object, not the non-existence of the jar. And since the cognition of the ground does not have the non-existence of the jar as its object, it cannot be the probans for it. Furthermore, the cognition of the ground is not the probans for the non-existence of the jar, because it is not the cause of the determination of that non-existence. For the determination of the non-existence of the jar arises from the cognition of the non-existence of the jar, not from the cognition of the ground. And since the cognition of the ground is not the cause of the determination of the non-existence of the jar, it cannot be the probans for it. Therefore, the cognition of the ground is not the probans for the non-existence of the jar. Nor is the ground the probans for the non-existence of the jar, because it is not invariably concomitant with it. For the ground exists even when the jar is present. And since the ground is not invariably concomitant with the non-existence of the jar, it cannot be the probans for it. Furthermore, the ground is not the probans for the non-existence of the jar, because it is not the object of that cognition. For the ground is the object of the cognition of the ground, not of the cognition of the non-existence of the jar. And since the ground is not the object of the cognition of the non-existence of the jar, it cannot be the probans for it. Moreover, the ground is not the probans for the non-existence of the jar, because it is not the cause of the determination of that non-existence. For the determination of the non-existence of the jar arises from the cognition of the non-existence of the jar, not from the cognition of the ground. And since the ground is not the cause of the determination of the non-existence of the jar, it cannot be the probans for it. Therefore, the ground is not the probans for the non-existence of the jar. Consequently, the non-existence of the jar is not established by means
When the fact that the existence of another thing (*anyabhāva*) consists in the absence of that [specific thing] is not accepted by others,
then those others maintain that the absence of that thing is a mere nothingness (*tuccharūpa*) entirely distinct from the existence of the other.

Otherwise, according to the reasoning already stated, if the existence of the other thing itself were the nature of that absence, then because of their identity (*tādātmya*), how could there be an absence of a relation between them?
And its establishment through direct perception was stated at that very moment, not by way of another alternative.

Furthermore, the phrase "that [inherence] belongs to that" and so forth is an explanation of the same point by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*); it is described according to the view of others as "inherence in a single substrate" (*ekārthasamavāya*).

For others, such as the Naiyāyikas and so forth, the two properties known as "producedness" (*kṛtakatva*) and "impermanence" (*anityatva*) are indeed distinct [from the subject] yet both inhere in one and the same substratum (*dharmin*). Thus, the relation is the inherence (*samavāya*) of the produced with impermanence in a single object, the substratum; or, as in the case of smoke, it is simply a relation. This is another example of a relation.

In this context, "inherence in a single object" refers to conjunction (*saṃyoga*); it is that very [conjunction] which is expressed by the word "inherence" (*samavāya*), because there is no regard for designating conjunction and inherence as distinct, since both are conceptual constructs. For others, however, fire and smoke inhere only in their own respective parts; thus, they do not possess "inherence in a single object" nor the relation of "container and contained. Therefore, the relationship between smoke and fire is merely a worldly one, based on the observation of smoke appearing above fire.
It has been stated that "the relationship between the produced and the producer" refers to the ultimate (pāramārthika) connection,
because, from the perspective of ultimate reality (paramārthataḥ), fire is the producer and the other [the smoke] is the produced.
Now, since the discussion was initiated with Īśvarasena, why is it stated that the relation as maintained by the Naiyāyikas also lacks existence in both the presence of another thing and its absence?
True; however, this was said for the purpose of refuting his view as well by way of a consequential argument (*prasaṅga*).

For previously, because the absence of the object to be negated is established by the perception grasping the "presence of another," no further perception in the form "there is no jar here" need be postulated for that purpose.
This was stated as a digression;

now, however, this is said by way of further context: when this absence (*tadabhāva*) is not established by a perception that apprehends another entity (*anyabhāvagrāhipratyakṣa*), then there must be another perception of the form "there is no jar here," characterized by the relation between qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*).
11. You have accepted [the cognition] as arising from proximity (*sannikarṣa*).

And in the absence of a relation, it is not logical for there to be a qualifier-qualified relationship (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*) between the existence of another thing and its non-existence, because that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Then, from what kind of contact (*saṃnikarṣa*) characterized by that [relation] could there be perception in the absence of that [object]?
Having thus explained the nature of the relation, he states its impossibility in this case: "It is not so;

for just as there is a relation between 'producedness' and 'impermanence,' or between 'fire' and 'smoke,' characterized by inherence in a single substratum (*ekārthasamavāya*) and so forth, there is no such relation whatsoever between existence and non-existence by which the existence of another thing would [constitute] the non-existence of this [thing]."
It would be a valid means of proof (*sādhana*).
For as long as two [cognitions] operate upon a single object in the form of a substratum (*dharmin*), there is a co-inherence (*samavāya*) of those two in that single object.

Furthermore, the "existence of another" (*anyabhāva*), which is designated as a particular location, exists in its own constituent parts; it is not the case that the absence of a jar exists in those very parts where that [existence of another] resides.
For in this way, it would follow that the jar does not exist in its spatial parts (*pradeśāvayava*), but not in the location (*pradeśa*);
yet its origination does not occur through those spatial parts,
for they, being substantial entities (*dravyātmānaḥ*), originate only another substance.
Furthermore, the absence of a jar is not a substance,
for only nine substances are admitted;
nor does the definition of a substance— such as possessing activity and so forth— exist therein.
Nor does it exist there in the form of a quality (*guṇa*),
for only twenty-four qualities are admitted,
and this [entity] is not any one of them.
Nor can it be of the nature of action, because it is not included among the five types of action and because it lacks the defining characteristics thereof;
for its defining characteristic is stated as "subsisting in a single substance" (VaiSū I.1.15) and so forth.
And this is not possible in the absence of that [existence],
nor is it possible in the form of a universal (sāmānya) and so forth,
precisely because of the lack of such a form.
Nor is there a conjunction between the existence of one thing and the non-existence of another, as in the case of fire and smoke, because conjunction is admitted only between two substances;
and it has already been stated that non-existence is not a substance.
Nor is there a relationship of container and contained,
since that too is said to be caused by conjunction, as in the expression, "jujube fruits here in the bowl."
Or it might be caused by inherence, as in the case of "the cloth is here in these threads.
However, conjunction does not exist for that which is non-existent and lacks the nature of a substance.
Nor is it inherence,
for inherence is held to belong only to the five categories beginning with substance;
and non-existence is not included among those five.
Furthermore, as long as there is no benefit to its own self, the designation "substratum" (ādhāra) is not possible;
or, if there were benefit, it would entail a relationship of produced and producer (janyajanakabhāva).
And that [relationship] is not something produced.
Because it would follow that it is an effect;
and its being an effect is impossible,
since [an effect] consists in inherence in its own cause.
Or rather, "being an effect" is asserted by you to be the inherence of existence (*sattā-samavāya*).
However, the "existence of another," namely the location designated as a place, is not its cause;
for it is accepted that only among substance, quality, and action is substance the cause. And non-existence is not [a substance].
Regarding the phrase "characterized by substance and so forth":
even when there is inherence of existence (*sattā-samavāya*), that which lacks it would still be the object of the cognition "existent," but not the object of the cognition "non-existent."
Furthermore, since the absence of a jar is possible even in the absence of a location, how could it be its effect? Nor does this [absence] possess a distinction with respect to each object,
because it is the object of a cognition having a single form.
Or, if [the difference] were due to the difference of related entities, then that consequence would apply even to universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth.

Furthermore, since inherence (*samavāya*) has just been refuted immediately above, how could there be for non-existence a state of being an effect consisting in inherence with the existence of its own cause?
By this, the relationship of produced and producer is also refuted.
Therefore, since there is no connection whatsoever, the existence of another thing cannot establish the non-existence of that [first] thing.
Showing another kind of connection, the opponent says: "There is the object," and so forth.

For just as an object (*artha*) is the *viṣaya* (the perceived) and a word (*śabda*) is the *viṣayin* (the perceiver), the relationship between them is one of object and subject (*viṣaya-viṣayibhāva*).

[S. 174a. In this way, there will be a relationship of object and subject between the existence of another thing and its absence, because the absence of a jar is made known by the existence of another thing called "the location"—this is the objection raised in the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*). The connection is that there would thus be a relationship between the word and its referent.
Of what nature is it?
It has the characteristic of cause and effect.
But how is it that the word has the status of being the effect of an object?
When there is the intention to communicate that [object], and when there is the desire to communicate the meaning, [the word] is employed—that is, uttered—on account of that.
Thus, there would be a relationship between the word and that object revolving within the desire to speak, characterized as cause and effect.
And even though both word and object possess the nature of universals (sāmānya) constructed by the intellect, nevertheless, [it is] through that which appears as the object...

Because the particular characteristic of the word (*śabdasvalakṣaṇa*), which is the basis for the conceptualization of the general category of the word, is brought forth by the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*), the relationship of cause and effect is expressed through that medium;
it is characterized by inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*).
The word "or" (*vā*) is used to express what is established by others;
for others maintain that the relationship between word and meaning is characterized by inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*).
Therefore, it is logical that there exists a subject-object relationship (*viṣaya-viṣayibhāva*), consisting of the signified and the signifier, which is based upon that relationship.

If it is argued that the same will apply to the non-existence of that (*tadabhāva*) and the existence of another (*anyabhāva*), he says: this aforementioned method is not possible here in the case of the non-existence of that and the existence of another.

For when there is the intention to establish the non-existence of a jar, the employment—that is, the establishment—of the existence of another, characterized as a location (*pradeśa*), does not occur.
Because the location is produced from its own causes even prior to the intention to demonstrate the absence of the jar;
and because, even when that intention exists, there is no absence of the presence of something else.
Therefore, how could there be a causal relationship between those two?
Or would there be an inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) mediated by that [relation], such that the status of object and subject (*viṣaya-viṣayibhāva*) could be postulated?
It might be thought: just as the relation of object and subject between a word and its meaning is caused by the relation of the probandum and the probans (*sādhya-sādhanabhāva*), so too [is it here].

Since the status of word and object as an example [for the relationship between presence and absence] is established merely by the phrase "also of the existence of one thing and the non-existence of another," he says: "For when... and so forth.
For the relationship of probandum and probans between word and object is based on their being cause and effect; otherwise, if they were distinct entities, that relationship would be impossible.

Likewise here, if the relationship of probandum and probans were established between the non-existence of that [word] and the existence of another, then by means of that [relationship], [the example would hold].
The relationship between object and subject would have to occur by way of the relationship between the probandum and the probans;

however, that very relationship of probandum and probans cannot be established in the absence of a connection— such as the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) and so forth— because otherwise anything could be the probandum or the probans of everything.
If it is asked how the sense faculty (*indriya*) is the basis for the establishment of its own object, [the answer is:
such a designation occurs because the sense faculty and the object give rise to a single cognition through a specific causal condition based on their mutual approach and so forth;
but it is not so in this case.
Because that [logical relation] is impossible between the existence of one thing and the non-existence of another;
and because the relation of probans and probandum, characterized by the state of sign and sign-bearer, is the subject under discussion;
and because that [relation] is impossible without a connection.

If it is argued that the relationship of probandum and probans between the presence of one thing and the absence of another is not based on any other relation, but rather is caused solely by the relationship of object and subject;

[the author] replies: otherwise, if no other relation is admitted, but the relationship of probandum and probans arises from the relationship of object and subject, and the relationship of object and subject arises from that [relationship of probandum and probans], then this would result in the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*).
And thus, if one [of the two] is unestablished, both would be unestablished.

Furthermore, if it is desired that the non-existence (abhāva), which is the possessor of the mark (liṅgin), be established—that is, inferred—from the existence of another thing (anyabhāva) serving as the mark (liṅga), then the non-aggregate (asamudāya) would be the probandum (sādhya);

for by means of the existence of another, only that specific absence is established. It is not because of an absence of relation in general that the relationship between probandum and probans is untenable.

And the word "ca" (and) refers to the fault of the absence [of the probandum] when the intended probandum (*sādhya*) is a composite whole (*samudāya*) characterized as property and property-possessor (*dharmadharmin*), which has entered into the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*).
If it is argued that the status of being a probandum is never intended for the composite whole in every case, he says:

"And likewise, if one accepts the status of being a probandum even for the property alone (*dharmamātra*) in its independence, then in an application such as 'the absence of a jar [is proved] because of the existence of something other than it,' the jar would [be absent] in every place and at all times."
Furthermore, non-existence would follow as a consequence.

For when a property (dharma) that is subordinate to a subject (dharmin) is being established in a particular locus, its existence is logical only there and only at that time, and not otherwise; thus, in all cases, it must be admitted that the composite whole alone is the probandum (sādhya), and not the property in isolation.
Here the opponent says: "It is not the case that the collection is the probandum, nor is there a lack of connection between the existence of another thing and its non-existence.
Why?
Because of the location and so forth," and so on.

In this case, the subject (*dharmin*), such as a location, is qualified by the absence of a jar—as in "there is no jar in this place"—and is thus established as distinct from a location that possesses a jar; therefore, having attained the status of a qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*), it is what is being proven.
It is not, however, the mere statement "the jar does not exist," where the jar remains a mere subordinate factor (*guṇabhāva*) of some other subject.
Therefore, since it is not the collection [of the locus and the property] that is the probandum (*sādhya*), how could there be the fault that arises from its existence?

Furthermore, on this view, the fault of a lack of connection between the mark (*liṅga*), which consists in the existence of something else, and the bearer of the mark (*liṅgin*), characterized as the substratum (*dharmin*) such as a location, does not follow.
Why?

Because the "other-being" (*anyabhāva*), characterized as a location distinct from the jar and so forth, has a connection with the locus (*dharmin*) such as that location, there exists a relation of identity (*tādātmya*).

For instance, you yourself maintain that the relation between a locus such as sound and properties such as being produced is precisely characterized by identity; the intention here is that such a relation exists in this case as well.
Consequently, he considers the statement "and because of the absence of a relationship" to be incorrect.

The proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntin), however, [proceeds] by means of the mark (liṅga) consisting of the existence of another thing, with respect to the possessor of the mark (liṅgin)— characterized by the property to be proven— which is called the absence of a jar.

Thinking that the absence of a relation previously stated does not apply to the subject (*dharmin*), and thus wondering how a subsequent [reason] could be connected to it, [the author], demonstrating the absence of a relation between the subject and the mark (*liṅga*) called "existence of another" (*anyabhāva*), says: "There is no non-relation between the mark and the marked (*liṅgin*)," which is then connected with "nor is there... [in the following verse].
Likewise, it is not that the non-establishment of the collection [of the reason] is the point;

rather, for one who speaks thus, the very lack of a relationship between the mark (liṅga) and the bearer of the mark (liṅgin), and the very non-establishment of the collection, [constitute the fault].
Why?

Because the very locus (pradeśa) and so forth, which is established as the subject (dharmin), is itself the "existence of another" (anyabhāva), and thus has the characteristic of being a logical mark (liṅga) consisting in the existence of another.

He demonstrates this very point: for when a certain locus and so forth is conceived by you as the subject, that very locus where a jar or the like is said not to exist by the world is [itself] that locus and so forth, in relation to that jar and the like.
A positive entity that is unmixed [with the object in question] and devoid of contact with it is intended as the logical mark (*liṅga*), and nothing else;

because from the perception of that very thing—namely, the perception of a location and so forth unmixed with a jar—the conceptual cognition "the jar is not here" arises for this cognizer as the knowledge of the probandum (*liṅgin*).
Therefore, that alone is the "other-existence" (*anyabhāva*).
For that alone which, being perceived, produces the cognition of the possessor of the mark (liṅgin) is called a "mark" (liṅga).
And a location or the like, when not conjoined with a jar, is exactly so.
Therefore, that very thing characterized as the presence of another (anyabhāva) must be accepted as the mark.

Therefore, how can there be the relationship of sign (liṅga) and signified (liṅgin)— that is, the state of being a sign or the state of being the signified— between that very same other-nature (*anyabhāva*) which does not even experience difference through its own exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*)?

For the sign itself cannot be the subject (*dharmin*), because once the subject is already cognized, the cognition of the probandum (*sādhya*) has occurred, and thus it is impossible to pursue the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and so forth.

Furthermore, since there is no other subject (*dharmin*), how could there be a relation between the mark (*liṅga*)— which consists in the existence of another— and that [subject], or how could there be the status of the whole being the probandum (*sādhya*)?

In the case of sound and producedness (*kṛtakatva*), however, although they are identical in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*), there is indeed a distinction based on the difference in their conceptual exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*).

Therefore, it is logical that even when the substratum (dharmin) such as sound is apprehended, if impermanence and so forth are not yet cognized, they are established by means of "being produced" (kṛtakatva) and other such reasons.

It might be thought: "By means of the conceptualization of a universal and a particular, there will be a single entity consisting of both the mark (liṅga) and the bearer of the mark (liṅgin). To this he says: "And in this present case of the existence of another (anyabhāva), the conceptualization of a universal-particular relationship is not possible, whereby—through the distinction between universal and particular—the universal could be the reason (hetu) and the particular the substratum (dharmin)."
For [the relationship between] the mark and the bearer of the mark must either consist in being established by a collection, or in a connection [between them].

Why is this not possible? He says: because the absence of the jar—the non-existence of the jar—is cognized precisely through the cognition of its specific [locus], that is, through the cognition of a particular location devoid of the jar.
