And since it is the specific [locus] itself that is the basis for the cognition of the absence of the jar, what is achieved there by the postulation of a universal?

If it is argued that this very particularity, while existing elsewhere, will attain the nature of a universal, he replies: since there is no persistence (*anvaya*) or recurrence of that particularity—which is distinct from the location of the jar—in another object of the same class, how can it possess the nature of a universal?
For a particularity restricted by place, time, and state does not follow after (*anveti*) another.
Right here he states the reason for the reinforcement: "The meaning of the proposition," and so forth.
For if the specific locus (pradeśaviśeṣa) devoid of the jar were indeed the subject (dharmin),...
And if that very [subject] is intended as the reason (*hetu*),
then the reason— characterized by the subject (*dharmin*)— would be merely a part of the object of the proposition (*pratijñā*), which is the aggregate of the property (*dharma*) and the subject;
for there is no distinction [of the reason] even from the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) of a part of the object of the proposition.
"The state of being a cause is unestablished from the perspective of experience.

Now, if one thinks that this fault shall not occur and thus does not accept as the reason a specific location that is merely devoid of a jar, but rather accepts "location in general" (pradeśamātra) as devoid of the qualification of being devoid of a jar, then he says: "And it is not the case that wherever there is location in general, there is the absence of a jar."

Even in a location where a jar exists, because there is still a mere portion [of space], the reason would be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). To show otherwise the relationship between the general and the particular, the opponent says:
"In such a place—that is, in every location where a mere empty space devoid of a jar stands before one, there is the absence of a jar; so how can there be inconclusiveness?"

The very cognition of such a specific location is itself the cognition of the absence of the jar; therefore, the relationship of sign (liṅga) and signified (liṅgin) between the existence of one thing and the absence of another is untenable. Demonstrating this, he says: "But of that very...
and so forth.
That specific location which is established as the subject (*dharmin*) in its state of being "bare" (*kevala*), it is precisely its "bareness" that is expressed by you through the qualifier "bare."
That very absence of the jar is called the "non-existence of the jar.

And that absence of the jar is established only upon the cognition of the bare locus (*pradeśa*) which serves as the logical mark (*liṅga*); it is not established at a later time as something distinct from that, in another form, like fire [is established] from smoke.
Therefore, once the object to be proven (*sādhya*) has been cognized precisely upon the cognition of that [locus], of what could that [absence] now be the logical mark?
It belongs to nothing else;
for while the absence of a jar— which was intended to be known— is established, nothing else has been intended to be known,
since the cognition of the absence of the jar occurs precisely upon the perception of the bare location.

Furthermore, this subsequent pursuit— namely, the following of the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) by means of the realization that "wherever there is a bare location, there is an absence of the jar"— is useless, because the probandum has already been cognized at the very outset. Since this is so,
it is established that the existence of another thing characterized as a bare location cannot be the proof for non-existence, because there is no distinction between the probandum and the probans.

Thus, that which was stated by the opponent in order to demonstrate that the mark (*liṅga*) has as its object a composite whole (*samudāya*) and its connection with the locus (*dharmin*)—namely, "because non-existence is established as a qualification of the locus such as a specific place"—is refuted precisely by the critique of their inseparable establishment (*apṛthaksiddhi*). However, when the demonstration of a connection through the relation of object and subject (*viṣaya-viṣayibhāva*) has been rejected, the opponent, showing the connection between the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*) in another way, says: "There exists a connection between the existence of something else and its own non-existence."
[The opponent claims: "There is that which is called contradiction;
therefore, because of the existence of a relationship [between them], the non-existence [of one] will be established through the existence of the other.
But the proponent of the final view (siddhāntavādī), not even conceiving of a contradiction between the probandum and the probans, asks: "What is in contradiction with what?"

The intention is that no contradiction between the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*) is possible here. The opponent, through ignorance of this intention, points out a contradiction: "of that [non-existence], such as a jar, which is desired to be cognized by means of the existence of another—namely, the nature of the bare locus (*kevalapradeśa*)—as its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*). Demonstrating that the opponent who speaks thus is stating something incoherent, [the author] says: "Indeed, what is it that the counter-correlate, such as the jar, is desired to be cognized by, such that by means of that counter-correlate, as the object of cognition (*prameyatva*), there would be [a relation] between the mark (*liṅga*) and the bearer of the mark (*liṅgin*)?"

Is contradiction (virodha) designated as a relation? If it is argued that the counter-positive (pratiyogin) is not intended to be established, but rather its absence (tadabhāva), he says: "But the absence which is the probandum (sādhya) is that of the counter-positive. [S. 178a]

[Kumārila, however, thinks: "Since this non-existent portion (*abhāvāṃśa*) is distinct from the existent portion (*bhāvāṃśa*), the non-existence of that thing is not simply another existent; therefore, how can the cognition of that [existent] itself be the cognition of its non-existence?"
For this non-existence is divided into various types such as prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and so forth;
yet, since differentiation is not possible for that which is a non-entity (*avastu*), it must therefore be of the nature of a real entity (*vastu*). As it has been said:
"These distinctions could not belong to a non-entity; therefore, it possesses the nature of a real entity."
[ŚV Abhāva 8ab] Thus it is said.
Furthermore, it is not logical that the very portion consisting of an entity (bhāvāṃśa) should be the portion consisting of non-existence (abhāvāṃśa),
because the former is cognized through the power of contact with the sense faculties.
And because the cognition of the other [absence] is caused by the non-conjunction with that [object]. As it has been said:
"When there is conjunction with that, the nature of existence is cognized as 'this exists';
however, the cognition 'this is not here' is likewise caused by the non-conjunction with that."
[ŚV Abhāva 26] Thus, how can the very cognition of that [object] be the exclusion of another? To refute this, he says:
"The isolation (*kaivalya*) of that other place—that is, its being solitary (*ekākitva*), its state of being without a companion."

That very deficiency of another counter-correlative, such as a jar, is "non-existence"; therefore, that which is other than it—the positive aspect itself—is what you intend by "the non-existence of that. The followers of the Sugata state that the aspect of the non-existence of the counter-correlative is not a separate, distinct property apart from that [positive entity].

And therefore, the cognition of that [absence] is precisely the cognition of the other-entity (anyabhāva), and that very non-cognition is the non-cognition of its counter-correlate (pratiyogin); that is to say, the non-cognition of the counter-correlate is the cognition of absence.

He thinks as follows: this factor of absence, which is postulated as a property of a real entity distinct from the factor of presence, experiences the nature of the absence of a jar and so forth precisely because of the deficiency of that [jar’s] form.
It is not otherwise;
and that deficiency of its own form exists even in the positive aspect of another entity.
For in the absence of that [nature], its status as a distinct entity would be lost;
indeed, that which does not lack a certain form does not experience otherness from it, just as a thing does not differ from its own essential nature.
Furthermore, in that case, even its aspect of non-existence would not be established;
the entire universe would result in being a single substance,
and from that, the consequence of simultaneous origination and so forth would follow.
Since everything would have to be applicable everywhere, the positive nature of one thing must necessarily consist in the very absence of others;
and thus, the cognition of that [positive entity] is itself the cognition of the absence of others.
Furthermore, the contact of the sense organ with that [entity] is itself the contact with the absence of others. So why is it said—?
If it is argued that the statement, "This is not here; thus,
it is caused by non-connection with that," was spoken with reference to conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), then this objection is indeed no refutation at all.

When, through perception, an object is apprehended as having the nature of a real entity consisting precisely in the absence of anything other than that [object]—due to the arising of its own form—thereafter one accepts a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) which expresses it according to how it was grasped.

Furthermore, this investigation into non-existence has been set forth by one who, in establishing the duality of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), examined both the object of cognition (*prameya*) and the means of cognition regarding non-existence; therefore, it should be understood from that very source.
Moreover, the apprehension of the existence of something other than that is necessarily itself the apprehension of its non-existence.

Therefore, demonstrating that it is not for the sake of establishing the non-confusion of entities, nor for the sake of the conventional usage of non-existence— namely, "this is not here"— that the postulation of a separate means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) called "non-existence" is logical,
he says: otherwise, if the apprehension of that [other thing] itself is not accepted as the apprehension of its non-existence, then...

If, by the determination of the nature of that other entity, there were no exclusion—meaning no rejection—of what is other than it and lacks its form, and if there were no cognition of its absence, then there would be no determination of it at all; that is, there would be no cognition of the very nature of that other entity.
What is the reason?

Regarding that [object] and that which is not its form: there is the specific form of that object, which is distinct from all the three worlds, and there is that which is not its form—that is, the form of another—which is not its own form; because of the non-discrimination, the non-separation, the failure to establish through distinction, and the failure to demonstrate without confusion between these two.

For that form is unmixed with the forms of all other things; if, however, that [form] is not reflected as such by the perception arising from its capacity, but rather that perception arises with only a vague appearance, then how could there be a determination of it by that [perception]? Indeed, it is not logical for a thing to be determined by a cognition that does not conform to the form of that thing—just as, for example, a person with jaundice cannot determine a white conch shell through a cognition in which the conch appears yellow, failing to conform to the actual form of the white conch.
Regarding the phrase "by means of cognition":
if it conforms to a specific form, how could there be a non-exclusion of others by that determination [of the object]?
Therefore, it is precisely because it does not conform to other specific forms that there is a non-exclusion of what is other than that.
"And thus there is an absence of its determination.
[The opponent asks: "Let it be so; what fault follows from that?
To this he says: "This worldly transaction (vyavahāra), which is recognized by all people, [arises] from the perception of some object such as fire," and so forth.

In some cases, with respect to that which is related to it, there would be no activity characterized by engagement for the sake of attainment, nor withdrawal for the sake of avoiding what has been seen or not yet seen.
Why is this?
Because this cognizer, even while not seeing fire, perceives through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) that which appears as a mixture of its own form and the forms of other things.
Otherwise, its nature as perception would be lost;
for if one does not perceive that which is unmixed, then even if one perceives the mixed, how could this perception belong to anyone at all, being like [the sight of] a clod of earth and such?
How is it that such a perceiver, who possesses this kind of mixed perception, perceives fire alone and not water and so forth?
However, because cognition manifests objects in a confused form, one perceives even water and such things;
therefore, why would one seeking water not proceed toward that place containing fire?
Anticipating the opportunity for an opponent's objection, he says: "By non-perception," and so forth.
For by means of a cognition in which fire appears, only the very nature of fire is cognized;
whereas the absence of water therein is known through the non-apprehension of water.

Thus, because of the discrimination between that which has that nature and that which does not by means of these two cognitions, the specific worldly transaction characterized by engagement and withdrawal is established.
The proponent of the established tenet (siddhāntavādin) asks: "What is this so-called non-perception?
For perhaps an opponent might say that it is merely the absence of the perception of water; therefore, he says: "If [there were] water," and so forth.
However, for Kumārila, the mere cessation of the perception of water—which is of the nature of a void—is certainly not intended as a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) for non-existence.

The non-arising of perception and the other means of knowledge is called the "absence of a means of knowledge" (*pramāṇābhāva*), according to the statement: "It is either the non-modification of the self, or the absence of cognition regarding another object. (Ślokavārttika, Abhāva 11).

However, that non-modification of the nature of consciousness—which consists in the absence [of an object]—must be admitted to be accompanied by a cognition in which another object appears, and not solitary;
this is introduced in order to lead the opponent to such an admission.
And thus, let the cognition of another object itself be the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) for non-existence.
What is the use of postulating a quality called "non-modification" for a self that lacks any means of valid cognition (*apramāṇaka*)?

Furthermore, you do not intend this so-called "non-modification" to be something distinct from the modification consisting in the cognition of other objects, because you have accepted that the non-existence of a thing is simply its being another state of being (*bhāvāntara*).

Moreover, the cognition of another object must be understood as occurring only when that object possesses a form with equal fitness (*yogyatā*) and is in contact with the same act of cognition, and not otherwise.
For it is through the cognition of that [object] that the absence of its counter-positive is established.
Indeed, it is not logical that the non-perception of taste and so forth should result from the cognition of color, nor is it logical in the case of objects remote in space and so forth.
Furthermore, the cognition of one thing appears only as the manifestation of its own specific form.
For if that [water] were manifested as another form [of appearance], the very non-perception of water would not be established.
And thus, the absence of the counter-correlate (pratiyogin) is indeed manifested through perception itself.
This statement is introduced in order to demonstrate that, regarding the conventional usage of that absence, it results in precisely the non-apprehension (anupalabdhi) as we intend it to be.

In that case, if non-apprehension (*anupalambha*)— in the form of the absence of the apprehension of water— is of the nature of a mere nothingness (*tuccharūpa*), then how can it be the cognition or determination (*pariccheda*) of any non-existence?
This is because determination is a property of cognition (*jñānadharmatva*).
Now, if it is not intended that this [non-existence] has the nature of a cognition, but rather that it is the cause of that [cognition], he says: "or it is the cause of cognition.
For it is not logical that non-existence—characterized by the absence of all causal capacity—should be the cause with respect to a cognition.
Or, if it were a cause, then because it would constantly produce that knowledge independently of any auxiliary factors, the cognizer would have only the knowledge of non-existence.
There would be no room for another cognition at all;
nor is it logical that the non-existence of this [water] should produce a cognition when it itself is not cognized. Thus he says: "How is even that absence of the perception of water apprehended?
If this absence of the perception of water were to produce the cognition of the absence of water while remaining itself unapprehended, then [it would do so] for anyone at all."

He states that very point: because of the establishment of the non-modification of the self as distinct from "the cognition of that absence of water-perception" or "the cognition of something other than that water, such as fire," and because even in that case, if one were to accept it, the non-modification of the self would not be established as different from it since it would be of the same nature as that;

and therefore, if the absence of water or the like were perceived even when there is no cognition of anything else—whether that thing itself or something other than it—then the absence of water and so forth would also be perceived during states such as deep sleep.
What is not perceived?
It has already been examined in the *Pramāṇaviniścaya* that even then, its absence would be perceived; therefore, this should be understood from that very source.

By mentioning "obstruction" and so forth, he demonstrates this: even the otherness (*anyatva*) of one thing from another depends precisely upon a form of capacity equivalent to that [otherness], and it is not to be accepted as independent of it.
Thus, the establishment of non-perception (*anupalabdhi*) is proven according to our description.
And when, in the manner thus stated,

the cognition of the absence of water through non-perception is not tenable, and the determinate form of the cognition appearing as fire is not admitted, then this cognizer who perceives fire, while seeing the fire—
Furthermore, one would not determine through a cognition appearing in a confused form that "this is fire, not water"; and failing to determine this,
because the form of water also appears therein, one who seeks that [fire] would neither stay nor proceed,
nor would one seeking water proceed [toward it].

For instance—that which is called "water" is defined as that which is capable of removing all thirst, heat, and so forth, and which appears in a cognition with a specific form unmixed with the forms of anything else.
This [object], however, appears as something entirely different, possessing a variegated form.
Consequently, since it is impossible to simultaneously carry out two contradictory actions—namely, engagement and withdrawal—the person who perceives this would fall into an insurmountable calamity.
Anticipating an objection from an opponent here, he says: "Precisely for that reason," and so forth.

I do not say that the cognition of the absence of that [water] arises merely from the cessation of the perception of water, which is of a non-existent (tuccha) nature, because that would entail the faults already mentioned.

However, from this very perception of a single, isolated fire, there arises the cognition of the absence of another thing—namely water—which does not appear therein, according to the statement: "or [the cognition] of another object.
The proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntin) asks: "How [is it] one? and so forth.
By what capacity, then, does the perception of that one thing bring about the cognition of the absence of others?
For instance: when that [object] is being perceived, one may understand that "that alone exists," but why should one realize that "anything other than that does not exist"?

Because one perceives that very fire which is currently being seen in its pure form, unmixed with water, and because it appears in the cognition of fire, the certainty arises that "water is not present.

For instance, if water were also present there just as the fire is, then it too would have appeared in the perception just like the fire; since their capacity [to be perceived] is indistinguishable with respect to their respective cognitions, the appearance of only one of them would be illogical.

Therefore, the appearance of one thing is invariably concomitant with the non-existence of another; thus, from that [appearance], knowledge arises regarding the non-existence of the other, and it produces the knowledge that "there is no cognition of another object.
Likewise, another object is described in that way precisely because its own nature is unmixed with the nature of others.

And that cognition is designated as "cognizing the other" precisely by virtue of having that [other's] form, since otherwise such a designation would be impossible. Thus, the very apprehension of the "other" is the cause for the conceptualization of the absence of that [other].
Thus the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādin) says:
"This very [point]," and so forth.
But has this not already been stated by us previously through such statements as: "When those two exist, there is no cognition restricted to a single form, because of impossibility"? [699]
Therefore, that very appearance of the isolated object, which is not in contact with anything else, is itself the non-existence of other things;
for that isolated object consists of the non-existence of others, and any other aspect of non-existence has already been refuted.

Consequently, because that non-existence is manifested by perception, there arises—by the force of that manifestation—a subsequent conceptual cognition of non-existence, which takes the form of initiating conventional linguistic usage.

However, nothing is understood by that [cognition] which has not already been apprehended; for if a cognition regarding another object—even though it is of the nature of perception—were to produce a cognition of the absence of that other object while that [other object] itself remains unapprehended, it could be established as a separate means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) called "non-existence" (abhāva).
To explain: the form of the single cognition of that [object] is experienced precisely as being devoid of the form of anything other than it.
Therefore, the very cognition of that [positive object] is itself the cognition of its absence;
for even in the case of conceptual cognition, there is no so-called "cognition of its absence" other than the cognition of a form devoid of that [object's] image.
It is only its conceptual nature that is additional.

Therefore, just as in the case where fire has been determined by non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpajñāna*), a subsequent conceptual thought (*vikalpa*) such as "there is fire here" is merely the engagement in conventional usage and is not a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) from that [non-conceptual cognition], as was stated previously; likewise, even a conceptual cognition of non-existence, or the cognition of another object by way of its result, is not a separate means of valid cognition called "non-existence" (*abhāva*) distinct from direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Therefore, since that very thing which we have asserted regarding the cognition of the non-existence of another is being asserted by you as well, why does this appear like a mere person [acting out of self-interest], such that—by not accepting that [our position]—you accept a separate means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) called "non-existence"? Thus he mocks him:
"Indeed, you say this now only because you have no other recourse, not out of impartiality; otherwise, why was this not stated by you right from the beginning?"
Concluding with the statement that the self has been thoroughly tormented by what is called the "net of craving" (ālajāla), he says: "Therefore, like one who does not see the shore," and so forth.
It is said that merchants aboard a ship release a bird, thinking, "Perhaps it will see the shore.
When it wanders everywhere but does not find the shore, it returns to the very ship; this case should be understood in the same way.
Since this position must necessarily be accepted, there is no purpose served by this direction of understanding which lacks any established foundation.

Thus, for the opponent who desires a relationship of sign and signified between the existence of one thing and the non-existence of another, this [position] fails because of the absence of a connection.

When the opponent had established that [the inference] was illogical, and it was objected that "in the absence of a relation, there could be no cognition of the non-existence of one thing through the cognition of the existence of another," Kumārila’s own position was set forth with the words "Certainly not from any relation whatsoever," and so on.

Thereafter, he sought to prove that "the existence of another is itself the non-existence of that [first thing], and the cognition of the existence of another is itself the cognition of the non-existence of that. Thus, the view imagined by Kumārila was presented.
The doctrine of non-apprehension (*abhāvapramāṇa*) as a means for determining the non-existence of something has been refuted incidentally; however, now—{p.
194.1} "And the establishment of the non-confusion of entities depends upon its validity" (ŚV Abhāva 2cd).
In order to refute this directly, he raises the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), saying: "If [it were] from the cognition of one alone," and so forth.

For if the exclusion (*vyavaccheda*)—that is, the negation (*pratiṣedha*)—of another were established merely from the cognition of a single thing in its isolation, then the non-existence of every other thing would be established without distinction in that very place where that one thing is perceived.
It is not, however, by way of grasping a specific distinction that it is said "of that alone" which is in a state capable of producing its own cognition;
for instance, this [object] is perceived as having a form distinct from other entities that possess an equal capacity,
because the cognition of it is restricted to that single form.
Likewise, it is also of a nature devoid of objects whose fitness is incomparable to that [object].

Consequently, since there is no distinction in its capacity to establish the absence of something else by virtue of having a form devoid of that thing, the cognition of the nature of the location would establish the absence of taste and so forth just as it establishes the absence of the jar;
or else, it would not establish even the absence of the jar.

Furthermore, as for this qualification that was stated—namely, "the non-perception of that which has reached the conditions for perceptibility (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*) is the means of proving non-existence"—that need not have been said.
Why?

Because even in the case of those things that have not reached the conditions for perceptibility, there is indeed an exclusion of cognition regarding them in that place by virtue of the cognition having that single form.

For instance: just as those things which have met the conditions for perception do not appear in a cognition possessing their single form and are thereby excluded, so too it is with those that have not met the conditions for perception; therefore, what is the purpose of this qualification "having met the conditions for perception"?

Thus, the prima facie position being established: if "exclusion of others" (tadanyavyavaccheda) means separation—that is, the establishment [of an object] as distinct from others—then that is indeed accepted.
However, if it means the non-existence of those [other] places and times, that is incorrect.

For that capacity by which one establishes the non-existence of something that possesses an identical nature of fitness and has reached the conditions for perception (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*) cannot possibly exist in the case of something that lacks an identical nature of fitness or has not reached the conditions for perception. "When those two exist, there is no cognition restricted to a single form, because it is impossible"—this is how the proof of its non-existence functions. And this is not...
In order to demonstrate that [the object] occurs elsewhere, he begins with the words "from the determination of a single self," and so forth.

That which appears in direct perception as standing before one is a single, determinate form; because of the determination of that [form], through the arising of a mental image corresponding to it and by the production of an affirmative conceptualization (*vidhi-vikalpa*), that which is other than it—distinct from it and separate from it—is [excluded].

The exclusion, differentiation, separation, establishment of otherness, and communication of the unmixed nature of that which constitutes the self or intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all those [entities] occurs [thereby].
But how is it that, through the very determination of one nature, the exclusion of its opposite nature is effected by perception?
To the extent that perception arises through the power of an object standing directly before it, let it apprehend only that very form.
But how can the entire collection of objects distinct from that [object] serve as its exclusion (vyavacchedaka) when that [object] is standing directly before one?
Therefore, the means of valid cognition known as non-existence (abhāvapramāṇa) must be accepted for the sake of that exclusion, because—
"And the establishment of the non-confusion of entities is dependent upon its validity" (ŚV Abhāva 2cd).
Therefore, he says: "from a cognition whose manifestation is restricted to that very nature."
For the nature of a single object standing before one is unmixed with other forms,
because all things, by their very own-nature, are established in their respective natures and thus possess a nature unmixed with that of others.
Otherwise, how could their non-mixture be established even through the means of valid cognition consisting of non-apprehension (*abhāvapramāṇa*)?
Because it would follow that such a cognition is erroneous when it attempts to establish the non-confusion of things whose forms are mixed;
for in that case, since the manifestation— which by its very nature is restricted to that [object's] own essence and is unmixed with the manifestation of another form—
is impossible within a perception that arises through the power of that single entity, the cognition would incur error, and thus its status as direct perception (pratyakṣa) would be lost.

Thus it has been said: "For that [cognition], being produced through the causal efficacy of the object, would indeed conform to the very nature of that [object]. (PVin I 40.12f: *yasmāt tad arthasāmarthyenotpadyamānaṃ tadrūpam evānukuryāt*).
Thus,
because that cognition— which has an appearance restricted to that very nature— is experienced through perception by means of self-awareness (*svasaṃvitti*),
the experience of that [cognition] itself is indeed what distinguishes perception from that which does not possess its form.

Exclusion (*vyavacchedana*) is the act of differentiating; and by the power of that very [differentiation], there subsequently arises a conceptual cognition (*vikalpaka*) which establishes non-confusion in the form: "This is not of the nature of another. This [conceptual cognition] grasps what has already been grasped, and nothing new is perceived by it, because the self—which is unmixed with other forms—has already been determined by perception itself, which conforms to that [self's] form.
Even if that cognition indeed has a manifestation restricted to its own nature, how can there be a differentiation of that [cognition] from another nature?
To this, he says: "For it is not its own nature," and so forth.
Because that which is the nature of that object—unmixed with the form of others—is not the nature of the remaining object which is other than it.
Because everything else has a nature other than that [object], for otherwise its distinctness would be lost;
therefore, cognition itself, appearing as restricted to that very essence, is the exclusion from others.
For it is not the case that an object must be grasped by the hand through cognition and then turned away from another;
rather, its "turning away" from another is said to be merely the imitation of its own singular nature as unmixed with the form of anything else.
Otherwise, if it did not turn away from other natures within its own domain, [it would fail to be a cognition].
In that case, if this object were not distinguished from another nature and were not established as separate, then there would also be a determination of the other nature within it;
otherwise, the very non-determination of that [other]—which consists in the determination of a single nature—would itself take the form of its exclusion.

Consequently, since there would be no distinction from the other nature, the determination of that [other] would follow, resulting in the absence of both engagement and withdrawal. Thus, the previous reductio remains: "For one who sees this fire... and so forth.
The phrase beginning with "api ca" [706] and so forth is intended to show that it does not merely exclude other selves, but excludes everything else from that self as well; thus he says:
"And that [object] standing before one, which is restricted by its place, time, nature, and state, [is excluded] from those whose natures are distinct from its own place and so forth."
Since this [object] exists precisely due to its own causes,
the cognizing intellect— by imitating that very nature which is restricted to a specific place and so forth by way of that [object’s] own essence—
excludes from its own object any deviation from suchness, namely, its abiding in another place, time, or intrinsic nature.
Then he distinguishes [the object] from that.

But why does he establish it as distinct from that which belongs to another location and so forth? To this he says: for in this way, because when there is a distinction from that which belongs to another location and so forth, the object restricted to that specific location and so forth becomes determined (*paricchinna*).
Because it conforms precisely to that form.

If being otherwise— namely, having another location and so forth— is excluded due to not conforming to that form, then both its being such [as it appears] and its being restricted to that specific location and so forth belong only to that very thing which is being perceived, and not to anything else possessing a different location and so forth.

Since it is thus, therefore, the conclusion of the first [point] is that by excluding—that is, by turning away from—what is otherwise (i.e., what possesses a different location, etc.), namely that which possesses such a location and so forth, one determines that [object]. Likewise, the conclusion of the second [point] should be formulated as: by excluding what is otherwise (i.e., what is not of such a nature), namely that which is otherwise, one determines that [object].

By the reasoning thus stated, the operation— that is, the activity— of a single means of valid cognition, whether perception or inference, establishes all entities within two categories, namely reality and otherness, precisely because it delimits its own object. Therefore, the non-confusion [of categories] is established solely by the power of that very means of valid cognition which delimits them.
What is the point of this conceptualization of non-existence?
Is it not the case that this is a function of conceptual construction (*vikalpavyāpāra*), namely: "This is not of the nature of another; rather, it is of such-and-such a nature"?
And since perception (*pratyakṣa*) is held to be free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpaka*), how can the establishment of non-confusion (*asaṃkaryasiddhi*) result from it?
Therefore, he says: "Its positive concomitance," and so forth.
For that perception is effective only when it generates the conceptual constructions of affirmation and negation regarding its own object;
and only then is it accepted as a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), not at any other time.

Therefore, because there is no unperceived portion of the nature of a single object, even when it is delimited in its entirety, its validity regarding [properties such as] momentariness and the like is not accepted; for, despite the presence of causes of error, it lacks the capacity to produce the cognitions of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) with respect to those properties.

It might be argued: "Even in the proof of the two-fold division [of existence and non-existence], let there be no postulation of a means of cognition called 'non-existence' (*abhāva-pramāṇa*) for the sake of establishing their non-confusion; rather, it will serve to establish the absence of any other alternative mode."

For it has not been established that perception has any function whatsoever in proving the non-existence of that [other entity]; therefore, he says: "by the exclusion of everything distinct from that," and so forth. Thus, by means of the exclusion—that is, the separation—of all things other than that which is being perceived, and through the establishment of the pervasion (vyāpti) by way of its being something else, the non-existence of any other mode—which lies outside the categories of identity and difference—is proven.
Therefore, even for that purpose, the postulation of non-existence as a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is not tenable.

Now, if it is thought: "Perception does not establish the pervasion of everything unperceived by way of its being other than what is being seen; so how could the absence of a third category be established by perception itself, such that the postulation of non-existence as a means of valid cognition would be rendered useless?"—to this he says: "Of that [third category] which is being postulated as a third category..."

Therefore, since there is no pervasion by way of being other than what is perceived, that perception does not exclude—that is, does not differentiate—its own object from that [other] object; nor does it exclude—that is, does not differentiate—the object conceived as belonging to another category from its own object. Consequently, there would follow once again the undesirable consequence that the entity, which is one's own object, remains undetermined.
For if that object—which has as its nature an identity unmixed with all other forms—is not delimited by that very nature, how can it be delimited by it?
Or, if it is delimited by that nature, how could there be no proof of the pervasion of everything by its "otherness"?
Otherwise, even a single thing would not possess otherness.
"Because the sign (nimitta) is the same.

Since this is so, therefore, when a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), such as direct perception (pratyakṣa) and the like, operates upon some object, it delimits that object by way of its specific, determinate nature.
It excludes that which is other than it and devoid of that nature,
by establishing it as being "other than that";
and it indicates the non-existence of a third category that falls outside of both identity and difference.
Because pervasion is established through the otherness of everything, or because the twofold nature of all things— which is the opposite of that [otherness]— is established; thus,
this operation of a single means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) has just been described, and it is now summarized for the sake of easy comprehension.

Demonstrating this, he says: For instance, when a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), such as perception (*pratyakṣa*) and so forth, operates upon a certain object, it excludes that very object from other forms— that is, it distinguishes it from them— and apprehends it in its unmixed form,
because in ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*) the object possesses that nature, and because perception conforms to the form of the object as it actually exists.
Why does it exclude other forms?

Because it determines that very [object] as having a single nature, devoid of other forms. Likewise, it excludes that which is other than this, determining it as indeed different from what is being perceived.
Why?
Because from its own object;
it does not merely exclude its own object from others.
"Even another [cognition] from its own object"—from what [source is this known]?
Because another form, being other, is not determined therein in its own objective support; and that which is necessarily undetermined must be distinct from that which is determined.
Since this is so, therefore that very same means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), which delimits a single object, establishes the absence of other modes,
but not that which is called "non-existence" (*abhāva*). Why is this so?

When that object is being perceived, because it is seen as distinct from others, the "otherness" (*anyatva*) of that other thing which is not delimited therein is its "distinctness from what is seen" (*dṛṣṭatadanyatvam*). By means of that, everything excluded from it is established; therefore, [it is] not [the case that this is not so].

And because that which is other than one thing does not exist as another—that which stands before one, excluded from all other entities—is established as being perceived through the mode of its very own nature;
thus, extending this same principle to other cases, he says: "By this, succession, non-succession, and so forth.
By this aforementioned principle, a cognition arises that conforms to the form of a single, specifically determined object.
Excluding everything that has a form contrary to it from its own object, [the cognition] establishes a twofold division and the absence of a third possibility.
Thus, whatever things exist in the form of mutual exclusion—such as succession and non-succession, permanence and impermanence, and so forth—they have been explained.
For instance: the intellect, by perceiving the succession of an effect as being without assistance from anything else, thereby distinguishes its non-succession as the accompaniment of other effects.
Consequently, the possibility of a third mode—other than succession and non-succession—is refuted by the establishment of duality;
for every arising of an effect that is distinct from successive existence must, by virtue of being other than that, abide as a second mode.
Thus, momentariness is defined as perishing immediately after arising; this is the manner of its determination at the time of its conceptual establishment.

In this way, cognition [establishes its object] by removing from its own domain that which possesses a nature contrary to it, and by establishing it in another mode as distinct from that; thus, there is no third category.
Having thus demonstrated the establishment of non-confusion based on a single means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), he concludes by saying: "Therefore..."

According to the principle thus stated, because a single, specifically determined entity is perceived, there occurs an exclusion (*vyavaccheda*)— that is, a differentiation— from that which is being perceived of whatever is other than it, whether it be of a similar capacity, its opposite, or lacking that form;
this is because that which is being perceived appears under a different form from the unperceived nature [of the other].

Thus, because the designation of its own object as having the nature of something other than that [object] emphasizes the state of being (bhāva-pradhāna), there is an exclusion, and non-confusion is established.
If, in this regard, it were intended that the absence of everything else is established there without qualification, then it would be a case of proving what is already established (*siddha-sādhana*);
for everything is, without exception, excluded from its own object by a cognition of a single form as being devoid of that [other's] nature.
Because no other form whatsoever appears therein.

Now, if it is intended that the non-existence of that place and time consists in the exclusion of everything whose nature is contrary to it, he shows that this is not tenable: "Not in that place and time, wherein that [entity] has its own specific nature."

An object is perceived that is distinct from the entire threefold world; therein occurs the exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) or negation (*pratiṣedha*) of everything else—whether it be another entity possessing a form with a capacity equivalent to it, or something otherwise.
For by whatever reason there is a negation of that which possesses a form with a capacity equivalent to it but does not appear therein, [that is the nature of the perception].
Since it is impossible for there to be a cognition restricted to that single form when [the object] exists, that [cognition], being invariably concomitant with its absence,

leads to the negation of it. Therefore, how could its absence be established if [the object] were not subject to the conditions of non-perception (*anupalabdhi-lakṣaṇa-prāpta*) and did not possess a form of equal capacity (*tadatulya-yogyatā-rūpa*)?

Summing up this very point, he says: "Therefore, everything that is not of the nature of that [object], being of a form contrary to it, would be established by a cognition having a single form of that [object]; and it would also possess the place and time of that which appears, meaning it would have whatever place and time belong to that [appearing object]."
Like what?
Like taste, form, and so forth.

For even when a cognition manifesting a form distinguishes a taste—which lacks that form—from its own object, and even though it establishes their non-confusion, there is no absence of those two (taste and form) from that place and time.
[The reason] is established.
And therefore, how could there be the non-existence of everything—even that which is in a state of incomparable fitness—therein?
Or else, why would the qualification "having reached the conditions for perception" (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*) not be stated?

Since this is so, therefore the proof of the non-existence of something, somewhere, at some time, arises only from the aforementioned non-apprehension— namely, from the non-apprehension of that which has reached the conditions for apprehension (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*), whose nature consists in the apprehension of a form possessing a capacity equivalent to it—
and not through generality, as others have said:
Where the five means of valid cognition do not arise with respect to the nature of an object,
there the means of valid cognition known as non-existence (abhāva-pramāṇa) functions for the purpose of awakening one to the existence of that object.
[Ślokavārttika, Abhāva 1; Tattvasaṃgraha 1647] Thus it is said:

for the non-existence of an object is not established merely by the non-operation of the five means of valid cognition when it has reached the conditions for non-perception, because even while that object exists, the non-operation of the five means of valid cognition is possible due to its remoteness in terms of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and so forth.

Having thus concluded this incidental discussion, [the author] addresses what was stated by the opponent: "Why is it that the very presence of another thing (*anyabhāva*) and the perception having that as its object do not establish its non-existence? Having refuted the status of the presence of another thing as a logical mark (*liṅga*) for that non-existence, he now refutes the perception having that as its object, saying: "The perception having the presence of another thing as its object," and so forth.
Furthermore, as for what was said—"Why is the perception of an object that has another existence not a proof of its absence?"—that is indeed accepted by us as a proof of its absence;
however, it is not as a logical mark (*liṅga*) in the manner you have described.
What is the reason?

For even in that case, when a perception whose object is the existence of something else (*anyabhāva*) is postulated as the means of proving non-existence (*abhāva*) as distinct from that other existence, the absence of a relationship is equal to the case of [proving] its absence;
for there is no relationship—such as inherence in a single substrate (*ekārthasamavāya*)—between that perception, which consists in the existence of another thing, and that absence.
Demonstrating the equality of this point with the argument "because they are not established separately" (*apṛthaksiddheḥ*), he says: "The manifestation of the mark," and so forth.

As for this perception of another entity which is said to serve as a logical mark (*liṅga*), since the non-existence of that [other entity] is established at the very moment that perception arises— namely, at the time it manifests in the form of a place devoid of that [entity], or at the time of its cognition— it is as follows: the experience of a cognition in which there is the manifestation of another entity distinct from the manifestation of that [specific object] is itself the experience of its non-existence.
He establishes that very point: for a cognizer, having first apprehended the existence of something else distinct from that [object], does not subsequently—
after establishing the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) of that cognition with the cognition of the other thing through its absence—
apprehend that absence by means of a proof-establishing instrument (*pramāṇa*).
What then?
One who apprehends that which is other than it, having a form distinct from it, simultaneously apprehends the non-existence of its counter-positive,
because that very thing has the nature of the non-existence of the latter.
For instance—the perception of the bare location itself, whose nature is not commingled with the location containing the jar, is precisely the perception of the absence of the jar.

Indeed, there is no difference in meaning between "there is no jar here," "this place does not possess a jar," and "it is other than that which contains a jar. Therefore, the perception of the bare location as being distinct from that which contains a jar is itself the perception of the absence of the jar.
The cognition "there is no jar here" is merely a memory because it apprehends what has already been apprehended.
If it is asked how this is known:

it is because immediately following the perception, without any intervention characterized by the means of establishing positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), [one cognizes] "this [place] is devoid of a jar."

Because it is established by the two subsequent conceptual constructions, "the entity of a particular location exists" and "this entity of a jar does not exist," there is no following of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) here.
Furthermore, since the example is unestablished, the apprehension of the absence of [the probandum] within itself is the proof for that non-existence.
He shows that very point by way of negative concomitance (vyatireka) with the words "And that [is] of that," etc.
If it is argued that positive concomitance (anvaya) also exists here, he says:
"For it is not possible in this way," etc.
Why is it not possible to demonstrate [the universal]?
Because of its apprehension as one: because that specific form of apprehension which belongs to that single entity unassociated with anything else does not exist anywhere else.
Now, if it is argued that the cause is the generality of the apprehension of what is distinct from that—namely, wherever there is the apprehension of a ground distinct from a jar—[we reply:]...

In each such case, the absence of a jar— as in a region previously experienced as devoid of a jar— is stated; for when a general demonstration is being made, even regarding the example, there exists no other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) such as perception to establish the absence of the jar in that previously experienced region devoid of a jar, since the apprehension has the existence of another thing as its object.
However, that very perception of the presence of something other than it is the means of proving the property to be proven, which is characterized by its absence.
And just as that [perception] requires an example for the sake of establishing its absence in the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*), so too does it require one for the example itself.
Likewise, in that case as well as in others, there would be an infinite regress of examples.
And in the event of such an infinite regress, there would be no comprehension of the absence of that [object] anywhere.
Since this is so, the establishment of the absence of something cannot arise from any mark whatsoever, whether it be the presence of something else or its perception.
If the existence of something other than that does not establish its non-existence, then how could it establish it as a logical mark (*liṅga*)?
To this he says: "That existence of another is established by the definition of perception"—because perception itself, being distinct from the intended apprehension, constitutes non-apprehension.
Being established by means of the non-apprehension characterized as "tallakṣaṇa," it would establish the conventional usage of non-existence;
but where, then, would this establish the conventional usage of non-existence? It establishes it when the cognition of a deluded person is the object to be proven.

However, for one who is not deluded regarding the apprehension of the object and indeed remembers the subject, the conventional usage of its non-existence is based precisely on perception; thus, in that case, non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) is not a logical mark (*liṅga*). How can the existence of something other than the ground, which is established through non-perception, be considered "non-perception" itself? To this, he says:
[§ 3. Having divided non-perception into three kinds, its analysis:]

Thus, having established the essential nature of non-apprehension by refuting all opposing views, he speaks for the purpose of explaining its divisions: "This aforementioned non-apprehension is threefold.
How so?
When the causal relationship has been established by a means of valid cognition that proves it, there is the non-apprehension of the cause."
Of what kind [of non-existence]? Of a non-existence that has been established.

Likewise, when the relationship of pervader and pervaded (vyāpyavyāpakabhāva) has been established, by the very force of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) that proves it, there is the establishment of only the non-existence of the pervader, and not of anything else; for otherwise, it would follow that the "non-perception of the pervader" (vyāpakānupalabdhi) itself remains unestablished.
And as it has been stated: "the non-apprehension of intrinsic nature.
Thus, there are three kinds of non-apprehension.
But how is the conventional usage of the absence of the cause and the pervader established, such that their absence is said to be proven?
Thus he says: therein, it is not only for that [object] whose non-existence is directly established as a conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) that this applies;

rather, in the case of the non-perception of an essential nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*), the establishment of the conventional usage of non-existence regarding the essential nature itself, and the establishment of another entity distinct from it, is called such precisely because it serves as the cause for establishing the conventional usage of non-existence.
That non-existence of the cause and the pervader (*kāraṇavyāpaka-abhāva*) is thus established.

The conventional usage of non-existence (*abhāvavyavahāra*) is established by means of perception in the form of the non-perception of another (*anyabhāva*), regarding the two things to be negated—the effect and the pervader.

When, due to these two having dissimilar objects, the perception of qualified [objects] is not established, then [the non-perception] establishes non-existence or the conventional usage of non-existence.
The word "or" (*vā*) has the sense of conjunction.

Now, one might ask: "Is non-existence also established as a logical mark (*liṅga*) even in the case of the non-apprehension of an essential nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*? To this he says: "But in the case of the non-apprehension of an essential nature," and so forth.
It is only the conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) regarding non-existence that is [established], not non-existence itself, because the latter is already established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Anticipating an objection from an opponent here, he says: "If, then, non-existent usage (*asadvyavahāra*) is established for those two which are the cause and the pervader, while they themselves exist—by what means?
By non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) consisting of perception (*pratyakṣa*), which is the establishment of another entity—one distinct from that cause and pervader."
It establishes the absence of another thing—whether it be an effect or a pervaded—and the conventional usage of its non-existence.

And that perception of the presence of something else serves to establish the conventional usage of non-existence for those two, namely the cause and the pervader, only when they have met the conditions for perceptibility; it does not do so otherwise. This being accepted, how [is it so]?
The application of these two—non-perception of the cause and non-perception of the pervader—is with respect to an object that is beyond the senses (*parokṣa*).

This occurs when the formulation of the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) for the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*) and the essential-nature reason (*svabhāvahetu*) is made: "Wherever fire is absent, there smoke is also absent," and likewise, "Wherever a tree is absent, or momentariness is absent, there a *śiṃśapā* is absent, or existence is absent. Thus, the formulation of the negative concomitance is carried out by including all things without exception.
For at that time, all objects other than fire and trees are neither perceived nor momentary;
and therefore, how [could they be so]?

Is the non-apprehension characterized by the apprehension of that which is distinct from it established as the non-attainment of the conditions for apprehension (*anupalabdhi-lakṣaṇaprāptatā*) of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*)?

If so, how could the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) of the effect-reason (*kārya-hetu*) and the essential-nature reason (*svabhāva-hetu*) be established through a pervasion that encompasses all instances?
Or, if that is not established, how can these two possess the capacity to prove [the probandum]?

Therefore, the opponent considers that the negative concomitance (vyatireka) must be accepted in some cases from mere non-observation alone, and the positive concomitance (anvaya) in others from mere observation alone;
thus, the proclamation of an invariable connection (pratibandha) is rendered useless.

The proponent of the established tenet (siddhāntavādī) says: The non-apprehension of the cause or the pervader is not employed as a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) at the time of demonstrating the negative concomitance (vyatireka) regarding an imperceptible object; that is, the non-apprehension of the cause or the pervader is not employed as a valid cognition.
Why?

Since there is no certainty regarding the mark (liṅga)—characterized as the non-perception of the cause or the pervader, or characterized by the absence of that [object]—and because those two non-perceptions are of the nature of doubt, and the absence of that object is itself doubtful, how then can the employment of these two be accepted at that time?
To this he says: "Merely," and so forth.

For when the relationship characterized by origination from that (*tadutpatti*) and the relationship characterized by identity (*tādātmya*) have been established— by means of the previously mentioned proof for the causal relation between cause and effect, and the proof for the pervaded-pervader relation between the reason and the probandum—
then, for those two whose relationship is thus established, wherever there is an absence [of the cause], there would also be an absence of the other, namely the effect or the pervaded.

Or rather, there must necessarily and invariably be an absence [of the reason], otherwise it would follow that [the effect] is causeless and it would follow that it lacks intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāvatā). How, then, could there be memory regarding the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) that establishes the necessary connection (pratibandha) by means of that [absence]?
These two non-perceptions of the cause and the pervader are employed for the purpose of demonstrating the meaning of the word "syāt" (it might be).

However, when a proof is based on the power of perception and non-perception, let its existence or non-existence apply only to that specific case where it was seen upon the perception of one thing, or not seen upon its non-perception; why then should it apply to all cases?

For it is not the case that when things such as cows and horses—which lack an essential connection—are observed to exist in a certain way in some instances, they necessarily exist in that same way everywhere; however, for a person, the observation of the presence or absence of one thing whenever the presence or absence of another occurs at some time or place would have to be considered a mere accidental coincidence if no essential connection existed. Likewise, powers are seen to differ among distinct substances due to differences in location and other factors.
When [the relationship] is established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it is necessarily the case that wherever there is an effect, there must be a cause;

and wherever that [cause] is absent, there too the effect is absent. Otherwise, if the effect were to exist without a cause, it would follow that it is causeless. And from that, it would follow that it must either exist eternally or not exist at all.
Likewise, wherever something has a certain intrinsic nature (svabhāva), there it possesses that state; otherwise, it would simply be devoid of self-nature (nairātmya).

Thus, it has already been explained at length previously that the necessary connection (pratibandha) can be demonstrated through the presentation of positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) by means of pervasion (vyāpti) alone, and not otherwise.
[725] Fire and tree—[726] their intrinsic nature. —T.
[§ 4. Conclusion on the three characteristics of the reason, the threefold classification, and the fallacies of the reason.]

Thus, demonstrating that the presence of the positive and negative concomitances (anvaya-vyatireka) exists only in the case where the property of the subject (pakṣadharma) is characterized by the non-apprehension of an essential nature (svabhāva-anupalabdhi)— because the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) establishing it exists there and not elsewhere— the author concludes by saying: "Therefore, this very property of the subject, characterized as essential nature, effect, or non-apprehension, possesses positive and negative concomitance because of the existence of a necessary connection (pratibandha)."

And since, by the aforementioned reasoning, there exists a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), it follows that [the reason] is pervaded by that part [of the subject]. This is because the pervasion by that part is ascertained precisely through the ascertainment of positive and negative concomitance, as stated previously.

Furthermore, because of the statement regarding pervasion by that part, [the reason] possesses exactly three characteristics (*trilakṣaṇa*), that is, it has exactly three forms (*trirūpa*) and is of exactly three kinds (*trividha*).

The reason (*hetu*) that is a prover is neither of another characteristic nor of any other [kind], because when the aforementioned threefold nature (*trairūpya*) is present, any other form is redundant; and when the aforementioned threefold nature is absent, even if one were to postulate another form, it would not be a prover due to the lack of non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*). Why is it that only a reason with the three characteristics and only of the three kinds is a prover, and not one of another characteristic or another kind? He shows this by stating "because of the non-deviation from its own property to be proven" (*svasādhyadharmāvyabhicārāt*), meaning that only that which possesses the three characteristics does not deviate from its own property to be proven.

Furthermore, since the capacity to indicate [the probandum] consists precisely in the non-deviation from the property to be proven (*svasādhyadharma*), the postulation of another form [of the reason] is useless.

Moreover, once the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)—which are based on the necessary connection (*pratibandha*)—are absent, there is no non-deviation from the property to be proven even if another form is postulated.

Therefore, by this [statement], the phrase "it is only threefold" means that the reason possesses exactly three characteristics, because the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*)—that is, the non-deviation from the property to be proven—is [defined by those three].

Because it exists necessarily by rule (*niyamāt*) through that [connection], and because no other form is postulated even when the necessity of the connection— namely, the pervasion of the "part of that" (*tadaṃśavyāpti*)— is not admitted, there are other fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*). Thus, those which are conceptualized as possessing other forms distinct from the three characteristics already described are fallacious reasons, because the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*)— the non-deviation from the property to be proven (*svasādhyadharma*)— does not exist in them.

The other meaning shown by the phrase "due to non-existence" (*abhāvāt*) is that [the reason] has as its basis the non-perception of the essential nature (*svabhāva*) and the effect (*kārya*), because these alone possess existence. [§ 5.
Refutation of those who assert additional forms in the definition of the reason.]

Regarding the statement that "the logical reason (hetu) possesses only three characteristics and no others," the author speaks while demonstrating the dissent of others: "Other Naiyāyikas, Mīmāṃsakas, and so forth, maintain that the logical reason has six characteristics.
What, then, are the six forms of the reason desired by them?"
Thus he says: these three are known as the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), positive concomitance (*anvaya*), and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).
Likewise, the fourth characteristic is "having an uncontradicted object" (*abādhitaviṣayatva*).

That whose object—characterized by the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*)—is uncontradicted, meaning not refuted by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), is so described; its state, that essence, is another characteristic.
Likewise, the state of having a desired singular number is another form [of the reason].

That causal substance which has a single number is "one-numbered" (*ekasaṃkhya*); that universal of the reason which has such a one-numbered causal substance as its substratum is "possessing a desired singular number" (*vivakṣitaikasaṃkhya*), and its state (*tadbhāva*) is the other form.

If the status of being a reason (*hetutva*) belongs to a manifestation of a reason (*hetuvyakti*) that is delimited by the number one and is devoid of a counter-reason (*pratihetu*), then it possesses the capacity to prove (*gamakatva*); however, this is not the case when it is accompanied by a counter-reason, even if it is associated with the number two— meaning, provided that no other reason, such as a "non-deviant contradictory" (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*), is presented.
Likewise, there are the states of being a cognition and being the object of a cognition;
for it is not logical that an unknown reason should be a signifier by its mere existence alone.

Among these various forms, that which is called "the state of having an uncontradicted object" is distinct from that [logical reason] only when the inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*), consisting of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) based on a necessary bond, is possible.
It does not have a separate characteristic;
however, since it has already been stated by that very statement that it consists of that [nature], it need not be stated again.
Why is it not a separate characteristic?
"Because there is a contradiction between sublation (*bādhā*) and invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*).

To explain: even when invariable concomitance exists as previously described, those who consider the possibility of sublation to exist state "having a subject that is not sublated" (*abādhitaviṣayatva*) as another essential characteristic (*rūpāntara*).
And this suspicion regarding its possibility cannot occur.

Because there is a contradiction with non-separation (*avinābhāva*) characterized by the impossibility of coexistence (*sahānavasthāna*), he says—establishing that very contradiction—"For non-separation... and so forth.
For the non-separation of the reason (*hetu*) is said to be its existence only when the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) exists.
However, sublation by a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) occurs only when that [object] is absent.

For if a means of valid cognition were to operate regarding the absence of that [object] while it is actually present, then because it would be erroneous, it would simply lack the status of a valid cognition; how, then, could there be sublation?
Therefore, that reason— possessing those characteristics and being inseparably connected with the probandum— would exist in the subject;
and in this case, how could the property to be proven not be present, such that there would be room for sublation?

Therefore, there is an impossibility of coexistence between invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) and sublation by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇabādhā*), because the presence of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) in the subject (*dharmin*) established by invariable concomitance and the absence of that [property] established by sublation by a means of valid cognition are contradictory— characterized by their existence through mutual exclusion— and thus cannot occur in a single subject.
To clarify that very contradiction, he speaks by way of mocking others, beginning with the words "For perception and inference...
When perception and inference subvert the property to be proven (sādhyadharma), they seize it by the neck and expel it from its own locus, the subject (dharmin).
And since the reason exists only when that property to be proven (sādhyadharma) exists— due to its inseparable connection with it—
it seizes the property to be proven by the throat as it is being led away and forcibly establishes it right there in the subject (dharmin).
Oh, how truly extreme is the instability of entities characterized as the property to be proven!
For instance, since those constrained by two machines would necessarily die due to the cessation of breathing,

[the opponent]— showing that there is no contradiction between the two [reasons] because their objects of application differ— states: "Apart from the subject (*sādhyadharmin*), the reason is invariably concomitant with the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) in the example-subject (*dṛṣṭāntadharmin*), but not in the subject itself."

Therefore, how can there be a contradiction between sublation (*bādhā*) and invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*), given that sublation establishes the absence of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) in one case, while the logical reason (*hetu*) establishes its presence in another?
Thus, even when such invariable concomitance exists, since sublation is impossible, the other characteristic—namely, "having a non-sublated object" (*abādhitaviṣayatva*)—is possible.
Even when such invariable concomitance and the other characteristics, such as having a non-sublated object, are accepted, those [reasons] are nonetheless fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*).

In order to refute the status of this as a fallacious reason (hetvābhāsa), which was established by the argument that "others arise from a different form," he says, preceded by a reproach toward the opponent: "So then, has this wretched and miserable subject of the thesis (sādhyadharmin) married a eunuch, and having wedded him, is he now seeking a son characterized by the property to be proven (sādhyadharma) by begetting upon him a husband who is devoid of the power to produce that very property to be proven?"

This very point is clarified: for what reason do you maintain that the probandum-property exists in the locus even when [the reason] is absent, since you admit its inseparable connection (avinābhāva) elsewhere than in the subject of the probandum?
Having pointed out such a [reason] in the subject of the probandum, how can it be said that "the locus possesses the probandum-property"?

For even though the property of being water (*ambhatva*) is invariably concomitant with salinity in the ocean, there is no establishment of salinity in water distinct from that [ocean]—despite the fact that such salinity is intended as the probandum—even in the absence of the property of being water.
Anticipating an opportunity for an objection from the opponent, he says: "Precisely for this reason," and so forth.
He explains this very point: "This might be your thought:

since a reason (hetu) might exist in the subject (dharmin) even otherwise—that is, even in the absence of the property to be proved (sādhyadharma)—as is seen in the case of 'waterness' and so forth, and because inseparable connection (avinābhāva) is admitted even with the exclusion of the property to be proved; for that very reason, it is said that the subject is one whose property is not sublated by the two means of valid cognition (pramāṇa)."

If, by means of both perception and inference, the property to be proven (sādhyadharma) is not sublated in the subject of the thesis (sādhyadharmin)— just as the quality of being salty is not sublated in the case of water—
then that [reason] possesses the capacity to prove;
it is not otherwise.
"Since we do not accept that the probandum is established by mere invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) in other cases, the aforementioned fault does not apply.

To this, the proponent of the tenet (*siddhāntavādin*) replies: "In that case, when the probandum is not established because the invariable concomitance of the reason with the subject (*dharmī*) is not accepted, and another form—namely, 'having an unsublated object' (*abādhitaviṣayatva*)—is stated for its establishment, then [what of] the reason?"
There is no efficacy whatsoever.
Why? Because the probandum is established even without a reason simply through non-sublation; thus, the reason is entirely ineffective.
For in this case, there are two possibilities: when the subverting means of valid cognition (bādhaka-pramāṇa) operates, would the absence of the probandum be necessary or unnecessary?

In that regard, if the first alternative is taken, then the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*) is necessarily concomitant with the operation of a subverting proof (*bādhakapramāṇa*), because it exists only when that [proof] exists and is absent when it is absent.

Therefore, in the case of non-subversion—that is, in the absence of the operation of a subverting proof—the absence of the probandum, which is necessarily concomitant with it, is also absent; thus, since the probandum is established, the reason (*hetu*) is indeed superfluous and should not be put forward.
Thus, by what other means could there be for [the reason] the state of having an uncontradicted object?
It might be thought: "Let it be that the capacity of the reason does not exist in the absence of the operation of a subverting means of valid cognition (bādhaka-pramāṇa)."

But when there exists a subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) regarding the subject (*dharmin*) of that which is to be proven (*sādhya*), then the reason (*hetu*) will possess the capacity to establish the probandum; therefore, he says: "Even in the case of subversion.
If a subverting proof exists, then because it establishes the absence of the probandum in the subject, [the reason lacks capacity]. Furthermore—
Since even Brahmā would be unable to bring about that state, how much less so by the sixth reason? For what power does the probans, as a reason, possess?
It is precisely for this reason that you yourselves state "having an unsublated object" as another characteristic [of a valid reason].

Now, if the second position is accepted— that when a subverting proof (*bādhakapramāṇa*) operates, the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*) is not certain because [the probandum] may still exist even in its absence— then, demonstrating that this too lacks the capacity for non-subversion, he says: "If there is no certainty regarding the absence of the probandum when a subverting proof operates, then this consequence follows."

Nor is it the case that [the reason] lacks the capacity to prove the probandum simply because there might be a subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) or because the absence of the probandum is possible; for even when there is no subversion, the possibility of the absence of the probandum remains, and thus even a reason associated with such [absence] is nothing but a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*). Regarding what was said—that "since the probandum is established by non-subversion alone, the reason is useless"—the opponent, demonstrating that non-subversion has a different meaning and thereby establishing the efficacy of the reason, says: "Not by subversion..."
Non-existence is intended as the absence of sublation;
what then?
It is the non-perception of sublation.
