And that non-perception by a person might occur in some place or other due to a deficiency in their capacity, even when sublation is possible; therefore, since the probandum is not established merely by the non-perception of sublation, a reason must necessarily be stated for its establishment. Thus, that is the domain of the application of the reason. For at that time, the reason, while establishing its own probandum, [is effective].
"How could it be incapable?

To this, the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādin) says: "Does the reason indeed fear that perception which constitutes sublation (*bādhā*), and not sublation itself, such that you would disregard even a possible sublation and insist that [the reason] must be employed only when that [sublation] is not perceived?"
Perhaps an opponent might say: "What will this wretched sublation (bādhā) do even if it exists? Its very apprehension is a demoness (rākṣasī).
Therefore, fear arises from that very [apprehension], and in its absence, the reason must certainly be employed. To this, he says: "In that case," and so forth.

In that case, he asks with an interrogative intonation (*kākvā*) whether, regardless of whether there is sublation from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), this [reason] should be employed when no sublation is perceived.
Perhaps the opponent might say: "This has already been stated; for what purpose is it being asked?
To this, he replies: "For what purpose is it employed?"

The intention [of the author] is that even if sublation (*bādhā*) is not perceived, if its possibility exists, there is no logical connection between the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*). The opponent, failing to understand this intention, says: "For the sake of establishing the probandum," because validity is accepted when there is an absence of a sublating cognition (*bādhaka-pratyaya*), he thinks that the establishment of the probandum is therefore entirely uncontradicted.

The proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādī*), suspecting that the establishment of the probandum is impossible even when sublation is not perceived if such sublation actually exists, asks: "Does that [sublation] exist anywhere? and so forth.

Furthermore, do you entertain the possibility that this reason might establish the probandum even when there is sublation, such that you would exert effort toward the ascertainment of its absence of sublation and employ the reason?
If you say, "It is so";
Thus, even when there is sublation (*bādhā*), if one accepts the capacity of the probandum and the probans, the condition of having an unsublated object (*abādhitaviṣayatva*) does not obtain.
Why?
Because even when sublation exists, this reason possesses capacity; that is, its capacity is accepted.
For that indeed is said to be the definition of a logical reason (*hetu*), namely, that without which one could not establish the probandum (*sādhya*).

It might be thought: "In the ultimate sense, the definition of a reason is the state of being uncontradicted by non-perception (*anupalabhyamānabādhatva*), not the state of having an uncontradicted object (*abādhitaviṣayatva*). To this, he says: "And thus," and so forth.

This being the case, even though the existence of sublation (*bādhā*) is possible, one would have to accept it and yet proceed with the application of the logical reason (*hetu*) based merely on its non-perception.
For if the application of the reason were not intended while accepting the possibility of sublation, then—

since there is doubt regarding sublation based on mere non-perception (because it is possible for some existing things to be unperceived in some way)— one would be employing a reason that is itself subject to doubt.
Activity itself would not be tenable.
Therefore, whoever engages in action even when there is doubt regarding something does so only by accepting the possibility of its existence.
And thus, just as a reason is employed after accepting the non-perception of a sublation, it should likewise be employed even when that sublation is perceived.

Since there is no distinction between the perception and non-perception of that sublation if one accepts its actual existence, it is not even logical for the absence of sublation to be a defining characteristic of a valid reason (*hetu*). Therefore, how could validity possibly occur in the absence of a subverting cognition if there is no necessary connection?
Anticipating an opponent’s objection regarding the possibility of sublation (*bādha*), he says: "Not when there is sublation," and so forth.
For indeed, when sublation exists, the capacity of the reason (*hetu*) is not admitted; how then could there be its employment even when that [sublation] is perceived?

The proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādin*) says: If this is so—that when sublation exists, the reason is considered incapable—then a reason for which the impossibility of sublation has not been determined is of such a kind that it would be employed despite sublation.
It is not [sufficient] by mere non-perception alone.
What is the reason?
Lest there be an incapacity of a reason—even when employed against one's own position—to establish the probandum, due to the possibility of sublation.

The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādin*) says: "If you think that because no sublation (*bādhā*) is perceived, there is an absence of sublation; and since, in the absence of a cognition that perceives existence, objects necessarily lack existence, the causal capacity (*sāmarthya*) of the reason is established"—the proponent of the final view (*siddhāntavādin*) replies: "What is perception? Is it sublation? and so forth.
For the perception of objects is the effect,
and an effect does not pervade its cause;
for causes do not necessarily possess their effects.
How, then, can there be an absence of sublation upon the absence of a non-pervasive apprehension,
such that the incapacity caused by the possibility of sublation would not occur for the reason [in question]?
And this is indeed accepted even by others;

for they admit that even in the case of what has been accepted as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), if a subverting cognition (*bādhaka-pratyaya*) arises at a later time despite no sublation having been perceived at the time of its origination, it is regarded as invalid.
Now, if it is argued that sublation is precluded when there is the non-occurrence of perception—even though such perception is not all-pervasive—then:
"For falsity indeed ceases effortlessly through the knowledge of the defect" (ŚV, Sūtra 2.52).
By this very logic, since the sublation [of the cognition] ceases upon the cessation of the knowledge [of its cause], he says: "Even so, the reason is futile.
Why?
Because the probandum is established precisely through the non-perception of sublation, even without the application of a logical reason.
What is the reason?
Because sublation is impossible when there is no perception [of it].
For instance: you maintain that where there is no perception of sublation (*bādhā*), sublation does not exist in reality (*paramārthatas*) at all;
and where it does not exist in reality, the absence of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) likewise does not exist in reality.

Otherwise, it would be impossible for there to be an absence of sublation (*bādhā*) in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*). Consequently, according to your own view, since the non-existence of the probandum-property (*sādhyadharma*) implies its existence, the cognition of the probandum would be rendered useless by the reason (*hetu*). Now, if you maintain that sublation does not cease upon the cessation of perception so as to avoid a contradiction with logic, to that he replies: even if perception has ceased, if the non-cessation of sublation is maintained, the situation remains exactly as before.

Since the perception of sublation occurs when the reason lacks capacity, there is no application of the reason; for whom, then, could "having an unsublated object" be a distinct characteristic (*rūpāntara*) of the reason?
Summing up this very point, he says: "Therefore, with respect to its own probandum," and so forth. Because, in this way, the reason is pervaded in all cases.

If one accepts the necessary concomitance (avinābhāva) with the probandum while the external pervasion is being sought, the employment of the reason (hetu) results in futility. Therefore, even if it occurs otherwise— that is, even when its own probandum is present, it does not occur, and even when its own probandum is absent, it does occur— the reason does not bring about, establish, or manifest any probandum whatsoever in the subject (dharmin).

Since one does not negate what is contrary to that [which is established], the employment or application of a reason that neither effects an affirmation nor a negation is ineffective; therefore, one who necessarily desires the employment of a reason must admit that the reason is invariably concomitant with its own probandum, and that concomitance is based upon a necessary connection (*pratibandha*).
And this [non-contradiction] depends merely upon observation and non-observation, as stated previously.

Since that [non-contradiction] is accepted, the contradiction between sublation (*bādhā*) and invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) is established; thus, in concluding, he says "Therefore, not... and so forth.
For this reason, because it is so, non-sublation is not a distinct property (*rūpāntara*).

If it is argued that, because sublation (*bādhā*) and invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) cannot coexist, non-sublation is understood when invariable concomitance exists, why then should this not be considered a different property (*rūpāntara*)?
To this, he says: "That indeed," and so forth.
For that [non-sublation] would indeed be a further qualification of that [invariable concomitance] according to the actual state of things (*vastusthiti*).

And according to the authors of the *lakṣaṇas*, a qualification deserves to be mentioned as a distinct category only if, even when that [qualification] exists, there might be an absence of another [thing].
For the relationship of qualifier and qualified is not possible at all in the case of identity (*svabhāva*) or deviation (*vyabhicāra*); it occurs only in the latter case.
He provides an example, beginning with "For instance," and so forth.
For although there is no presence of "audibility" and so forth in the similar instances (sapakṣa),
and although there is presence of "visibility" and so forth in the similar instances, there is no connection with the subject of the thesis (sādhyadharmin), namely sound. Therefore,
because of the existence of both concomitance and deviation between these two, the relationship of qualifier and qualified is adopted as a distinct definition [of the reason].

If it is argued that "the same will apply here as well," he replies: "And this [objection] which was just stated is not possible when there is non-contradiction (*abādha*) given the existence of inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*).

Since non-contradiction necessarily occurs whenever there is inseparable connection—and thus there is no deviation—how could there be a relationship of qualifier and qualified, or how could it deserve to be adopted as a separate definition?"

Thus, sublation is not possible in the case of a reason that is invariably concomitant with the probandum (*sādhyāvinābhāvin*), nor in the case of a contradictory reason (*viruddha*) that is invariably concomitant with the opposite of the probandum (*sādhyaviparyayāvinābhāvin*).

According to the manner stated, when there is no reversal [of the reason], it is indeed a valid reason; however, because it is employed where it does not belong, it is called a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*).

Since this is so, therefore the absence of that [sublation]—the lack of sublation—is not to be stated as a separate characteristic for these two, the reason and the contradictory, distinct from their positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), which consist in their respective natures.
Because deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is absent, it is impossible for it to be a different form [of the reason]. Furthermore,

since sublation (*bādhā*) cannot occur when there is an inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*), due to their contradiction, there is no possibility of defects such as contradicting direct perception (*pratyakṣaviruddha*) and so forth, even in the case of a thesis (*pratijñā*) whose meaning is already implied, provided that a reason possessing the aforementioned characteristics is employed.

Since those [faults] have already been rejected by the very definition of a valid reason (*hetu-lakṣaṇa*), how can the absence of sublation (*bādhā-viraha*) be stated as another characteristic (*rūpāntara*) of the reason?
Furthermore, the description of such impossible [faults] is fruitless; this is the intended meaning.
If it is argued that there is the possibility of employing the thesis alone, he says:
"Nor even," and so forth.
For when the employment of the reason is absent, the thesis alone is not employed.
Because that [thesis] is accepted as having the reason as its object;

and therefore, the authors of the treatises need not state defects of the thesis, such as contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣaviruddha*) and so forth. However, since the venerable Dignāga observed various misconceptions regarding what is to be proven and what is not to be proven, he formulated the definition of the thesis (*pakṣa*) even for that which is unfit for formal employment (*aprayogārha*), whereby non-thesis-hood (*apakṣatva*) is established by logical necessity.
By the word "ni" (in *na ni*), there is no statement of what is contradicted by valid cognition (*pramāṇaviruddha*);
rather, the definition of the thesis (*pakṣalakṣaṇa*) is excluded from being over-extended (*atiprasakta*).
"Because that which is doubted alone is the probandum (sādhya), and because a proving means of knowledge does not operate upon that which is sublated by a [contrary] means of knowledge.
Having thus refuted the property of having an unsublated object, he says, while refuting another characteristic: "By this, in the case of inseparable connection (avinābhāva)..."

By demonstrating the impossibility of sublation (*bādhā*) existing [simultaneously], the intention to express a single number (*ekasaṃkhyāvivakṣā*)—which was stated as the opposite of the fault of the "non-erroneous contradictory" (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*)—is refuted and rejected.

The opponent asks: "How?"—in what manner is it that just as there is a lack of coexistence (*sahānavasthāna*) between sublation and invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*), so too is there a lack of coexistence between two counter-reasons and their respective invariable concomitances?
"In that case, the very desire to express the number one would likewise have to be rejected.
Showing the parity [of the two positions], the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādin) says: "One," and so forth.
For a single reason is indeed endowed with the defining characteristics.
How can it be non-deviant from its own probandum?
If it were to exist only where its own probandum exists, otherwise its definition known as "inseparable connection" (avinābhāva) would be lost.

In this very same subject (*dharmin*), that [reason] is one possessing those characteristics; yet, in that same subject, there is another counter-reason (*pratihetu*) which is contradictory. How, then, can it be endowed with the characteristics of a valid reason? Because the very existence of another property—which is contradictory to and subverts that which is to be proven (*sādhya*) by the first reason—occurs precisely when [the first reason] is absent, and not when it is present; thus, due to its necessary concomitance (*avinābhāva*) with the subversion [of the probandum], it is a "counter-reason" (*pratihetu*) because it is equal to the subverter, being equal in its impossibility of being subverted.
Thus, [the objection] has been refuted.
In this very context, intending to state another refutation, he says, beginning with "Moreover" (*api ca*), while offering a distinction:

"In reality" (*vastutaḥ*), that is, from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārthataḥ*), for whom no counter-reason (*pratihetu*) is possible—is such a person [the possessor] of correct knowledge (*samyagjñāna*)?

Is the reason intended as one that establishes the opposite of the proposed probandum (sādhya)—that is, a cognition contrary to it—on account of which its characteristic is stated to be the "intended singularity" (*ekasaṃkhyatva*), or rather, is it that for which no counter-reason (*pratihetu*) capable of proving the opposite of that probandum has been demonstrated, even though such a reason might exist in reality? Not seeing this further fault, the opponent says: "And what of it? and so forth.
"If it be granted that either the former or the latter alternative [is possible], what fault is there?

To this, the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādin) replies: "If a counter-reason (*pratihetu*) which is impossible is accepted as the cause for correct knowledge and so forth, then this intended singularity of number would lack its defining characteristic (*alakṣaṇa*)."
Why? Because it is impossible to determine that for which, in reality, there is no possibility of a counter-reason (*pratihetu*); this is what is meant by that term.
And this is stated with reference to the position of others;
for the opponent maintains an invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) based on observation and non-observation, even when no necessary connection (*pratibandha*) exists.
For the opponent maintains that there is an invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) based on observation and non-observation even in the absence of a necessary connection;
consequently, it is possible for such a counter-reason (*pratihetu*) to exist.
Since that [counter-reason] might occasionally occur even if it is not being perceived, its actual absence cannot be definitively ascertained.

For us, however, who maintain that the invariable concomitance (avinābhāva) is based on a necessary connection (pratibandha), the impossibility of a counter-reason (*pratihetu*) is indeed well-ascertained. This is because, when the necessary connection— characterized by identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*)— has been established through valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and a single reason has thereby proven its own probandum in a given subject (*dharmin*) by virtue of being invariably concomitant with it, it is impossible for another reason of that same character to prove a meaning contrary to it in that very same subject.
The possibility of a counter-reason (*pratihetu*) is suspected because two contradictory natures cannot coexist in entities;
and when there is the possibility of establishing such contradictory properties, it is that very [counter-reason] which [is suspected].

"Because it is impossible to establish, through a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the existence therein of the first [reason], which is inseparable from its own probandum. It might be thought: "Even if it is indeed impossible for us to ascertain the non-occurrence of a counter-reason (*pratihetu*) in the case at hand, nevertheless, why should the definition of a reason—which is established by the singularity of number intended to convey the impossibility of a counter-reason—not be applicable?"

Thus he says: "For one whose nature is not ascertained," and so forth. Since a probans (*hetu*) whose essential nature (*svabhāva*) is unascertained does not possess the characteristic of being a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), it lacks the quality of being a "property of the subject" (*pakṣadharmatā*), just like a doubtful [probans]—this was the previous proof.
Nor can that whose characteristic is doubtful be a reason; for if that were so, nothing at all would be a reason, which would result in the non-existence of reasons.
This is the justification for the statement that "fallacious reasons (hetvābhāsa) arise from that [doubtful case] as well.
It might be thought: let that alone for which a counter-correlate is observed be non-reason, since it possesses the status of a counter-reason (pratihetu).

However, for that [reason] whose counter-reason (*pratiyogin*) is not observed, there is in reality no possibility of a counter-reason. For in such a case, the actual possibility of a counter-reason is not even suspected, because a suspicion of sublation cannot occur without a sublating cognition (*bādhakapratyaya*). As it has been said:
"But as long as a subverting cognition has not arisen, there is no groundless suspicion.
Therefore, he says: "For when the defining characteristic is equal," and so forth.

This means that for that [reasoning] whose defining characteristic—consisting of the mere observation and non-observation which serve as the basis for the invariable concomitance—is equal to the suspected counter-reason (*pratihatuhetu*).

When a counter-argument— a counter-reason (*pratihetu*) that subverts [the original reason]— is observed in that case, it gives rise to a suspicion regarding the possibility of such a counter-reason even among those [reasons] whose counter-arguments do not appear, provided they possess characteristics similar to it.
What is the reason for this?
Because there is no distinction between one whose counter-positive is unperceived and one whose counter-positive is perceived;
for indeed, there is no difference between that [non-existence] and the other such that its occurrence might not be suspected.

However, since the non-perception of that [opposing factor] might be possible due to a deficiency in human capacity and so forth, why is it said that "an apprehension [of an opponent] cannot be without a basis in valid cognition"?

Now, if a specific feature (*viśeṣa*)—characterized by a logical connection (*pratibandha*)—is desired as the determiner of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) for a perceived counter-reason whose counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) is not perceived, such that the apprehension of the possibility of a counter-positive comes to an end;
then, provided such a specific feature exists, that specific feature is the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of the reason.
What is the reason? Because,

due to that specific distinction, the reason— being definitively certain and having its counter-thesis eliminated— determines its own probandum in such a subject (dharmin), since a counter-reason is impossible therein.
That which is not of such a kind—lacking those specific characteristics—is a perceived counter-reason (*pratihetu*); being devoid of that definition, it would not be a valid reason (*hetu*).
And thus, even if a counter-reason is observed in the case of what is not a valid reason, what does that have to do with the [actual] reason?

He says this because the intention to specify a singular number (*ekasaṃkhyāvivakṣā*) is made in that context for the sake of excluding such [a counter-reason], since that exclusion is already achieved by the very statement of the aforementioned invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*). Thus: "And so, when a counter-reason is impossible for a reason endowed with those specific qualifications, the intention to specify a singular number is useless—that is, purposeless.
Since no counter-reason possessing those characteristics is possible if one accepts the aforementioned qualifications, what is there to be excluded by the intention to specify a singular number?"
[This is stated] so that for him there may be the state of being a producer of an effect.

Furthermore, the intention to specify the number "one" is made in the definition of a valid reason (*hetu*) in order to exclude the fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) known as the "non-erroneous contradictory" (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*).

Moreover, since a counter-reason (*pratihetu*) is impossible in reality, if one requires a specific reason characterized by a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) in the definition, then even the "non-erroneous contradictory" does not become a fallacious reason.
Then, since there would be nothing to be excluded, what would be the point of intending to express the number "one"?

Showing this, he says: "Therefore, because one accepts a specific definition of the necessary connection (*pratibandha*), that definition of the fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) known as the 'non-erroneous contradictory' (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*) would be discarded—that is, it would not be possible.
But what, then, is the definition of that non-erroneous contradictory?"
Thus he says: "In its own characteristic," and so forth.

When two reasons, each possessing its own characteristic, fall upon a single subject by way of contradiction—acting as proofs for mutually contradictory probanda—that is the "non-deviating contradiction" (*viruddhāvyabhicārī*); such is the definition of the non-deviating contradiction.
And that [simultaneous existence of two causes] is not possible when an invariable connection is admitted;

for when a single reason possesses an invariable connection with its own probandum through either identity (*tādātmya*) or origination (*tadutpatti*), it is impossible for a second reason of that same character to exist in that very same locus (*dharmin*),
because it is impossible for entities to possess two contradictory natures.
Because the superimposition of contradictory properties is the defining characteristic of difference,
how could there be any possibility for a second reason that does not deviate from that [object] to exist therein?
Now, if the definition of a "non-deviating contradictory" (viruddhāvyabhicārin) is lost when such a specific distinction is possible, [then what follows?]
Or, even if the intention is to express the number one, there is still no consequence of the absence of a reason;
so why was it said that "there is an absence of a reason"? To this he says: "And not"—meaning certainly not—of that specific [relation] characterized as a necessary connection (*pratibandha*).
Since the impossibility of a counter-reason (*pratihetu*) is determined in reality,

you yourselves must specify the essential nature (*svarūpa*) characterized by identity (*tādātmya*) and causality (*tadutpatti*), just as we have specified it— that form in dependence upon which we perceive the possibility or impossibility of a counter-entity (*pratiyogin*).
Where that distinction does not exist, there the possibility of a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is merely imagined in an inference based on scripture;

however, where that distinction does exist in an inference proceeding by the force of real entities (*vastubala*), there a counter-correlate is impossible. Since this is so, that distinction of yours simply does not exist—you do not even know that distinction.

Thus—therefore, even in every case where the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) is not perceived, there must nonetheless be a doubt regarding that counter-positive. Strengthening that very doubt, he says: "Even for one who has seen a counter-reason," and so forth.

For even in the case of one for whom a counter-reason (*pratihetu*) is observed, prior to seeing the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), no specific distinction is perceived by the other [reason]— which has never seen a counter-correlate— at which point one could know, "The counter-correlate is possible here, but not elsewhere. This is because positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), which are based solely on observation and non-observation, are identical in all such cases.
Nevertheless, because a counter-positive (pratiyogin) was subsequently observed there, the suspicion that a counter-positive exists everywhere in things of a similar nature does not cease.
It might be argued: "In those cases where a counter-positive is possible, it is certainly sometimes perceived;
however, in those cases where it is not perceived even within a human lifetime, it simply does not exist."
"In that case, such a cause will exist;
so how can there be an absence of a cause for us?
To this, he says: "And not," and so forth.
For even in those cases where a counter-reason (*pratihetu*) is possible, that counter-reason is not always perceived by cognizers;
for the perception of those who do not see all things does not pervade the existence of all entities, because of the presence of obstacles and deficiencies.
But surely, in a case where the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is never perceived by the cognizer at all, how can such a suspicion be raised? Thus it has been said:
"As long as the cognition of sublation (*bādhajñāna*) has not arisen, suspicion is without basis."
Likewise, another [instance]:

when counter-arguments had been presented by a lineage of disciples prior to the appearance of Kumārila— counter-arguments conceived by that very person endowed with extraordinary power of insight— the suspicion regarding those [arguments] for which no counter-argument had been seen throughout one's life ceases upon seeing him.
Therefore, how can it be said that the suspicion is without basis?
For even the passage beginning with "tulyalakṣaṇe hi" has already stated that the possibility of a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is indeed a cause for such suspicion.
Nor can one who suspects the possibility of a counter-correlate be turned away from it merely by the taunt, "one might imagine (*utprekṣeta hi*)," since the possibility of its cause remains.

Therefore, one must state some reason capable of dispelling the suspicion of a counter-example (*pratiyogi*), as we have stated: "When there is certainty regarding identity (*ātmya*) by virtue of a subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) in the case of the opposite of a svabhāva-reason, there is the determination of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) therein;
and in the case of an effect-reason (*kāryahetu*), there is that determination because the relation of cause and effect is established through the aforementioned perception and non-perception."

Since, according to your view, the suspicion of a counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) does not cease in every case, for that reason there can be no certainty regarding the counter-positive; namely, the form of determination such as "here a counter-positive is possible" and "here, however, it is not possible. Therefore, because the definition of a logical reason (*hetu*)—which consists in its having a counter-reason (*pratihetu*) that is in fact impossible—is not established, no reason at all exists for those who maintain the intention to express a singular number (*ekasaṃkhyāvivakṣā*) and so forth.
It might be argued that a reason whose definition is not ascertained cannot be a valid reason; thus, the conclusion is:
"In this way, is it intended that whatever is in reality incapable of having a counter-reason is a cause for the subversion of correct knowledge?"

Having thus refuted this first alternative, and desiring to refute the second alternative, he says: "The connection [of the words] is that 'then, that which has not demonstrated a counter-reason (pratihetu) is accepted as the cause of the error of right knowledge'.
And showing that this position is indeed favored by the teacher Diṅnāga as well, the opponent says: "As the teacher Diṅnāga said:"
What does he say? "In that case," and so forth.
For when the teacher Dignāga stated that audibility (*śrāvaṇatva*) cannot in any way be a reason for exclusion (*vyavacchedahetutva*), the opponent replied:

"In that case, when a grammarian accepts that 'sound-ness' (*śabdatva*)—which is a specific universal (*sāmānyaviśeṣa*)—is eternal, then this property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) characterized as audibility would indeed be a valid reason (*hetu*)."

When the opponent has stated, "Sound is eternal because it is audible, like the nature of sound (śabdatva)," the Teacher replied: "If some Vaiśeṣika or other proponent were not to point out a reason for non-eternality— characterized by being produced, being dependent upon effort, and so forth— with respect to this subject (dharmin) called 'sound,' then this [audibility] would be a 'reason' that is a counter-reason (pratihetu) as previously described."
"Thus it must be.
Having thus provided the testimony of the venerable teacher’s words, the author of the treatise, raising his fist and crying out, says: "Now this... and so forth.
For when some explain that even the Teacher himself intended this, it leads to a very great calamity; because it was spoken by the Guru, it ought not to be made public.

Indeed, it is not proper for those who uphold justice to reveal the faults of their gurus; yet, by those same principles, it is neither to be withheld nor concealed. Thus, since both [options]—either to defame our gurus or to neglect justice—are impossible, how can this most grievous calamity be endured?
"Not in any way whatsoever.

But what is the fault here that makes this so much more difficult? He says: "First of all, this reason characterized by audibility, with respect to real entities such as sound and the like, [proves] its own probandum—reality (*tattva*), namely permanence—and those things which have that as their nature, which consist of that."

Having established that the authority [of scripture] consists in its being heard from those persons—such as the Mīmāṃsakas, Grammarians, and others—and having thereby joined them with prosperity, namely heaven, and with the supreme good, namely liberation;
for it is thus: as long as one does not abandon the afflictions (*kleśa*), one attains heaven, which is the reality of things.
But by abandoning the afflictions (*kleśas*), one becomes intent upon *nirvāṇa*.

Alternatively, when the eternity of sound is realized, through the authority of the Veda, by performing the *agnihotra* sacrifice as prescribed therein, one attains heaven; and through the study of the Vedānta, one attains liberation (*apavarga*).
Furthermore, at a later time, by a person such as a Vaiśeṣika who possesses intuitive insight (*pratibhā*) and a specific kind of wisdom (*prajñā*), [another] reason (*hetvantara*)...

By means of the demonstration of a counter-reason (*pratihetu*), that capacity which this [reason] previously possessed for proving its permanence— [a capacity] existing when the counter-reason was not presented— is now uprooted and removed by that demonstration.
Thus, those entities are displaced from their possession of permanence.

And having caused those persons who take that as their authority to fall away from the attainments of heaven and liberation, the reason characterized by audibility— being unable to protect itself due to its lack of power— goes to the forest of asceticism like a king whose kingdom has been lost,
on account of his own misdeeds; what can we say to this?
Thus, having ridiculed this position, he points out the fault by saying: "The power of a person's intuition," and so forth.
For when a reason is accepted without a counter-reason being demonstrated, then the status of being a proof is admitted to be produced merely by a person's intuition.
Consequently, in reality, nothing whatsoever is obtained that is either a proof or a non-proof.

For instance: when a counter-reason (*pratihetu*) is not presented, it is a proof (*sādhana*); but when one is presented, it is no longer a proof. Thus, the status of being a proof would come to depend upon the ingenuity of the person.

Furthermore, if the status of being a reason were admitted for a reason whose counter-reason is not presented, two alternatives arise: is the reason, in ultimate reality, possessed of that property (*taddharmabhāvī*), or is it not?
And [is it] "one that possesses that property"?
Regarding the first alternative therein, he says: "That is the reason which is first employed;
if, by its very nature, it exists only when that probandum-property exists—possessing such a character because of the acceptance of the necessary connection (pratibandha) as described by us."
If that which is intended is accepted as it is, how could it be made otherwise? How could something that does not possess the nature of that [result] be produced by another cause?
Not in any way. What is the reason?
Regarding the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of things characterized as causes— namely, that which consists in their existing only when the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) exists—
if there were an absence of its contrary (i.e., its non-existence when the property is absent), and if both were invariably concomitant with their own respective properties to be proven,
then by virtue of their very nature, if both were present in a single locus (*dharmī*), two contradictory natures would belong to that one thing.
Furthermore, two contradictory natures cannot belong to a single entity,
because the superimposition of contradictory properties would entail the loss of its unity. If, on the other hand, it is the second alternative, then it would not possess those properties.

Even if the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is absent, how could there be a proof for anyone at any other time—even in a state where a counter-reason (*pratihetu*) has not been shown—given that you do not admit any necessary connection (*pratibandha*)?
It is not a proof even then; it is certainly not a proof only in the state where a counter-reason has been shown.
Summing up, he says: "Therefore, by way of intrinsic nature," and so forth.

Since the intrinsic nature of entities cannot be made otherwise in this manner, and since a single thing possessing two contradictory natures is impossible, therefore, from the perspective of ultimate reality, each by its own...

Since a counter-reason (pratihetu) characterized by that same nature— namely, the nature of being an effect or an essential property— is impossible for the two reasons, the effect-reason and the essential-property reason, which are inseparable from the probandum and possess the characteristics as previously described, the "intentionality of a single number" (*ekasaṃkhyāvivakṣā*)— that is, the state of having a single intended number— is not a defining characteristic (*alakṣaṇa*). It does not constitute a definition.
What is the reason? He says: "Because there is nothing to be excluded.
For a counter-reason (*pratihetu*) is described as that which excludes the intended singularity of number.

And since that counter-reason (*pratihetu*) cannot possibly exist for either the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) or for the two types of reasons—namely, the effect (*kārya*) and the essential nature (*svabhāva*)—how could it possess the definition of a [valid] reason?

Thus, regarding these two forms, their occurrence is only possible when the aforementioned invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) is absent; even if one were to admit another form, it would still be nothing but a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*). Therefore, the meaning of the statement "the fallacious reasons are other than those" has been explained.
To refute the notion that [the reason] is already known, he says: "Furthermore, knowledge... and so forth.

The state of having an uncontradicted object and the state of having the intended singular number belong only to the reasons of effect (*kārya*) and essential nature (*svabhāva*), because when there is an inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*), there is no possibility of a contradiction or a counter-reason; thus, since there is no [other] thing to be excluded, even though it is a property of the mark (*liṅga-dharma*), that [inseparable connection] constitutes its definition.
It has been stated that it does not exist;
however, "cognition" (jñāna) is the state of being known (jñātatva),
because it is precisely this that is expressed by the abstract suffix (bhāvapratyaya).
For instance, that which is called "cognizedness" (*jñātatva*) is the ground for the application of the word "knowledge" (*jñāna*);
and that [ground] is indeed knowledge itself, because the conventional usage "it is cognized" occurs only when that [knowledge] has arisen.
And since that is not the essential nature (*ātmarūpa*) of the logical mark (*liṅga*), how could it constitute the definition of a logical mark?

Even if the generic form (*sāmānyākāra*) appearing in conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is established as the logical mark, nevertheless, it does not possess the property of being a logical mark within the cognition itself;
for this [generic form] is not an independent logical mark.

As it has been said: "Since independent conceptual distinctions rely upon [words] that correspond to their actual referents, if one were to understand the object from an object imagined by those [concepts], there would be no attainment of the actual object at all.
Therefore, this [conceptual distinction] is established as a logical mark (*liṅga*) precisely by taking an external thing as its basis.

Because the perception of the actual thing is lost when one conceptualizes the probandum and the probans, and because the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) does not persist anywhere [in the conceptual domain], conceptual constructions— which merely recollect its properties—
display various forms of identity, difference, and exclusion; yet, due to their indirect connection with the real thing, they are non-deceptive.
And it has already been largely stated that [the universal] is based on the designation of signs such as effects;
yet its own nature, consisting of those effects and so forth, is not known.
Furthermore, the general form appearing in conceptual construction is not at all the very essence of the conceptual construction itself.

Because that which is formless contradicts the nature of a real entity (*vastu*), and because that circle of conceptual reflections lacks the nature of a universal (*sāmānyātmatā*). For even though it is not external, it is determined as being external; and although it is not persistent, it is taken to be persistent, thereby possessing the character of a universal. But if this is so, how can it have the nature of a conceptual construction? As it has been said:
And how could that which is non-different from cognition become a separate object?
"Therefore, this apprehension of a single nature in objects is a false appearance" (PV 3.70f.).
Thus, it is not a property of the cognition that serves as a logical mark (*liṅga*).
Establishing this very point, he says: "Of what nature," and so forth.

When the question under consideration is, "From what kind of cause is the object to be inferred (anumeya) to be known?", the treatise-authors describe the essential nature of that mark (liṅga) which is non-contradictory for the person who is the cognizer. Of that [mark]...

Having established through differentiation that "this cognizer is for the sake of seeing form" and that "wherever that form is possible, that is a means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), whereas that which lacks that form is not a means of accomplishment," one relies upon activity based on the conviction that the intended object is present in that which has been established there as a means of accomplishment.

Likewise, this being the established principle, that which constitutes the essential nature (*ātmarūpa*) of this mark (*liṅga*) must be its defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), just like its status as a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) and so forth; it cannot be that which is its extrinsic form (*pararūpa*). This is because the mark is an instrument of proof only when it is known; therefore, it is logical that the knowledge of the mark—which serves the purpose of establishing the probandum (*sādhya*)—is the defining characteristic of the mark. To this, he says: "In the production of comprehension," and so on. If the mark is intended to have its definition consisting merely in the fact that knowledge is useful for the production of the cognition of the inferable object, then an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) follows.

He states that very point: if the definition of a logical mark (*liṅga*) were based merely on its utility in producing such a cognition, then the object to be known (*prameya*), the person who is the knower (*pramātṛ*), and— by the force of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*)— conjunction, inherence, and the like, as well as light, mental attention (*manaskāra*), and so on, would all possess the status of being a logical mark.
Regarding this, he states the reason: "For even when those [factors] such as the object of cognition (*prameya*) are absent, there is no cognition of the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*).
To this, the opponent, seeking to bring about an undesirable consequence, says: "In that case, the inclusion of the term 'ascertained' (*niścita*), etc.
If, because it has the nature of another, cognition does not constitute the definition of a mark, then what of this which was stated by the Teacher?

"Existence in the object to be inferred and in what is similar to it, and non-existence in what is not"— regarding this "ascertained," the inclusion of the term "ascertained" has been made by you, yet it is unnecessary.
For instance: certainty is indeed the very nature of the mark (liṅga).
If that [certainty] is its defining characteristic, why is it not accepted as cognition? Because certainty is precisely consciousness, since it is a specific state of it.

The proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādin) says: It is not that it should not be stated, but rather that it must certainly be stated; for the inclusion of the term "ascertained" (*niścita*) serves a different purpose than the mere presentation of the form of the logical mark (*liṅga*).
Demonstrating that very difference in purpose, he says: "In the similar class (*sapakṣa*) and the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*)" and so forth.
For others accept a reason as a means of cognition merely by its presence in the similar class and its absence from the dissimilar class alone.
The term "ascertained" (*niścita*) is employed in order to indicate that for these [two], the reason is not capable of establishing the probandum by mere observation alone;

for it is observed that even when observation and non-observation are present—that is, when they exist—the reason lacks probative force, as in the case of [the argument]: "He is dark-complexioned, because he is that man's son," and so forth.

Since this is so, for that reason, it should be understood that the term "ascertained" (niścita) is included in the definition-sentence in order to make known the following meaning: that a logical reason (*hetu*) is a means of cognition when it is qualified by its presence in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) and its absolute absence in all dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*), and when it is qualified by its presence— characterized by identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*)— in the similar instances and its absolute absence in all dissimilar instances.

This is what is meant: a reason becomes a prover only through those very presence and absence in the similar and dissimilar instances which have been ascertained by the operation of a means of valid cognition that establishes the necessary connection;
it does not become so merely by some kind of observation. It is for the purpose of making this point known that the term "ascertained" (niścita) has been employed.
Concluding the present topic, he says: "By that," and so forth.
Since the term "ascertained" (*niścita*) was employed solely to indicate the specific nature of existence and non-existence, and not to denote another form [of those two],...
Furthermore, it is not logical for that which is of a non-self-nature to constitute a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇatā*);
therefore, the form of another cannot be the characteristic of the logical mark (*liṅga*).
This is because by means of that other form, such as cognition and so forth, no specific feature of the form of the logical mark is expressed.

But surely others also accept a reason as indicative by virtue of its presence in the similar class (*sapakṣa*) and absence from the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*); moreover, it is their very observation and non-observation of these two that establish [the reason].
So for what purpose is the inclusion of the term "ascertained" (*niścita*)?
Thus, for this reason he says: "For those two," and so forth.

Even though opponents maintain that the logical reason (*hetu*) is indicated solely by presence and absence, they nevertheless establish presence in the similar class (*sapakṣa*) and absolute absence in the dissimilar class (*asapakṣa*) based merely on the observation and non-observation of presence and absence.
Nor do those two [types of reasons] succeed in that way,
because even for things lacking an essential connection (*pratibandha*), the occurrence or non-occurrence of existence and non-existence may somehow be observed or not observed in certain cases.
Therefore, those two which consist in the nature of "the reason existing only in the similar class (*sapakṣa*) and being entirely absent in the dissimilar class (*asapakṣa*)"—

Existence and non-existence are to be understood through the operation of that means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) which establishes their existence—that is, by way of its having as its object the proof of identity (*tādātmya*) or causal origination (*tadutpatti*).
Why? Because there is no other means.

For if this were not accepted, the presence of the reason only in the similar class (sapakṣa) would occur when all things possessing the reason are seen to be concomitant with the probandum, and its absolute absence in the dissimilar class (vipakṣa) would occur when all objects lacking the probandum are perceived to be devoid of the reason;
and this is not possible for one who does not perceive everything.

Because there is no other means [of establishing this], for that reason the word "ascertained" (niścita) is employed by the author of the definition in the definition itself in order to demonstrate those two specific states of existence and non-existence.

Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that certainty regarding existence and non-existence is obtained simply from the statement of them as being established by valid cognition (pramāṇa); otherwise, their very existence would not be established?
To this, he says: "Even though," and so forth.
By this very statement— "its presence in the object to be inferred and in what is similar to it, and its absence when it is absent"—

which merely expresses the existence and non-existence in the similar and dissimilar instances without depending on the inclusion of the term "ascertained" (niścita), although the occurrence of the valid cognition that establishes that existence and non-existence is indeed implied.
But how can there be an implication of the occurrence of that [reason] based merely on the statement of its presence and absence, without the inclusion of a definitive apprehension?

To this he says: otherwise, if the occurrence of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) that establishes it were not implied, then the existence—which is the establishment of the essential nature—of those very presences and absences in the similar instance (sapakṣa) and the dissimilar instance (vipakṣa) would remain unestablished.
Why is there no proof?

He says: because the determination of the existence of the object of knowledge—characterized by its presence or absence—and the establishment of its own nature, are dependent upon the existence, which is to say the arising, of the cognition through which it is perceived.
For objects are not established by themselves independently of perception.
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that everything would be established as everything.
Therefore, whether something is of such a nature or not of such a nature is determined solely by the arising of a cognition possessing that specific form.
Since this is so, in all treatises and in the world, the determination of the existence of an object of knowledge is established even without an explicit verbal apprehension of it; that is its proof.
It "draws in" or implies the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes the existence of that [object].

Furthermore, because the composition of a treatise is for the sake of others, it follows by implication that the operation of the means of valid cognition which establishes its existence is implied; this is the connection.

But what kind of composition of a treatise is it, which—being for the sake of others—implies the means of valid cognition that establishes the existence of the objects of knowledge as established by itself?
Thus he says: "The three-featured logical mark (*trirūpa-liṅga*) is that which is concordant and leads to the attainment of the object desired.
Even if the composition of a treatise for the sake of others (*parārtha*) is of such a nature, how does it imply the operation of the means of valid cognition (*sādhana-pramāṇa*)?
To this he says: "Those who [know] its form"—that is, the form, the essential nature (*svabhāva*), of that three-featured logical mark as taught in the treatise.
Practitioners do not know [it],
and therefore they do not engage with the intended object on the basis of that three-featured logical mark (liṅga) or what is stated in the treatise;
for that which makes an unknown object known does not induce engagement by its mere existence alone.

Since it is thus, therefore, because it serves as an indicator for others—that is, because it makes known to others—the cognition of the three-featured logical mark (*trirūpaliṅga*) as that which prompts action is established. Although the inclusion of the term "ascertained" (*niścita*) might seem redundant, nevertheless, it is those two alone—the presence in the similar class (*sapakṣa*) and the absence in the dissimilar class (*asapakṣa*)—that are specified by the treatise as being of a particular form, namely: "presence only in the similar class" and "absence only in the dissimilar class. This is how some, such as the Naiyāyikas and others, [understand it].
Others [hold that] by mere observation and non-observation— those observations and non-observations which do not establish a necessary connection—

they establish [the probans as a cause] merely on that basis, thinking "precisely because of this. Therefore, for the sake of refuting those disputants, the Teacher employed the word "ascertained" (niścita) in the definition, and we too accept it.
If, however, there were no misconception on the part of others, then this [reasoning] would not be employed at all.

Why, then, should one not accept positive and negative concomitance—consisting of presence and absence in the similar and dissimilar instances, which are the objects of perception and non-perception—as being distinct? To this he says: "Even when they exist," and so forth.

Even when there is the observation of the presence of the reason in some similar instances (*sapakṣa*) and the observation of its absence in some dissimilar instances (*asapakṣa*), there remains doubt regarding positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) in cases such as "He is dark-skinned, because he is that man's son.

To explain: positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is the existence of the reason only where the probandum (*sādhya*) exists; and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is the non-existence of the reason wherever the probandum does not exist, by way of pervasion (*vyāpti*).
Moreover, even when the presence of the reason is observed in some instance where the probandum exists, its existence does not follow everywhere by that alone,
because there is no necessity for the coexistence of things whose natures are not intrinsically connected.
Likewise, even when the absence of the reason is observed in some instance where the intended probandum is absent, it is not necessarily absent everywhere whenever that probandum is absent.
Because that [absence] does not necessarily follow from the absence of that [cause], since there is no necessary cessation of the latter upon the cessation of the former.

Therefore, it is shown that the existence and non-existence in the similar and dissimilar instances, as previously described, are established only through the operation of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) that establishes the connection (pratibandha), and not otherwise; thus, with the aim of refuting misconceptions, he says "therefore," and so forth, indicating that the term "ascertained" (niścita) has been employed.
Because we accept the inclusion of the term "ascertained" (*niścita*) as established by the Teacher—since this is our own position regarding other [interpretations]—he says "by us.

Thus, having demonstrated that the inclusion of the term "ascertained" is for the purpose of excluding disagreement (*vipratipatti*), and that it need not be employed when no such disagreement exists, he says the following, showing by this very logic that "known-ness" (*jñātatva*) is not a distinct property (*rūpāntara*): "Since..."
"...also," and so forth.
"Distinct from this" means distinct from the three-fold nature (trairūpya) consisting of the property of the subject (pakṣadharmatva) and the others.
Why? [Because...]
Because it is understood—that is, apprehended—by the very statement of the three characteristics through the implication of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes them.
Like what? Like the meaning of the application (*upanaya*), [which is understood] from the statement "because it is a property of the subject" (*pakṣadharmatvāt*).

Just as the meaning of the application of the reason is understood by the mere statement of its being a property of the subject, since that [statement] consists in demonstrating the existence of the reason in the subject (*dharmin*).
And since the statement of the property of the subject (pakṣadharma) possesses that very form, the application (upanaya) is not a separate form from it;
likewise, knowledge arises from the three forms [of the reason], because it is understood by the statement of those very forms.

On this point, the opponent, seeking to establish an undesirable consequence, says: "Even in the case of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)," and so forth. If knowledge is obtained through the force of the statement of the three characteristics (*trairūpya*) alone, then it should not be stated separately from that; alas, then negative concomitance should not be stated separately from positive concomitance, nor positive concomitance separately from negative concomitance.
What is the reason?
Because both [positive and negative concomitance] are understood from the employment of either a positive instance (anvaya) or a negative instance (vyatireka).
Furthermore, their separate mention has already been made.
"In that case, since 'cognizedness' (jñātatva) also possesses the three characteristics [of a valid reason], it too should be mentioned separately even though it is already implied.
To this, the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādin) replies: "No, because of the reason," and so forth.
There is no difference between positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), but rather they possess distinct forms.
To explain: positive concomitance is said to be the presence of the reason in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*), whereas negative concomitance is its absence in the dissimilar instances (*asapakṣa*).
Furthermore, these two do not exclude one another nor are they mutually included, because their intrinsic natures (svabhāva) are distinct as they consist of affirmation and negation respectively.
Nor is it logical that what has a nature distinct from something else should be included within it.
[Objection: But if positive concomitance (anvaya) and negative concomitance (vyatireka) are of different forms, how then is the logical mark (liṅga) said to have three aspects (trairūpya)?
For it is not logical that its two selves should be mutually distinct,
since the distinction between entities is characterized by a difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
This is not a fault.

Since it is stated that these two are not included [within the categories of cause and effect] only insofar as positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) are established— or rather, not established— and not otherwise,
how then are these two established?
This is by resorting to a distinction made through conceptual exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*).
Thus, these two indeed possess distinct forms;

yet, even though there is a difference in their exclusions, in the ultimate sense (*paramārthatas*) there is no difference, and so it is said that "a single logical mark (*liṅga*) possesses three characteristics."
How then is it that it was stated previously [at 771]: "There is no difference whatsoever between the meaning of these two, except for a difference in their application"?
To this, he says: "A single sentence," and so forth.

We maintain that a single statement, whether formulated by way of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) or negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), conveys both the positive and the negative as having distinct characteristics; it is not the case that the nature of one thing is stated to be the second. This is because these two, though mutually distinct, constitute the single meaning of the sentence.
Regarding this, the opponent says: "But not in that very [case]," and so forth.

The intention here is as follows: the mutual inclusion is urged by relying upon the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) as set forth in the defining statement (*lakṣaṇavākya*).
And that [positive concomitance] indeed exists.
For instance—in the defining statement "existence only there" (tatraiva bhāvaḥ)—the absence [of the probans] in the absence of that [probandum] is understood by virtue of its meaning;
and here, in the phrase "necessarily absent in the absence of that," [the presence of the probans] when that [probandum] is present is implied.
For when there is no necessary connection (*pratibandha*), the absence of one thing does not entail the absence of another.
And that necessary connection, consisting in identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*), takes the form of "presence when the other is present.

Consequently, since both [presence in the similar instance and absence in the dissimilar instance] are understood through a single, specific defining statement (*lakṣaṇavākya*) that establishes presence in the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) and absence in the dissimilar instance (*asapakṣa*), a second statement need not be made.
And thus, because they are included within the meaning of a single sentence, it is difficult to maintain that these two possess distinct natures.
Consequently, what was stated—that "even positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) are not separate"—remains exactly as it was.

The proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādin*) says: this statement, in the form of "existence only there" (*tatraiva bhāvaḥ*) and so forth, implies and establishes both [concomitances].
Why?
Because of the capacity [of the reason] to establish both;

for there is a restriction—that which pervades [the subject] is "present only in the similar class (*sapakṣa*) and absent only in the dissimilar class (*asapakṣa*)"—and since this formulation with its exclusive limitation (*sāvadhāraṇa*) is inseparable from the implication of the second [alternative], it is inseparable from the establishment of the second.

Nor does the mere fact that both are presented by a single sentence imply that they possess a single nature, for even things with distinct natures can be presented by a single sentence. Furthermore, although both are understood from a single definition-statement, their separate mention is for the purpose of restricting their formal application: in the application of similarity (*sādharmya*), [there is no mention of] dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*).
A statement should not be made;

and in the case of an application based on dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-prayoga*), a statement of similarity (*sādharmya-vacana*) is likewise unnecessary. Furthermore, it is not for the sake of establishing another aspect that was not understood through a single expression. Nor is it the case that, by means of stating the three characteristics (*trairūpya*)—which serve as the basis for knowledge—and by means of composing a treatise (*śāstra*) for the purpose of providing a definition for others, one establishes the existence of the object of knowledge (*jñeya-sattā*) as something distinct from the three characteristics themselves which reside within the knowledge.
Since there is no purpose in restating knowledge already obtained through demonstration, it is not logical to mention it separately.
It might be argued: "In that case, even when isolated, the two would not be included within the meaning of a single sentence, as they would be mutually non-different in their intrinsic nature."

Since they will [be included] therein because they are included within the meaning of the single sentence itself, he says: "But not merely by being included, the presence and absence in the similar and dissimilar instances—standing alone and independent of the meaning of the single sentence—mutually imply one another;
for we observe that even things of distinct natures are included within a single sentence."

But surely, even though existence and non-existence possess a necessary connection (*niyamavantau*), they are each independent; thus, if they imply one another, that same consequence would apply to them independently as well. To this he says: "And those possessing a necessary connection are established by sentences containing restrictive particles (*sāvadhāraṇavākya*); they are not independent, but rather necessarily conjoined. Why?"

Because a restrictive statement (*niyama*) possesses a dual nature—consisting in the presentation of both existence and non-existence—it is thus the case that by means of a restrictive statement, neither positive concomitance (*anvaya*) nor negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) alone is expressed. Rather, the second is understood through its inclusion within that very [statement]; however, the two, being mutually exclusive, are expressed together by a single sentence.

Concluding the demonstration, he says: "Therefore, by the statement 'existence only in that very [subject], namely in the similar instance (sapakṣa),' it is not meant that there is existence *only* in the similar instance.
What then?"

There is also non-existence in the dissimilar instance (*asapakṣa*); likewise, by the statement that there is "non-existence alone in the dissimilar instance" made by the other [definition], it is not merely non-existence that is expressed, but existence in the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) as well.
For if it were merely one or the other, it would imply the second by its very nature, such that there would be no separate mention of these two.

Therefore, when positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) are intended as existence (*bhāva*) and non-existence (*abhāva*), they are indeed of distinct forms; so how could there not be a distinction between them?

Alternatively, if they are expressed by a single restrictive statement (*niyamavat vākya*), then since both are understood from that very sentence, a separate mention of each should certainly not be made.

Yet, that [separate mention] was made not for the sake of making known what was previously unknown, but rather for the purpose of restricting the formal application (*prayoga*); this has already been stated.

It might be thought: just as positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), characterized respectively by existence and non-existence, are not identical with one another and thus possess distinct natures from each other, so too cognition is indeed distinct from the "three-fold nature" (*trailakṣaṇya*) propounded by the weapons of the opponents' definitions;
it is not included therein.
Thinking that there might therefore be another form [of existence], he says: "It is not so;

for while positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), characterized respectively by presence and absence, are mutually non-inclusive, knowledge is not non-included within the three characteristics (*trailakṣaṇya*) as propounded in the treatises that define the characteristics of others."
Why?

Because it is characterized by others (*paropalakṣaṇāt*). "Others" refers to those who are characterized; that is, the treatise by which they are caused to have a cognition whose object is the three-fold nature (*trairūpya*). Therefore, because the three-fold nature that is cognized—which is the knowledge already grasped—is non-different from that [treatise], [the three-fold nature] exists within the knowledge already grasped.
The meaning is that [it is] because it is included within [the three-fold nature];
therefore, there is no other definition than the three-fold nature (*trairūpya*).

This is the collective sense here: if "cognizedness" (*jñātatva*)—which is the ground for the application of the word "knowledge"—is, according to the manner stated, said to be knowledge itself, then it does not constitute a distinct entity from its own mark (*liṅga*).

That is not its defining characteristic. Furthermore, if it is argued that the state of being an object (karmabhāva) is called "cognizedness" (jñātatva) in dependence upon cognition, even then, since the establishment of the existence of the object of knowledge depends upon the existence of the cognition, it is precisely the establishment of the three-fold character (trairūpya) that implies the cognition which establishes that existence.
Therefore, since the status of being a reason (*hetubhāva*) is established even without being explicitly stated when it depends upon that [triple-character], its separate mention need not be made.

Likewise, because it is not excluded from the triple-character (*trailakṣaṇya*) taught in the treatises intended for the instruction of others, and because that knowledge has not been grasped [by the opponent], [the reason is valid].
